If you want a game that isn't online and will last you quite some time, about 100+ hours for everything to be handled, then you have found your game, if you want a game that will test how long you can exist on one game, you have found your game, the game has events from time to time, where you fight certain, giant bosses, there are some giant bosses in-game additionally as well, whenever you want to play them, and you get legendary gear for overcoming them, however they are not easy, given how now we have a nightmare, above hard, difficultly in addition to enemy scaling to your level, we are reaching ¼ Dark souls difficultly here, side quests, looting, tomb raiding, and Arena horde modes, I hate the races though haha!
Now for presentation, while I thought Assassin's Creed Unity was nice, Assassin's Creed Origins on Patch 1.10, the current latest, and overall, has turned and taken It's rightful place as being the best appealing in visuals and overall detailing given the attention to detail in Assassin's Creed Origin's characters, musical score, and detailing of the setting presented in Assassin's Creed Origins itself, you will not be disappointed, and I would recommended that Ubisoft takes two years to release an other Assassin's Creed, if we get another Assassin's Creed Origins.
Ending : Note .
Take the name, Assassin's Creed out, there is no reason for any hardcore gamer out there, or just an open-world, RPG, fan, buying this game, you shall not be let down, and you will connect with the characters and possibly find yourself, finally playing, other Assassin's Creed ones, such as Assassin's Creed One for example, and, we have Steam refunds to help you, shall you distaste the game, or ran into any game-breaking problem, not that you should in my honesty and personal experience, for any Assassin's Creed fan, massive or not, buy the game.

Civil War II has the makings of bing one of the best strategy game available -- especially on the Civil War, definitely an underserved topic.  It's extremely complex, but that translates into a realistic feeling:  war is complex.
Unfortunately, AGEOD has dropped the ball in 2 major areas:
First, the bugs.  Almost all players have commented on them, so it's the game, not individual computers.  In a campaign, the game crashes about every 3rd turn.  Fortunately, reloading the game with a previous save allows the war to go on.  Except I reached March 1863 and encountered a hard crash that's unrecoverable, recurs after reboots & reloads.
That's hundreds of hours down the tubes.  (I'm running an i7-3770 w/ 64 GB RAM & 4GB VRAM, Windows 10).  The game's been out almost a year -- 6 months since the last patch.  Obviously AGEOD has taken what money suckers gave them and gone on to other projects.
The 2nd problem is balance.  In my games, whenever the USS Monitor meets the CSS Virginia, the Confederate ironclad is obliterated in a single battle, leaving the Monitor unscratched -- and able to navigate the Atlantic in winter to reach the Florida keys without refueling.
It's impossible for the South to capture Washington.  There are over 1000 points locked into the city, ready to be released any time a Southern unit steps foot in Montgomery County (even if the unit is retreating from a minor skirmish in Frederick MD).  Not only that, a union army of about 500 points suddenly appears in Fairfax VA out of nowhere.
Don't capture and then exit a union town.  A unit suddenly appears out of nowhere and retakes the town.  Though only 17-points strong, it can withstand seige by a 200-point division for more than 5 turns.
Sigh.  CW II would be such an interesting game, if only AGEOD could invest just a little more time to fix the remaining problems.
JULY UPDATE
Good news!  The December 2016 update has resolved the crashing problems -- at least, so far.  Hurrah!
Play balance...?  What were those Southerners thinking?  How could they think they could take on the North?  -- Given the North's vast super-overwhelming edge in troop numbers, industrial output, and technology?  (It's like the Union has more troops in Washington/Alexandria alone than the entire Rebel army!)  Is that authentic?  I donno.  Ask Robert E Lee....
The South's "saving grace" is that usually a huge avalanche of Union troops runs up to the defender's front line...  (Or more like, oozes slowly in the general direction, maybe, sometimes.)  And they just sit there.  And sit there some more.  Nothing happens.  Sitzkrieg.  For turn after turn.
Hint:  Supply is the thing.  Everything depends on having good supply trails.  Spend the 1st year making depots to the site of future campaigns.
Hint 2:  The only Southern strategy is to create an impregnable defensive line.  Don't think you can launch any offensive operation anywhere at any time.  (Although be ready to make a limited thrust to take advantage of Northern errors.)

Its exceptionally original stained-glass art is undeniably the game's most accomplished and arguably only strength. That it offers such unique and lovingly crafted visuals makes its frailties in just about everything else all the more disheartening.
Interestingly, you choose dialog options for all characters, allowing you to customise the story's delivery, albeit without branching paths or consequence. This is a linear experience, reinforcing the storybook analogy.
Retelling stories by putting image shards back together is pleasantly relaxing.
A few original ideas were unfortunately poorly implemented despite their freshness. There's a weird face-off mechanic that plays like a stats game where the rules are not always clearly laid out but simple enough. Merging roads is a very clever trope but its execution is just a matter of reordering simple patterns in sequence.
Little effort seems to have gone into the design of the game mechanics. Many interactions end up feeling peculiar or clumsy. In particular, dragging items feels technically awkward when the game expects you to position them in very specific and arbitrary locations.
The top goal banner acts halfway between a humorous narrator to the story and a stern guide that tells you exactly what to do. Multiple pop culture references abound, including Reservoir Dogs, Lord of the Rings, Cluedo, Mass Effect, Super Mario and many others that add to the game's carefree tone.
The soundtrack features pleasant music that constant looping unfortunately renders repetitive. The gibberish voices may be a hit or miss depending on your preferences.
This is not a typical point and click adventure, so players looking for a short but interesting tale with minimal interactions may find something to like here. Despite its charm, the game is too lacking in proper gameplay and genuine puzzles to heartily recommend.

The game runs smoothly, does not bug, nor do I experience screen tear or lag. That's a big plus because technically, its well coded.
The plot is decently interesting as a whole with little loop holes but do not provide any gripping turning points or decisions that most enjoyable plots have.
My criticism with the game is mostly design related, because they feel redundant, unbalanced, trivial, or unrelated, all of which hurt mainly because it breaks immersion;
1) Why did the company put in a reputation/karma system but make it that the only thing that gives you 'bad' karma is finishing off an opponent? No one in that universe considers sparing enemies you beat within an inch of their lives in self defense to be chivalrious. Actually, using excessive force stopping short of murder is also not really chivalrious in reality either. You can argue that being a♥♥♥♥♥♥to a fragile sexually abused girl or insulting a nurse who's son is a drug addict is bound to give you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ reputation, but meh, not really. And then there's the lack of redemption. Reputations can improve or recover, but in this game it can't.
Also, the premise is that Mars is an unforgiving and dangerous place, right? It's not strange to protect yourself by finishing off an enemy that just tried to kill your life, because it's likely they'll come after you once they're on their feet again. So, is it immersive to be a "bad" person because of it? Maybe in reality, but not on Mars (in tandem with the rest of the story).
2) What's the point of making money if it's so easy to find parts for crafting, and items are so cheap in the store? The economy is very unbalanced in that if you loot the containers you come across and clean up the enemies' drops, you will have everything you need to craft everything you need. Even if you didn't bother looting everything, you're so rich or things are so cheap that money is not at all valuable. (But at the same time, lore-wise, 5 serums (less than a piece of scrap metal sold in a store) is the equivalent worth of a person's life).
3) The game is very short for the plot-line covered. This is the feeling I get watching the latest season of Game of Thrones, where the bad guy or whoever dies shortly after their character is developed (barely) enough for the audience to care and feel bad about. Case in point, the big bad and the dragon (tvtropes) have their differences and politics games in the back but the audience can't relate until the last cutscene of the game. There's a lot of intrigue that technically occured throughout the plot but the dialogue is so shallow, it's hard to really appreciate it fully.
4) The side-quests occur pretty much in tandem with the main quest location and wtvr else -wise, and don't require extra effort to seek, do, fight, etc. All side-quests occur along the paths of the main quest anyway so by completing the main quest, you finish could its contents simply by talking to npc's you happen across. That's not entirely a "side" quest. Most of them got nothing to do with the plot. Why am I looking for counterfeit coins again?
Overall, it's worth the $1 I paid it for on Humbl Bundle.

Quick Review. Great game for the price, especially for a indy RPG title. Don't expect anything outstanding as a triple AAA RPG such as Mass Effect which most have compared this to. For what it is, it delievers and I am happy to have played through this game. I didn't trust it, and only got it due to Humble Bundle low tier. I am happy to say I was mistaken.
The story and environment itself is the selling point here more than anything. You will love it or hate it. Personally it sat well with me.
Small things however do make this a lower than Triple AAA title which I hope will be fixed for the sequel.
1. Mouth animation. What the hell, I can't be the only person to notice this. In sub quests it is god awful and some time in the main quest itself. It isn't game breaking, but it is irritating if you ontinue to stare directly at it.
2. Odd pacing. The monsters you face in the earlier levels that make a return later briefly IMO are the hardest thing in the game next to enemy swarm. To place them so early, and to have so many made you really have to build supplies early. Once you built supplies for this said area you are pretty prepared to coast through most of the game as long as you visit shops and stay on your toes in large groups. Which I don't mind but the you can't do it one way then jump to the other it is unsettling. At least to me.
3. Have more of your dialogue options actually have outcomes that effect more often. This is a common complaint to any multi-dialogue or choice option RPG but with the small environment given it missed the chance to really stand out and go above and beyond other titles in the genre.
4. Tedious enemies. This isn't something I mind as much, but others might. Over halfway through the game aside the casual boss whom has played the same as normal enmies you will encounter 5 enemy types....5. So if you don't like the linear beat-em-up RPG style or are loving the story. This could be very concerning.
With the price it is right now however, and the story aspects being above par the generic RPG IMO. This is a good title to buy and play through on a weekend. Or maybe even a bit more if you tend to play less hours in a game day. Hopefully more see and enjoy this title.
I hope and expect great things for the sequel now that they are getting a larger budget, and will be getting it.

Good ♥♥♥♥ing god this game is frustrating but good.
Giana is a platformer game with the gimmick that you can switch between two personas during gameplay which have different powers (a dash and a twirl which lets you slow your descent). The controls are tight and responsive but there are some minor problems with hit detection. Switching sisters also switches the music and backgrounds and there are two distinct styles and it’s really cool how the background objects morph into each other. The visual styles are very nice and colorful and it’s nice to have a cherry game admits the browns of modern games.
The platforming is really nicely done with LOTS of different things you can encounter which gives each level its own variety. Additionally, each enemy looks and acts different for both sisters which increases the total amount of variation. The difficulty curve is nice with gradual inclusion of more challenge. HOWEVER, the ending levels are just super frustrating. There are long periods of precise platforming without checkpoints and it’s so ♥♥♥♥ing hard. On top of that, you have to collect most of the gems and not die that much in order to 5 star the level. Normally, I wouldn’t care but you can't play the last level until you do and it’s really annoying.
For those seeking a challenge, this is your game. There are about 5 game modes that get increasingly harder and some of them are just insane (beat the entire game in one life). HD 4000 users: ~45 fps with everything set to low.
Overall, great game. Play it and enjoy. If you're looking for a challenge, you're going to spend lots of hours on this.

This will be a review that I will update over time as my playtime progress's, I only have 3.6 hours at the moment and so I was not going to even write a review yet but after seeing countless people complain saying it is a bad port, full screen is broken, game constantly crashing "omg square enix sort yourself out" etc. I decided I had to at least start a review to counter their negative ones.
The game is final fantasy meets pokemon with a kingdom hearts feel with cute art and puns for days, as I said I only have 3.6 hours playtime so far but all of that playtime has been me playing in fullscreen, no crash's or anything negative, the game has worked perfectly fine for me which is why I felt the need to write this so people do not see the complaints of some people and go "great another bad port with loads of issues, not going near that game" as I said I am not saying that those peopel did not have those problems but for me it has worked perfectly fine.
The game has a "cute" feel about it and each of the charcaters I have met so far seem unique from each other, there has been moments where it has made me laugh so far and other times where I have gone "HA" at a bad pun. They do a lot of fanservice in this game for fans of final fantasy with eastereggs and references or nods to other final fantasy's but in a way that do not seem out of place if you do not recognise it.
There are a few different battle system elements you can configure, including making it a old school final fantasy turn based game where when it is your charcaters turn you can take as long as you want and there is another that is more modern final fantasy where it is in like final fantasy 13, that the battle is continuous and does not stop when it is your charcaters turn.
Another comaplaint I have seen is someone saying that they had to use keyboard and controller to naviagte in the game but I have only used a controller and have had no issues what so ever with navigation.
Please keep in mind that some issues that some people have had are just what they have experianced personally and regardless of the given impression from their reviews that it is the norm for the game; are inaccurate as myself and other people have had no problems what so ever, so do not base your opinion on this game solely on a few issues some people have had and assume that you will get it too or that it is a terrible port, because my experiance and that of others contradict that notion.

Aviary Attorney takes the Ace Attorney formula and runs with it. Multiple endings, side quests, as well as the ability to lose and keep playing. For more info, check out my review:

This may seem like just another Phoenix Wright clone, but it is so much more. This game definitely pays homage to the Ace Attorney series, but it stands on its on two feet. The game is witty, amusing and generally gets you invested in the characters. The replay value of this game is big positive for me. The fact that you can start trail completely unprepared is not a bad thing.
1. It's realistic that you can't have all the time in the world to comb all of Paris for clues before a trail date. So sometimes you miss some, so what? Live with it.
2. It allows you to learn from your mistakes and replay the scenes if you want to or just continue the story.
3. It allows for different outcomes throughout the game.
This game doesn't just stop and say, "Sorry you lost, try again?" It continues the story and lets you live with your mistakes. Too few games do that. I HIGHLY recommend this game to people who love the Ace Attorney games and to anyone who just likes a good story laced with humor and bad (good) puns.

Yes, it's a Phoenix Wright clone, and no, it doesn't really make any improvements to the basic formula. But it does defy certain expectations, such that the story actually goes somewhere. The writing isn't incisive enough to actually get it there, but the fact that it addresses real issues puts it in about the 90th percentile, as far as these things go.

A wonderful variant on the tried-and-true Ace Attorney style.
Unlike the AA games, Aviary Attorney has a much stronger emphasis on the investigation part of the game, while the court sections are rather brief, but both are handled well. There's a push for greater realism in the court part of the game: while you can do the whole Phoenix Wright thing and find the real criminal and force him to confess in court, it's not always a requirement for a not guilty verdict. Simply demonstrating reasonable doubt IS sufficient.
It's also notable that the investigation sections have an action limit: going to a location to investigate it takes a day, and wasting time can mean the difference between mere acquittal and catching the real culprit -- or even outright failure -- since the trials are on fixed days that can't be moved.
But failure actually isn't the end in Aviary Attorney. The game has multiple possible endings, and failing cases can be necessary for some. In this way, the way you play the game determines not only the outcome, but also the tone of the game itself: idealistic play will result in an idealistic game, cynical play will result in a cynical game, and wacky Ace Attorney play can result in a wacky Ace Attorney game.
I laughed, I cried, I got punched by a lion. 9/10, could use meatier trial sections but great game nonetheless.

The art style was  enough to peak my interest in this game but what hooked me was the world and stort this game had to tell. Aviary Attorney is a game that made me step back at the end just agast with amazement and the feelings that only a good story makes you feel. This game is truly a work of art and I recommend it wholely. I will say coming to this game knowing as little as possible is highly recommended and will greatly improve your experience.

I found this game disappointing.  A court game lives or dies on its dialogue, and this dialogue is either boring or downright bad.   To add color, one of the suspects speaks in fake-Cockney, sprinkled with words like " 'ave" and "sayin' ".   However, he also says okie-dokie, a glaringly American term.   Although the drawings, the music, and the names are French, and the game is set in Paris, there's no French flavor at all to the dialogue, no French epithets or turns of phrase.  The two investigators you're guiding aren't well characterized -- the sidekick makes bad, not funny-bad, just bad, puns, and the lead investigator is solemn and rebukes the sidekick.   Finally, evidence searches are literal pixel-hunting: when the background is a cross-hatched engraving with lots of detail, it's almost impossible to guess which object is unusual and which is part of the original drawing.   I wound up sweeping my mouse across every part of the page to try to find objects.

The bad reviews almost stopped me from getting this...This is why I am writting this review. I ended up getting the game and was very very happy with it. It has a tremendous amount of depth, features and choice options on how to manage your side of the conflict. I really enjoy the strategic and regional level choices, while coordinating supply and unit command formations.
I hate bugs and I hate crashes, when i read that in the reviews it was very dissapointing and I almost didn't purchase the game. If you are experience crashes, there are several suggestions in the forum as to fixes. For me personally I used the userpath.ini delete fix and thought that worked very well cutting down on crashes. Also something to note, you can get the game to auto save between 3-12 turns...so crashes or tech issues shouldn't stop anyone from playing as you can easily recover, and sometimes just reprocess the turn.
Immersion, This game via its strategic and regional level options combimed with supply, unit production and army configurations is defintely a deep, rich and immersive experience. The map is huge, has many fiters and the wego system is by far the best system to be used on this kind of game. I want to really reiterate that, some games I don't think its great for and this is the first game I've truly been able to say, is better off for having the wego system as it provides the best gaming experience for this war/era.
This is not for the light hearted gamer nor the total war style of gamer. This is actually more realistic because in a grand strategy sense you are not some godlike presence that can order every individual unit on the battlefield. You do choose who commands your bde, division, corps or armies, you do get to build up these types of units and combine them to make your composition of forces, and if you pay attention to the ground your fighting on, supply, unit cohesion and all the other factors the game takes into account, you will do well. However, if you take 20k men into a seige, tell them to assault the walls with no arty support, guess what, ur men are gonna get slaughtered.
I personally spend 1-2 hours per turn, the game does 2 week time frames, early in the month for the first two weeks and late in the month. This works great because the game using the wego system processes each turn into 15 days. So coordination of forces matter a lot and in reality u have every single day of the war being played.
I had never been a fan of the ageod battle system, I personally dont think its right for the american rev period, nor do i think its right the for world war one era, for the civil war and the napoleonic era though its really is the most realistic and superior system for those time periods. I encourage you if you are a grand strategy fan, to try it and give yourself a few days of playing to get used to it. I believe like myself you will see the benefit and the beauty of the system in this time period for this title.
You will absoutely get your monies worth if you put in the time to learn the features and options. The Grand strategy genre is my absolutely favorite and those are the games I really excell at because of all the different things you have to manage. I know this isn't billed as grand strategy because you can only play two sides, but the amount of choice, different options and features in the game make it a grand strategy title to me. Indeed, I wish they came out with a game like this that allowed u to be any country in the world like a lot of the paradox titles allow you to do.
All in all i highly recommend this game if you love history, the civil war, and grand strategy games.

First Impression:
I can't suggest anybody but a retired gamer play this.  Only they would have the time to play such a complex game.  Not that I don't like complex.  I love Dwarf Fortress and Hearts of Iron III.  But in this game they somehow mixed complex with abstract information.  For example, a battle result screen covers the whole computer screen but I can't find where it says who won.  And also, it measures a unit's strength by giving it a 'power' number.  Hmm..how about just telling me how many soldiers or horsemen or artillerty it has?  It makes judging how much force you have in a certain stack kind of hard.  Is 230 a good number?  What about 890?  And this, of course, is not a solid number - as weather, terrian, and other factors can change it during the battle.
Once again, let me point out, that I have played and enjoyed complex games.  Norm Koger's The Operational Art of War, with the 160 page manual, for example is a great game.
But this game....
Organizing your units has been made more complex than it every needs to be.  Units who are part of a chain of command do better than those out on their own - which makes sense.  But forming Armies and moving them can take much of your time.
Sadly, for such a complex game, the political and economic parts of game are nothing but you triggering certain events that cost money and victory points and so on.
There is also supplies, training, transporting, and so-on, so-forth.
The UI is the most complex I have ever seen and the tutorials are good for what they explain.  But I would say they cover about 50% of the game's interface and do not even touch on the naval forces or blockades.  Even the manual points out that tooltips are needed because many functions are not covered in the manual.  Let me repeat that.  The manual states that many functions are not covered in the manual.
You will not even be able to get a refund as the tutorials will take you more then two hours.
I strongly suggest this game only for gamers who a lot of time, who love the American Civil War, and are willing to spend a few days learning how the game works.  Other wise....skip it.

This is an excellently designed game which brought hundreds of hours fun for me.  It is not for the light hearted as you will spend hundreds of hours engulfed in the game.  Not as complex as some but has tons of options and historical detail.  It was a perfect mix of options and complexity for me.  For those old enough to remember, the game play and options are very similiar to the old boardgame Civil War by Victory Games.
One of the best Grand Strategy Civil War games made to date.  If this is what your are into, consider it a must buy.

Steep learning curve that pays off greatly once you understand the game. Make no mistake this one is most likely going to appeal the most to hardcore wargamers, that said I think if you have interest in the genre this is an excellent place to start.
Stick with it and you will get hooked!

It's Final Fantasy Pokemon.

This is a combination of Kingdom Hearts, for visuals and feel. Pokemon as the games essence - RPG-based capturing and evolution. With all the characters, and creatures, being of previous Final Fantasy games. All tied up with an immersive world, story and characters. With crisp contemporary graphics, and well acted voice over work.
The gameplay does come across a little intensive, and confusing. At first. Especially if you've seen it out of context, or haven't been tutored. But it looks complicated, yet isn't, but has enough simple explanations with opening tutorials as well as depth, especially later in the game, to allow for you to challenge yourself on hard difficulties or with side bosses.

Here's hoping). And that the characters, and places, are alternate versions of those you know from their respective games, all existing in the world that WoFF is set in.
it's new original characters, concept and use of an entire franchise spanning almost 3 decades is worth your time, and money.
I'd DEFINITELY recommend it if you are an Final Fantasy fan or newcomer!, unless you find yourself allergic to the typical trappings of such games (you can see the typical zomg 30 fps outrage on the forums already). But it’s still a Final Fantasy game… isn’t it? ;)

This could be a great little casual game if it was actually finished. It is not a true flight sim and to prove it, there is no support for customising controls and if you are lucky enough to have a flight controller, you will find the throttle is useless. I could not even find a button to accelerate at all, so ended up using a gamepad. Controlling the planes is not that bad at first though they always seems to be turning left a little . The starting plane seems to lack lift and is constantly falliing. Its not really an issue until you try to bank sharply, and find yourself falling too fast to do anything. The second plane on the other hand is always climbing. Again not to bad except for the fact it is extremely slow and climbing slows it further. It struggles to get enough power to climb when taking off, which is bad considering the number of runways surrounded by hills. the constant climbing also prevents it building enough speed to finish many of the timed missions. The third plane is the worst so far. The rate of climb is so severe it makes landing difficult. the amount of force you need to counter it is also likely to give some side input. the problem there is that this plane is also very responsive making it incredibly hard to fly straight. This means that landing are ridiculously hard, trying to counter the uplift and land straight so as not to run into something or roll. I have yet to unlock the fourth plane, but already dreading it. One thing they all have in common, is a useless rudder. Pressing it will turn you only a few degrees, no matter how long you hold it. When you release it you will  have to endure some wild swaying back and forth until it settles close to the direction you started.
The graphic of the game are pretty basic but FPS sux, badly. With the game only using maybe 20% of my CPUs capacity, and GPU barely registing any use, I can only get an average of 11fps even on lowest settings and smaller resolution. Higher detail was barely worth the 4fps I ws getting. The only major differnce was on lower settings I could actually see things through the clouds at 300metres, that completely block visibilty on high detail. For those not familiar with the metric system, that is damn low, under the minimum legal flight altidude in many countries. So having no visiblitly of anything on the ground makes it damn hard to land. Night time, which is somehow 14hrs long,  has a similar problem. In this case though it is more from lack of design. Fair enough you cant expect lights in the middle of nowhere, but some runways have drum barrels that remain unlit, and base runways have power and still no lights. Not even the buildings have lights.
The games missions are something I really like. There is a good variety and you are given a choice of three at a time. Even here though there are some issues. The worst being some timed missions are too short for the capabilities of the second plane. Another annoying set are ones requiring you to go though a series of waypoints to your destination. Thats fine if you are taking tourist sight seeing, but why do I have to fly in a needless zigzig when someone needs something urgently. Even worse, why do I have to fly the whole zigzag on the return trip? To make it worse quite a few waypoints are hidden behind mountain. Isnt the idea to set way points to avoid obsticles? Also they are white and set at 300m. The exact altidude to be hidden by clouds, which seem to always be around. A lesser complaint would be the fire fighting missions. You fly through a series of waypoints and drop something on the fire when prompted. Exactly what you drop and how you can drop it multiple times is something left up the imagination it seems.
I did enoy playing this game at first, but the bad hadling mixed with pathetic fps made it more of a chore flying the third plane. Add in the terrible night landings and hidden/useless waypoints and I honestly cannot recommend the game in its current state.

tl;dr: the reason only 3% of players have the "Green Optimization Award" achievement isn't because the game is hard, but because the game becomes unplayable in the end.
This is a good programming puzzle game that is badly let down by some trivial, but intensely irritating, flaws. I actually don't want to leave a negative review, but I can't ignore its glaring problems. Since the positive reviews outnumber the negative ones, I'm leaving this review to add some constructive criticism.
Programmers will breeze through the puzzles in no time, about a single-digit number of hours to complete. The game only gets interesting when you try the optional optimization challenges (get your program under a certain size or speed). Programmers need to do these optional challenges otherwise there is no point in even playing this game. They are interesting challenges, but they're also where things go bad: the bad UI makes things unplayable. Here's why:
1) You can add comments to you code, as well as labelling memory locations...but it's done in the most annoying way possible. You don't type in your comments with the keyboard, instead you "write" with the mouse. Oh, and the field you get to draw/write into is very small, and the pen you draw/write with is very thick, so you can barely write anything. A comment such as "P is prime" hardly fits. Really infuriating. I've seen some awful programming environments, but this is the first one I've seen that actively discourages you from commenting your code.
2) The maximum program run speed is far too slow for some of the more advanced optimization challenges. One of the puzzles will take 3:30 to run at max speed (although you can get it down to about 2:20 when you optimize it). That's too long, and will become an unnecessary test of your patience.
This isn't a petty complaint. Let's put that 3:30 into perspective. 3:30 means you can only run your solution 17 times an hour. That's 3:30 of waiting, maybe about 20 seconds to apply a fix, then another 3:30 to see if it worked. Rinse, repeat, get frustrated. That means you can only try about 15 things (trivial stuff like small fixes) an hour, so that particular puzzle becomes dragged out to a ludicrously painful extent. You spend a lot of time just waiting for the puzzle to run, and hardly any time working on your solution. Imagine if your favourite IDE did that. You get the picture.
As an aside, that particular puzzle also trolls you by supplying the single-item list as the final input (after the 10 item list that accounts for most of the 3:30 runtime), so if you have a bug that happens with the list-of-only-one-item (an edge case, that's why they test for it) then you're going to have to wait 3:30 for that bug to appear, then additional multiples of 3:30 to test each of your fixes.
3) Dragging and dropping program instructions is needlessly laborious. The maximum HRM program length is 255 lines (although I think the longest HRM program I wrote is about 70 lines). Let's just say, without spoiling anything, you **might** get near the 255 line limit while trying to solve some of the optimization challenges. That's a lot of dragging and dropping! If you double click an instruction the game appends it at the bottom, which isn't helpful as most of the time you are likely to be working on an inner loop. Instead of adding it to the bottom, double clicking should have inserted the instruction after the last one you added. That would have been a big improvement.
These complaints may sounds trivial, but they aren't. The big optimized programs have lots of jumps, etc and it quickly turns into a mess of spaghetti code (that's ok, it's just what happens with asm code). You can only see about 16 lines of code at a time, so it becomes very easy to lose track of things. You could add some labels, but the labels are painful to add! You're bound to make mistakes as a result of the UI, and then the UI punishes you for those mistakes by making you to wait 3:30. Now you see how the game itself becomes the biggest problem. These problems only start to make themselves apparent when doing the optimization challenges. At that point you have to wonder why you're even bothering with HRM. You can find loads of programming challenges/golf/puzzles out there, just do one of those instead in your favourite development environment where you can add comments with your keyboard, don't have to wait 3:30 for a trivial program to run, and you can see more than 16 lines of code at a time. Go pick something off Project Euler instead, and challenge yourself mentally instead of challenging your patience or your ability to draw text with the mouse.
A saving grace is that HRM supports copying and pasting programs. It's often less frustrating to copy your code into Notepad, work there, and copy it back into HRM. Shame the comments/labels don't go across in a way that's readable, but that's because they're mouse strokes not text.

The game represents programming as it was in the very beginning – when a kilobyte of memory costed thousands of dollars, and an hour of machine running time cost more than a programmer's paycheck for a month (while computing speed of a computer the size of a building was several
slower than any modern "weak" laptop), they went to ridiculous lengths to optimise away
kind of inefficiency they could. And there are actually two criteria to work on, depending on what you need more (that is, what your hardware limits you to).
This game gives you a bunch of mostly trivial tasks (starting from "pass input to output" and up to "calculate prime factors for each given number") and asks you to "instruct" yourself in how to solve them (which is basically equivalent to writing a program in a very limited version of Assembly – about a dozen most primitive operations). Initially you only have "input" and "output" operations, but you'll get a new operation whenever it's needed for solving the task at hand. After you reach the first "milestone", you'll be introduced to the optimization challenges – "preferred" length and average run time values for your programs (personally, I found that moving the last part of a loop body before its beginning is a surprisingly effective technique). You'll also get "optional" branches with more interesting (but also trickier) problems to solve; though the main branch also gets quite tricky later on (I found it quite funny, that on the last problem, whenever I tried optimising for time, I somehow ended up also reducing program size, on every step).
In short, it's a neat game with several hours worth of fun brain exercise, that also makes you struggle with doing simple things enough to appreciate the fact that no one actually
(and definitely shouldn't) program this way for at least half a century.

LD;DR: If you like Ace Attorney, GO FOR IT, NO SECOND THOUGHTS.
Now for a slightly more, say, eloquent review:
First of all, in order to set my bias status: I am not a Kickstarter backer, and a fan of the Phoenix Wright series. Mind that I do rarely wright reviews (pun intended) and I really really want to see a sequel of this game.
That said, this game exceeded my expectations in many, many ways. I was at first quite happy to buy an Ace Attorney clone and to my uttermost surprise right on the second case this game seemed like it would fit on the "pupil surpasses master" category. I was correct.
Why should you buy it:
It's not only really well written and crafted, It feels way more dangerous than Ace Attorney. You see, the trials have dates, and you better get the job done of asking the right questions and collecting the correct evidence before the trial day otherwhise
. If you do a poor job at investigation phase, you will fail...
...and that's the best part. Failing doesn't mean you will get a "game over" screen. There is a special case that might go in threee different paths depending on your performance and decisions.
It's a delightful twist to the Ace series, while it doesn't have a Bioware/Telltale range of storyline paths, it doesen't feels like you're been railed visual-novel style. The text is clever, the smart and non-lazy use of Creative Commons art works marvelously, the plot twists are quite twisty indeed and if you think this game is full of puns, well, you're wright (strike two).
You'll more than once think "well, that escalated quickly".
And to end the "why should you buy this" rant: it's amazing how a pun-riddled game about antropomorphic animals performing mundane tasks can be quite a banquet for though.
And don't worry about the
, for they're few :
- A little glitchy here and there, I particularly had a lot of trouble with sound and had to lower my sound config in order to have it working properly.
- The interface is quite pretty looking but messy and non-intuitive sometimes. Examples: 1: there is a blackjack mini-game that would benefit a lot from a "Replay" button without the need to go through dialogue again in order to play it. 2 : The main map of the game is quite messy, sometimes it tries to prompt you with a special cinematic and the prompt has exactly the same color of the background so is quite easy to miss. Besides, it does not tell you the day the trial will occur, nor allows you to check your evidence and suspects folder.
Buy this game wright now and you wont regret it (strike 3. Im out).

I also want to say that there's some genuinely funny moments that made me laugh hard; but it doesn't ever feel too forced.

Probably one of my top five games released in 2014. It's a shame practically nobody knows about it, it's super fun. So fun that I actually went out of my way to review it because I feel like it deserves more attention.
To sum up the game, I would say it is a speedrunning fast paced game based around mobility. If you played Dishonored and liked the blink mechanic, you'll love this.
The aesthetics, graphics, atmosphere, and soundtrack are all fantastic. The gameplay is super fast paced, but the overall pacing of the game is good. It introduces new mechanics at a good pace and doesn't overload you with information. Then, it tests you on it all.
There's a great feeling when you manage to pull off something crazy such as pulling off a crazy stunt that you think that the developers probably didn't realize you could do. But the thing is, the developers did know probably. The map design is phenomenal. Because the game takes entirely in the sky, every single thing placed is deliberate and every jump calculated. So, when you pull off that crazy jump, you know at the back of your mind that you beat the developer's challenge that you didn't even know they were challenging you to.
Deadcore is one of the few games that I've actually wanted to go back and replay. Because you unlock new mechanics and powerups, going back and replaying levels to see new areas that you can reach and collecting "sparks" (which reveal new parts of the level) is super satisfying. Beating a level five times faster than you did originally is a great experience that really shows off how much you've progressed, through mastering mechanics and unlocking the new ones.
Also, if you're looking for a good story, this game doesn't really deliver I think. The story is entirely given through text files which you can collect. I haven't really read them, so it's possible they're really good. However, I like to leave it up to my imagination to come up with an explanation for the game and I feel like reading the logs might ruin it a bit. I might be completely wrong, but just be aware that this is not really a story driven gamemode. Your goal is to get to the top, not to save the universe.
This game is almost flawless, but it is important to point out the flaws.
For one, even though
everything in the level design is deliberate, I did manage to find a few things that I clearly was supposed to come back to later. For one, at the beginning of a certain level if you are observant enough you can find an alternate route. Getting to this route would normally require a powerup that you would unlock if you went the normal route, but you can use some of the nearby launchers to get there. Maybe this was intentional, maybe not. I did this in my first playthrough, and I was able to beat it without the pretty important powerup, as you don't actually need it for the alternate path or the rest of the game. When I finished the game and realized what had happened, I felt kind of punished for being resourceful and observant.
Secondly, similarly to the first, there was one point in the game where you could get to a "spark" (which, once again, unlocks new sections of the game which require mechanics you unlock later on) by playing around with the environment a bit. Once I got to the spark, I realized that I clearly was not supposed to be there since it was impossible for me to progress without the mechanic I hadn't unlocked. This one is a bit more forgivable since I had to go out of my way to get there and I felt like something was wrong.
Thirdly, one of the last enemies you encounter in the game feels really cheap and unpredictable and can really screw you up. For a game based around perfection and speedrunning, getting killed in a nearly unavoidable way is pretty annoying. Definitely the only parts of the game that I really disliked the design of and felt like it was more artificial difficulty than challenging.
Finally, there are some small bugs with the instadeath lasers and gravity fields. Sometimes they don't work, sometimes they're unclear, sometimes they don't reset properly. It's extremely rare when it does glitch out and typically it only glitches out at specific parts of the game, but if they get you killed when you're hauling through the level as fast as you can, it can be frustrating dying for no reason.
Anyways, if I had to give this game a rating I would probably give it a 9.5/10. It's almost completely flawless and easily worth the $10. One of the most fun games I've had. Provides a solid challenge while being fair almost the entire time, in a way similar to Dark Souls almost.

Good
* Looks great, impressive that this was made with Unity.
* Gameplay has multiple mechanics rather than just jumping.
* Lots of checkpoints, never far from where you die.
* Small dev team (5 people) are highly active on the game forum.
* Fairly priced.
Bad
* No antialiasing option ingame and forcing MSAA through drivers doesn't do anything. Since the aesthetic is almost all straight lines, jaggies are quite noticeable.
* Really obvious microstutter regardless of frame rate. Even at a constant 120 fps, it looks like 40 fps. Others have mentioned this in the forum - devs are looking into it.
* Some of the gameplay mechanics. For example, many times you will have to 'dash' between horizontal laser beams. Since it's first person and you can't see your character model, there's a lot of guessing at first to know whether your character's hitbox will hit the lasers or not. The gravity shifting mechanic in the second half of the game can also be very disorienting as it constantly shifts your camera automatically. Not a fan of the perspective changes in a fast-paced first person game.

The game is a pretty simple RTS with basic gameplay and building menu, still, that isn’t necessarily a bad thing. While the buildings and units are few, when compared to other modern RTS titles, this makes it perfect for any newcomer to the genre, just like C&C did back in the day, it is easy to learn but hard to master.
Gameplay is pretty simple in the sense that you start with your HQ and the first thing you should do is build a refinery to harvest resources, which are located in various nodes scattered throughout the map. You don’t need to order your harvester to harvest resources, it will automatically do it for you. Building is also as simple as it gets, click a building on the menu and choose where you want to place it and that is it. The only thing you need, besides money, to have a building functioning properly is power, which can be obtained by building more power plants.
While unit variety is rather small, this makes it easy to know which unit counters which, even if you’re no military expert. Also, due to their simplistic design and stylized blocky visuals it is very easy to distinguish different unit types amidst the chaos of battles. One other thing worth noting is the fact that each type of unit production building (barracks, motor pool and air control) has its own queue but if you want to train units faster you can just build more buildings of that type.
The game offers a 25 mission campaign as well as a 10 co-op missions. These missions don’t really have that much story to them other than some text on the selection screen but I feel that these missions are supposed to be some sort of tutorial for what is really the true experience, skirmish, for they gradually introduce you to new units and buildings. Missions offer 3 different difficulty settings and you can replay them in order to complete secondary objectives which will unlock new units for you to use and also unlock more starting units.
Skirmish supports up to 8 players on 10 different maps, and if you don’t fancy getting destroyed by veterans on the multiplayer, you can always just play with AI that has various different difficulty settings to choose from.

This game is for the old school RTS fan.  I've been playing Command and Conquer for over two decades.  I've purchased every game in the series multiple times (aside from CnC4, thanks EA for destroying the entire franchise).  I've been dying for a good, solid RTS without a bunch of crap or unnecessary complication thrown in for the sake of making the game "seem different".  This game doesn't need a gimmick like that, it is good in its own right.
For those of you who don't know, Petroglyph made this game.  They formed Petroglyph after Westwood shut their doors (thanks again EA, seriously) and from what I understand some of the original Westwood team is still under the roof.  And for that reason, I'm thankful.  They've taken the original, successful formula of CnC and turned it into a fantasic game.  If I could hug these guys for helping to keep the RTS scene alive I totally would.
The game is base building, army forming, and sweet, sweet destruction.  Buildings don't have their own build queue, additional buildings decrases build time.  Multiple nuke silos don't add multiple nukes, they're on a timer...just like old school CnC.  And don't expect much warning before a nuke hits - it's four beeps and BOOM.  There are additions to the original CnC formula - for instance, an engineer heals all unit types near it.  You have two types of helicopters - a light with MGs and a heavy with missiles.  There are two types of defense turrets, which come in very handy as a failsafe around your base.  The tech tree is in full swing, you will have to do some basic learning of the tree to streamline production.  It's exactly what an RTS should be.  Not overly complex.  It has complexity and the deeper elements lay in battle tactics and strategy, but you don't have to worry about managing multiple types of resources.  You can focus your time on battle strategy...which makes the game very fast paced.
I only have ten hours into the game, but I've beaten the campaign and played some co-op campaign.  The campaign is varied and fun, the mission types are mixed up quite a bit to provide variety.  The co-op campaign is a blast if you play with a friend, it's like a skirmish or multiplayer game with a set of objectives.
Campaign difficulty goes up and adds additional objectives to make it more of a struggle.  I enjoyed this as it helps you fine-tune your build/battle strategies.  The campaign is long too - I think it was close to 25 levels.  The art style is great - it's like they put Minecraft into one hand, an RTS landscape in the other, and smashed them together like handfuls of yogurt.  The buildings are destructible, which adds another layer to the gameplay.
To wrap up, if you love CnC or enjoy RTS games - don't hesitate.  This is a great game, and at $15, it's a steal.  I had a blast running through the solo campaign, plan to complete the co-op campaign with a friend, and see a lot of replayability in terms of skirmish and multiplayer online.  The Petroglyph team also seems to be organizing online free for alls with the devs with awards for winning the match.  Last week it was a $20 Steam gift card (more than the game itself costs).  Again - great RTS.  Please support Petroglyph, they keep it old school.

Akin to a previous reviewer - I'm British but have a deep fascination with the ACW - the sheer bravery of men fighting a 'modern' conflict using Napoleonic tactics both humbles and appalls me. However enough ruminating - the game itself offers a very entertaining model of the strategic military aspects of the war.
Leadership and command ratings of the various generals are brilliantly realised - which is somewhat of a disadvantage with the game as it has a large bearing on influencing tactics i.e. rush to get your most able generals promoted as early as possible - but , as wargamers. we have the invaluable benefit of hindsight to know that Grant, Sherman, Forrest, Cleburne et al were extremely capable - the enjoyment is in giving them opportunities to shine in other theatres and to change the course of history.
Related to this is the extremely well realised Army and Corps structure - with the most able generals 'marching to the sound of the guns' and turning a desperate situation into a glorious victory. It also makes historical scenarios repeatable as it's extremely viable to tempt an opposing force into a seemingly winning situation only to throw a nasty surprise his way ala Lee and Jackson.
Supply is another strength of the AGEOD engine - it's possible for many a glorious victory march by a well led force to flounder in the face of cut off supply routes.
My only issue so far (playing as the CSA) is that compared to the first incarnation of the game (Blue and the Gray) is that the Union AI appears less apt to stretch my resources in the western theatre or with his naval superiority - but that might be due to me being more prepared for these eventualities.
I'd recommend this game to fellow ACW affeciandos - however it won't be to everyone's tastes - you either enjoy the AGEOD engine and it's sometimes annoying fatal crashes (but every turn is auto saved and in terms of hours played they aren't that frequent) or you don't.
In short the best strategic game of the Civil War you're likely to find.

The games engine allows you to organize your army as you see fit. When you do, many minor or major factors apply which can be game changers for the next battle. So make sure you use the system of organization wisely (brigades, divisions, corps, and armies)

The first time I saw Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams was back when Greenlight first started before any game had been Greenlit.  It stood out not only because it looked graphically and artistically good, but also the entire level would appear differently depending on the character's transformation.  It was on a different level of polish compared to other Greenlight games.
The gameplay revolves around the character's transformation from regular to punk mode, enabling a different skillset as well as morphing the environment.  It's a fairly enjoyable platformer that requires a degree of precision to beat levels, so expect your character to die quite a bit, but because of this the game doesn't feel very fast paced.  Also although the levels are varied, sometimes they don't feel exciting, but that might just be my expectation that I want to move faster through the game than how the levels are designed.
The boss battles are fun except for the last one which I found to be a chore.  The concept behind it is cool, but after repeatedly dying to it, it gets bothersome in each attempt to have to wait for the boss to go into its next phase of attack before I can act as well.  Each long animation it does for preparation felt tiresome to watch after a while.
Although I listed some negative aspects of the game, overall I found it to be a worthwhile platformer to play.

A pretty competent game with some decent level design and music (it's been stuck in my head for days!), but it's sorely lacking in the "X-factor" department to make it stand-out from any other game. And with all things considered, the world-swapping mechanic which is lauded by the game's description & other reviews is not much more than a gimmick, and you'll be hard-pressed to remember much about the game after you're done with it.
You may also have trouble finishing the last 1/3rd of the game because at that point, as the recycled art assets, music, and enemies will start to become pretty monotonous. And the last boss -- which is where I quit playing the game -- was also very poorly-designed and frustrating because waiting for it to go through its sequence of moves took
. I counted, and whenever you respawn the boss takes around 15 seconds to begin his first attack. And the maximum time it took in-between attacks in his sequence was 26 seconds. It all adds up and you'll get frustrated from the boredom of waiting, rather than from it being difficult.
I'm putting specific emphasis on the boss because I honestly can't remember a whole lot about the game (the boss is fresh in my mind right now), and it ruined any little sense of momentum I had in the last few levels. It really does become a blur of tedium towards the end, and the mandatory-to-progress "Collectathon" aspect of the game especially wore thin by then.
With that, the "Rise of the Owlverlord" expansion was actually really good. I initially went into it with extreme reluctance because of how mind-numbing the original game was, but I had a great time with it. The level design was interesting and varied, and had a much speedier pace due to the design and being able to bum-rush them since a collectable-quota was not required to progress. The boss was also enjoyable and challenging. Took me about 50 minutes to beat the 7 levels.
Overall, I'd stay clear of this game though, since there are much, much better platformers out there.

This is a charming game absolutely riddled with flaws. For ~45 minutes of casual play at $3, I'm giving this a thumbs up more for what could have been, versus what actually is.
The stained-glass aesthetic is enjoyable and the characters intriguing, but 45 minutes is absolutely not enough time for this story. The minigames were great and varied, and the battles actually well composed and very interesting for this genre of game.
Unfortunately, the story lacked polish...in fact, it almost lacked story altogether; it was a true hodgepodge of story pieces mashed together in a barely coherent plot. Everything occurred far too quickly, and the dialogue, though amusing at times (including a few on point references) lacked depth of any sort. I do believe that were the story stretched to a four-hour game, the gameplay itself would have grown repetitive, but with the sort of charm and ingenuity to genre displayed here, I have no doubt the developers COULD have continued down a path of inserting more combat, new mini-games, and the like.
I enjoyed that the point-and-click aspects of this game were logical (perhaps unusual, but logical nonetheless). My main complaint in so many P&C games is that the puzzles are so obscure I have to reference an online walkthrough (Deponia, damn it all, I'm looking at you!), which takes away from the fluidity of the gameplay. Message Quest, what it lacks in so many areas, does some of the basics right, and for that it earns a thumbs-up from me.

It's adorable and creative, and I love the stained-glass aesthetic and sense of humor, but it's SO short -- it only takes about an hour to beat the game, and you only complete a fragment of what is clearly a larger story. Will that story be revealed in sequels? Expansions? For the low price and level of time investment required, I guess it's not a huge deal whether those questions are answered or not, but I would love to see this expand into a longer, more substantial adventure.

I downloaded Carpe Diem because it was a free visual novel game that popped up in my featured steam client. I usually download any free games I find, especially if its a visual novel, so its no surprise that once I saw it I downloaded it. Sometimes I skip the trailer like I did this one, but the game itself laid on my desktop as a game that was untouched for a couple months because I didn't feel like playing it. And so today I decided to look at it because I wanted to play a game.
I looked at the trailer and I kind of actually got interested, and looking through comments I realized it was a very short game, which is very normal for a first visual novel for the company it was made from. So, I decided I would try it. I opened the game and decided to play.
SPOILERS AHEAD - SORT OF LONG REVIEW
Now in my opinion, I didn't exactly like the game, which is surprising coming from me since I am easily amused, entertainted, interested, etc... especially with visual novels (my favorite type of game) It just had some faults in my eyes such as the music (when I got to the starting screen it kind of confused me because the beat seemed really out of tune and kind of made me cringe. The same music also played over and over in the whole game.  I suppose I can understand why, since it was a very short game and stuff but still, it got kind of annoying.
Now I'm the type of person who can listen to the same thing over and over again and literally never get tired of it. I guess I got irritated with it because the beat, it was pretty but it just wasn't my type of music - like I said before the beat made me cringe, it seemed out of tune in my opinion.
Another thing I didn't like is the writing. I don't know who wrote it but their wording was just so plain, I'm a big writer so I'm pretty critical about this stuff I guess, but it just seemed to plain and too many baby words and went way too fast and stuff. I didn't get much of a feel from anything, especially since 97% was just talking. Which leads to another thing; most of the talking seemed unnecessary and boring. Maybe thats just me as I'm not that big on Slice of Life, I at least need a sad twist or something exciting to happen.
There was a sad twist at the end SPOILERS; Ai ended up being a robot that would malfunction soon. Okay, I didn't really expect that which I like but it just went too fast and the wording was so simple I didn't get that sad about it. I was sad but I didn't cry or anything, it was more of "oh thats kinda sad." and then went on. I guess one reason why I decided to play the game is because of how short it was (if I had to go through an hour of that I wouldn't have made it; which is the only reason I pushed on to the end) and because the ending was supposed to be sad, like said though, it wasn't that sad.
The tags also set me off a little, "psychological horror" mostly. Nothing in that game seemed scary psychologically. Maybe its just me, but I'm scared very easily actually, one reason why I stayed away from the game for a while because I thought there was actual horror in it and thats usually not my cup of tea. Also the "cute" tag was a little misplaced too. It had some nice cute parts but not something I would put a tag on as "cute", if that makes any sense at least.
One of the only good things I saw was the graphics; that was a little cute I suppose, I liked how it was drawn and stuff but again, it disappointed me with the lack of backgrounds and such. I would have appreciated it if they changed the background into the shops they went to, as well as show her in that dress she picked. But it stayed the same basically, there were only like, four backgrounds or whatever, and the lack of facial expressions also bugged me.
I can understand why there are so many positive reviews but a lot of them I don't agree with. The game didn't make me think as much as others did I guess, maybe I'm not that logical or whatever but by the end of the game I kind of felt like I wasted my time all in all. Literally all I thought when I got the badge "what are you doing with your life?" is why was I playing this in the first place when I had better things to do. So no, I would not recommend this game unless someone likes a ten minute boring game. This is actually my first review though.
Only game I've completed to 100%. Would ask "What am I doing with my life" again.

I don't mean to be a downer, but I don't see what all the fuss is about this game. It's
short and is basically a single scene (with a couple of minor variations based on the single choice you get) that sets up what's supposed to be a big, heart-wrenching twist at the end. Unfortunately, it just didn't work on me. Probably the biggest flaw in the game is that the twist was
predictable and easy to see coming- the game's description just gave it away to anyone with a hint of genre-savviness as if it were written in twenty-foot high flaming letters. The other problem is that the entire story lacked any context- I never really got a feel for either Ai or Jung before the twist dropped and the game ended (although Jung
come across as an aggravating git who I couldn't stand at all).
You could talk about the game's "metatextual meaning" or some such nonsense, but it's honestly just too short for that sort of thing to really work. Bizarrely, while the twist is meant to strike more at the kind of person who really gets into games like this, the kind of gamer who obsesses over and forms a strong attachment to their favourite "waifu", in my opinion that kind of person will just see right through how blatantly manipulative this game is trying to be. I know I did. I practically rolled my eyes when the game flat-out asked "What are you doing with your life?"
Look, I'm not trying to disparage the efforts of the creator, but I really don't see why this 5-minute long (10 if you play all 3 paths, because each of them double up on one of the scenes from the others) one-note "gotcha!" story has such high rating. Yes, it's free and yes it's not really
but it was nothing special. I'm sorry, but I've played much better kinetic novels (and this
a kinetic novel, not a visual novel, despite the single choice on offer). The idea could potentially expanded out into a much longer and more in-depth product, but as it is if feels sorely lacking.

This is low key the most under rated RPG ever. Yes the budget may have been like 2 cents and it may have been way too ambitious of a project but the end result is still very much worth checking out. If you are like me and don't really care about all the fluff Bioware has been adding to their games recently, but still like their stories and characters, this game is for you.
Important note: They got a lot of new voice actors and re did a lot of the bad voice overs. So the annoying voices in the trailers are not actually in the game (although LOL@ Innocence randomly getting a British accent)
Pros
+Story very enjoyable. Not a huge grand adventure but still I found it interesting, and found most characters to actually be pretty good.
+The setting is amazing and I hope at some point it can be revisited.
+Visually very beautiful. (Design wise, graphics themselves are ok if you care about that lol)
+The combat actually has a lot of fun elements to it, and I also enjoyed the character custimization. It doesn't play like most other WRPGs, but I didn't really mind although I know some do.
+Roy is a preset character whose pretty defined but you still have a lot of flexibility with how he acts in conversations. Compare to auto dialogue mess Shepard from ME3? I'll take Roy/Temperance any day.
+So many good ideas LOL normally I would not suggest this but a bigger company needs to buy Spiders and give them some $$$ and direction. Once they have those 2 things they could honestly be the new Bioware.
Cons
-The game is small scale. There won't be a billion items to collect or places to explore. A lot of simplified elements but honestly who actually cares? I don't get much out of endlessly exploring desolate areas (Thanks Skyrim for bringing this awful trend back)
-Combat can be wonky and annoying at times

The game is pretty short which could be a pro or a con. Also I still don't know if I find the virtue names cliche or really interesting. Maybe its best there probably won't be a sequal, I can't imagine there are that many virtues left for them to pick from for new characters lol

Mildly challenging and very fun to play.
On the art: the graphics seem impressive on the surface, but if you look closely (as others have said) there's a high amount of texture reuse. The clouds are also 2D projections which follow the player's gaze. But none of this actually affects gameplay, besides ruining immersion a bit. I think the sound design is awesome, though, and overall I think this game takes many inspirations from Portal 2's style. (edit: I feel as if later in the game, the developers stopped striving for a 'wow effect', which is okay, I guess. There's only so much 'newness' to go around. I noticed when I went back to the first level from the third.)
On the gameplay: I like it. Platformers have classically been the prerogative of 2D or 2.5D. It's very nice to see a 3D platformer, and intriguing to see how unconventional and innovative platformer mechanics have been shown in this game. Another thing I like is the freedom for the player to explore each "level" and choose their own path, seamlessly (through that level, not through different levels in the cycle), apart from areas where the player cannot go "back down".
Imagine playing as scout from TF2, but with the ability to freely air-control your way around obstacles like those people you see jumping around in CS:S or CS:GO
Deadcore is really challenging and immersive gaming experience.

Comparisons to Ace Attorney are inevitible, as they're intentionally self-evoked here, but Aviary Attorney does have more than enough to it that makes it a much different experience.
For one, the game is more about breadth than depth. The main storyline only took me around 4 hours to complete, but my playtime double going through the game again to see alternate paths and the other two endings. Each trial has multiple outcomes that can affect the story in different ways ranging from a few small details to three distinct endings. The game has a lot more replayability to it than the linear Ace Attorney games, and that's not a knock against Ace Attorney either, the linearity allows the game to provide a much more in-depth story.
That's not to say the story in Aviary Attorney is lacking; far from it. What starts off as a silly bird-lawyering game escalates into a turbulent tale of rebellion and violence, with three potential outcomes. The game is far darker than Ace Attorney ever gets, and the scope of your actions is far more reaching than the relatively minimal stakes the Ace Attorney series sticks to. There's a variety of characters with interesting personality quirks and a good dose of humor as well, the game can still be fairly lighthearted at times, but going in expecting something as over-the-top silly as Ace Attorney would be a mistake.
The gameplay also differs a fair bit. For one, it's much more fast-paced. Investigations are done a day at a time, and you have a limited time to get everything done that you need done, making it possible to fail any trial if you don't have proper evidence (or simply present the wrong evidence too many times). The first case is fairly trivial to complete, but it's possible to miss some crucial details in the second case and the third case is actually quite strict as far as what you need to do to ensure a successful trial, while giving you more options than you'll know what to do with. There's a bit of a trial-and-error element but when you have a sense of what you're missing or what you did wrong, it's not too hard to put the pieces together and have a perfect case after only a replay or two. And replays can be done fairly quick as the text is all fast to skip.
If I were to have any real problems with the game, it would mostly come down to three issues. First, path 4A is a bit... awful, storywise. It forces one of the main characters way out of character to push an overly dramatic and hard to take seriously storyline, though since the player intentionally has to initiate this ending, perhaps it was done on purpose? Either way, I wouldn't consider this ending "canon", and it's only one of three.
The second issue is that there are a fair few instances of script breaking, where the game will have assumed an event took place even if it didn't. This tends to only occur if you intentionally try to screw up things though, and the only major script break I encountered was a result of intentionally failing the first case early, though there are certainly others to be found.
The third issue, and this is only a minor nitpick, is the price vs. length issue. 8 hours is what it took for me to experience the vast majority of what this game has to offer (some branching dialogue paths and two failure states I didn't achieve that wouldn't change much in the long run) and while it's not impossible that I'll revisit it in the future, it still feels either a tad short for the price or a tad overpriced for the length.
But I digress, anyways. It's a very well-made game with a great story, a unique and interesting art style, and there are bird puns. I quite enjoyed my experience with this game, in spite of the small issues I have with it. Definitely recommended.
