Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams is a platforming game that allows you to switch between two versions of one character, you have an innocent looking girl with blonde hair and light blue dress then you have this red haired girl that seems to be heavy on makeup and dressed in a punk style. The environment alternatives with the character that you chose which seems to show the side of the character which is currently hidden away, yet the music that plays seems to be according to the character that you have currently chosen. It’s a very peculiar game to say the least and I personally love the art style and how much detail the developers have put into both alternating worlds. The characters only have one move or action that they can execute but you can alternate between your innocent side and punk side at any given time during that move or action.
In terms of the story... Well, let's say its there but almost non-existent but don't worry, I won't spoil it for any of you. I don't think the game needed a strong story to begin with, I mean it has the protagonist and antagonist which for a platformer is all it really needs. It has enough content to keep even a person like me who is usually very story driven interested.
In each level you will usually spend 5 minutes or more, depending if you're keen on collecting the gems lying around in the level. There are enough levels and gamemodes to offer you a good 10-15 hours of gameplay to keep you entertained which for the price is not bad. The levels are very varied and well laid out with traps and enemies but it’s far more forgiving than Super Meatboy or Blood of the Werewolf is.
The music is great, it has a fantasy feel to it and I love the alternation between calm and the edgy metal when you switch the characters.
The game modes are as follows:
Easy- Pretty self explanitory, its the the easiest mode to choose from and offers more checkpoints than the rest of the modes.
Normal- I found normal to be challenging enough, good for people that aren't looking to be pampered.
Score Attack- Sort of a mix between racing against the clock for a better score and collecting as many gems as you can+defeating enemies for bonus score.
Time Attack- Race against the clock as you try to beat the fastest time, although only if you're hunting the achievements. I personally wouldn't recommend it for the reasons that I will state in a moment.
Hardcore- If you die at any point during the level, you get sent back to the beginning aka no checkpoints to save your♥♥♥♥♥
Uber Hardcore- The good old days of gaming where you have to go through ALL of the levels from start to end, if you die you get sent back to the beginning of the first level. This mode will kick your♥♥♥♥♥and call you its♥♥♥♥♥♥
All that being said, while I recommend this game there are some gripes with it. The levels sometimes are a bit too big and you can find yourself getting lost often especially during the time attack mode because even with the arrows placed to guide you where to go you will need to know your way around the map. Its strongly recommended to use a gamepad, the PC controls are kind of bad.
There's no level restart, I repeat there's NO LEVEL RESTART, that means that if you die during Time Attack Mode you have to quit back into the menu and select the level again OR you can finish the level and get sent back into the menu and select the level, either way you're looking at about 20 seconds of wasted time when the developers could have just put such a simple but helpful option.
I'd be lying if I were to give this game a negative review though because I enjoyed it thoroughly, its a decent platformer that adds a few nice gimmicks here and there. That's all I can say about this game, I give it a 6/10.

I loved the original Giana Sisters from the 80's which is why this game caught my interest. This game certainly has some of the charm of the original, but there are too many flaws in it for me to recommend it.
The world changing mechanics are a nice idea, but they are confusing and too underdeveloped to feel intuitive. When standing on a platform you often change the world and the platform disappears, sending you falling making you do the same platforming segment again and again. I don't have a problem with the platforms disappearing as such. I have a problem with the visual clues not being clear enough. How am I supposed to know if a platform will disappear or not? The visual clues are there, but they are so damn subtle that when you are playing a hectic segment, you just fail, fail, fail and fail again. Very frustrating. It's a general problem with the game. The graphic style is all over the place. So many colors everywhere and so many layers that you just can't tell what is going on. It's the same problem I had with the latest Red Alert game. It lost focus and became this color infested mess of a design that you almost couldn't tell your units apart. Same for this game. Often times you die from falling in "acid" because you thought it was water. And often you land on a spike and die, even though some of the crystals you pick up are very spiky. Signals are so mixed! And with the world changing looks all the time it just gets even more confusing.
Anyways, it's certainly not a bad game by a long shot, meaning that I actually like the gameplay when I take it extremely slow. I'm just so disappointed that they didn't think of these things. Or maybe they did and they just ended up working so long on the game that they couldn't see the flaws anymore. It happens. Sadly.

I'll start by saying it is by no means a bad game.
Music and visual styles are great, but both have issues. Music is VERY limited in the game. You hear the same few tracks over and over. They're good, just not varied. Art style is great, but every now and then a foreground object gets in front of a hazardous object. And you die from it. So the camera angles and foreground objects needed work. The visuals also work against it from time to time, having to swap dimensions to avoid certain hazards, sometimes one or two will blend in with the world transforming, so you may not see it until you get hit by it.
Controls are clunky, your default attack runs out but keeps the momentum of movement, often causing you to die to an enemy just out of reach that the game forced you to attack. Or forcing you to rebound in a way that'll possibly get you killed, and will do in some levels.
The game also can't decide if it wants to hold your hand or not, as 3even during the final world you're still getting tutorial billboards, but they completely neglected to mention something else that isn't so obvious. Case and point, they never mentioned you can duck under harzards while on a rail, but 3 worlds later they're happy to remind you to use your basic ability to fall slowly, or tell you "you can swap dimensions to make the next few walls transparent".
It's also short as all hell, you could beat the entire game in less than 3 hours easily.
Still not a bad game, just flawed and needed some more work, polish, and testing.

I was quite disappointed with this game. It has a pretty cool sci-fi setting, and the main characters from what I've experienced so far seemed decent enough. But the gameplay is just so rough around the edges that the game becomes a test of patience a lot of the time.
The combat seems fun and all. Some battles in the beginning were quite fun, especially with the whole chaos going on aboard the space station. However, that whole area was just gunfight after gunfight. And when you're not engaging in gunfights, you're crossing vast areas doing nothing but walking, like the first plains area right after the space station. I spent a good minute or so crossing it, then died in a battle, then had to cross it again, two more times.
And shortly after that there was a car driving section. The control for the car is quite awkward, and I ended up giving up when I kept failing to make it over a gap between the cliffs whilst trying to dodge enemy gunfire. It's not my idea of fun. If you thought controlling Mako in Mass Effect was bad, think again.
In addition to frustrations in the gameplay, the game also crashes a lot. You can't save when you want, and checkpoints are quite far apart, so every time the game crashes to desktop, you lose a lot of progress.
There are some good ideas present regarding the setting, and some of the mechanics are nice, like doing dodging manoeuvres during gunfights, but in general the game feels very rough and even unpolished, with no regard to the player's time, so I can't recommend it.

Advent Rising is a game that I randomly found. I saw many steam reviews saying that it was one of their favourite games of all time. And had a person in my steam friend list who also was super excited about it. So, I recently played the game to find out if it was all nostalgia or if it really is a masterpiece.
You start the game off by getting on to a spaceship and receiving your training. You visit an alien form that warns you of another alien group that is about to attack. When you return to the ship it is under attack and you have to escape. I have to say the first 2 hours of the game really felt boring to me. The gameplay felt like you were just going from room to room killing aliens. The only positive was that you have choices in the beginning. Which you, sadly and strangely, don't have as you continue further into the game.
After those initial 2 hours it finally starts to get interesting. Also your weapons are levelling up and you are unlocking new cool powers (It comes over weird in the story that you randomly unlock new powers though). The game has so many powers and weapons that I haven't been able to try them all out. This may be because you are limited to one weapon or power per hand. Also, I have to say that the end bosses were pretty challenging overall, I wasn't expecting that. The driving sections in the game can become really exciting, except if you have to shoot. In the end the game took me 10 hours to complete on normal difficulty.
The story is pretty well written and had me coming back to the game. I am sometimes amazed that they actually did what they did with the story. I reached a part of the game that made me wish to stop playing, but the story helped me push through it. There are times when the story felt cheesy and cheap (And sadly the not CGI cutscenes looked really poor). It is also obvious that the screenwriting took inspiration from movies popular at the time of the game's release. The game has many slow-motion animations while jumping or finishing an enemy to make it more cinematic. This is pretty cool but after a while it can be really irritating, because you are just waiting for the animation to end.

The most recent game by Swery65, the 'auteur' game producer responsible for the gloriously batshit Deadly Premonition. And on first blush this had exactly the same spirit as DP, though wrapped in mechanics of a Telltale/Quantic Dream bent instead of the open world RPG trappings. So you explore each level talking to the weird characters therein, doing simple side quests for them and advancing the main plot of travelling back in time to try and solve the murder of your wife. 'Action' scenes play out using the usual sort of QTEs you've seen before and while they're relatively fun it manages what all these kind of things do and takes your attention 100% from all the entertaining looking nonsense that you're 'controlling' making it probably something more fun to watch than to play. Overall it's a bit clunky and repetitive but it's engaging enough given the general weirdness of it all. And then...it ends. Like just stops dead on a cliffhanger. It was originally planned to be an episodically released games but after the intro part and first two episodes were released as an initial package nothing else was ever delivered. Swery has since left the company that developed it and has made no bones about the fact that it's dead so, that's that I suppose? I don't think I paid very much for it so I got my money's worth but if I'd realised how utterly unfinished it was I'm not sure I'd have bothered.

Review after 39 hours
I am a Sudden Strike veteran. As many others. I always preferred Sudden Strike Forever than Sudden Strike 2. I don't even consider the third chapter.
I was looking forward this game but at the same time I was sceptical, due to the disappointment of SS3 and the way sometimes games nowadays are done and released.
I was positevely surprised and I recommend this game 100%.
The spirit of Sudden Strike is there and they have introduced a number of things that are very good (shells bouncing on highly-armored tanks, crew of artilleries responding to fire when attacked, etc...).
- Graphics and animations are very good and of course huge improvement compared to the old titles.
- Interface is also good and very easy, in particular if you are used to the old games and Men of War series.
- Sound is great and the music is excellent: it is dynamic and I loved the "drumroll" from time to time in the single player. Just great.
- Single player campaigns (21 missions in total) are not so short and they are challenging. I
: they are not linear so you have new objectives in the middle of the mission, ambushes, retreats, being outnumbered. It's very nice,
- Multiplayer came out not completed and that was a shame. Anyhow the dev team released some patches and in particular added the classic "zeppelin" mode that many veterans asked. Now it is very good despite there are still problem of connection and you have to be aware that the scale of the battle is smaller (map size and number of units) than old Sudden Strike games.
- In terms of zoom, range of sight and range of fire the game is balanced and enjoyable as it is. Nevertheless everything is "smaller-scale" compared to the old SS games. Sudden Strike 4 could definetely benefit from an increase of zoom out. range of sight and range of fire.
- Units miss experience and that is a pity because in previous SS games you could have your "hero" units thanks to XP.
- Infantry is very nice, although the officer is missing the binoculars, but it is never enough. We always need more infantry!
It appears that the dev team cares about this game. It is good as it is but it has even the potential to become a great game, an authentic jewel and a even more authentic successor to the glorious Sudden Strike.
Keep up the good work!

As someone who played a lot of Blitzkrieg 1 as a kid this is a surprisingly good followup to that. It's got the bombastic feel of COH with artillery raining down, tanks blowing up to pieces and infantry getting flung around like ragdolls. While it's not exactly realistic(I mean in COH you could repair tanks to full health for example), the battles are smaller and more focused compared to the older Sudden Strike games. I'd compare this to COH for the bombastic action and the first Blitzkrieg game on the mechanics, like towed artillery and limited troops(which I don't get why people think you could build them on the field like C&C)
It can get slow and methodical as you set up your artillery and resupply/refuel your tanks while your infantry creeps until you make contact with the enemy. The graphics and map design are really nice with good explosion effects and environmental damage. The sound and music are good as well although I'm a bit miffed that all faction briefings and in-mission dialog are all done by the same actors which loses some immersion. Even your infantry survive mostly impossible bombardings but get shredded by other stuff which can lead to some frustration.
It can get a bit annoying to micromanage your troops under pressure but the pause button is pretty handy for these kind of situations. There's no autosupply function for your supply trucks so you'll have to manually order them separately for fuel and ammo. The missions are varied in which it seems a bit short at first(looking at you Market Garden) but they open up for bigger operations with even more options like artillery and air support for you to use and they take some time to finish. Line of sight seems strange although positioning your infantry in the front or calling in recon planes allows you to gain a larger sight. The star system based on your performance isn't something I'd call amazing but it gives your troops better options although I'm not sure why hand grenades aren't standard issue in the first place and I wish infantry was selectable by squads instead of individual troops(although you can group them).
I hope they add more missions and flamethrowers which are sadly not present. Also it runs smoothly on my aging rig although there are some weird audio loops which will hopefully get patched out.
Otherwise it's a pretty good single player romp.

Only 2 or 3 of the cast even come close to that.
Second, the humor. I didn't laugh once throughout the movie. Most of the parody of office politics are overdone and obvious. The punchlines are weak and badly timed. I have no idea how this thing is labeled a comedy.
Third, the script. I have highest hope for the script. Independent projects, as opposed to big-budget productions, can always pull something totally out of the left field. It turns out to be nothing special. I admit the mystery kept me interested for a while. However, the set-up and acting gave away fairly early who's the murderer. The movie did have a twist that I could not predict but I did expect something similar. Events always foreshadow what will happen next. Characters who perish all raised dead flag. I correctly predicted who will be the next victim on all but one occasion. Anyways, nothing will blow your mind unless this is your first experience with the mystery genre.
The rest are hit and miss. Sounds are okay but I dislike how the music is used too often to set the mood. It makes the movie feel even more like a stage production. Cinematography is actually quite good. To me, how the camera moves adds more suspense than the actual script.
Last but not least, Noureen is a huge letdown. She's the only cast member I knew before the movie. However, it felt like she was casted just for that one underwear scene. Worth it I guess since the scene got marketed heavily with the movie. Her acting is so inconsistent as if she does not exactly know what her character should be.

Well worth every penny. Steam should do this more often.

Alas, no, I'm not the director, and a darn shame too, since he actually made something relatively unique. I made the review to add to the positive review count so more people could see the film! But, since at least somebody out there asked nicely for an honest review, here goes:
The movie was worth every penny because I got it for like $10, and bundled with another movie to boot (which I have yet to view but you haters can bet I will be leaving something positive over there, too!) It was not a blockbuster extraordinaire by any stretch of the imagination, but it had cute moments, and I saw it as a more modern interpretation of Ten Little Indians (And Then There Were None) by Agatha Christie. Night Shamalamadingdong quality), or if they were expected, could have easily gone any number of different ways.

This game should be called 'Mars: Evasive Rolls and Gophering'  because that is virtually all you will be doing.
Things you can do in Mars: War Logs, listed by frequency:
Sick Rolls: You will die almost immediately without them. 90% of your battle strategy will be somersaults, side rolls, and back rolls).
Getting things for apparent invalids: Everyone needs something, and, yes, it is on the other side of the bland and lifeless map.
Listen to mind-numbing dialog and fifth-rate voice acting: The mish mash of accents and hammed-up acting is intense.
Sell all your items one by one: You know how most games allow you to sell items two, or even three, at a time? Not Mars: War Logs. You must sell everything one by one, even if you have fifty of them. Enjoy!
Crafting objects that are way more expensive then just buying them: To craft a health injection costs 20 serum, to buy one costs 8. Do the math.
Putting sick plates on your dusty clothes: Now you can look like an awesome post-apocalyptic warrior, or maybe you can look like Kevin Costner in The Postman.
Actually fighting: When you aren't busy gophering, crafting, and getting lulled into a rage-coma by the silly acting and storytelling, you can beat enemies with improvised weapons. Yes, we are far into the future, but due to apparent reason guns, laser swords, and fun weapons don't exist in this sparse world. You get to beat up on your enemy with light fixtures and mole creature bones.
Pros of Mars: War Logs: You will be momentarily distracted from all the evil in this world by this catastrophe. You will get to practice your digital gymnastic skills (except for jumping, because why jump over things when you can roll right past them?).
Cons: Playing Mars: War Logs is a lot like playing Solitare. It's basically a way to tell your friends and family that you are exceptionally bored and have nothing on your plate at the moment. It's inviting people to give you a menial task to do, much like the NPCs in Mars: War Logs. Don't let it happen.

Time to write a review... FOR JUSTICE!
The facts are these:
#1: The writing is charming, witty, and quite punny (and there are a few jokes for those who speak French)
#2: The art style is boldly different, yet somehow nothing is lacking in the visuals. The details are beautiful and every new character/animal has a completely fresh design that is great to see.
#3: The story itself is extremely interesting. Each case warms you up to the over-arching narrative that takes some detective-work on the player's part to piece together. Will all these facts collide in the developing Chapter 5? I hope so.
#4: While hilarious, the story also takes itself quite seriously. One wrong move on the player's part could result in a death, not just a "game over." In this spirit, the story is grounded in the very real setting of revolutionary France, allowing the history buffs a bit of a spree through tumultous times.
#5: The so-called "negative" reviews of this game are actually worth a read, because most praise the game in the highest fashion. Some bird-brains just can't wait 5 days for one of 3 intricate endings to be polished and delivered. A miscommunication, at best. Having played all three endings (the delayed ending cannonically last, in my case), I would say it was well worth the short wait.
The Verdict:
GUILTY of being a wonderful romp through mystery, art, wit, and great characters. This game is worth a play (or three), and I take off my hat to the developers. I, for one, am happily looking forward to the promise of even more in the future. Due process and all that.
Review ADJOURNED.

Despite the premise, this game is less an Ace Attorney-clone and more of its own beast. So whether you'll like this game or not depends on your expactations: if you want to scratch that Ace Attorney-itch, this game might disappoint you. There are 4 cases in total, but only half of them follow the Ace Attorney-formula; the other half "plays" a lot more like graphic novels with easy puzzles/cross-examinations. However, if you are looking for an unique graphic novel with fantastic writing, go for it - these strong points make me recommend this game.

Though I do recommend this game, I feel like some of you might be surprised by the actual amount of content in the game.
There are 4 cases in this game with Case 4 having 3 different parts depending on the results of Case 3. Though this seems like a lot of content, I was able to go through the game in approximately 8 hours at a leisurely pace. I have no doubts someone could get through this game in 5 or less hours.
I will say this game has great music, art, and dialogue. You can definitely feel the love and effort that was given to these areas of the game and I loved it. It truly felt refreshing.
The story however is short and, in my opinion, a little lacking. All of the cases are quick and have rather simple scenerios. Especially Case 4, where investigation is streamlined and we are given short and simple endings. Case 3 probably took the longest but only because you have to go through it fully twice to get both the endings.
Now, at it's modest price tag of 15$ (compared to Ace Attorney's 35$ on release) you get a comperable amount of time for your dollar. However, don't be expecting long/intricate cases or a thrilling plot. But do prepare to chuckle whenever Sparrowson speaks.

Is Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams worth your purchase? Likely
=TL;DR=
GS;TD is the crowdfunded sequel to the infamous original Great Giana Sisters platformer, which was seen by Nintendo and most players as a clone of Super Mario Bros. I wouldn't exactly call it a clone, but it's definitely a rip-off the classic. Twisted Dreams escapes that problem and makes itself to game to be loved by "collect everything" style gamers, and masochists, and looks good doing it. A great game for platformer fans.
=Presentation
The premise of the character is a bit confusing, as the game is called Giana Sisters and you clearly see one of the two "sisters" being abducted in the opening cutscene. But official developer descriptions refer to the girls as personalities of the same Giana. I guess the idea is that the other sister is imaginary, yet part of Giana's personality.
Twisted Dreams has a pretty nice asthetic with a bright, and colorful dream world for Punk Giana, with metal-esque backgroud music that transforms smoothly and convincingly into the nightmare world for Sweet Giana with it's more pop-ish style music. The transformation of the worlds when switching sisters is very slick and I would like to see how the developers made it happen. Much of the music comes from the band Machinae Supremacy, which I will be looking out for now. The sound effects are fitting and what I expect - though the coos and screams of Giana will annoy some players.
=Gameplay=
The gameplay is very simple and easy to understand early in the game. Sweet Giana can jump and also twirl to get a second jump and also slowly descend, similar to Princess Peach from Super Mario Bros 2 while she is in the spooky world with "sweet" music and can change personalities on the fly to Punk Giana to also jump and have a secondary flaming cannonball attack, similar to Blanka's from Street Fighter. This attack can help in enemy aided jump sequences, objects that propel the attacking Punk Giana, and breaking Super Mario Bros style blocks (that don't contain gems like the original, or coins like SMB). You die in one hit unless you pickup a shield for an extra hit, and lives are unlimted unless you play Uber Hardcore, which ends your game if you die. I thought I might eventually give that mode a try if I beat the game, until I got to the first boss level which I was massacered in (but eventually beat after dozens of deaths. F*** that boss).
The level design is generally fair and relatively forgiving, though not flawless. The first level or two clearly point out "death pits", and your main path, making you think that this will be the case throughout the game, but not all the death pits are as blatantly obvious in the later levels, which is irritating if you're trying to collect all the gems without dying for extended playthroughs (though, at this point, you should probably have memorized the level pitfalls, or be able to consult a guide). Trial and error and level replays are key to perfect level playthroughs, but perserverance will get you through the main levels and end game (though, you may have to replay some levels to get the minimum star requirement for the last level). The near exception to this rule was the first boss battle, in which I died waymore than I liked to admit, but it also wasn't the smoothest first boss battle I played and some of the boss attacks where a bit unfair. I've also had unexpected results when using the cannonball attack in certain segments, which is fustrating to die after hitting an enemy RIGHT after coming out of the cannonball animation.
Progression only comes in the form of unlocking new game modes including score attack, time attack, hardcore and uber hardcore and replaying levels to get all the gems and 5 star ratings. You don't level up or unlock powers, though a few more mechanics are thrown at you during the course of the game; such as pairs of ghost that are only active in the sweet or punk world and can only be killed by special light shafts in the level. Winning the game is all about your play skill and not what you unlock or luck (except for enemy spawn/patrol locations). I've spent about 4hrs for halfway at the game, so maybe twice that or more for completion. Extra holiday and Dieselstormers promo levels are included free, and there is an expandalone title "Rise of the Owlverlord" if you want more.
=Conclusion=
Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams is a no brainer for platformer fans, collect-a-thon gamers, and masochists. It's very solid has a great look and soundtrack, though, nothing about this is remarkable for somebody with limited time and is only looking for the most premium and interesting games, or the types that have no interest in cute games. $15 is probably a fair price for the entire package, though unless this is a must-play for you, you can just wait for a sale or bundle.

If you have played any other AGEOD games and you have an interest in this period, this game is a must have. If you're an American Civil War buff, this game is a must have. If you want to learn about the American Civil War or the War of Northern Agression, this is a must have. I guess what I'm getting at is that you should seriously consider this title.
Pros: extremely detailed (army leaders, units, army organisation, you name it), appealing graphics, advanced AI, historical events (e.g. suspend habeas corpus) and extremely detailed
Cons: extremely detailed - a history book and online video tutorials will help you here :), the manual (version 1.04) is missing information on national decisions (very small con, because you can just refer to the tooltips instead), and some stability issues (experienced a couple of crashes) - however there's dedicated support by email and forums (not on steam, on developer's website) full of people who can guide you through any issues
Buyer beware - you may become extremely addicted. Seek professional help if you connect a caffeine drip and play non-stop for 7 days. :)

If you have a younger gamer or two to entertain, then Message Quest is a great little game for a rainy day - the description of it as an "interactive picture book" is spot on. For the rest of us, there are more engaging games available on Steam for the same price.
Message Quest is certainly a cute way to pass the better part of an hour, and all the bright colours and light humour make that hour a pleasant one. Yet my personal feeling is that this game should have been marketed to children, rather than being released as a purchasable game for adults on Steam.
Now don't get me wrong - there isn't anything wrong with short games at all (Limbo, anyone?). But there's a difference between a game which is short because it was developed to be so, and a game which is short because you're flying through every challenge without blinking. If you're able to read this review, then chances are you'll also find Message Quest's simple little puzzles a little
simple to be satisfied with. For example: a recurring objective throughout the game is to "dust off" dirty panes of glass, revealing what's underneath. To dust, you click three times.
Objective complete!
And that's why I feel the developers have really missed a trick here. The simple and colourful selection of puzzles, along with the bright, cheerful art style and the overarching "moral of the story" message, would go down really well with children. It's just a shame that they aren't really Steam's target audience! However if you're reading this as a parent of school-age children, then Message Quest will be a great addition to your Steam library. Note: Message Quest does require a basic-to-fair level of reading ability, so either make sure you're on hand to help if your little gamer gets stuck on a difficult word, or turn it into a family activity and read along with them as they play. :)

I could not just play and not come back to give appreciation. Besides, it would be too lovely to see other game creators made games inspired by Message Quest, so here are the most shiny features (warning, small spoilers) :
- character fights,
- graphics,
- the BO and its freely given Steam soundtrack,
- the faint humor that seems to hesitate between dark and burlesque,
- bits of a simplistic spoken language (I don't know if it's made from a real one)
- the reference to Esperanto,
- the dialog system making the player decide of what every character says, showing the player how something someone say can be interpreted differently and heard a conversation in a lighter or darker direction, but also saying that there can be more than one reason for a happening, and that, well, no one is perfect (not even the narrator),
...All of these elements made my heart sing, long to hug every character, and broke through my usual misanthropy for a few hours.
End of spoilers.
The only negative point I can find is that I found the plot weak, and with too many unexplained things by the time it ends. But that may just be a wrong impression due to the devs not being native French or English speakers : which may have let to so some sentences in the Prologue / Epilogue not being turned in a way that gave sense and cause for the events of the game.
If it was possible, I'd wish for two things :
1. Getting to listen to the characters' songs and battle attacks in the Soundtrack
2. Getting to play the whole game in Esperanto ♥

Take part Mass Effect, part Halo, and throw in a dash of Star Wars and you get Advent Rising. This is the utmost praise, however, as Advent Rising is a fantastic game. It is clear that Mass Effect borrowed heavily from this game as the Geth seem to be ripped straight from it. The fiction behind the story is some of the most engrossing sci-fi I've seen in a while, which is no surprise since it was written by Orson Scott Card.
The gameplay is third-person, with the use of guns and special powers. The guns do feel really nice, but I found myself using the powers more often, especially in the later game. The level design is superb as well, and I never felt lost, even in some of the bigger environments.
The game is not without it's faults, however. Consulting
is a must for essential fixes, but I still had a fair number of issues. There were graphic anomalies when things got intense and there were lots of explosions. cutscenes would sometimes hicup as well, although the dialogue did not skip. The most annoying thing were the game crashes which happened a handful of times. Thankfully, the game saved at the exact point of the crash so nothing was lost, but still annoying.
Iffy port aside, this game is fantastic. It really is a shame we will probably never see the planned sequels as this game builds a very promising lore and world around it. It's certainly worth playing, just know that it will probably never get a proper finale.

I played Advent Rising twice over the course of the ten-some hours I've played it on Steam. I went through the first time saving Gideon's fiancé, and the second time saving Gideon's brother. This is really the only, somewhat, major choice in the game. It really only affects who accompanies you through the early game, and a portion of the post-credits game. The first time I played through legitimately and on normal difficulty. The second time I used a cheat to give Gideon infinite health and energy so I could take a bunch of screenshots without getting killed or running out of energy for the things I was trying to screenshot.
The early game it consists of a space station, a few cutscenes, your one major-ish choice and the Human planet. These are amongst the least interesting parts of the game. Earth also has a lot of Vehicle driving. The Earth Vihicle controls aren't good, but the Vehicle itself is hardy enough to endure all the things you're going to be running into. If you've ever heard someone tell you a game takes X amount of time to get good, this is the sort of game they're talking about.
After escaping the destruction of the Human planet Gideon starts to get super powers as is the entire concept of the game. Playing with the powers is, quite simply, a blast, combining their primary and secondary fire modes with one another is easily the game at its best. No other game I've played has captured the growth of a being to super powerful levels quite like this, and more games should take note.
The designs of the Aliens, the enemy A.I. and variety of enemies is decent. There's room to grow, and the A.I. has its hiccup moments, but there's nothing terrible in regard to these things. The Alien Vehicles you'll pilot in the late game even manage to control better than the Human vehicle you pilot in the early game.
The music is stunning. Great. Lovely. No complaints. The story has its moments, but a lot of the lines characters speak are just goofy. If you can handle a bit of awkward and goofy dialogue, the story still isn't a gem, but it can be an enjoyable and adventurous romp. The voice acting is hit and miss, but even the worst is forgiveable and the later game's dialogue, voice acting, story and music just managed to bring me in more and more, where the early game, again, was very goofy and awkward.
I'd like to keep praising the game but . . . it's a really terrible port. I've never seen the original Console version's cutscenes, so maybe they were always like this, but on the PC they look terrible and I'm told many Cutscenes are missing from the original release. It's sad. There is a patch to add them in, but the download for the best quality and most scenes restored is large, and oddly slow considering my decent connection speed.
The problems go beyond cutscenes. Bugs. Lots of bugs. A few issues in the early Human planet vehicle sections with terrible 'vehicle platforming' for lack of something better to call it, Lots of crashes. Lots. Graphical glitches, very limited graphical settings and many more things work against this game.
Advent Rising, as a console game ported to PC, is a very, very flawed game. It's also a very fun and entertaining game, and by the end, despite some very real flaws, I'd forgiven the flaws because I really did just want more, and that feeling only grew after the credits rolled and revealed a decently long post-credits sequence and boss fight, that ended in sequel bait.
A sequel that never came.
;_;
TL;DR - It's worth playing and can be a lot of fun, but prepare for bugs, crashes and some frustrating elements muddying up some legitimately fun times. Your tolerance for goofy/awkward dialogue/story telling in the early game, and a very bland start to the game, will factor a lot into whether you can enjoy this game, and get to its meat.
-
EDIT:
After coming back to the game, again, and a again, since my original review, my feelings on Advent Rising haven't changed. There are so many new and old games I play, and never touch again. This one I've come back to repeatedly. Maybe that makes me a fanboy, but, I feel it says something about the quality of the game (in some respects) and the strong base further entries could have built on.

Advent Rising is scifi adventure following a human named Gideon as he teams up humans and aliens alike to combat one of the most powerful forces in the galaxy. In this epic scifi story many aliens hold humans at a near god-like stature and have been on the search for them for many years believing that they posess vast powers. The aliens find the humans just in time to warn them of a major threat that is heading there way and could be the end of the human race.
The story in Advent Rising is nothing short of excellent. I bought this game on sale and did not expect to play for very long, 3 days later I have completed the game. The story is just that entertaining. Each section leaves you wanting to see more of the story unfold. You are in for a treat with this one.
While the overall gameplay is that of an early 2000s game (which this game is) the combat is very addicting. You will be using melee, a huge variety of guns and even special abilities you unlock which are very fun to play with. There is nothing like throwing an enemy into the depth of space using your telekinitic-like abilities or boxing an enemy inside a forcefield and watching them kill themselves. You can also control turrets, drive land and flying vehicles all with their own weapons and abilities. The boss fights each have a specific strategy and it can provide quite the challenge to figure out.
The game is not without its flaws though. While the combat is addicting, the style in which the enemies approach is very repatitive and sometimes the targeting system will work against you. I found myself aiming manually as opposed to using the target system due to this. Also the game tends to crash randomly after cutscenes. Luckily the game saves quite frequently so this is not a major issue, but is still rather annoying. There is also one bug where the game can't recognize proper input if you have a game controller in. This is easily remedied by unplugging the controller though.
Advent Rising was far more than I expected it to be. It was one of the better stories I have played through this year. The gameplay is repetitive at times but the combat is still very satisfying. There are a few bugs with the game but they are not decision breaking. The story alone in Advent Rising is worth the full price tag. If you find it on sale it is a steal.

With the new update bringing ending 4-C, I can finally recommend this game with good conscience. Not that the game wasn't good before, but it was imcomplete prior to the update, which is worth mentioning.
Anyway, with that out of the way, Aviary Attorney is a fantastic game with great art and writing. Characters have interesting anthropromorphic animal designs, the characters are likeable and memorable, and the dialogue is clever. Fans of the Ace Attorney series will definitely find a lot of similarities from that series in this game, but there are enough differences and new twists to make this game worth it. For example, there are branching paths (you can get three major endings in fact), and it is possible to fail cases and continue the game with your failure affecting various portions. Investigation segments are also a lot of fun due to having to choose carefully on where you choose to investigate. If you make poor choices, you might not get all the info and evidence necessary to save your client.
Overall, I highly recommend this game, especially to fans of the Ace Attorney series.

A decent adaptation of a classic. As far as board games go, this one is heavy on the whims of the dice, and a 6-player game with the computer takes several hours to complete. Interesting twist that you get XP for finishing a game, and this in turns grants minor boons to apply to all singler player future games (along with achievements, if you're into that). Nice to entice replay. Graphics are nothing special, and the computer can be aggravating (it seems the AI wants to go around attacking one another than win the game). Because of game length, you can exit anytime and the game saves your spot.
For new player, you choose a character that has unique abilities and then try, subject to extreme dice whimsy, to make yourself stronger by having encounters in the outside of the board, with the goal of entering the middle of the board and eventually the center, which requires you obtain a particular item and be strong enough to face specific tough encounters. This game is nice in that if a player dies, they're not out of the game and restart without items. To win the game, someone needs to reach the center, which has a Crown that each round casts a spell that has a 50/50 chance to deal 1 damage to everyone else. Anyone who dies from this damage is out.
My major complaint is the AI. I'm not sure it ever tries to win the game.
Worth a go if the game is on sale, wouldn't pay full price with the AI as is.

Very complex game but I like this game. I am British so I don't have any real feeling of immersion playing the American Civil War but like any strategy game its the act of fighting a strategic war, with historical troops, and finding out about things you didnt know about that makes this game really interesting. The Civil War is an interesting period of history as well in that both sides had it tough, the war was a long brutal one, with much movement and innovation. So its an interesting conflict to play.
The mechanics in this game are spot on. For example you dont move alone you move at the same time as the enemy does, so you have to predict where they are going to be and often you can get surprised. So thats very realistic. Far more realistic than attacking a paused enemy. Also you have very detailed heirarchy of troops including armies and corps, a lot like Paradox's Hearts of Iron 3 in fact. You get bonuses to things like supply and attack coordination for being well supported and organised which is good.
You can use gunboats to support your attacks, You can syncronise your attacks, You can even have neighbouring friendly armies 'march to the sound of guns' and automatically move to support you in a battle.
Pretty much everything you feel should be in the game is actually in the game, and this game is far more polished than the first game.
The only downsides are that the game might not be all that stable - many crashes have been reported and I had a critical error crash in the first tutorial, five minutes into the game on my first turn's generation, but none in the actual game since. Also the GUI is rather bland looking compared to the lovely period one in the first game but its far easier to see whats going on and there are mods to add cosmetic improvements to it.
Overall I would say this is probably the most complex strategic game I have ever played. The complexity does put you off playing it unless you have a bit of time and brain power to spare, but for those who love very deep strategy games this is about as deep as they get.

While still having a lot of the surreal charm of Sweary's first game, there are higher production values and more consise storytelling then in Deadly Premonition; which leaned very heavly into it's low budget for a lot of it's ironic charm. The game was origonally a Kinect game, that actually was well talored to the platform(despite it's lack of support from microsoft later on.) The motion controls translate into a mouse pretty seemlessly in this well made port.
There's a lot of interesting mechanics layored into what is essentially a point and click game. The conversation choice system is a new spin on it, where it's less about making a choice, and more an attempt to understand and "sync" with the main character David by figuring out his personallity. There's a lot of small mouse over details that you need to hold to get all the bits of information about it, which can be cute or cutting details about characters and objects. The mechanics really help you get into the head of this quirky detective, and going back through chapters to find all of them through cutscenes or places that you forgot to double check ties into the psuedo-time travel naritive in a somewhat meta way.
Unfortunatly, most of the plans of a second season have been canceled at this point (even after the chance of revival at it's steam rerelease.) and it's a shame that a game with such a great opening act wont have any closure any time soon if even. If you are hoping purchasing this game will give you a fully played out narrative, it's very unlikely at this point, but if you don't mind being left in the dark and just want a taste of something new in interesting, I highly recommend this odd little half-made game.

In the masterfully crafted "Mars: War Logs" (which is in fact a war-diary), we are transported to a martian "anti reality", where societal norms regarding sexual orientation are questioned and examined in series of autisticly voice-acted scenes populated with uncanny-valley robo-people. "The War", (referenced in the title), is actually culture-war being fought not only on the Martian landscape, but within ourselves.

:
In this game, you play  a man metaphorically questioning his own sexuality whilst constantly being thrust into combat scenarios  where the only way to survive is to forcefully bludgeon others with handcrafted electro-phalluses.  Our  protagonist hails from a martian colony called "Aurora";  a symbol of cis-genedered norms. Aurora issues "virtue-names" to each inhabitant  like "temprance", "honesty", "morality", "steely-dan" and "jazz-organ" as if to imply a life of freedomless societal predestination.
Our doucheburn-wearing antihero held rank in "The Source". "The Source" is a guild of "technomancers", a group of pick-up artists who have dedicated a lifetime of hot-gluing wires and glowsticks to their bodies in a misguided attempt at peacocking. Rejecting this worldview, he is cast down into a dirty man-prison festering with debauchery. It is in this gay-underworld that our protagonist takes his first steps in breaking away from breeder-culture and changes from his assigned name "Temperance" to "Roy", the name of a gay space-cowboy.
All is well in the Brokeback Mars Mountain-Prison until one day a strapping young bronco named "Innocence" appears one day, in the shower room. After defending him from an attempted♥♥♥♥♥♥(yes that's what happens), "Innocence" thanks you and becomes your new buckaroo-boyfriend. Innocence then keeps a scrapbook, where he draws fanart about the main character, and talks about his feelings.
After bonding with Innocence by digging through trash bins, rubble heaps and rotten mushroom patches for a few hours, Roy and his young buck decide to "break out of the closet" by stealing a train, and returning to Aurora. Ideally, this is where where they will organize a "resistance" that will pridefully march in the streets and overturn societal norms.

:
The gameplay consists primarily of combat and dialogue. The dialog feels largely forced, much like the expectation our protagonist feels to conform to society. Your character is almost entirely sent on errands, in an effort to highlight the meaninglessness of life without freedom. You are both figuratively and literally wasting away in a prison! This nihilist gesture is surely to underscore the overarching theme of resisting cultural assimilation and cisexual assumptions.
In a bold move, the extended metaphor of sexual discovery is manifest in akward camera angles during combat. The audience is constantly asking questions like "what am I really trying to see?" and "who am I, in all of this?". The camera encourages you to explore new ways of seeing reality.
The enemies you fight during combat consist of your sexual rivals in the prison, cave dwelling testicle-mutants and pick up artists wearing rave-gloves. Despite the fact humans have clearly terraformed Mars, you are restricted to fighting with nailguns and crude batons. You must therefore "assert dominance" over your foes by forcefully employing these erotically-shaped instruments in a symbolic display of fertility and potency.
However, with the slow response speed and erratic camera movements, much like the theme of the game, the real enemy is yourself, thus highlighting the thematic motifs present in the story.

:
In another bold artistic gesture, the developers decided to maek every mesh appear as robotic and lifeless as possible during the dialogue. This is clearly an allusion to a dystopian reality, where "every cog has its place" and personal freedom is stifled. Every landscape is a exercise in monotony and every texture is visual litter.  Everything, (even your clothing), is covered with the same blurry rust, soot and grunge; a clear attempt to give Mars a literal and figurative sense of 'uncanny valley', a fitting location for our symbolic tale.
I feel like this Idea could have been explored more throughly, hence the 9.

:
If you're the right kind of player, itching for a game to make you question yourself, social norms, and why you spend money on Mars: War Logs, this is a game that will raise the right questions. I have never seen a game so experimentally break the 4th wall by intentionally crippling core gaming features in service to a noble theme.
Sadly however; I cannot recommend this game. I don't think most people are ready for this. Mars logs is simply ahead of its time.

Advent Rising is one of those games that tries to tell a very good story behind some relatively good 3rd person dodge shooters with some fancy-shmancy powers. The result is a bit of a mixed bag though, but for a 10 year old game it held up pretty well. Unfortunately, the game is sort of a sleeper hit that never was popular enough to finish the other two games in the trilogy.
The story penned by Orson Scott Card (Ender's Game, etc.) has the Wyeth Brothers (you control Gideon, the younger brother) be the pilot taking the ambassador to a first contact with a race of aliens who worship the humans almost as Gods, and they bear bad news... while they are perfectly peaceful... their enemies, known as the Seekers, are about to wipe out all the humans, and they will be here in days.
And just as the shuttle head back for home, the Seekers arrived early with a full fleet, and started to invade the human space station. Fighting through the chaos and waves of aliens cutting through the hull and marines defending till the last, Gideon witness the Seekers appear to be scanning humans as they execute them. He was able to get his brother to escape pod, but his fiancee Olivia had been captured or lost.
Pod landed on the planet, but there's full enemy action there too. Fighting through more enemies, they arrive at the city, fought through more enemies, reached the general in charge, but was told they need to find a ship off the planet... Seekers are using asteroids... any one not getting off are dead. As the asteroid bombardment begain, Wyeth brothers have to run through a collapsing base to locate the last available ship...
Well, I've barely covered 1/3 of the game so far. Later Gideon discovered he has powers that he barely knew how to tap, and with the help of some friendly aliens, he may survive long enough to figure out what is going on... And let's just say there's enough plot twists left and right to keep you guessing.
The game itself is third-person with some vehicle sections. Basically you control this guy, very athletic that can jump, pinwheel, dive and roll, and so on. He can also dual-wield two long weapons (or short) and achieve phenomenal accuracy if you lock on to the targets. So the game basically is a lot of shooting and jumping around, even a few fisticuffs when you have no weapons (and later, fight with your powers). The problem is, you only have two active attacks, and if you need a third or a fourth you have to remap them and things get dicey, and in the late game boss fights you will need more than two attacks. Consider this a hint. :)
You do get to drive a vehicle sometimes, and the "Scythe" is almost a bit like predecessor to HALO's Warthog. Your brother or allies will get in and man the gun for you. And it handles pretty well. It also has a bit of a booster for the more difficult jumps that you may sometimes need to make. And yes, you can run enemies over. Seekers also have hovertanks that you can borrow. There are also sometimes stationary turrets you can appropriate against Seeker gunship/dropships.
Graphics is obviously a bit dated by current standards, but not excessively so. Animation is decent, and while architecture is a bit square-ish it's not too bad.
Good story, lots of action, though a bit cliche-ish at times. This game really needs a bit of love, even though it's a decade late.

An old game, sometimes doesn't agree with steam, but a good game.
The storytelling is a little awkward with rapid jumps in time, introducing new powers with the same animation makes them seem a little less important, and you're regularly thrown into new environments that you become a little shell shocked to the ambiance - and likely can't appreciate the fullest of the worldbuilding. Similarly, the controls are a little awkward at certain points. I don't mind dual wielding rifles, given the statements about recoil in this universe - but more importantly, the Throw ability is a little hard to use. Normally I wouldn't complain, since there are many otehr abilities that work without flaw - but the Throw ability is used in a number of boss fights.
Now, even with all of that? I enjoyed myself.
It was a unique narrative, in a unique world. A lot of different faces, mixed characters, some of whom I grew attached to more than others. The deaths of characters stood out to me, and though I wish there was more choice - I can safely say that this game doesn't parade behind an Illusion of Choice system. When you have to make a choice, which may be rare - but given this game's age I can understand that - you still greatly appreciate the results of your choice.
Combat is interesting, and but not a change of pace from the usual archetypals. It's relatively smooth to go and decide what you want to equip, though knowing how much more XP you need to level a skill requires going through multiple menus. Having said this, I really like one thing about this game: You cannot max everything. I do not think, unless you play on easy, and grind away at mobs tirelessly, will you max all of your skills. That makes your gameplay choices a little more meaningful, and my character reflected it.
In short? Yes, some of the voice acting isn't great. Its an old game. It can be clunky in some places, but all in all - I recommend fans of High Science Fiction pick it up. We'll never see a sequel, but we can smile at what was Advent.

A charming, if challenging platformer. A collector's gem, literally, There is 300-700 gems per the 30+ levels, with a lot incredibly difficult to collect. The originlal Giana Sister's was pulled from shelves years ago for playing to simillarly to the Original Mario Bros games, but this iteration feels like a truely unique experience.
Each level is rated on a star system, where more stars are given based on the total amount of gem collected, and the least number of deaths. The main game mechanic is swapping between the two sisters abilities, Both have a basic jump ability, with one sister able to do a fiery dash charge, and the other sister has a spinning glide to move further. Each of the sisters has her own soundtrack too, with one being a typical sugary bouncy track, the other a punk metal tinted soundtrack which balances out the game.
Only disappointment is the repetition of the game content. The same enemies, general level lay-out and soundtrack get stale by the end. The additional levels, (Holiday themed, which are completely different) do help offset this, DLC is available, but your money would probably be better spent elsewhere.
There is some unlockable artwork and incredibly difficulty settings for those that beat the game and are looking for a steeper challenge.

An "8 bit" themed C&C style game where the focus is more on your army as a whole, and less on individual units. I've been waiting for an RTS like this for a while. I loathe modern RTS games (beside Grey Goo maybe) so this allowed me to play in a way I haven't been able to since the early Red Alert series.
Pros:
- Game focus is on the macro scale of things. (Out-army the other side)
- Clear view of what's going on.
- Easy hotkeys to remember.
- Building one structure at a time allows you a chance to think about your army strategy.
- Tough AI that seems to be reactive rather than just on a loop.
- Awesome retro music and clean art style that really captures your senses.
- Nice blend of old-fashioned and modern RTS resource gathering. Though, I miss my units just sucking up gems and chrono-leaping back to my base.
- Fast games that don't drag on.
- Simplified gameplay but a challenge to master.
- Single-player campaign missions offer up 25 levels and there are 10(or 11?) Co-op missions. The campaign has tons of replayability since it offer's bonus objectives and cross-mission advancement in the form of starting resources. This is only the first faction too! According to the devs, each faction will have their own campaign.
- I can finally stop playing my crash-inducing RA2 copy.
- Tons more I can't bother to list. :P
Cons:
- Wish I could garrison buildings.
Side notes:
- A lot of people say this game lacks all the structures and unit types other C&C games did, but that's intentional to allow for fun streamlined gameplay, yet still capturing the essential unit types. Engineers can heal too so they're more useful than in the Red Alert series.
- This game stands on its own. It doesn't need to be compared. It delivers solid gameplay and even expands upon the foundation that many other and I find ridiculously fun from RTS of old.
Thanks for reading my review! If you enjoyed the original C&C games, and have grown tired of the distracting mechanics that define modern day RTS games, then play 8-bit Armies!

Let's get the elephant in the room out of the way first. Yes, one of the variants of the final chapter is missing from the game at the time of writing. But it will probably be back in fairly soon and you don't have to pay for it, so I don't really see the issue. Also, you only get the particular version of the chapter if you ♥♥♥♥ up the previous one. So, uh, don't do that, I guess.
Speaking of elephants in rooms, you may have noticed that all of the characters are animals. The art style is actually one of the game's strongest points. And I don't say that often. The fact that they're animals is hardly important to the plot, beyond a few puns and maybe cats clawing people to death. It's a neat way of having all the characters be visually distinct without resorting to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ anime drawings. And despite the game being a visual novel, there are quite a few charming little animations to give things a bit more character.
The gameplay is pretty inventive, but sadly underutilised. It's like Ace Attorney, unsurprisingly. There's an investigation phase, where you talk to witnesses and look for clues, and then the trial phase, where you present evidence to contradict the witness' testimony. It's all very talky. The key difference with Aviary Attorney is the time limit during the investigation phase. Each place you investigate will take you a full day, and you have only a limited time before the trial starts. If you faff about going to the same locations too many times, or in the wrong order, you might not have all the clues ready for the trial. Which means you might not get the best possible ending.
This is something a lot of mystery games lack- an actual failure state. Too many allow you to click on everything until you find the solution. It's neat that the game doesn't patronise me by making the solution too obvious.
It's not all perfect though. I found the game to be pretty easy- I got the best ending for every case on my first try. I mean, it probably helps that I've played Ace Attorney and Danganronpa before, but even if you haven't, the game heavily hints at where to go next during the investigation phase, and the trial phase usually has fairly obvious contradictions. If you don't know what to do during the trial, just press every statement. Eventually, someone will say something like "I bet you can't prove that the witness owns a massive blood stained knife", at which point you present a bloody knife with their name signed on the handle.
The trials are also very short. There's only really two full trials to sink your teeth into. The first case is more of a tutorial and the fourth is just an excuse for some story. Not even particularly good story, the variant I ended up with (the one you get for succeeding in Act 3) was all about protecting a character the player doesn't care about. I can't really blame the developers, it's enough for the price tag, but I guess Ace Attorney has spoiled me into wanting more.
Besides the last act the writing is actually pretty excellent. It's funny, and not just "funny by video game humour standards". Legitimately funny. It also completely avoids the common mistake VNs make of describing a thing we can already see because it's a VISUAL novel.
In short:
Pros:
+Excellent writing
+Unique art styles
+Interesting investigations and trials
+Likeable characters
Negatives:
-A little on the short side
-Too easy
-A few mild bugs
-No log to reread dialogue that you might have missed
-Slightly incomplete
In short, it's a unique game that's worth experiencing despite its flaws. I hope the developers can explore some of these ideas more fully in a sequel.

Take a journey through the fowl world of late 1840's France on the verge of another revolution as legal eagle attorney extraordinaire JayJay Falcon a hard drinking but dedicated defense attorney, accompanied by his faithful chirpy comic relief sidekick Sparrowson in Aviary Attorney. Can you get your clients off the hook or will they find their goose is cooked? Bird puns out of my system let's get down to it!
Gameplay is greatly inspired by the Phoenix Wright series. Anyone experienced in those games will easily understand how this game works. You'll wade through sticky tangled webs of court room drama. Scour the cobblestone streets and back alleys of Paris for clues, make decisions on whether or not to use less than legal methods to obtain evidence, examine witness testimony, use logic and deduction in order to put all the pieces together to present your case. All the while coming to discover serving "justice" can be a messy complex affair.
The first thing to probably hit you is the astounding whimiscal caricature artwork that's highlighted throughout the game. Along with the backgrounds that range from smoke ridden taverns, to that of genuine historic sites and palaces of 19th century Paris. The anthropomorphic characters make up wonderfully strange an beautiful imagery. The artistic style of Jean-Jacques Grandville very much stands out for it's ability to conjure up such fantastic characters. The background surroundings you find yourself in are mainly borrowed from old illustrations that you would find in ads, catalogs and publications of the time. Pairing these two together and piecing them into a story results in a remarkable great looking game.
Music consists of many wonderfully orchestrated classical scores. Including the very fitting and recognizable "Funeral March Of A Marionette" that many would recall from it's use in the Alfred Hitchcock television show. Everything sound wise fits in with the period and serves to enhance the dramatic tense undergoings of the court room.
Writing and plot can make or break this type of game. Luckily the story is full of some great moments. Especially as you delve deeper into each case. The story likes to leave you with certain doubts by unfolding the dastardly truth along with the glaring cracks that make up our imperfect sense of justice. It leaves you with some thought provoking feelings as you consider the different possiblities and motives of each case you're assigned. The writer seems to make good choices as to when to inject humor and when to take itself more seriously. It keeps the over all atmosphere and tone to each scene consistant and immersive. Resisting falling into the trap of trying to hard to slap you in face with jokes, which can be tempting to do in this type of game. Nor does it always take itself to seriously and knows when to use timing to deliver a good joke.
All in all it's a very interesting game that any lover of adventures, visual novels, and of course Ace Attorney games will appreciate. I would personally rate Aviary Attorney overall as a 9 out of 10. Highly recommended good fun that draws you in and makes it hard to put down.

Veterans of Ace Attorney may find the few poses for each character a little disappointing, but it never feels as if the game could have used any specific additional pose. The backgrounds are quite excellent as well.
The music is quite nice and the voice bleeps are fitting and actually an improvement over the typical Ace Attorney ones, if only because of their larger variation and style.
The game is rather short. But so is the story. The length of the game matches the story well and it never feels as if the pacing is too slow or too fast. The price is however a bit too much for the length of the game.
The story is generally well written, even if short. However, the integration with the gameplay falters at times. The good ending is a bit of a meh deal, especially with the rather lacking investigation and trivial trial. It is a bit of a let down compared to the rest of the game. But aside from the ending, it is quite interesting. There is a good underlying story going on beneath the cases you take on and it is just right in intensity, you know it's there, but it's not screaming at you.
The main problem with the gameplay is the ability to bumble the investigation, ruining your chances at the trial. This game makes it obvious why the Ace Attorney games don't let you do that. It's not just "oh dear, i am failing this trial", but you also risk missing major parts of the story simply by never getting that far in the investigations.
The game has had a rather rough release, with poor testing and an obvious Christmas rush. Time will save the game, even if the developer has repeatedly proven themself unable to obey their own deadlines.
Overall, do play this game. But you might want to wait for another sale and the game being finished.

is a 3rd person sci-fi action RPG. On a Mars that's been cut away from Earth for decades, Roy "Temperance" is an Aurora soldier stuck in Abundance P.O.W. Camp 19 that wishes to escape back to his home city of Shadowlair, just to find out the Technomancers have taken over the government.
Good base story that reflects a rich universe, much larger than the span of the game. While the graphics themselves are sub-par for 2013, the aesthetics are excellent, showing a dry planet built from scraps where people have obviously grown beyond their resources and no supplies are expected. Combat gameplay works well and prevents you from just going flailing about or shooting all in sight: you need to think and react properly to the different ranged or close-ranged attacks, blocking, leaping and hitting when the time is right, and the A.I. actually does a great job at becoming much more strategic and challenging at higher difficulty levels. Also, ranged weapons are under-powered, a good thing as it forces you to make use of the melee combat mechanics. There is an interesting, although limited, crafting system for upgradable items.
The voice acting and cut scenes are bad, and I mean it: out of sync voices, long awkward pauses between character reactions or interruptions, bad character animation, all so much more dated than the game itself is. The maps feel just as dated: floor surface is polygony, there is no climbing or jumping over 1 inch obstacles, invisible walls and "decorative" stairways or ledges your character should so obviously be able climb on, it reminds me of the one thing I hated in the map layout of
. The story is rushed, as so many concepts are introduced or teased at but get no development whatsoever. There is barely any equipment you can purchase (a few suits and a few sticks, some of which are not upgradable).
★★☆☆☆ - Forget it
I wish I could recommend this game, but in all honesty it's not that good. The writers obviously wanted to bite on much more than they could chew, as the game introduces concepts meant to rival the biggest modern RPGs or sci-fi stories out there: Mars being cut from Earth, futuristic guild wars, mysterious ruins from the first colonists, serum (body fluid) being used as currency, that and so much more gave the game a lot of potential, none of which is exploited in a significant way and all end up falling flat. Still, the setting's potential is enough to have me interested in its recent spin-off
, hoping it'll be any better.

3rd person, action, RPG with melee combat.
You play as a Technomancer, a gifted individuals who are forced to go through hard training to master their force talents. Story takes place on planet called Mars, in time of war and poverty that followed soon after the colonization. Story is about different groups of people fighting for control over the land and resources.
RPG element includes three character skill trees, perk system, weapon and armor modification and crafting of support, utility items (like medkits, explosives, etc.). You have a variety of abilities available, some allow you to enchant weapons, others protect you from damage like electric shield, some do damage or stun enemies like arc lightning shock, etc.
You mainly use melee weapons, like metal pipes modified with different attachments you make with metal scraps and hardware found throughout the game. Ranged combat is really limited to one shot nail guns, grenades or Technomancer electric abilities. You can craft and place traps, that are useful if you're surrounded by enemies.
There's decent amount of missions and side missions available, some have choice and effect element, so pick your answers wisely. Good amount of voiced dialogues. Reputation system in game was a bit weird, I didn't change from Neutral all game, though I didn't do anything bad, nor did I juice the downed enemies. Main currency in the game is pretty much human blood, as far as I understand, and was kind of weird.
You can have followers in game, five in total, two of those can be chosen by joining one or other group of people, one is partially available and two are available pretty much throughout the whole game. Two males and three females as far as I could tell. You can romance females, if someone wondering, though there's nothing special, just hugging and groping.
Visually game looks poorly, a lot of low resolution textures for 2013 game, model quality is bad, animations are poor, voice over quality is decent. Game has a lot of glitches, texture clipping, hovering objects, bad lighting and other sort of things that could be fixed in post-production.
Overall game was fun experience, but lacked serious polish. Some missions were hilarious, I also liked typos in text that made no sense, and weird naming for drugs and nurses advice for cutting someone's jewels off. Don't know if it was intended, but apparently you can bed both female followers and then chose which one you like more.

Furthermore, the developer does a good job of replying to Steam members with questions about the game, and he also releases a significant update at least once a month, as well as smaller, unannounced updates here and there. The low price tag of $7.99 is also more than enough reason  to give the game a try. With the relatively frequent updates, the game will likely only get better, so I would definitely recommend it to anyone who is a fan of survival/crafting games.

My experience with the Sudden Strike series is too minimal to have any kind of nostalgic attachment to it. At a glance SS4 seems to stay close to the previous titles, perhaps slightly streamlined but not to its detriment. It scratches the same itch I've been treating with the Men of War series. SS4 trims down some of the complexity of MoW in favour of a more focused and polished experience. There is no base building or unit production, you work with what you're given.
What I love about these games is the strategic creep across a map, slowly pushing a frontline trying to minimise losses, capturing enemy materiel and balancing ammunition supply. Sudden Strike 4 caters to this well and can keep you engaged in a single mission for hours. Mission design has enough variation to keep things interesting but the maps are really well designed, beautiful and rich in detail. Normal mission difficulty seems to be fairly well balanced, it rewards cautious advancement and makes you think twice about your next move, while careless play will be punished.
I would've liked to see some further effort put towards sound design, it's not bad but it lacks a little something, some ambiance and roughness... the battles sound too "clean", if that makes sense. Voice work is also something that needed more work but there's only so much you can do given a limited budget.
I've only tried the multiplayer briefly but enough to gather it's not to my liking. Considering the solid gameplay I think there is much potential for a multiplayer mode but not in its current form. It should be scaled down a notch and rework the reinforcement mechanic alas, I understand why it would be bad business to put great effort into it.
All things considered I reckon 40€$ would've been a better value proposition for this game at launch, if you're on the fence about this one, buy it once it's on sale for that or less.

Honestly this reminds me of the old Codname Panzers games, but with an extra couple layers of complexity and realism to keep it fresh. I'm all but certain that the rifle model for the soldiers is actually the exact same one from almost 10 years ago...
Anyways, 9/10. Would recommend.
