This game feels like it tries to be The Witcher 2 in space. It has very similar mechiancs, and a very similar combat system. While I can't say it succeeds, it's definitely very enjoyable.
The graphics aren't very impressive, and Mars is very monotonous and boring to look at.
The combat is fun and sometimes challenging, though since there are only a few different enemy types it gets repetitive fast.
The voice acting on most characters is pretty bad, and the dialogues aren't very well written for the most part, but they do the job in telling the story. There is a companion romance option, but it's so badly written it feels like they put it in last minute just to make sure the game has a sex scene. "Hey I like you" - "Oh I like you too, and now that we're finally alone with the entire crew watching, wanna f**k?" TRUE LOVE.
That being said, the story and the world are interesting and well crafted. A lot of thought was clearly put into the backstory, and I did feel intrigued to know what happens next at every point in the game.
The RPG elements are all there, some better than others. There's also a morality system but its effect on the game is so tiny that it really doesn't matter if you're "good" or "bad" (i.e. if you're bad you get more money, but if you're good shops sell to you for less. Ends up exactly the same... and doesn't matter either way since there is no reason to buy anything in the shops anyway). There is a significant choice to make at the end of the 2nd act which does alter the story, and isn't as obvious as good/bad, so I did enjoy that one.
I really like the weapon customising system. It was new and innovative - You start with a pipe or iron bar or something like that, and you craft it according to your will. Add a sharp piece at the top and you have an axe, put a brick there and it's a club. Put iron on the bottom if you want a hilt, or leather if you want a better grip.
Overall this game reaches far and doesn't quite get there, but it's definitely worth the ride. Hell, if they ever make Mars: War Logs 2, I'll probably buy it as well.

You're a timberman, and your goal is to chop down a tree while avoiding branches. Seems kinda boring, but trust me it's really fun.  So you have to chop as many logs from the tree as possible before either the branches on the tree or the timer kills you. It's not an easy game and takes some time to master. You get better, makes more progress and unlock more stuff. It's very rewarding for all your hard work.
The game has a singleplayer and a multiplayer. The singleplayer is you alone chopping down the tree, trying to get the best score possible. Because you can unlock a lot of new "timbermen" to play as and unlock achievments based on how many logs you get. It gives the game replayability where you every time get a new goal to reach. The multiplayer is eiterh dual or 4-player where you fight against other players being the fastest timberman. You can defeat the other players by chopping much faster than them to get their time-bar decreased  while dodging branches, or you can hope they hit a branch themself. It has a ranking system based on skill and rank, where skill counts on how good you are on singleplayer and rank counts on how many people you can defeat on multiplayer while climbing the leaderboard.
At times the multiplayer can get really competitive and exciting. The MM system is a bit unstable and you can lose connection sometimes. Sometimes you match with ppl at rank 20.000 while you are 1.000 which makes it a bit unfair for the low rank player. Also it takes a bit of time before everyone accepts games (drops out etc.) and it can be frustrating. But the devs are good with content updates and bugfixes where they keep on pumping out more content for the player base. A big thumbs up for the good work the devs do.
It's a cheap game (7kr), and works great as a time consumer. Really good pixel graphics, addicting sound/music, good fps and fun/simple gameplay. Give it a try!

Blast to the past!
This game is sheer awesomeness with the total reminder that C&C is still alive today! My Only problem with the game was the AI constantly rushing which the devs fixed this recent patch by giving the AI some personalities! Which was kind of awesome!
Some Ideas:
- New Units; Maybe Special units for 'Factions' ? Rocket Heli's Tanks and Armored Cars are the norm to rush. Creating a Front line then back line. Granted Arty can just decimate the grouped units but I think there should be some hard counter unit to the spam.
- Resources. Once you run out.... that's it, you kind of have an awkward stalemate. Or you make the guy waste his army on you then counter attack to win (it's how I've won recent games) C & C Generals had Oil Derricks: Which always generated $200 no matter what. Even if your supply ran out. You of course had your drop zones, hackers, black markets of the respected factions getting income.
Since the Money Cap is much lower, you can spam freely. If it was raised, like the Nuke being 5k as other games, and give some buildings that can generate some funds periodically it can be an even better game!
It can even be as simple as a fix as just giving the current oil supply a larger supply or longer for it to run out. I understand the game wants to rush action, but sometimes the game can go back and forth creating a longer game to which the game must provide the players with resources to keep it going!
Maybe go back to the supply crates and use oil derricks as the steady income (such as the old Generals and Red Alert days)
- Nukes: As stated above 5K seems like a good cap for the super weapon. GRANTED I love how it's set up now to only be used as a harrassing tool or Unit Clearer. It doesn't do insane dmg to buildings (4 needed to destroy HQ) but it decimates units. Since you can build multiple speeding up the time, at 4 you have about a 1 minute cool down. I think the starting timer should be 6 mins. or 5 mins, just to keep it from being too spammy.
- Spam. As mentioned alot this game requires you to SPAM! My original play style was sit back, and turtle. In this game doing that may cause your death. You must be prepared to RUSH, and SPAM! With that said, it's an interesting thing to see a game WANT to make you spam units. It's by now means over powered because a well placed Nuke destroys the spam. But there should be tweaks to it.
- Walls. Westwood..... come on man you know it's true.
- Some form of Formation, as when units clump together since the nature of the game is SPAM, it messes up when you attack. I guess this can also be counted as a counter.
- MAPS! MORE MAPS! The current maps are made excellently with a good sense of strategy needed for each map. I think once the dev's add a bunch more maps, it'll create even more re-play ability.
With that said... it's an awesome game and it's only getting better. The points i've listed above are really the only main things I have with this game. I think if the dev's can incorporate at least a LITTLE of what i've mentioned this game can TRULY excel even further than it already has.

Initial Release Review:
Think of this game as an arcade version of Command & Conquer.  This game is fun.  I loved old school Command & Conquer, and 8-bit delivers.  The graphics are blocky, and the sounds and action is a bit gamey, but the simplistic strategy that was C&C is there.  The former Westwood staff did a good job on an initial core game.
I am no longer recommending this game, however.  I had hoped that it would be popular enough to bring in sales to continue development, but the staff is already resorting to releasing paid DLC just a month after initial release.  Should people continue to fund the game or buy the DLC, perhaps the game will pan out into something great, or perhaps it will become abandoned, which is a more likely scenario.  Should you find this game years down the road and everything is on a bargain clearance, it is worth the purchase.  However, I cannot, on good faith, fund further development of this game.  I am a consumer and not an investor, it is not my job to fund development.
Cons: Units drive through buildings and there aren't a lot of units.  The factions aren't that well balanced as of June 2016.  There are two factions at the time of this review, but you have to buy the second single player campaign, bummer.  The Devs state they want to add more factions, like a version of NOD or perhaps USSR or Allies (speculation).  If the game doesn't sell, this may be a quick run on the bank resulting in abandonware.
Summary: If you are a true RTS and even C&C fan, do yourself a favor and pick this up on sale.  If you want to fund development of this kind of project, then do your homework and buy in.  The more folks that buy it will add funds to the dev's coffers and they will be able to add cooler features like Warcraft, Red Alert, etc.  However, you will probably have to pay for all of those addons on top of what you already spent.

Gameplay: Here's my biggest issue with the game. While you can change between two Gianas, it gets gradually harder to do, especially around stages 3-1 and beyond. Bosses have memorable patterns, but they aren't easy despite their 3 hit life bar. I also want to mention that Purple Giana's ability isn't always spot on for me. It could be my controller ( lol Gamestop Controller ) but sometimes pressing Up+B would make me go diagonially forward and would lead me to a death because of it. Difficulty is old school, it demands your patience and if you're not willing to try again, then this game isn't worth it.
Final thoughts: Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams was never a bad game from the start. But I wouldn't pay full price for it either.

Wow.  I have done programming work as part of my profession, I have a bachelor's in CS, I've been programming for over 20 years, and this game is amazing.
Firstly:  If you are new to programming or not even new yet, great!  This game is a great introduction.  Just IGNORE THE OPTIMIZATION MILESTONES.  Focus on finishing all the levels, then you can worry about that.
If, however, you are like me a professional programmer at times, this game's optimization challenges can still provide a great challenge.  I just spent what felt like 2 hours (probably more like 1 to 1-and-a-half) trying to optimize the runtime of Level 20 (multiplication) and half the time my program didn't even work correctly, let alone optimally.
Protip: The program doesn't end until you go to the Inbox while it's empty.  Doing so before a jump, rather than after, can make the difference in optimizing number of steps taken.  Also, it's not literal steps -- it's number of instructions followed, so which floor mat locations you use doesn't matter.  Jumps count as a step but jump targets do not.

As for the story, the characters are fun and memorable, and well deliver plenty of chuckles (albeit likely no full belly-laughs).
The big problem dosen't rear it's ugly head untill late in the game, in my first playthrough I reached a branch in the story where I had not gathered the correct evidence for an impromptu trail, resulting in a text screen that read something along the lines of "Sorry, this ending is unfinished! Check back in two days!" And the game crashed.
Not that it's super relevant, but it's but more than two days, almost a week.
Nowhere on the store page does it advertise this being an uncomplete game, nor does it label it with a "Steam Greenlight" or "Beta" nomiker. This game had a kickstarter, and was delayed at least once, so why not wait the extra time and release the full game? I cannot reccomend purchasing this in the current condition (12/30/15), and possibly cannot reccomend a purchase even if this unfinished ending is patched in. This is lying to the customer, you NEED to advertise that your game is NOT finished, an improumptu text screen is simply NOT enough. Since this part of the game was almost 4 hours in, a refund was not possible, but if it had been I would have gotten one. Skethy Logic games needs to properly address this situation, as it is a dangerous practice in video gaming, and plagued what was otherwise an extremely pleasent experiance.

Note: This review was orginally negative before being changed to positive as a result of the 1.02 patch. I have saved the original review down below for future reference.
----------------------------------------------------------------
Let's get the obvious out of the way: Aviary Attorney is clearly inspired by Ace Attorney. Everything from the gameplay, the type of humor, the dialogue and courtroom sessions are incredibly similar to the Capcom classic. Hell, the initials of the two series are the same and I doubt that due to coincidence.
If you like Ace Attorney, I'll cut straight to the chase and say it: You'll probably like Aviary Attorney as well and it’s worth your money.
To go into detail, the game functions very similarly to Ace Attorney. You get a client coming in to defend them from a crime, usually murder. Then you have several days to wander to different areas of Paris, interview witnesses, gather clues and generally stick your beak where it don't belong. At the end of that period, you have a trial where you cross examine witnesses, present evidence and find contradictions.
So far, so Ace Attorney, right? The similarities go deeper: The main character is a bumbling and struggling defense attorney with a puntastic assistant. The prosecutor for the first case is inept before being replaced by your hoity toity high class rival who delights in insulting your skill. Many characters debate the true meaning of "Justice"...etc. etc.
So what sets it apart? Why buy it when Ace Attorney 6 is announced.
Well for one, there's no guarantee that Ace Attorney 6 will ever make it out west with the latest title in the series, The Great Ace Attorney, unlikely to ever release here so.....you don't have much of a choice.
But yes, there are some changes from the Capcom series that sets this title apart.
The most obvious is the art style. Aviary Attorney's most well known feature is that all the characters are anthropomorphic animals taken directly from the works of the 19th century French Caricaturist J.J Grandville. The art has been touched up in places, mostly to add animations such as blinking eyes and beaks/snouts/muzzles moving. They're not extensive by any means but are done quite seamlessly with a minimum amount of "original" artwork to fill in the blanks. (For example, one character pulls out a gun and a sharp eye can see that the outstretched arm's cross hatching isn't quite as detailed as the original art, indicating it’s a new change for the sake of the animation).
Some people might be turned off by the black and white visuals but I greatly enjoyed them as they gave a real picture book feel to the game and it’s always nice to see a game that increases the appreciation for classic art.
This extends to the music in the game which is also lifted mostly from 19th Century French composers of the Romantic era such as Hector Berlioz and Camille Saint-Saëns (as well as some original tracks made by the game's composer) which sounds absolutely beautiful.
When compared to Ace Attorney, the graphics in Capcom's offering are definitely better (though I like the style of Aviary's more) but the musical tracks are a no contest to Aviary Attorney, as much as I like the music in Ace.
This all fits in perfectly with the time setting of the game: 1848 Paris. If you know your history, you'll know that 1848 is a pivotal year for France and you will get embroiled in France's real life history one way or the other. (Err....but with some liberties taken of course. It's a game about anthropomorphic animals after all).
But how is the gameplay? I won't lie; the investigating and interviewing processes in Aviary Attorney are pretty simple. Especially when compared to the multiple games in which Ace Attorney has had to grow out its staple of gameplay mechanics (i.e., adding in forensics, multiple angles to a crime scene.....etc.). Due to being limited by using J.J Grandville's art, the creators couldn't create incredibly complex locations for the game's crimes and therefore, all the cases seem rather simple when compared to the genius of Shu Takumi's crime drama writing. Aviary Attorney has the very simple mechanic of simply talking to witnesses and clicking on various objects in the background to reveal items and even the latter is only in special locations designated for investigating.
Overall, the game's cases are simpler and shorter than that of Ace Attorney. Still intriguing and interesting but not as good.
But Aviary Attorney has an ace up its sleeve, time and branching pathways. In Ace Attorney, it’s not possible to advance unless you have all the evidence you need to win the upcoming trial. You can keep switching around the various locations available to you till you find that one person or one event that will propel the story forward.
In Aviary Attorney, when the game tells you "The trial will commence in three days" You're on the ♥♥♥♥ing clock. Visiting most locations will consume an entire day and if you overlook a piece of evidence or go to the wrong locations, you can very well end up in court short of the evidence you need to clear your client. This is most evident in Case #3 which can end up in three different case #4s depending on how well you utilized your time and dug for evidence. It is entirely possible to go to the wrong locations and ♥♥♥♥ up the trial. Another possibility is you get a partial success. In case #2, you can clear your client but still not expose the real criminal, giving you partial success and access to case #3 regardless.
On top of all this, you have a money system in the game. The main character (J.J Falcon) has a wallet to carry his francs in which he can spend on various items in the game. You can usually get around paying by bringing another item or by clever dialogue choices but the currency mechanic means you can just skip some of the tasks in the game if you wish (As J.J Falcon says when asked for money or food in exchange for an item "I'm done with this fetch quest nonsense, just take the damn money").
Overall, Aviary Attorney isn't as good as Ace Attorney but does a lot of stuff that Capcom should really look at and implement into their series to break it from its linear structure. The writing Besides, Aviary Attorney is 15$ while Ace Attorney games are over double that so the shorter game time is justified by the discounted price.
As of the time of writing though, some bugs in the game remain. The steam overlay still does not work (A "bug" EA and Ubisoft will no doubt love to have), Saving is still not working (Saving and quitting sends you back to the last checkpoint, the beginning of the day) and achievements are still not implemented.
The devs have promised to fix these in addition to announcing a bonus chapter and a Linux version. So you might want to hold onto your francs if you these things bother you.
See you in court, monsieurs!

I want to start by saying that I love the visual style of this game, and it got me into playing an attorney game even though I'd never played one before. The writing is cute and engaging, and the characters can be a lot of fun.
But on the whole, I've found the game disappointingly buggy. Sometimes it's just that the dialogue options haven't been thought through properly (for instance, if you need to choose a character from the list of characters you know to accuse of something or to ask about, and you choose the wrong person for the storyline, the characters will say something like 'Who is that person?' even if it was a friend of theirs, which makes things very confusing for the player, since you start worrying you pressed the wrong button or something). Once, in Act 3, I asked about an unimportant piece of data and midway through discussing it the dialogue skipped back to a previous conversation on a different subject.
Sometimes the bugs are bigger. It's already been noted that depending on how you play through, Act 4 may not be accessible to you at all. I made a mistake in Act 3 and Act 4 isn't accessible to me, so I went back to play from Act 2, but when I try to load Day 1 of Act 2, it bugs out and gives me an illustration, but no characters or dialogue and I can't move forward. I feel that this game has a pretty hefty price for mostly text-based gameplay if it's going to have this many game-halting problems with it. It's not just the unfinished Act 4, there are a number of serious and confusing problems that really affect the experience or sometimes terminate it altogether. Especially if the game is going to be so unforgiving (going to a location that I had a lead for a day earlier than I was apparently supposed to caused me to fail my goal in Act 2), and going to halt your progress if you make certain decisions, then it really needs to be able to reload properly from previous days.
I think this game could be really great, but it's lacking polish and completion in several serious areas, so at the moment I don't think it can be said to be worth $15 or even $13.

Ok, so I just ended up rewriting this whole thing to be more clear and not so rambling. As a disclosure, I got this game in a Humble Bundle awhile back and just recently I thought I would try it out after seeing a video of Scott Manley attempting to play it.
I really want to like Tharsis. The idea of a space survival game loosely along the lines of Apollo 13 and Alive sounds like it could be very interesting. The ship design also looks like something I need to build in Kerbal Space Program for an interplanetary mission.
Unfortunately, I found this game to be more frustrating than fun.
The tutorial is extremely basic and doesn't really explain much of anything other than how to do the most basic actions. It doesn't provide any advice or guidance on how to actually play the game or what things are important.
There are some missions on the main menu that act kind of like an extended tutorial, but this were apparently added in a more recent patch and the existing tutorial doesn't even acknowledge their existence. It just throws you into a frustrating game where you are almost guaranteed to lose because you don't really know what you're doing.
This leads to the first major problem with this game: the learning curve. It's extremely steep and unforgiving, even on easy. Unless you're a fan of this type of game, you'll probably be turned off on this game in the first hour like I was. At least that's soon enough for a refund. After reading some forum posts and a few guides, I've tried to perservere a little longer and made it a little farther (last turn on easy), but I'm still finding myself more frustrated than entertained.
Much of the game feels like it's luck based on the RNG and that the game is out to get the player. There is a strategy game under there (and after reading some guides I can almost beat the game on easy), but again, if you're not familiar with the genre, this is not at all obvious to the player. Even with good strategy and planning, a few bad RNG results can quickly ruin an otherwise good playthrough.
The last major problem I see fundamentally has to do with the setting of the game. Nearly all other rogue-like and rogue-lite games put you as a hero facing impossible odds where the expected outcome is death, and it's a miracle that you'll succeed. In other words, they set the player's expectations appropriately.
Tharsis does a very poor job of this. The intro video has a line talking about how the mission had prepared for any type of emergency. Once you get into the game though, it doesn't feel like this at all. The entire game feels like a comedy of errors that would be appropriate in Kerbal Space Program, but not at all what a real space mission would be like.
Every turn (one week) two or three major systems fail and you have to scramble to repair the ship or everyone dies. Because of the dice rolls, the crew frequently feels utterly incompetent and unable to do their job, and the ship feels like it was designed and built to the worst possible standards. Each week, each crew member can only do actions in one module.
The end result of this is that the game just ends up being frustrating. Which is a real shame, since I can see the bones of a great board game under the surface. With some tweaks to the setting and mechanics, I can see these rules being repurposed into a much more enjoyable game. Unfortunately, the game as it is now is not something I would recommend to anyone but a die-hard fan of the genre.

Despite many negative reviews from critics, and despite some flaws, for the most part I enjoyed this game and thought it was solid. The story takes place in a gritty, dystopian, almost post-apoc setting and spans 3 chapters. There are a lot of sidequests and character interactions, and the game tends to alternate between big open areas and linear levels, which in my opinion provided a nice change pace.
Perhaps what I liked the most was the levelling and the combat. The fighting was incredibly fun, a little awkward at first, but easy to get used to. And the customization of your weapon and armour is great. You get to find various tools and crafting parts that you can use on your gear to give it additional bonuses of your choice. The levelling had 3 different mastery trees - combat, renegade (support abilities like healing and stealth), and technomancy (electrical powers). The levelling happened very frequently, which was great too, since you didn't have to wait for ages to get to the skills you've had your eyes on.
The story and setting are pretty interesting. I personally found chapters 1 and 2 to be brilliant, but chapter 3 fell flat on its face. It almost felt as though the game was rushed at the end. What was most interesting perhaps is how at the end of chapter 2 you get a choice of split paths to join one of the 2 factions, which changes some things in chapter 3, but ultimately you end up visiting the exact same locations regardless of which faction you go with. The premise of split paths for the final chapter is fantastic, but the execution resulted in a diluted experience. Going with the Resistance at least was a half-decent attempt at a conclusion that presented some more moral choices down the line. But going with the general felt like it was added into the game at the very last minute just for the sake of having this split path feature.
The game also had 3 romance options in it, but this too felt rather lacking and devoid of much dialogue. A few other NPCs felt like they should've gotten more screen time than they actually did, like the bounty hunter friend of the main character. But apart from that, most characters were rather interesting.
Overall I'd recommend this game. It's a decent sci-fi cyberpunk RPG and I was immersed for the duration of playing it, even going as far as trying out both story paths for its somewhat disappointing conclusion.

There is so much to like about 8-bit armies, it's clearly a love letter to the days of Command and Conquer and in the vein of games people have been pleading to EA to make for the last decade. I'm one of those people, in fact just recently I did a play though of Yuri's revenge and was pleasantly surprised to still find the game fun to play and engaging.
However my experience with 8-bit armies was not as great.
I picked it up for the co-op campaign and what I found was that the AI was uh..."challenging." So challenging in fact that they were given many advantages over the players. Access to more units, more money, faster building speed and worst of all, the ability to micromanage perfectly. Units designed to counteract other units have the ability to zero in on the unit they work best against even when there are dozens of units on the screen and mow down troops in a matter of seconds. This made bonus objectives like "don't use rocket troops" or "build no turrets" feel insurmountable. It maybe my imagination but it felt like my units lacked any sort of direction at all on top of all that.
Worst of all was on many occasions, the AI was allowed to make several artillery units, place them just inside the fog of war and bombard your base repeatedly. Sending out troops to deal with this was futile as they were easily and quickly overwhelmed. Perhaps the most annoying part of this was that once the AI had destroyed a random number of your buildings they would leave, give you enough time to rebuild, then return and repeat the process. AI could only seem to be overcome by building turrets down every street and once the missions  allowed the AI to build air units along with artillery, this strategy no longer worked.
I would be willing to let them work on it and wait, but the game is not in early access and so I have requested a refund. I hope they will continue to work on it as there is a lot of potential but I cannot recommend it at this time in it's current state.

This is a hard game to rate as it has a good amount of issues to deal with, but also a quite interesting idea. In the end it boils down to the question if it is worth your time and money.
The presentation in both the graphical style and the choice of music is very good. You get a good amount of film noir kind of detective tracks and also a good selection of melacholic tracks which both fit the the setting well. The cell shading look of the game also works really well.
The story is well presented and while (most of) the characters are over the top, as a whole it makes the game what it is. The only two locations (okay, let's say two and a half) are also well designed and allow for a surprisingly interesting exploration. Along with this goes the amount of collectibles that you can find throughout the game and that give the game a good amount of depth.
Why didn't I rate the game as recommended then? First and foremost it's the length of the game. The 'season' consists of two episodes and a prologue and they take you between four and six hours to complete. The game ends on a horrible cliffhanger and most likely there will be no season two (for understandable reasons, but it still leaves the game feel very incomplete).
The other reason (and a much more subjective one) is the use of QTE throughout the game. Even in cutscenes you are supposed to look for small button prompts that give you attentional info and credits. The real problem for me were the longer QTE fights in the game though. There is no setting for them and I'm pretty sure that the game punishes you for failing them. I barely managed to get through all of them without retrying, but it was far from a pleasant experience. The other problem with the gameplay is the use of credits to buy food to perform actions to get credits. It just doesn't feel like it's needed to add this mechanism, even if it sometimes creates the need to plan your course of action a bit ahead.
Overall it's surely an interesting game and if you don't mind QTE and can get it on sale, please have a look. For 15$ I found the game to be lacking in content and the amount of cosmetic DLC seems questionable to say the least.

The Gianna Sisters series has a long history of being compared to Super Mario Bros.  You have a couple of sisters (not brothers) jumping around collecting jewels (not coins), defeating enemies by hopping on them.  But the similarities don't go much further than that, and this entry into the series has so many unique features that you'll forget the plumbers even exist.  Right off the bat, the game is much prettier than anything you've ever seen in the Mario series.  Switching back and forth between the sisters causes the entire world to transform, allowing you to solve puzzles.  For example, some doors and bridges exist in one version of the world but not the other, so you'll have to switch back and forth frequently to progress.  The world's transformation sequence is very quick but eerily beautiful.

There's also certain gems that only a specific sister can collect.  The sisters have very different special moves, each befitting the character's personality.  So even though you'll probably have a favorite sister early on (I'm betting the redhead), you'll end up using both characters equally. This is a probably well-meaning game that fails to deliver to the audience most interested: the newbie programmer. The game has a charming premise, which is underdeveloped. Although your character is moving upward through a dystopian corporation, this is less fleshed-out than the world map in early Mario games. The sound design is suitable and unintrusive, but nothing to write home about. More importantly, the game design suffers from expert myopia. It's essentially a teaching game (or to use the 90s buzzword, an edutainment game). While it could be a fun way to learn visual programing, in reality the teaching game genre is merely used as a framework, and is entirely neglected. There are no actual hints for a stumped player. The coding language the player uses is artifically hobbled by a lack of the most basic functions fundamental to languages handling maths. The player must execute relatively simple programming tasks with elaborate contortions of unsuitable functions, like determining if numbers are equal without an actual comparison function of any sort. The newbie codemonkey will feel it is cheating to look up answers or even hints, likely unaware that porgrammers pull code from documentation and github all the time.
For experienced coders, this will be a fun puzzling romp with a robot apocalypse skin. For aspiring programmers and those with less than perfect math scores, it will quickly devolve into an exercise in frustration.
*I have not reviewed it for accessibility. This is a single-mouse-click based game. Keyboard controls are not available. Audio is not required to play. Color is not required for understanding and playing - it is mostly sepia with some arbitrarily red or green items.

Human Resource Machine is a puzzle/programming game by the devs behind World of Goo and Little Inferno.
It makes you code not with the fancy sophisticated constructs of programming languages, but with a very limited set of instructions the likes of which your processor really understands. It is basically a very cute, very graphical introduction to assembler languages and to programming in general.
The game starts with simplistic problems and an extremely limited set of instructions, but the difficulty ramps up quite a bit until you finally tackle typical programming problems like Fibonnacci and prime numbers, sorting and so on.
Besides all the programming puzzles, the game also tells you a story that I will not dare spoil here, even though it is not, by any means, a story-driven game.
If ever a programming game could be accessible to non-coders, this would be it. At the same time, behind its cute graphics and visual gimmicks, it really is a programming game.
If you're a coder, you should give this one a try, if only to afterwards go back to your favorite language and sigh in contentment for all the syntactic sugar making your coding experience so much more comfortable.
If you've ever wondered how computer actually compute data, this is the game for you.
If you're a big fan of puzzles and brain teasers, this will probably give you a headache in a good way.
If you fit in none of those categories, I would only advise getting this game on sale, as you might go into anaphylactic shock ;)

I am writing this review immediately following "100%"ing the game. I found this game on kickstarter when it was just about to be funded. I have been a fan of Phoenix Wright ever since it first came out for the Nintendo DS, and have played every title up to now multiple times. So when I saw this game I thought that having a new set of characters in a new universe with the same game formula, that it could definitely be something special. First off, the art and the music of the game are absolutely fantastic. The art and the music are definitely some of what my favorite parts of the game is. Going into the game, my thoughts were as follows: Space? Yeah! Cannibalism? Hell yeah! But in reality, not so much. I thought that being a survival-based game with random events confronting your crew on its way to Mars, that the concept was somewhat similar to Sunless Sea, a fantastic rogue-like which has you captain a ship in similar circumstances (though on water). Tharsis, unfortuantley, was much different, and this was due to the mechanic of dice. See, when confronted with a broken engine, or a food shortage, your crew gets to roll dice, and the higher the number, the more likely you can deal with the event successfully. And that is where this game falls short of Sunless Sea, in that, while there's always an element of randomness, events are not entirely beyond your control or your decisions. In Tharsis, the roll of a dice can mean the difference between fixing the command module or having your ship disintegrate in space. While I like the look of the mystery meat served in Tharsis (looks like steak), the sheer lack of control over events makes it a hard game to succeed at. Overall Score: 7.6/10

Sometimes, often, trying to fight all the fires is a bad plan I had an event turn up around turn 3, -2 hull a turn but 3 injury results and about 22 ish to fix...I could have assisted up, got the research running and get a good fix reserch fished out...all resource intensive, but it IS a 2 hull a turn tax, so I was looking for ways

People get caught up in the must fix everything mind set, when really, food, dice, health and hull are all resources and all need consideration. Took me a few goes some 'unfair' losses that in retrospect maybe my fault to get a grip on the game

If you can't handle a game sometimes going south when you've done nothing really wrong, again not the game for you. What a comeback for this franchise. I've been playing the AC games off and on for years beginning with AC 1, 2, Brotherhood, Revelations, 3, 4, Unity and Syndicate. The series has seen many highs and lows, but without a doubt, this is the best the series has been in years.
Plot // A generally satisfying plot overall. While the main plot isn't the best the series has had to offer, it's still good and offers some very interesting perspectives about the overarching plot of Assassins v. Templars as a whole. On the other hand, the side quest stories are very interesting and refreshing and really provide many interesting mini-stories. Some are bland, "please rescue (insert name here) Medjay" quests but many have interesting little twists within them. Some side quests even provide bits of lore and help to deepen the main plot.
TL;DR - Good main storyline, fun side quests with interesting stories within themselves
Gameplay // By far the biggest changes to the series in this game is in the gameplay. In this iteration of Assassin's Creed, prepare to collect loot, level up and fight some tough bosses as this game is as action-rpg as you can get. The combat system has been revamped in favor of a more technical and methodical system. Instead of readying your finger to counter and one shot enemies, you now have to watch their movements and time your attacks accordingly. I was playing on hard and a miss-step or two could get you killed pretty easily so you do have to be much more careful this time around. The skills you can acquire are pretty useful and there are alot of them. The weapons types are pretty varied and all feel unique, especially the legendary weapons. There really isn't any "uber god-mode" weapon that breaks the game so mix and match as you please. Overall there's a ton of content to be had here from beginning to end. I really hope that the developers continue to make Assassin's Creed games in this style as I feel it is really fun and refreshing.
TL;DR - Fun and new combat system with a focus on patience and timing. Lots of skills. A bunch of content. Cool tombs and you can fight big♥♥♥♥♥elephants.
Technical // The game looks stunning and ran fairly well in my experience, my FPS would dip a bit in large cities but I was never too bothered by it. I noticed that many Ubisoft games have been including pictures next to settings options so you can get an idea of how different everything will look when you change that setting which is very nice. I experienced no crashes and minimal bugs, nothing game-breaking. Mostly clipping which I've kinda come to expect in these games at this point.
TL;DR - Looks beautiful, runs good, no real game-breaking bugs, some clipping.
Music & Voice // Music was alright, nothing I would really listen to outside of the game. Unlike the AC2 soundtrack. The in-game musicians in some cities did play some really nice music that would help build the atmosphere really well. I'm also very pleased with the voice acting in this game, it all sounds believable and fitting to character. Abubakar Salim did particularly well with Bayeks voice, I hope to see more of him in the industry.
TL;DR - Alright music nothing really stands out compared to the soundtracks of earlier entries in the series. Pretty good voice acting.
Conclusion // A really great experience overall and I believe this game to be the best Assassin's Creed to date. If you're returning to the series this is really different from the previous games, but better for its differences. If you're new to the series this is probably the best the franchise has to offer so far, however, I would recommend also trying AC2 and AC4 as those two are amazing in their own right.

Graphically this is a very impressive game, but I found the plot disappointing, especially the later parts which seem strangely rushed. For a game supposed to describe the origin of the assassins, the story is really just a basic revenge plot with uninteresting antagonists who seem to have no deeper motivation than being parodically evil. The main character is well acted and the trauma he suffers at the beginning of the game is handled well, but the engaging parts of the narrative are spread far too thin, and padded with so much grinding that the game more often than not feels like an MMO. The assassin order is thrown in almost like an afterthought, and when it comes to the overall sci-fi metaplot of the Assassin's Creed universe, Origins adds next to nothing.
Still, it is an amazingly beautiful game, and it might be worth playing just for the spectacle. I don't regret buying it, but in retrospect I wish I hadn't preordered the game (especially not the deluxe edition). Also, I'm sorry to say that this will probably be the last Assassin's Creed game I buy. I liked Origins far better than Syndicate, but the series as a whole is just not good enough to keep me interested anymore, especially the modern day plot which has been standing still for four games now.
So buy this game on sale, as long as you don't expect too much in terms of story, but skip the season pass and everything to do with microtransactions.

The problem is that the target audience of this game, the people who can synergize with it, is very narrow. The only people who will really catch the message are those fans of the visual novels, anime and manga that take their hobby a step further in a bad way.
And yes, we could talk about that all this could have been executed in a better way; in the end what we've been reviewing until now its the idea per se, not the product offered here. The point is that it could seem that a better execution could have permitted that this game, this message, arrived to a wider audience, but I don't think so. The message this game wants to send us is very simple. You don't have to adorn it more because the public it aims for is rarely talked about this theme. A one on one conversation about this conflictive topic, from a position that usually inspires safety and comfort: it's the only thing you need to get this message through.
In conclusion, this is a niche piece, executed in a simplistic way (but let's no forget that this is the author's first work, Eyzi, who happens to be an indie developer that works by him/herself), but very interesting and that will surely work with a lot of people. Deffinetively very worth of checking out.

Message Quest ends very quickly but has enough going for it to provide a decent gaming experience: while the puzzles and fights are easy (just manipulate objects to find an items, solve jigsaws etc..)  they at least make sense in the context and are funny enough to not become downright boring. The story is pretty straightforward but Feste, with his chronic laziness, short temper and nervous breakdowns manages to elicit at least a few smiles and offers a good alternative to the usual brave or tragic characters populating the genre.
It's a game that'll surely sit well with younger audiences while mature gamers will have to come to terms with its simple nature and basic gameplay if they want to enjoy it properly: for less than 3$ it wasn't bad at all and the art style alone is worth praise.

《D4：Dark Dream Don't Die》，可以翻译成《D4：暗梦不灭》，但是游戏处处都体现不出来”梦”这一主题。虽然主角大胃羊可以通过一些证物回到过去，但是依然看不出“梦”在哪里，好在目前只是出了第一季，也许后面的故事会讲的更清楚些。好了，我们回归正题，其实在本人看来D4真的是一款很不错的文字冒险类游戏，这里我不得不提一款剧情神作——《致命预感》，之所以要提及，是因为《D4》是《致命预感》的精神续作，而且后者在本作中也有不少客串。有兴趣的可以去查一查这款游戏，另外，本人强烈建议大家去看优酷达人博伟制作的《致命预感》全程剧情解说，相信我，你一定会有所收获。
D4第一季的主角大卫·洋（大胃羊）曾经是一位警察，十分擅长曲棍球运动，有一天他的妻子佩琪在自家浴室里遭遇杀害，佩琪临死前向大为透露了一句“Look for D”。为了查出真凶，大卫走上了侦探的道路，并发誓不找到凶手誓不罢休。然而，就在佩琪死亡的那天，大卫获得了一神奇的能力。它可以通过一些关键证物回到过去，因此大卫打算利用这个能力去寻找线索并改变过去所发生的事。
先来说说优点吧。
1，本作的画面采用了半写实半漫画渲染的风格，之所以这样说，大家可以去参考下《波斯王子4》的画面表现，简约而不简陋。
2，游戏的对话很丰富，玩家可以操纵大卫和NPC就不同的问题聊很长时间，如果英文过关的话，你会发现这些对话的措辞大多都很有趣，要是英文不过关的，虽然不能说寸步难行，但肯定会从对话中失去一些乐趣。
3，本作的音乐绝对是一流的，气氛渲染几乎完美。（网易云音乐里能搜得到）
4，人物的塑造十分到位，以自己是波士顿人而自豪的美食专家泰迪，神秘兮兮却十分可爱的猫咪少女阿曼达，魅力十足并且隐藏了什么的的空姐奥维利亚，彬彬有礼但是精神又有些不太稳定的空乘服务员飞利浦等等，只要玩家能耐心与其对话，这些角色都能够给玩家留下很深的印象，这一点可以说从《致命预感》中完美的继承了下来。
5，游戏中的解密并不复杂，游戏中同一个角色会有好几个支线剧情，多与其对话就能解开了，从支线先当中玩家可以更清晰的了解NPC的故事，甚至可以预测出他们接下来的命运。
6，游戏的收集要素很丰富，像是衣服，食品，杂志，勋章什么的，数量非常多，在阿曼达那里购买到一定程度可以触发新的事件哦，喜欢收集的玩家一定不要错过。
再来说说一些不足。
1，首先就是优化，本作的优化确实不咋样，掉帧现象频繁出现。
2，保存机制存在严重问题，没错，是严重问题。本作虽然是自动保存，但是极度不可靠，到了检查点之后退出游戏，再选择继续游戏时，会从本章节开头重新玩，叫我非常恼火。
3，与NPC的对话虽然有趣，但是有些则过于冗长，能在精简些就更好了。
总体来说，作为一款文字冒险类游戏，我个人认为本作真的是一款不可多得的佳作，然而这款游戏的销量并不好，并不是说游戏的水平不行，而是它出现的时间并不恰当，毕竟这个时代的游戏市场都被那些主流大作占据了，玩家们的眼光也越来越挑剔了，或者说玩家们变得越来越浮躁了。我真的很希望大家能抽出一点点时间来关注这些小众游戏，不要老是沉浸在大作的海洋里，往往这些小众游戏的内在是十分巨大的，乐趣也是别样的。最后，希望有生之年能玩到第二季（认真脸）

I'm 5 missions in and I feel this game is a beautiful slog at best and a boring tedious shoot-the same-units-from-as-far-away-as-possible-for-a-few-minutes-to-a-half-hour-until-you-can-advance snoozefest.
I really enjoy the models, effects, and particles. Watch a round bounce off a slanted piece of armor, or explosions kick up debris and ragdoll bodies, that's great! I mean I LOVE the way grass is parted by infantry or tanks roll flat swathes through rows of corn..
..but the UI doesn't do a great job conveying information about unit functionality. The UI is simple and boxy and explains controls but does nothing to explain the strengths or weaknesses of a unit. Can you penetrate that front armor with this tank? Will a frontal angle deflect shots from that tank? Will this anti-tank 'rifleman' actually do anything? Why do units sometimes just 'surrender' and hold up weapons? Is there a morale stat hiding somewhere?
Every tank feels the same except when it's determined the front armor can't be penetrated and the sides take little damage and you're forced to try and hit the rear before his turret and main gun destroy all your units.. then you're fighting a losing battle and can do nothing before it's too late.. Not that you 'can' do much with sufficently strong tanks in your way.
Infantry are weak and practically useless.. Enemy riflemen will eat machine gun bursts like sponges (go take a MG42 and attack two or three riflemen and watch how they suck up those bursts like candy).. Meanwhile with your infantry, after carefully navigating a forest while prone and holding fire get chewed to pieces as soon as an enemy finds them.
Oh, and shooting a trench with direct hits 20 times with assault guns (spgs) and mortars before my infantry can advance isn't how I wanted to spend my time.
And how come when I double click to move a unit 'faster' sometimes vehicles remain stationary? Requiring me to re-submit a command? Or worse, spin in a circle exposing their♥♥♥♥♥to an enemy? ("Didn't I give you a directional move command? Oh now you're going to just kill yourself, great!")
And tank visibility range is a joke, even with the periscope upgrade and bino touting lemers popping out of the hatch, enemies always somehow engage and attack outside of visibility range.. You'll learn to basically 'prone sneak' with 'hold fire' on a single infantry unit to gain a small potentially temporary range advantage, before he's mowed down by the closest vehicle to be aggro'd and you're being hit from the fog of war again.
I don't know, maybe some patching can fix this, but something just doesn't 'feel' satisying about combat.. it feels boring and monotonous.. Sometimes things kill too easily other times you're watching mortar shells and grenades make direct hit with little effect. ("Two grenades of sharpnel stuck in the gut? No problem, I still have half my HP remaining!") Why have a sniper who has 10% extra range when a rifleman shoots him dead after advancing a few inches anyway? Or an MG which is less effective than a submachine-gun?
I dunno, maybe I'm missing something.

Good old Sudden Strike Returns
I've been playing Sudden Strike series since I was a kid and this game certainly brings back many of those good old experiences: capturing enemy vehicles, limited fuel and ammo, combined ground and air attack, etc. Although nothing astoundingly new is added compared to Sudden Strike 3 a decade ago but, hey, who cares, it's Sudden Strike anyway.
The overall gaming experience is good and to show it, I have to compare it to Blitzkrieg 3, another sequel of my childhood memory which I happened to have purchased. SS4 has good singleplayer Campaigns with interesting walkthrough and moderate difficulty while the Campaigns of B3 are dull and absurdingly hard (and you can't save the game back when I played it). The armor penetration mechanic works perfectly for SS4, a King tiger can eat shells for breakfast when angled properly, while in B3 I wonder whether it really exists, as the very same King tiger can be frontally damaged by Bazooka rounds and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to death by hand grenades! AIs in SS4 are also much more intelligent and well organized than those in B3, making the game nonlinear and changeful. Getting ambushed and counterattacked by AI is kind of fun experience.
That said, currently the game still needs some improvement for sure. There are bugs that will hamper the game experience. To mention a few, the vehicles will get stuck occasionally and keep turning in place, wasting a lot of fuel. When you dismantle crew from a supply truck during refueling, the soldier doing the refueling will stay outside as if the vehicle is still occupied. This will be a problem during retreat missions as they still counts as friendly and are unable to control. However, these bugs are not fundamental and I still enjoy the game as a return of the classic Sudden Strike series. Totally worth it.

As an indie game, I find the rating of Mars: War Logs unfair.
I admit I played the game just now, as of January 2015. I have no idea of how bugged it was - apparently it was, according to other reviewers - but in my hands ran just smoothly.
Based on such remarks, here are my opinions on the game:
The setting and the artwork are nice, with a flavour of steam-punk style. After all, Mars is the red planet.
Dungeons, caves, and maps in general are a bit repetitive.
Dialogues are just fine. Perhaps they lack a bit of depth, though they are just enjoyable as such. The story is nice and leaves plenty of room for other episodes.
Animations are well made. It is nice the way it slows time down when opening the wheel menu or while counter-attacking.
It is a pity that jumping is not available, although it would be useless considering the game mechanics.
RPG mechanics are OK; the characters evolves by spending points in the three branches or potentiating already unlocked skills.
Combat may be the weak element of the game. After getting acquainted with the commands and the combat mechanics, the most successful way is to evade all the time, hit'n'run. If AoE skills from the Technomancer's branch, that becomes even easier.
Equipment is also lacking depth. There is a lot of different weapon and armour upgrades, though it is rather difficult to find upgradable pieces during the game. The nice point here, is that you can adjust your gameplay by choosing the desired upgrades - which, by the way, also change parts of the look of the upgraded item according to their stats.
Crafting also appears to be incomplete and could be improved a lot.
Overall, I believe this is not a "< 60 game". As already state, based on the opening remarks, I would rate this as a 65, at least.

Sony Vegas 13 Platinum is a video and audio editing program. In this review will be some common questions you might have about this program and the given answers through experience.
- multiple text, video and audio editing tracks
- tons of effects and transitions to use and mess around with. Most effects have multiple sliders to very precisely adjust the shape and intensity of the effect at hand
- panning, cropping and animating of the effects and screen area
- extensive text and media generators
- clean interface with simple and advanced options/viewing mode
- the option to export video and audio separately and in various formats and quality settings (PC specs do not influence this negatively). This also means you can use Sony Vegas as an audio converter to create music playlists and gapless albums (export to .mp3, .FLAC, .ogg, etc.)
- the ability to zoom in on the timeline up to the point of editing individual frames which is perfect for seemless cuts and precise placement of media
- ... and many many more. I've been editing for over 70 hours now and I've barely scratched the surface, so to say.
This program is excellent for making gameplay and montage videos, as well as meme videos, music videos, YouTube Poops and anything that comes close to these. And of course anything more basic than this like slideshows and creating (gapless) music albums.
There are a lot of videos about Sony Vegas so any and all issues you have can be resolved quite easily. The only real nuisance is all the different versions of Sony Vegas so it's possible that a tutorial video does not match your exact version of Sony Vegas. Just a thing to be wary of.
Furthermore, most things can be learned within minutes and you'll be able to replicate them and practice with it easily. Sony Vegas has a built-in help tool that is able to help you at the start and for future reference.
There's one thing that instantly comes to mind: crashes. Sony Vegas is known for crashing occasionally but by taking a few precautions in mind this will only be a minor nuisance/occurence:
- save your project regularly, despite the autosave
- do not modify or delete footage or audio
(preview). This almost always results in a crash in my experience
- give the program time to load when applying effects or adding media
It's been crashing some times on my end but by taking the above in mind I was able to prevent it a lot and if the odds were against me, still reduce the downtime to a half a minute at best and no loss of material. It's just a thing to be mindful of.
However, people have said it crashes upon startup or rendering. So far that hasn't happened to me even once.
I usually don't make videos longer than ±8 minutes so I can't say much about it but people have reported issues with working on long videos (an hour and longer). It's probably safe to say to look at other video editing software, maybe even in the professional department, if you plan on working on something long/cinematic. Keep in mind that you also need to export it all which takes quite a while for greater lengths, especially in high quality.
The longer the video, the more the assets and the higher the quality, the larger the required disk space. I would recommend to make a folder dedicated to your projects and to store all of your media and assets in. I myself bought an external hard drive for it, which works like a charm.
There's one thing you should consider before getting this program (or any video editing software): do you just want to make basic videos with text, cuts, simple fades, etc? In that case consider to save your money and just stick to Windows Movie Maker or similar basic video editing software. I worked with it for a while and it gets simple jobs done well and an ideal program if you don't plan on making videos often. It's simple but useful, often underestimated by a lot.
If instead you want to spend some more time trying and putting in effort to make good videos and enjoy having a lot more tools, options and overall more workspace, this program is exactly what you're looking for.

This game started out as a fun little assembly programming puzzle but got tedious pretty quickly.
The story and style are exactly what you'd expect from a 2DBOY /  Tomorrow Corporation game (World of Goo, Little Inferno). Kind of cute and whimsical, but with a story utterly disconnected from the gameplay without much of a cohesive plot.
If you've never done any sort of assembly programming this game could serve as a nice introduction to it; a bit of a  challenge while teaching some of the basics.
However, if like me you have done some programming you'll probably find yourself getting annoyed with it pretty quickly. It has:
-No boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT, etc.) which seriously limits the scope of what puzzles can be in the game.
-No "branch on positive result" operator, despite there being negative and zero variants. This doesn't stop you from solving anything, but it forces you into writing some really inelegant solutions in order to work around this pointless omission.
-Comments and labels that need to be drawn letter by letter. You aren't required to use them, but if you do hopefully you have good handwriting using a mouse.
-No ability to set constants; you have to use whatever the game provides you. This means you pretty much have to solve the problems how they expect you to, no creativity allowed.
-A run time that even at the fastest setting will take a few minutes of sitting and waiting for some of the longer puzzles to complete.
All in all I think this game fails pretty hard, as its core audience is people with some interest / experience in programming but it doesn't respect that audience. It wasn't even all that challenging, I found I spent more time fighting the interface to get my solutions to work than I did actually thinking up solutions.

I wanted to give this game another chance before I wrote a negative review.  Well, I did - two more chances, in fact.  So here's why I think you should avoid it.
Tharsis acts like it's giving you a lot of options.  You can decide that the damage over in medbay isn't worth fixing at the moment and grow food.  You can assign crew to life support to recover precious dice without food.  If someone's morale has taken a beating, send them to the ops room and let them recover.
What the developers - and all the people saying what a wonderful game this is - do not tell you is that the situation quickly spirals out of control.  You can ignore that measly one hull damage problem in the cockpit, sure... but then next turn you've got two or three new events.  The fact you had five hull and could afford to lose one suddenly doesn't matter so much when you're looking at two more events that both trash your hull too.  Now you've got to fix that two damage one immediately or you'll be dead in space.  This brings up the biggest issue I have with the game: totally unfair RNG.
I have lost games because someone with three dice moved in to finish repairs on a system only to get three fives... when fives were declared to be voided, and I'd already used my assists up when the first person went in to start the fix.  Or they need to get just two repair - just two, that's it - with the single die currently available to them... and they get a one.  Hit the roll button again and it's another one.  Great, now I have to divert someone else to repair it or just take the hit.
You can't even use the ship's systems safely.  One game I had someone with full dice, five of them, go into the hydroponics bay to get some food grown.  This restores three dice, so having some food around helps a lot.  In order to actually produce any food, all you have to do is get two dice to come up with the same number.  Three will get you two food.  Rolling five dice makes it extremely likely that you'll manage this, but instead I got a 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6.  I saved the 4, figuring that rolling four dice I'd be almost certain to get either a duplicate or any of them at all coming up 4.  I got 1, 2, 3 and 6.
This means that not only did I totally waste that person's turn, I also wasted one of their dice because you lose one every time you roll for anything.  The next turn he was down to four dice, I didn't have any food, and the problems he could've been very helpful fixing up were still there.  The same system applies when trying to repair the hull.  Other systems require you to roll 5+.  The only one that you can actually be certain will help is the life support, and having someone go there specifically to restore their dice isn't a very good option - they burn one die in order to roll to use the system, and then get two back for a net of one more die.  If you're really lucky they'll get doubles and can restore four dice instead.
tl;dr - bad luck will kill you. Between bad die rolls and events conspiring to kill whatever you're already weak in, all the skill in the world won't save you if you don't get lucky.

More words:
This game is the most excellent time-killing game I've played. Easy to pick up and put down at a moments notice, I often find myself playing it when I'm waiting for something else, only to get immersed into it and just continue playing anyways.
The gameplay is simple: you use one of many provided button combinations (you can use a keyboard, mouse or controller) to chop either the left or right side of the tree. Keep chopping until a branch hits you (via chopping on the wrong side) or the timer at the top runs out from going too slow (which is a non-issue until your score gets really high).
The unlockable characters also give motivation to play, and
The passive online mode is a nice touch; the game actively searches for multiplayer lobbies while you play single player. There's an option to turn this off as well should you only wish to play in singleplayer. If you want to play multiplayer only, there's an option for that too; the game will search for an open lobby, and if there isn't one, it'll automatically create a lobby for you.
My only complaint about the game is the music; the only song is a short chiptune song that speeds up in intensity the more you play, and resets after you die. It's catchy at first and the idea sounds good on paper, but I personally find it rather distracting and annoying after a while. Fortunately, you can turn off the music (and the sound effects if you want) in the options menu and just play your own music instead.
Overall, I think the game's simplicity is its strong suit, which is why it's priced as such. I'd say it's worth it if you find yourself wanting something to kill time while waiting for something else, or if you just have some spare change lying around and want a cheap and simple game, especially if it's on sale.

Wow.  Quality artwork.  Great story.  It's short but what a journey.
This is a point-n-click style game.  A few puzzles, not very many and not very difficult.  And a few "battles" as well.  Awesome graphics.  There are voices but it is a nonesense language just for background effect, but it does portray the emotional state of the characters well.  (Reminds me of an exercise in drama school where we had to do a scene and the only words we could say were "Mary had a little lamb".  IT's amazing how much you can portray by voice inflection and stuff like that)
You help the main character become a reluctant hero.  He just wants to sleep instead of doing his job.  You have to literally drag  him with the mouse to the edge of the screen in order for him to move on.  He complains all the way through the game.  He has to deliver a message scroll to a hero in order to save the land from impending destruction.  Along the way he meets other characters that become involved in the story.   I won't spoil anything for you, but there is a neat thing they do in the game after you reach the "end" of the story they do a flashback and show what happened earlier but from another character's point of view.  It gives a different twist to the story.  Very nice storytelling.
One of the main puzzles is to create a path across a chasm by choosing small pieces that will fit together.  Then there are the battles.  You have to battle by choosing from a few options, like damage opponent or heal or defend, but they are not written that way.  They have phrases that are specific to the characters.   There are some battles where you have to do more strategy that just attack and defend.  There's also an option to increase attack or increase health.  So spend some time alternating between those and healing and then once your attack is high enough you can go for the kill.  Though you don't actually "kill" anyone.  It's more like you defeat them, they give in to your demand.
There's lots of humor in this story.  Sometimes it even breaks the fourth wall and talks to you, the player.  I love that kind of stuff.  Oh, and the game is kid-friendly.  I dont' think there's anything that will offend anyone.  It's really a game for all ages.  It's not neccesarily aimed at kids but it's not aimed at adults only.
Graphics are cute, charming, kind of like stained glass or woodcuts or mosaics artwork.
Total playtime: about an hour or so.  There are a few hidden things if you want all the achievements, so you might have to replay some sections.
tl;dr version:
great story
great art
point-n-click gameplay
some puzzles (easy to medium)
voices but not in a real language (like the schoolteacher in the old Charlie Brown and Snoopy movies)
1 hour playtime
much potential, but weird and not really fun

Before I'll say anything about the game, I'd like to tell you the type of gamer I am. I am the 'easy crowd' - easy to impress, with little expectations. I tend to avoid writing reviews in general, since what can one voice change in this big mess. But this time I've felt that I have to.
D4 is a great game. The story had me make a new theory of what had happened with each new piece of evidence discovered, untill its very end. The QTEs were good, with the exception of few that were in my opinion unnecessary, though they did add some of the... let's call it arcade... feeling to the game. The controlls might feel a bit clunky, but after some time with the game you can get used to it.
In short - I loved the game. It delivered what it was supposed to deliver - a good story.
So why the negative review you might ask? Well, the answer is simple. The game is dead. The story has been cut-off at a second episode. This is not a season 1 of the D4. This is a mere prologue, the first two episodes, and a bunch of regrets after learning that there will be no more. Of all the questions that were given to you at the start of the game maybe two were answered, with more unknowns popping up throughout the 'gameplay'.
My personal experience of the episodes:
The prologue felt like a good introduction to the tone and type of story that will be told.
The first episode was rich in content, and for its duration I tried to figure out who, what and where - a good thing if the plot involves solving a mystery. The 1st episode was quite fleshy - At few points I was hesitating to go forward afraid that it'd be the end of episode, and I've missed something, only to be proved wrong moments later.
The second episode felt like the first episode, though now I've gained the confidence from ep 1 that 'this important thing will not be the end of the episode'... and I was proven wrong. The ending of 2nd episode feels rushed to say the least. As if somebody just cut it in already developed point, and then slabbed the credits to it.
For this reason I hate this game. Just as I've started loving it, it left me. The main reason to buy it, is to be disapointed in the end. If that can be called a game, then warm clay can be called a brick.

A decent piece of editing software with the stability of a quadamputee on a tightrope.

For the price, it's a decent editing tool for quick edits and even more advanced ones such as chroma keying etc.
Nowhere near as high as quality as other edting software but for the price this is possibly the cheapest alternative to software such as Sony Vegas, Preimer Pro/After Effects. Highly recommended for begginers as it's easy to use, boot and render times are decent.

Again I highly recommend to people who want a simple editing tool that doesn't cost a small fortune.

I'm a veteran of the series and it goes without saying that I spent countless wonderful hours in SS and SS2 and even a few painful ones in SS3. However when SS4 was announced I realized that it would be difficult to recreate the magic of the early games and at the same time gather a new, younger fan base. Times have changed, guys and game design needs to adapt to current trends!  Therefore, while expecting it not to be the same as the first ones, I still thoroughly enjoyed the game and for me, it has enough elements to still be counted as a worthy SS successor.
What was enjoyable:
- Creative, logical and varied objectives in the campaign missions
- Absolutely gorgeous maps!
- The logistical aspects of your army <3
- Tiger B is unstoppable if used adequately. Seeing tens of projectiles bouncing off its armor is poetry in motion :)
- Historically accurate units based on the date of the mission, FINALLY!
- French and Polish units to fight against, even though just in the early missions of the German campaign (which, like the beautiful maps, is a testament of the love and attention the developer put in this game)
Flaws:
- Some annoying pathing issues that everyone can notice
- Weird animations for ground attack aircraft
- No fighter aircraft?
- Different doctrines are not necessary. Having all the perks available for use would be truer to the franchise. However the progression mechanic is not a bad idea but could have been done better in my opinion (more/better units unlocked, veterancy for them, etc).
- Multiplayer is bad and needs more depth but this doesn't ruin the game entirely for me.
In conclusion, the game has its flaws and I can understand why some players felt underwhelmed by the experience. However the game isn't bad and can only get better if content will continue to be added to it.

It's basically assembly logic puzzles.
I highly recommend this game for non-programmers who are interested in challenging themselves to learn the basic logic of programming or who want to try and solve puzzles via programming.  However, it isn't going to teach you the syntax of a language or anything like that.

He said he enjoyed it, but that it wasn't very challenging.  So I don't know if it will become challenging at that point or if it's too simple for programmers, however, I think it's worth taking a look at for anyone.

Tharsis is ultimately a game about dealing with the hand (or dice) you're dealt. Some things are influenceable, you're able to slightly rig the odds in your favour, but at the end of the day you are at the whim of the dice. Of course, if you rigged the odds properly, their whim shouldnt have much of an impact. If you play it properly, you should only have a handful of instances that are completely out of your control, and if those fail, you should have a backup plan ready. In fact, you should have multiple.
Yes, extroadinarily, somehow a game relying on rolling the dice is actually a lot more skill than luck based. I've played plenty of roguelikes, I've played strategy games that relied a little too much on the RNG, this is not one of them.
Please give this game a chance. Maybe not on full price, but on sale it is a good addition to your library that can keep you occupied for more than a few hours.

tldr:
- If you like FTL, Renowned explorers (RE) or solo quick board games
- AND you are willing to count the odds / like optimisation tasks
- AND accept that output is "dice" dependant
- AND game is on steam for 5E
give it a try, otherwise better avoid it.
Long version:
For me it is quite enjoyable - I like "optimization tasks", but this game is not for everybody.
Game is not forgiving and sometimes you just get unlucky, but if you manage the risk, it is winnable (definitely on normal).
There is no noticeable story and the replayability could be an issue for many players.
FTL and RE are more enjoyable to play, but Tharsis is much quicker and straightforward, so it could be good choice for quick relax. (You may argue. that they are completely different games, but I like them too, and I put them into the same category.)
Pros
- Audio, Graphic.
- Rules are easy.
- Counting odds+prediction+optimization => win
Cons
- Story (ending).
- Replayability (questionable)
- Limited choice of crew members / strategy
- Straightforward (=not many surprises, it is just like optimisation tasks)

Really is hard for me to decide whether to be positive or negative about this one, but when in doubt go for the negative.
The positive qualities of the game are just slightly outweighed by the negatives, unfortunately.
First off, the game isn't /that/ hard. Not compared to lots of other "hard" platformers on steam at least. Not easy, no, but not that difficult either. That's not a bad thing though; in fact it's about where I like games to be in terms of challenge most of the time. The problem is that it gets to that difficulty pretty quickly and then never really gets noticeably harder. 1-6 is the first hard level and then after that the game does nothing to really challenge you until the final boss.
Another big issue I have is some technical issues. Most notably, occasionally the dash move will stop short of your intended target leaving you to die by face-ramming into the enemy you were attacking. This happens a bit too frequently to ignore it. The dash can be unreliable in general, too, but that's the biggest problem I've seen with it.
Though, the *real* issue I have with this game is the tedium. All over the place... the game slows its pacing to a crawl. Way, way too often. By the end of the game you've gotten no less than 3 ways to move reeeeally slow around levels. And the bosses get worse and worse about it too. The first boss is decent. The second boss requires a bit too much waiting. The final boss is simultaneously the most difficult part of the game and INSANELY BORING. It takes no less than 4 minutes to defeat him (via 3 hits) due to how long a hit cycle is, and that's just plain inexcusable. As well, the levels tend to feel like they lacked variety. There's only ever forests and castles, essentially. 1-6 is a cave I guess but it's forest-y and 2-7 has this ocean ruins aesthetic but it's really castle-y, and the rest of the levels literally don't stray in the slightest from the two main ones. And since the level objects remain mostly the same the result is what feels like rather unnecessarily repetitive level design. On top of that some of the levels hardly feel cohesive; on a few occasions there are levels that will have a random short water section at the very end for what feels like no reason at all other than to extend the level a bit.
The game can be mildly fun at times (3-6 for example is pretty fun to play) but too often I found myself not having much fun at all. Not the worst in its genre by any means, and maybe you'll like it more than I did, since it's not terrible at all, but certainly you could do better than this.

General verdict is that it’s really great, and comes strongly recommended, especially if you’ve ever enjoyed any of the Ace Attorney games. There are some significant and insignificant bugs and typos at the time of this writing (December 27th, 2015), but the package as a whole is more than good enough for me to forgive some rough edges. (Pro tip: don’t adjust options at the title screen. Wait until you’re in the game proper. I had to uninstall and reinstall the game a few times until I figured out that was what was making it stop responding to me.)
It’s a visual novel about lawyers practicing in 19th Century France, except everyone is a creature from the illustrations of 19th Century satirist J. J. Grandville, set to music by the romantic era composer Camille Saint-Saëns.
The whole thing has a very Hatoful Boyfriend kind of feel to it, and not just because of the static images or the birds: this is a game that has a completely ridiculous premise and uses that to draw the player in to a grim tale of political strife, asking questions about justice and revenge. Parts of it seem to be direct responses to Ace Attorney scenes, too - a lot of Ace Attorney moments get flipped on their heads here.
That’s not to say it isn’t really funny when it wants to be - it’s freaking hilarious when it feels like it! That’s another thing that feels really Hatoful Boyfriend about the whole proceeding, but it’s certainly its own thing, and it got its talons in me really deep. Can’t wait for the third ending to get fixed!
tl;dr: While there are some bugs still, it’s highly recommended for visual novel fans, especially if you enjoyed Hatoful Boyfriend and/or any of the Ace Attorney games.

Should you play Aviary Attorney? Yes with a hint of maybe. All in all it will be best to wait to purchase this game until the developers release the debugged and complete version.
AA is a fun playthrough for fans of both of the game's major inspirations (Phoenix Wright/Ace Attorney and Hatoful Boyfriend). It has its fair share of comedy and puns (although many of the puns will require minimal knowledge of the French language), and in the later half of the game, it has a great original overarching plot centering around the setting of pre-revolution France. The game also features a great original classical soundtrack and engaging graphics styled around 19th century etchings and caricatures.
At the moment, the game remains incomplete though, and this makes is a bit hard to recommend the game, especially with the high price point (for a short visual novel). The first half of the game will feel boring to Phoenix Wright players, as it nearly carbon copies the first Phoenix Wright game through the first two cases. Many bugs abound in the game that make it hard to understand why it was released (do not open the options menu from the title screen, and the save system is a mess). While the game boasts three endings, one of them is listed as "Coming Soon" and there is little knowledge as to whether this means pay-to-play DLC, a forthcoming update, or that it will ever come at all.
Should the bugs be worked out and the game completed, it's well worth your time and money. If this ends up being the final version of the game, I still recommend it, but would urge players to wait and not pay more than $5 for the product presented.
