Enjoyed the game. Purchased it at the regular price and don't regret it, only wish it would be a tad longer and perhaps allow somewhat greater freedom of exploration (though the most of the areas that appear throughout Chapter 2 are explorable from the get go).
One of the common gripes I can see in other reviews is the combat system. It's much different from what I have seen in most other RPGs, and I would say that it's challenging to master. In fact the difficulty level of some battles seems to be quite inconsistent, as I don't remember having many problems fighting my enemies in latter stages of the game (except for a boss fight in the latter portion of the game, which featured a completely unique type of enemy), but some battles in the beginning were frustrating and at times overwhelmingly difficult. Groups of enemies are really, really hard to dispatch at first, and the companions that we have available serve as little else than a distraction. They don't ever seem to get any better as well.
Character developement is fairly straightforward, featuring three skill trees - Combat (meaning melee combat); Renegade (ranged weapons and explosives, stealth, healing and a very useful "blinding skill"); Technomancy (magic, sort of - this tree becomes available after the first chapter). I'm not entirely sure if they are well balanced, as a full focus on Combat with a few points here and there in the other two trees allowed me to be nigh invincible towards the end of the game. Combat is, in general, fast-paced and rather dynamic.
What I liked most, however, is the way that the player improves their equipment. Crafting is possibly the only real means of improving ones gear, as both armours and weapons in their basic versions provide little improvement over each other. Their full potential is unlocked only by craftable upgrades. In fact, the main reason to acquire new armour or melee weapons is to get the ability to craft more advanced upgrades.
Voice acting ranges from fine to downright terrible. I hear that the dialogue quality has lost a lot in translation from original French, and it does sound a bit odd at times, and some sentences actually don't make sense. Not a lot of that however, at least after the patch that actually included improved voice acting for some characters.
The story is so-so, although hardly groundbreaking or surprising. That said, it had one or two unexpected twists before getting to a rather predictable ending.
The general theme of the game is described as 'cyberpunk'. I would call it 'cyberpunk-ish' at best. There is little to no advanced/futuristic tech to be experienced, it just seems more like a dystopian vision of a forgotten space colony, whose inhabitants have slowly devolved.
To sum up: I would recommend this game to patient people, who would like to try their hand at something a bit different. A pretty solid indie game, which you just might want to buy when it's on sale...

Vehicles absolutely dominate over infantry, especially seeing as tanks can instantly squish through infantry. I am not kidding. So many of your infantry taken by surprise could be wiped out in a second if a tank showed up to roll over them. They just cut through them, no pushing or shoving, just
. So there is no such thing as an infantry heavy build or anything such. You build tanks and helicopters ASAP, infantry is simply there to make sure you don't get rushed in the first minute. Infantry are further made redundant as Transport Helicopters can either load 5 infantry or 5 tanks. Which would you bloody prefer?
You can only construct one building at a time. So, for example, in the moment you either choose between the machine gun or the barracks. You cannot put down a blueprint or queue the building (as far as I know) and decide which one gets built first, or just so you can tend to other things. You do not need engineers to construct buildings, they just start going up (and really slowly). I tried to use my engineers to boost the construction time but this feature does not seem to exist either.
The Nuke was an exciting idea but it is basically a ring of death on the battlefield. It takes a few minutes to prepare, you launch it, and any units in the ring are blown up. It does damage to structures, but will not one-hit them. So it is a utility best used on a large group of enemies. However it is very easy to avoid this and move away from it, it is accompanied by a noise, a ring, and a delay on when it lands. This contrasts with other RTS games like Company of Heroes which only gives a small flare on the map, or a ring on the minimap, or even just a sound queue making it a little harder to dodge when engaged. It feels really lackluster and non-special.
Buildings are produced only to unlock the units that coincide with them. You build a barracks to unlock infantry and so on. They do not provide upgrades or any other sort of functionality like other RTS games such as Warcraft would have them do.
There is a single 'faction' in the game. So no unit differentiation or bonuses. There is a faction coming up which looks like a wizardy-fantasy campaign. Though I have not seen confirmation that these will be free, and I worry that they may end up as DLC you need to pay for.
They aimed it to be casual, and an introduction to RTS for new players. They succeeded in the former. However, would anyone really desire to play further RTS games after this I wonder? When I was younger the only board games I were exposed to were Chess and Monopoly. If I had never had a flatmate that loved card games and board games I wouldn't have dreamed of picking up a hobby I now really love. So why show newcomers to a genre really basic, boring, mechanics and say "Here's your intro to RTS games!". You don't need to do that, you can have a really deep game that newcomers can have a lot of fun with too so long as you provide the materials to learn. An effective singleplayer campaign, a ranking system, in-game hints, dev tutorials.
Don't bother. If you want an intro to RTS games find something that looks really cool to you and put some time in to learn it. Learning it isn't always fun, neither is getting your♥♥♥♥♥beat. But it's a competitve game and some people have the jump in time-played. It wouldn't be any different here, and you're barely getting a game!

Mediocre "2.5D" platformer with gorgeous graphics but precious little else. The novelty here is that Giana can switch between a light world (enemies include owls and bunny rabbits shooting love hearts) and a dark one (demons, skeletons etc.). In one world she has the ability to rocket violently in any direction; in the other, to float a la Dixie Kong. Many of the platforming challenges revolve around switching between worlds to access environmental features that exist in one and not the other.
Following the lead of Trine, graphics are full 3D models; the backgrounds in particular, with features morphing between light and dark, are spectacular. But there is a reason that precision platformers have tended towards 8-bit chic, and it's because genuine precision is very hard with 3D effects. Hitboxes aren't always clear, foreground and background elements can hide hazards, etc.
What really lets Giana Sisters down, however, is the level design -- levels are long, repetitive, unpleasant and uninteresting. Perfect scores require collecting upwards of 700 gems in each level. The soundtrack is also incredibly grating.
For other, far better games with the same world-switching gimmick, try Guacamelee or Eversion. A vastly superior game with similar 2.5D graphics is Donkey Kong Country Returns.

Idea and setting of the game are nice. Sadly, execution of the game mechanics is utterly horrible. Where do I start...
Inventory system. There isn't any. You can hold only a single item. If you want to pick up another you have to drop the current item, or teleport to your stash (called "the case") and drop it there. So the item management gets incredibly tedious, you never know what items you currently have unless you go to the stash and back all the time. And if you don't bring everything to the stash you can easily lose an important item somewhere in the level; good luck finding it again. How could anyone think this is ok?
Active zones. They are not marked in any way. No visual clue, the cursor doesn't change, nothing. The game wants you to click everything just to check if you can manipulate it or not. To add insult to injury, objects have no description and to show their names you have to hold mouse button over them for a second. I don't think I've ever seen such user unfriendliness in a modern adventure game.
Levels are huge. Huge and extremely nonlinear. And of course, there is no map. For people with bad sense of orientation (like me) it was hell to navigate through the game.
Last but not least, the puzzles. There is only one type: the "what the f- am I supposed to do" puzzles. Their mechanics are completely obscure, random, they make little sense in context of the surroundings and the clues are sparse and very vague. Often I didn't even know there is a puzzle to solve! Combined with the inventory system which hates me, I gave up on all puzzles very soon (they're optional) and just collected ribbons to get to the end as fast as possible. And I'm sure it was not intended to be like that.
This game is the definition of unfun. If it wasn't too late, I would have asked for a refund.

=Review Revised=
Quick Review: This game is frustratingly difficult, even on the “easy” setting. Between the RNG and the mechanics against you, it may turn off many. I originally did not recommend this game, but have changed my recommendation as it is really interesting and a neat game worth checking out, just expect some unpleasantness on your first few playthroughs.
Basics: If you’re looking for an idea of what this is, it’s FTL meets Yahtzee. You will command a crew of 4 unique characters along a randomized mission where every week new problems arise on the ship, and you must repair them. Along the way, you must also manage health, hunger, hull damage, crew stress, and assists to protect you from hazards. The goal is to survive until you reach Mars.
You will be managing all this with the use of dice. A problem will require a target total dice roll to success, you roll, add what you like, re-roll the left overs, and that’s that. If you roll the target or higher, it’s repaired, if you fail, you take a consequence. The game does offer 3 constant randomized research cards which you can dump spare dice into for quick help/recovery. As weeks progress, all problems will also be accompanied by negative status effects for specific values, if rolled. For instance, you may lose 1hp, or a die, if you roll a 3 in the engine room. These negative hazards are where much of the frustrating difficulty comes.  In fact, you probably won’t complete the game unless you just give up from the beginning and leave certain sections of the ship damaged every turn, beginning to end, so as to focus your whole crew on the big areas. If you have strategy OCD, like me, about repairing everything, getting all your food and items prepped and good, strategizing and maximizing a plan, this will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
Tharsis is less about successfully winning and more about losing well. You just remember that when you’re salty and typing a review, like I had.
Presentation: Very nice. The environments work, music fits the theme, and the UI and general design is smooth.
Issues: I doubt a developer or director will pass by this, read it, and take any to heart, but here are several criticisms and suggestions for future patches and/or sequels.
-Difficulty: The easy mode isn’t easy enough. It is brutal and capable of wiping a team, early in the weeks, even with optimal play. There is so little room for flexibility or failure, it’s absurd. Again, I can understand a challenging roguelike with this mentality, but you have a Normal and Hard mode to do that with. If you want to open up your game to a larger audience, and retain their attention to the end, and already have an “Easy” mode then go further with it.
-Lower Easy mode repair targets. Hitting target values in the 20s and 30s while 3 hazards are out, on easy, is a bit much.
-Begin the game in better condition! Easy aside, your characters are nearly dead and out of dice turn 1. You can’t even partake in cannibalism that early. This is fine if the difficulty of repairs didn’t spike so suddenly; thus giving you a chance to recuperate and prepare.
-The ramp up in difficulty is excessive. Like many of these complaints, it’s an either do this or that acceptance, not both/all.
-More playable characters. To me, though it’d honestly probably make the game much easier, it’d be fun to have 6 active characters rather than 4. I like the idea of a team working on repairs while a Captain goes around refilling dice, or the team is able to focus on a large problem while one member is free to think about food or stress or research or abilities or hull. Perhaps just another easy mode only suggestion, but it’d certainly increase fun factor.
-Roguelite character experience. The bitterness of a game over would be majorly assuaged by persistent character levels and bonuses. For instance, the Doctor, upon so many repairs/missions/heals/turns/whatever ranks up which improves the ability to heal +1 on a 5+ value to “on a 4+ value”. Then, on another rank up, on a 3+ value. Maybe the Doctor heals +2 to all module crew later, maybe it’s +1 to whole ship rather than module. If you follow this idea out, it makes the late replays even far more interesting and dynamic. It’s incentive to play new teams, to level up, to take a defeat and come back stronger with more tools.
-The last critique is based upon the systems commentary trailer. In it, Craps was discussed as an inspiration over simple dice games because of the persistent excitement it allows. An example of high stakes was presented as the framework. As a Las Vegas resident, allow me to point out the appeal of Craps: the opening roll out, the point, and the secondary round(playing the field, rolling for point, placing odds, etc). You see, Tharsis sets the point with repair targets, and then proceeds into the secondary fundamentals of research/skills/module skills as side bets on a field, I get it. The game lacks a roll out though! This is, bar none, the most exciting and appealing part of Craps! It’s the only bet in all of Vegas where the odds aren’t absolutely battering you; in fact odds on the line are no house favor!  When you see movies with people playing dice it’s always “seven! Winner! SEVEN! WINNER!”, and everybody is excited, and there’s champagne, and scantily clad women blowing on dice, and Sean Connery… mmm…  Where was I? Anyways, this game lacks the roll out excitement of a lucky 7. It begins by establishing a low odds point, bypassing all excitement of rolling a lucky jackpot number, and it just becomes a grind of “will I still hit my point? At least?”. If you want a Tharsis closer to the excitement of Craps, you’d have no repair target, just a problem and consequence (a bet). Upon reaching the module, the character would have a come out roll to determine the difficulty of the target. This difficulty roll out would also have a “lucky 7” special value which completely and happily solves it. You could have one single die be odd colored, and upon the roll out of it coming up a 6, or whatever, it counts as a win. You can also two-edge this, like Craps, by making the odd color die roll out a 1 which makes the situation even harder (crap out). Based on this system, the player would roll out, establish different difficulties of point, and then have a field of side bets depending on the outcomes of the first two steps. RNG games need that possibility of a jackpot, an easy win, the thing you need to blow on the dice for. By just constantly denying the ability and dumbing it down to simply achieving a point, you’re placing all the odds in the house and hoping your hypothesis of “more to lose” will carry players through the slog.
I only take the time to point out this stuff because I genuinely enjoy the idea of this game and wish a little more for it. It’s a hard pill to swallow as it stands in its current state.
Recommended, but with reservations.

As someone who has been playing TERA for the past four to five years, I can tell you a lot of things about the game. I'm played all of the classes, but have just stuck with only a handful, so my views may be slightly biased.
But long story short: you want to kill time? Here's an option.
Anyways, here's my long summary of TERA which will have a TL;DR at the end for you guys that don't care.
TERA's mechanics are relatively okay, although the option to link attacks just makes it so that people rarely have to move their hand to press the actual attack buttons themselves. It's just hitting space bar multiple times, while your character does some fancy-smancy attacks, that look oh-so-difficult to use to non-TERA players. (HAH.) Battle tends to differ, obviously, from class to class, but for the most part, it's relatively fluid. (Although, sometimes little incidents will occur and it's usually gracefully hiliarious.) Honestly though, if you're new to games such as these, TERA is actually easy to pick up and even with the recent nerf patches, it's also very forgiving.
Speaking of which, TERA can easily be played solo, never ever joining a guild, or in a group. Either way, you're pretty much set—until you get to level 65, which is the current level cap. Unfortunately, one of the larger quests is to complete a very big raid where 100 players have to kill 4 dragons, all at the same time or they will be re-set. Because of the large amount of players, it's almost absolutely necessary for players to join an active and medium-sized guild to complete this. Not only that, there is obviously certain equipment that one needs to join these raids. Even with those in guilds, you have to have this equipment, which can be crafted through drops of other other level 65 dungeons. (Mainly from Lilith's Keep, the worst dungeon to ever exist. If you like constantly dying, this dungeon is the one for you. I hate it, mainly because I've gotten stuck in that one for a few hours after our only healer decided to ditch.)
Continuing on: dungeons. Dungeons actually happen to be my favorite part of TERA, mainly because you have a chance to party up with a random set of other people of varying classes to clean out a dungeon. Dungeon queue times tend to range from a minute to about twenty minutes, depending on the difficulty and level of the dungeons, which isn't half bad, although it is annoying to wait around for that long. You're also free to solo dungeons. Dungeons also happen to be split between raids and dungeons. Raids, although there's only I believe two of them (possibly three; I don't really know that part ha), which basically means there's more people and a slightly longer dungeon. A bit of an excitement in somewhat of a meh game.
With TERA's lore, the only thing I can say about it is: horrible. If you're looking for some more in-depth and less cheesy, TERA isn't the thing for you. Honest to god, they've spiced it up and changed the beginning portions throughout the years, but it's just simply boring. The tutorial is okay, but personally, only when you near the level-cap is where things become a little bit more interesting and even that just gets eh. Definitely not a game for those lore lovers, unless you like cheese. It's pretty dang cheesy.
Which brings me to grinding. TERA grinding isn't half-bad when you're simply following the quests. There's a few areas that make me want to stab something in pure frustration, but past that, not bad at all. Dungeons, on the other hand, can be an incredible pain. In some of the dungeons, there are in-dungeon quests that you must complete to continue the storyline. Fun Fact: Dungeon monsters are extremely difficult to kill. Another Fun Fact: Your party members that you randomly joined probably have already completed or are ignoring the story quests. Have fun solo-ing that quest and dying multiple times, getting completely ignored by your party members! (You'll usually have to start the quest immediately as you get into the room.) On the other hand, grinding for items is just. No. No thank you. If you've managed to save up quite a bit of gold by selling and brokering (selling to other players) and doing quests, then that part may help you a little bit in getting the items necessary for crafting. But mainly, crafting items have to be earned through quests and occasionally, it just takes too dang long to grind for certain crafting items which will push people to use the cash shop. Even then, though, it may not sometimes be guranteed that you'll get the crafting item.
And with the cash shop comes the fun extras. With TERA, it only seems to hover around that point of ALMOST pay to win once you've hit the level cap. (Grinding is still an option.) If anything, you can still get certain things like clothing skins and crafting materials through in-game drops or fashion coupons. (Fashion coupons are also drops that have recently become slightly more difficult to get. But they tend to be dropped from larger monsters.) It's not too bad.
Another thing that's a bit interesting about TERA, since recent patches, they've attempted to balance out most of the classes and they did pretty well. (We're going to ignore the whole race issue. Come on. No one can lie about that. Elins are top dogs, sorry, it's horrid, I know.) They took away some abilities that I'm going to miss, re-organized when you get each ability, and etc. Before that, ninjas were extremely over-powered, with them easily carrying dungeon parties and cleaning house under 10 minutes, alongside gunners as well. Now, it's a bit more grindy and all classes seem to push out less damage, which is fine by me. Although there's some issues I have with these nerfs, for the most part (and most classes), it isn't half-bad.
TERA graphics. What...are graphics? Ha. TERA is run on an older engine, which not only makes the loading in slow, but causes FPS to either remain low or jump around. The visuals in some areas, though, are gorgeous. My personal favorite actually happens to be Heartwood. For the most part, a little bit on the dry side. However, if my old toaster laptop can run TERA, then for all of you fellow toasters out there, here's a game to look at!
And with that comes bugs and glitches. Sometimes, you can get stuck in certain parts of the map that are absoutely freaking ridiculous. One can usually unstick themselves with ease, but there is an official Unstuck button available to those that are utterly stuck. Yes, I know getting stuck in certain items is a common thing, but the reason I mention it here is that it can actually get you killed if you get stuck in certain areas and getting stuck in certain areas of the map is a constant. Not only that, there seem to be more bugs popping up throughout the game. Monsters will not return to their positions after they've been out of their zone for too long, certain monsters won't properly trigger, monsters that you've triggered on different floors will suddenly pop out of no where in your face, and not to mention the dreaded elevators that if you don't get on right, you'll literally fall through the floor and to your death. I do think this is because the lack of attention En Masse has been giving to TERA and Bluehole...? I'm not sure what they're doing anymore. (En Masse is currently working on two other games. One that recently came out, while the other's open beta has just begun.)
In my own personal opinion, I do think TERA will come to an end in the next two years or so, or maybe hang on for a little bit longer due to the small but very active fanbase. So play while you can but don't get seriously into it.
TL;DR
+ Relatively Easy to Pick Up Gameplay
+ Plenty of content to do or re-do
+ Still plenty to do before the paywall
+ Solo or Party
+ Classes all different
- Graphics/Old Game Engine
- Lore
- Gender/Race Walls
- Bugs, Glitches
- Maybe ending soon
CONCLUSION: You want to waste time? Sure. You in for the long haul? No.

TERA is interesting to say the least.
Combine a fun combat system and an addictive collect-athon and you get hours and hours of eye catching game play.
The plot itself is kinda cliche, you are defending the realm from a race of super beings who are invading , this plot is common in the mmo category. However it branches out more and more as you go, creating steps you need to accomplish so you can level up in order to solve the next task.
I really enjoy leveling up my character, they have a wide variety of weapons, armor, and skills you can earn by completing missions. And as you go, those earnings can make a huge difference in battles.
The only bad things I have to say about the game is that it can get repetitive. There are a lot of missions where it is you killing the same monster a certain amount of times. And the only reason that it doesn't get too boring is because of the combat mechanics. However, even with that exception the boredom eventually settles in after you have been playing for a long time.
In the end, TERA is a great game. However, I suggest you play with other friends. It makes the experience more entertaining, and can lead to some great dungeon runs. The battles are awesome as you level up, and I think it certainly worth the time to do so.

Most people say that this game teaches you programming basics. In my opinion it teaches you how NOT to be a programmer.
Sure, you get an introduction about how a computer thinks, but the game makes you find the most complicated solutions for the easiest problems which gives you a false view on how programming really works.
For example, you get the task to multiply two numbers. Instead of just multiplying them (like you would do in a real code) you have to store them (like variables), add them and keep checking and changing the variables until you've done the multiplying process. And then repeat it.
I realize that a lot of important "codes" are missing in order to make the game more challenging, but that's not what I expected from reading the reviews.

A lot of the negative reviews are from programmers who already know how to code who say it's too easy. I am not a programmer. Here is my review.
You play an office drone in the mailroom of a large corporation, tasked with menial jobs like sending boxes from the inbox to the outbox, adding numbers to them, subtracting numbers, reordering them, sending only primes, alphabetizing, etc. along the way. As you progress, there are little bits of "story" that just seem cute at first but then become hilarious as you realize the world outside is changing in strange ways as you while away the years in an office. I was pleasantly surprised that this game even had a story at all.
As for the coding itself. You have a limited amount of commands, so your code is never going to be super efficient. (Ex. You have to divide quite often, but a divide command is unavailable, so you have to do an excessive amount of subtraction to get the same effect). A lot of the fun comes from trying to figure out non-obvious ways of achieving tasks that are simple in the real world with what you have. There are also challenges for optimizing your code, either with the minimum amount of steps or the minimum amount of commands. The coding style is with little boxes that you arrange in a list (no typing code), some with arrows to redirect your sequence. It's most similar to the coding system Scratch, for reference.
Pros:
+Great art style
+Good music (although repetitive, but I never got sick of it)
+Speed/efficiency challenges for each level add replayability
+Harder bonus levels that you can skip if you don't want the challenge
+Cute little story
+Slick UI, with only minor issues (see Cons)
Neutral:
~Minimal story, so don't expect one and you won't be disappointed. In fact, I was pleasantly surprised at what there was.
~Mouse only. This isn't really too big of an issue, but there are ways to add notes to your code to help you keep track of what you're doing, but you have to write them by had with your mouse, which is kind of annoying. Definitely not game breaking, and it also allows you to draw pictures if you want, which did come in handy at times.
Cons:
(None of these are game-breaking. Just little annoyances)
-Code is very inefficient, so you end up with really long bits and it's easy to forget what parts of the code are doing what. You either need to use the note function to remind yourself what you're doing or debugging your code will be a nightmare. When changing one thing led to tons of errors, I often just deleted everything and started from the beginning just because it was easier than figuring out what I had done.
-No way to select chunks of code for easy delete. If you wanted to get rid of half of your 40-command-long-code, you had to delete each command by hand, or just delete the entire thing at once and start from scratch.
Overall: 9/10. If you're a programmer, you might find this too easy. Go play SpaceChem instead. For the average gamer who likes logical arguments or amateur coding, you'll find this to be a hoot. Cute little game. Overall playtime for me: 15 hours, all levels (without doing optimization challenges).

Assassin's Creed is the kind of series where you can never tell going in whether or not it's going to be good or not, thanks to the overall quality of the franchise constantly vaulting between good and bad almost randomly. Because of this I didn't initially have much hope for Origins, but ended up pleasantly surprised.
The Ubisoft formula is still wholly in-tact; if you're here because of your life-long passion for climbing towers and controlling animal populations to make handbags then you'll be right at home. Alternatively, if you like having fun, you can do that too, because this time they decided to add another layer of game onto Assassin's Creed by blatantly copying as many things as they could from other, better franchises, by which I mean mostly The Witcher 3 with little bits of MGSV.
The overall system of progression, the formatting of the sidequests, and even a lot of the general UI feels like it was copied from Witcher 3's playbook, and while the more RPG-like presentation of the combat might turn some people off (namely the people who were hoping to go in and mash the counter button until they can chain execute 20 people in a row while eating your controller) I think it's overall a pretty welcome improvement. The action combat feels like it's at least trying to require some skill and timing now, and the stealth has been improved with some new tools despite some things being a little silly, like the new ability to curve your arrows' trajectory.
It is slightly dampened by the sheer size of the game and its map, however, and it seems clear that they didn't have enough of an idea to actually justify how big the game's world is. While in the games Origins copies the sidequests are practically a reward of their own thanks to the characters and stories, the quality of the ones in Origins are as varied as the overall quality of the series they're a part of, with some of them being great and some of them barely being worth starting, let alone finishing. They're mostly passable, but by about 3/4 into the game I was ready to just start riding from one main objective to the next because you can only save so many wives' husbands or children before it starts to sink in that most of those husbands use the same models and most of those children have the same voice actors, and that most of their stories are just excuses to stab some people. Some of the side quests from the previous recent games have been dropped as well, like the murder mysteries, which I thought was disappointing since I actually liked those in the last two.
The main questline is generally more interesting than most of the series' campaigns, and though it does have some pretty bad padding near the end it's not overly offensive, and certainly not as bad as AC2 suddenly grinding to a halt until you collect 30 codex pages. Bayek is a pretty interesting protagonist, and while I didn't really like Aya you thankfully only have to occasionally deal with her and play as her even less. The same applies to the obligatory shoehorned modern day segments, which are barely even in the game at this point, though if you're the one person out there who actually still cares about that then there's various things to read out there too.
Overall, this new formula is better in some ways and worse in others, and I think in a setting that could offer more variety in the sidequests it could be great. They definitely seem to have thought that their idea was better than it actually was and overstretched the game because of it, but I think the year gap in between this and the last Assassin's Creed paid off in a lot of ways, and I'm looking forward to seeing how they can improve on this new style. It's still not as good as any of the games they copied, but it's a welcome start towards making the series feel like more than just a color-by-numbers yearly sequel.

I went to re-play Dream Daddy after some time away, but before I started Dream Daddy I decided to see if there were any new dating sims worth playing. Much to my delight, I found Purrfect Date! This game is so much more than a dating sim. It's a visual novel and mystery (with cats!) and I love it. I've played through it twice now and I keep finding new things, which keeps me engaged, and makes me want to play it again. The repetition at the beginning of the first few chapters does get a bit tedious, but thankfully the game developers seem to recognize that by the last few chapters and speed things up. If you like dating, cats, mysteries, surprises, clever writing, and/or all of the above, I would definitely recommend this game.

: I purchased this game after some deliberation when I saw it featured on Steam for a brief time; I'm not a follower of the developer's other work.
Purrfect Date is a visual novel with an empthasis on the
part championed by Oliver Age 24 & Ruby Bae (a cute British couple I presume).
This is evidently a passion project that took over 2 years to develop because they've recently put out a challenge wanting only 1000 retweets for them to get Purrfect Date tattoos!
For anyone who came here with the impression that this is an erotic novel featuring raunchy dialogue and bestiality: you're in for a surprise.
There is endearing affection, romance and love waiting for you if you want to make those decisions but for anything more explicit - you'll have to look elsewhere.
What may at first glance appear like yet another "edgy" indie dating sim with the typical flourishes of memes and over-the-top humour is actually a game with a complex & interesting story with plenty of mystery to keep you on your feet (or paws?).
The game also featuring intricate characters (you know a game has done well with its writing when you're able to relate to characters and to see both things you like & dislike about them) which could only have been fleshed out more if the game was even longer.
This game is also plenty of fun if you and/or a friend decide to do the voice-acting :)
As someone who doesn't read too much fiction because they prefer the authenticity and nuance of real interactions - I can say this game is ticking the right boxes.
Overall I'd reccomend this game to anyone who has the patience to read, gets pleasure from trying to work out a mystery, likes a dash of humour and doesn't mind too much when things get adorable! =(^w^)=
The story of Purrfect Date is written by Ruby and has plenty going for it due to its satisfying length and the mystery interwoven - it is hard to really capture this experience in a review without providing spoilers, but as mentioned before, the novel part is the
aspect of this game and where the game really shines; hopefully you end up loving the characters as much as I do (Trixie & McMurphy ♥)
The somewhat linear nature of the game means the best experience will be on the first playthrough. Unfortunately this meant that repeat playthroughs (for curiosity or achievements) can be a bit of a chore due to the amount of dialogue that needs to be skipped.
The good news is that someone raised this on the forum and I understand the Devs are planning to implement a feature to skip dialogue - in the meantime autohotkey programs can be used.
In terms of gameplay, this isn't one of those visual novels where you have to juggle a bunch of stats and use trial-and-error to progress (looking at you Long Live the Queen).
Other than choices during dialogue, here are the gameplay mechanics:
This game features an OST by Oliver Age 24 which is about 45 minutes in length -- it offers a reasonable variety and is used appropriately for the scenes in the game.
I enjoyed the quirkiness in places but feel this didn't really stand out too much - feel this is mostly because the story is much longer than the OST though.
The artwork in the game was created by Dan Lish - feel it is a bit difficult to really comment on this aspect because I've not played many visual novels / know basically nothing about artwork :P
The style is generally colourful, tropical and a brush of cute with more somber artwork to align with the darker sides of the story - I found it charming but not sure what else to say!
Few gameplay mechanics helped to keep focus, could have had more music but overall an excellent story with pleasant artwork.
Some advice for the first playthrough: take your time, enjoy the cats, make choices carefully and try not to stay up past 4 o'clock in the morning!

As of writing this review I am 29 hours in and I intend to increase that number. Wow, where to start... I have played a few dating sims in my time but none of them have captivated me like this one.
Purrfect Date is a combination of a dating sim and a visual novel.
POTENTIAL SPOILERS AHEAD! I do try my best to not mention the most important ones however.
I won't say too much to spoil things for you but what I will tell you is that the story can and will change based on the decisions you make. At first the story seems overly cheerful with humor and action sprinkled on top. You are a scientist arriving on Cat Island to act as the professors research assistant. It is your decisions that truly make this story interesting as things get dark,
Each person seems to notice it at different times but they are always there to notice providing you know where to look.
The story and writing hooked me, even when I thought I had finished playing, there are the other options and decisions that I didn't choose before that still need to be explored.
If you are the kind of person to get attached to characters then prepare for a rollercoaster of emotions. I myself couldn't get enough of
and my heart hurt whenever I done something that caused them harm or sadness.
You yourself must make the decision on how you spend your time on the island. Research with the professor? Maybe you just want to explore the island? How about those cats? This is a dating sim after all and yet you can ignore the romance part all together if you wish-but why would you want to even do that?
This may surprise a number of people but the soundtrack of this game has become my personal favorite. I am listening to it right now as I type this review! These are currently the only songs I have on my cell phone too, I like them that much.  The OST helps set the mood of each scene perfectly, making the moments either magical or even heart crushing.
The music is so incredibly powerful! I believe it will be much easier to understand my love for it once you have played the game yourself however as once you have the music linked to the scenes in the game that affected you most personal it adds a special touch to them.
This game is not only a dating simulator but also a visual novel. Reading has always had a stronger and more lasting effect on me than any movie or TV series. Because your own interpretation of things becomes a strong factor here there is no telling how you may feel in the end.
The characters in this game are very easy to get attached to.
They each have had so much effort put into them, giving them their own unique traits and [some more than others] incredibly charming personalities. I will be honest, I went in to this game very skeptical as so far very few dating sims have given me any 'feels' at all. The 3 cats I mentioned earlier however- any options that could harm them were things I could not bare to try [at least until my inner achievement ♥♥♥♥♥ came through].
You
become attached to these characters, if you somehow find a way not to then...how did you even do that?
Wow... this game was so much more than I expected. I got this as a christmas gift and I never expected it to become my favorite game. Some people may think I have already spent far too long on this visual novel. I loved this game so much that I went to the developers asking if they had merchandise, because I need some in my life.
The story had me hooked, I wanted to know everything. I replay it and then realize how I missed something the first or second time I played-I can see myself playing this for many more hours yet.
The music adds so much to this game, helping to express emotion to each scene just as it is supposed to. Sometimes I had to fight shedding a tear because I got so into it.
The characters. By far the part of this game I loved the most was the characters. I have never wished characters in a novel or game to be real before, not as much as this at least. The personality in these characters can feel so real and it really does get hard not to fall for them. Dating simulators are meant to capture your heart and this game does just that, leaving you wishing there was so much more.
Do I think this game is worth it's price? Yes! I didn't even pay for it myself and yet I would have gladly done so. I may yet buy it for a number of my friends so that they can go on the same epic tale that I experienced. The game is also currently on sale, though today is your last chance to take advantage of that for a while. I strongly recommend this game. So much so that I have never put such effort in a review before. I really hope this game gets so many more people as hooked as it got me. This game is truly special and I hope your experience will be as wonderful as mine was and will continue to be!

Mars: War Logs is an indie rpg developed by Spiders who recently brought us Bound by Flame. Both games look exciting first, but suffer from certain problems which break the gameplay.
Pros:
There are still a few parts of the game, that may persuade the player to give a chance to the product. The graphics are okay, there is not much to see, but overall the places and people are believable, however do not expect anything fancy. The game kicks off better as it progresses later. I liked the soundtrack in the main menu, which gives the mood. In the early fights also the combat feels good, I had the feeling that something good will come. There are customization options also, which are somewhat in-depth. You can reinforce your gear, both weapons and armor for example with different materials. There are also options to make things out of junk, like medpacks, ammo, etc. The story and dialogues are consumable, nothing really poetic or anything, but it is still one of the better parts of the overall experience. You also have some optional choices which will influence your reputation.
Cons:
And, here comes the cons, because the game has a lot of them. As I got involved into bigger and harder fights I started to see clearly how the combat system cannot handle them. When you face more than 3 enemies at the same time it is starting to get difficult to plan your moves. The target system is not working as intended, and without it you can hardly keep track the movement of the enemy. Usually I get about half a minute before Innocence is incapacitated and all the enemies rush at me. The best tactic is to flee, but there is simply not enough room to do so. The skills also need time to activate, and as the opposite fighters are moving fast, it is almost impossible to use them due to interruption. Overall combat is a mess, nothing more. Also the are problems with the corpses. After some fights I needed to search after the bodies, because they stuck into the wall, and cannot be seen right away. The places looks tiny, corridor-like and they feels alike. The theme itself is not that bad, but is not a rule that each of the sections need to look almost the same.
Overall, I can recommend this title only to those who are really die-hard fans of the rpg genre and have the patience for this.

Sudden Strike wasn’t among the first RTS games I ever played, yet I hold it dear for another reason. It was the first strategic title which taught me both to rely on tactics instead of spamming units from a base and the most important thing of it all, it paved the way for the history buff you’re reading right now. Sudden Strike 1 & 2 along with the Age of Empires and the Total War series, will forever be recognized by me, as the reason why history fascinated me from a young age. No book or boring teacher could have achieved what a couple of excellent RTS games managed in my case. So you’ll have to forgive me if I’m biased about Sudden Strike and its successors.
I shall still judge the game fairly and criticize its flaws, rest assured. Sudden Strike 4 is released 16 years after the title which spawned this excellent series. It may have shifted dev/publisher hands since then, yet the formula has been improved far more than hindered. For a Steam debut, Kite Games have proven themselves a capable team and Kalypso Media Digital deserves even more credit for reviving a franchise whose last attempt was in 2010 (and even then if was unworthy of the Sudden Strike name). So if you want to experience the origins of a game which relies on pure combat & tactics, you can find the Sudden Strike Trilogy on Steam.
I hope you don’t expect me to narrate or even go into detail about World War Two, since I can probably talk and write for hours on end, in regards to this topic. I definitely don’t wish to bore you. No, I won’t make comments about politics and propaganda either. Or “the good guys” and “the bad guys”. Remember:  a soldier no matter on which side he serves, is still someone’s son, husband or friend. And a soldier’s death is as much of a tragedy as that of a civilian. Many of them were too young to be married or fathers themselves and they were drafted into various branches of the armed forces without being asked if they’re willing to die for something as abstract as “patriotism” or “the fight against evil”. Military leadership doesn’t care about cannon fodder afterall. History is indeed written mostly by the victors, but facts that occurred 70 years ago can’t get as twisted by time and malevolence like let’s say, the Middle Ages.
Players shall get to experience Sudden Strike 4’s tactics from the perspective of the Allies (US+UK & USSR) but the Axis is sadly represented just by Germany. Sad to see Italy and Japan neglected, especially since the Rising Sun’s Imperial Army was portrayed in Sudden Strike 2. Alas, there are plenty of historical missions to choose from and learn a good deal of history in the process. Seven missions for each of the three campaigns. While they have different start dates (1939 for Germany, 1941 for USSR and 1944 for the US/UK troops), the campaigns all end in 1945. As expected, a historical approach with no deviation from the norm. The missions themselves upon completion, shall unlock clips with original footage from the war and texts which go further into detail about casualties and outcomes for each operation. Any fan of history shall appreciate these extras.
Sudden Strike 4 has been released two months after Blitzkrieg 3, its “arch-nemesis”. Ironically they both feature highly (and skillfully) modified Unity Engine assets. Powering two of the best pure tactical RTS’ in 2017, is no small feat. Unity seems to be almost everywhere on Steam. From the subpar dollar-bin “game” which could be developed by nearly everyone, to intricately detailed real time strategies such as Sudden Strike 4. Of exactly how much detail are we talking about here? Well the kind, which features tank battles over frozen lakes (unfortunate units can sink, once the ice breaks from the artillery fire), moving vehicle parts, such as antennas and suspensions, not just the wheels or tracks and last but no least, foliage moving in the wind. The perfect cover for an infantry ambush or simply a relaxing sight to behold.
I could almost not believe it that Sudden Strike 4 is a Unity project but for all its pretty effects, there are some obvious cracks into this digital reflection. The first games in the eponymous series, featured persistent wrecks and unit corpses. The fourth rendition has unfortunately opted for them to vanish within 30 seconds. You destroy an enemy tank or a unit of your own, meets an untimely end. In less than a minute they vanish from sight as if nothing happened over there or anywhere else on the mission map. And this is truly ridiculous since it’s 2017. Powerful CPUs, more RAM than you can use and equally capable GPUs, have made PC games further the rift between them and their console alternatives. I refuse to believe that the PC version of Sudden Strike 4 couldn’t handle persistent fallen units on the battlefield. I don’t care about the limitations of the PlayStation 4 version, Kite Games.
I don’t wish to write a full-fledged rant, but I understand at least partially why the game has received some of those negative reviews. For me, it’s not the price that was the issue. Instead I am bothered by how this game shoots itself in the foot. On one hand you have a lot of beautiful in-game effects and on the other, you can’t even hide the user interface or HUD entirely. You like epic screenshots and the various objective markers, mini map, group selector or information displays are standing between you and a perfect image of the battle? You’re out of luck, pal. At best you can hide the objectives tab. By contrast Blitzkrieg 3 lets me transform my Steam screenshots of that game, into wonderful 4K screenshots. Yeah, speaking of resolution, at least Sudden Strike 4 didn’t disappoint me with its frame rate and stability. Maxed out, 4K@60fps constantly.
The soundtrack is decent, if nothing special. The voice acting for the narrators and mission commanders is abysmal though. American English accents for the Red Army and Wehrmacht campaigns? For real? Not even some impecabble British accents to go with the villain cliché? It really breaks the immersion and I couldn’t ignore that. Thankfully, the units themselves, the regular rank and file speak in their native tongues. I couldn’t understand a single word of Russian and I still struggle with German, yet I respect and demand authenticity beyond anything else in my historical games.

By comparison to similar titles, Talisman: Digital edition is a terrible digital port of a board game.  The UI leaves A LOT to be desired, and so many of the flaws are things you would think should be obvious.  Game issues range from minor annoyances to downright broken bugs.  The AI actions also seem completely bizarre; I can rarely fathom why the AI does what it does.  With all the bugs and interface issues that have been present, complained about, and ignored for years, Nomad Games is clearly just milking this cow for as much cash at it can provide.

This game, has to be one of my all-time favorites, amazing world, amazing story, and one of the few times I've really cried during a video game and to that I say, just play it for yourself.  But before you do play it, just some words of advice for you to get the most out of this game.  You can complete this game just by finding these ribbons throughout the game, which kind of trivializes the entire experiences.  There are optional puzzles in this game and they provide a lot of the story along with notes that you find throughout the world and both make the world feel as though it’s living and breathing.  I encourage you if you want to truly fully experience this game, complete the side puzzles and read the little bits of exposition, and if you get stuck do not hesitate to look up a guide, I repeat DO NOT HESITATE TO LOOK UP A GUIDE to 100% this game.  You get so much more out of the story, and trust me the story is amazing, it may seem nebulous at the beginning, but once you have all the info you can scrap from the world it all comes together in a beautiful narrative, that is really, really worth the time and effort.  Also if you do 100% this game there is a second ending, and it adds to story just that much more and really makes you understand everything.  Sometimes the puzzles while they are really interesting are just really obtuse, and don’t feel bad if you don’t get it, just try it out for yourself, and if you aren’t figuring it out, use a guide.
Also one big flaw with this game, there are some bugs in it, not like game crashes or graphical bugs, but things that won’t let you progress and you can’t seem to figure out why, like you just needed to re flip a lever to progress.  For this, again, LOOK UP A GUIDE, a video guide may help a bit more here, but most of the time, you won’t be able to realize the bug, but once you see how things were really supposed to go you’ll be able to see what went wrong and how to fix it in game no problem.
All that said, if you like, say, old point and clicks, or games with really deep stories, than this game is a must, but even if you don’t like those kind of games but are still interested, than still try out this game, it may be an awesome experience for you.  Really this game is amazing narratively, it's just a matter getting past the sometimes annoying quirks/bugs and getting past the sometimes fairly obtuse puzzles to enjoy the narrative fully.
TL;DR: This game is awesome, but take the time to 100% it, and DON’T BE AFRIAD TO LOOK UP A GUIDE, can’t stress this enough, but if you put in the time and effort the game will give back like no other.

In this game, you play as a professional puzzle solver, who has travelled to a curious village to help a bunch of helpless villagers who have all conveniently lost the fourth slider wheel from their combination safes, broken all of their projectors, and rearranged their homes and workplaces into Myst-like puzzles. The game does a good job of capturing that classic Myst feeling of wandering around an expansive puzzle-filled area for 20 minutes, flipping a lever to test it out, flipping it back after wondering whether or not you were actually supposed to flip it yet or not, and then exploring for 20 more minutes until everything finally starts to come together.
The only problem is the strange inventory system, in which instead of having a typical inventory system, you can only carry one item at a time, and have to warp back to your "Case" (which acts as a hub between the different maps) and place items on the various shelves in the main room to store them. It's not as inconvenient as it sounds since the transition between the map and the case is mostly seamless and the shelves are right beside where you arrive in the Case, but it's also somewhat glitchy - at one point early on, one of the safe wheels found in the Case itself vanished after I put it on a shelf and went back to the map, and it never came back. It was presumably a spare wheel since I was able to fully complete the game without it, but if it were to happen to someone else to a more important item it could be game-breaking. But the inventory system also lends towards the "fun confusion" factor of the game, because since a somewhat large amount of items can be picked up and stored in the game you're never as sure whether you need to use a particular item as you would be in a game where you only had three items in your inventory. This was particularly relevant in my case, since on two separate occasions the instructor gave me a friendly reminder that I could store items after picking up an item, and in both cases, that item was a bottle of alchohol. This led me to believe that the bottles might end up somehow being important, and it wasn't until the credits began to roll that I realized that there was no great alcohol puzzle, and I didn't actually need a shelf full of 30 bottles of the village's finest cider for anything other than a good time.
Overall, if you like puzzle games, especially exploration-based ones, this is a pretty easy recommendation. The story is great, and the puzzles are challenging. It's worth noting that while almost all of the real puzzles are optional and completing them only fleshes out the backstory, you won't really get a good experience if you just wander around collecting the ribbons that are the only thing completely necessary to finish the game, but if you're looking for a reasonably challenging puzzle game then this is a great choice.

A thoughtful, heartwrenching tale about a patient suffering from dementia, and the tragic events that took place in the seaside community they grew up in. Themes such as loss, love and the beauty of the mundane echo throughout the game, which on a full playthrough took me around 10 hours.
Visual and sound design come together beautifully in Ether One. Soft, melancholic tracks complement the watercolour aesthetic, and an attention to detail gives each area a vibrant, lived-in vibe.
The gameplay design is pretty intriguing. There are two main pillars. Exploration, and puzzle-solving. Exploration simply involves walking through each location, and finding all ribbons to progress the story. It's not as linear as it sounds though. These levels are sprawling. The environments tell additional stories, some self-contained, but most tied loosely with the main tale. Through scattered notes, diaries, and voice overs you learn about the inhabitants of this small, seaside town; a town that slowly lost its relevance as the decades wore on.
The puzzle sections are optional, but make up the bulk of your gameplay time. As you explore, you will stumble upon projectors, which can be restored by interacting with objects and buildings, in a similar vein to classic adventure games. These puzzles vary from stupidly easy, to obtusely hard, which can be problematic if you're aching to 100% the game. I know many people find the puzzles frustrating, however, they really aren't necessary to enjoy the game's story in full. They're really more like collectables. You do the ones you can, and puzzle the rest out later if you want.
It was a masterful stroke for the developers to do this. Instead of alienating players of either exploration or adventure games, both could experience the beautiful story while playing the game as either or.

I've played this game for a few hours.  While it supposedly is a game based on dementia, I'd call it a exploration game with a story line mostly revealed by solving puzzles.  The puzzles are largely solved by finding objects/clues that enable certain actions to be taken.  When the requisite action for the puzzle have been taken the puzzle is considered solved.  It can be tedious.
First off, the installation went a little oddly, I had to restart the game before it ran smoothly.  I didn't have any further issues with the performance but others have reported issues.
The game play seems fairly open in that you can find the objects and solve the puzzles out of order within a given level.  There are some bugs (or possibly arcane order requirements) that cause one to have to repeat the actions required to solve many of the puzzles.  I find this annoying even if one chgaritably assumes this is intended to simulate the confusion of dementia.
So far there is no tricky jumping such as in Talos for example (i.e. easy navigation).  In fact, the player motions are very hobbled even in areas where a player ought to be able to easily jump (ala HalfLife).  Restrained motions degrade the exploration aspects to that of poking around in persons underwear drawers (yes, really).  Also the many of the bathrooms doors can't be shut when you enter them (that's quite a flaw).
The game is built on the Unreal Development Kit (UDK).  Graphically, the game itself is rendered more like a comic book than like a typical 3D (not saying that's bad but it is not using much of the UDK capabilities).  The game supports Nvidia 3D vision well if you like that sort of thing in a comic book rendering scheme.
The audio is overall quite reasonable but the controls for audio are minimal.  Also the keyboard controls options are limited (a reflection of what is needed in the game).  I didn't try it with game controller as yet (in this game it might be preferable to a keyboard/mouse).   The walking pace is rather slow (even if you run).  The action controls are a bit awkward and do not repond uniformly across the game.
I'm torn in my opinion of this game -- while It certainly has a few interesting puzzles, it's no Talos or Portal.  The clues it provides are rather peculiar/obtuse and some clues IMO are non-sequiturs.  The voice acting is adequate.  I sometimes find the game play compelling but more often it feels tedious.  I can't honeslty rate it a thumbs up even though I like the game enough to have played it for several hours.  I suggest that you first read the helpful negative reviews and if you still want to try this game, wait till it's on sale.

Loving the game visually, similar in art style to Borderlands. Story concept is interesting, but feels like it's only doing the bare minimum to keep me interested in seeing where this goes. Feels predictable so far, so I'm hoping for a fun twist somewhere along the line.

Tera is a fun game. It does some things well. And some things poorly. It's biggest faults are its updates make older items, etc. useless, its free-to-play nature makes micro-transactions completely rediculous, and its end-game content is lacking. There is very little hand-holding, and you can do things or not do them, and move on. It will not be remembered as the best MMO. But I think it will be remembered fondly as a stepping stone in a positive direction.
Let's get micro-transactions out of the way. You don't "need" to ever buy anything to enjoy this game, or even do well in it. You can use it to buy costumes, EXP bonuses, and pets. But none of that is necessary to play. However, the standard costumes suck compared to purchased ones, and accessories and such are pretty cool. And here in lies the problem. Everything is recockulously expensive. Like, I'm not sure if someone messed up the currency conversion, expensive. Add to that the RNG nature of a lot of purchases, and having items not cost an even number of EMP, but not allowing you to purchase small amounts. Really makes the whole experience rage-inducing, or even worse, addictive. Regardless, it's a complete disaster. But I enjoyed the game for free. So I purchased a few things to reward the Developers.
I see a lot of complaints about Elins, and gender locked classes. But I guess I don't have a stick jammed far enough up my colon to care about "little girls", or "breast physics". I actually like the idea of locked classes, though gender-locked is a bit odd. It shouldn't hurt you to play female characters to get, what, three or four classes? My theory is that game devs have to make all new skills, animations, gear for new classes. And players mostly play female characters(and purchase in game stuff for them). So they go where the money is. I'd bet if they sold more male stuff, there'd be male-specific classes.
I wish they had been more organized with updates, etc. so that they'd not have so many, now useless items. Or at least make them worth hundreds or thousands of gold, and not just worthless. And even current items, like crystals, are just spammed at you, but have no value. And there are no quests to explain upgrading/enchanting items to new players. I hope you like Google-sensei. Basically the game is messy if you've played for a while, or stop playing for a while, and get back into it. And they don't advertise special events by email, so unless you log in, you'll miss free character slots, etc.
My favorite thing about the game is the customization of the player(even though creation really could use an update), and the interface. You can set up everything how you like. Even use a controller(but I wouldn't). You "can" make your characer over-sexualized, completely goofy, formal, or festive(for every holiday). Add pets, and mounts. Buy, and sell, "all the things".
The game is really fun, but the armors lack modesty. 8/10 wanted to play ninja but didn't want to be a todler.

D4: Dark Dreams Don't Die is probably one of the strangest things you'll ever play if you choose to do so, but if you are a fan of adventure games with the main focus on storyline, you probably should. You play as David Young, a retired detective of the Boston Narcotics who now spends his time trying to solve the murder of his wife Peggy, after they both have been shot by a mysterious character whose name begins with "D". As David managed to survive the bullet in his head, he lost every memory of that night, but in exchange he obtained the ability to go back in time by touching mementos, objects that have been involved in a particular scene in the past, allowing him to go back in time to that same moment. Aided by his ex-partner Forrest Kaysen, David manages to get his hands on some important mementos related to Peggy's murder, allowing him to travel back in time and solve different puzzles and side-quests along the way. What makes this story weirder than anything else you may have experienced before are the characters, as from the cat-woman Amanda who managed to move into your apartment without reason and without previously knowing you after your wife's death to the mysterious Roland Walken, the game is filled with strange characters that will constantly keep you engaged in the story and make you wonder which one of them is the one you're after. The biggest disappointment in the story is that it ends too soon and without a proper closure either; the game follows an episodic format, however at the end of the season there are only 2 episodes plus the prologue, which can be completed in less than five hours. There are plenty of satisfying things to keep you preoccupied along the way as each side-quest will help you gather more information on each character and reveal their true intentions, but disappointing enough is the fact that in the end they don't really matter, as the outcome will always be the same cliffhanger ending no matter what information you gathered along the way and which one you thought to be the killer.
Originally designed as a Kinect game, the game made the transitions to controllers quite well, something that I strongly recommend if you're playing on PC with a keyboard and mouse in mind. Using your controller makes the game simple and entertaining to play, using basic movements and the right analog to turn around since the game always gives a 360 degrees view from each point. You will spend most of your time interacting with objects, but even in the most basic of things the game doesn't let you put the controller down as opening the fridge requires a quick turn of the right stick, turning the TV on requires yet another action to use the remote and so on. Even during cutscenes you will often be prompted to observe a certain object, gathering more information about it. Observing is something you will do a lot in this game, especially if you're a completionist, as the game has achievements and rewards based on the amount of objects that you observe and interact with in each episode. Observing can sometimes be fun, as moving your hand over an object will give you a short description of what David thinks about it, and while this is an useful thing for important objects, it does become very repetitive for objects you will encounter often, such as credits. Among the objects that you will encounter, you can collect a lot of them, starting with the drinks that restore your vision, a power that allows David to highlight every useful object in his sight and food that will restore your stamina, which will slowly be depleted as you perform actions. Apart from that you can collect credits, clothing articles and bandages to heal your wounds, but even so the world often feels empty of the objects someone would normally encounter in particular scenes, as every item that you can interact with is either food, stamina, credits related or part of the case you're following. The biggest hightlight of D4 however are the fighting scenes, where you will have to quickly respond with basic movements and button presses in action-filled cutscenes that never seem to get boring to watch.
D4 goes for an anime look, which doesn't look bad at all and totally fits the weirdness and silliness of some of the moments the game will throw at you, especially those food eating sessions with Forrest Kaysen that have a special touch of humor. D4's biggest graphics-related problems are the lack of variety in environments as there are only three locations that you will visit for the entire game and the maximum resolution being locked to 1440x900, but even so D4 is not about being realistic or breathtaking, and for what it is, the overall design suits it well.
Ben Pronsky does a fantastic job as the voice of David Young, with other well-known actors in the gaming industry such as David Lodge, Carrie Keranen, Liam O'Brien or Chris Tergliafera completing that circle of believable voice acting that makes the characters unique and strange enough to be in mood with the tone the game wants to set. The soundtrack is amazing, especially the tunes playing in the background of each fight scene, but the sound effects could use a little more variety here and there.
As mentioned before, the game can be completed in less than five hours, but if you're a completionist going for all the achievements you will most likely complete it a second time. There are a lot of customization items for each character from some of the most popular gaming franchises such as Gears of War, Fable, Killer Instinct or Rock Band, but apart from choosing the ones you like to actually wear there is no reason to collect and buy all of them.
If you like adventures games with great stories and you're ready to experience a little bit of strangeness as well, D4 is the game you are looking for, however keep in mind that this is a story above anything else game, so don't expect any complex gameplay or longevity since the game can easily be completed in one session and on top of that the ending does make the entire thing more like a preview for something greater that is set to follow.
This games a perfect example of the good die young.

So what happens when you have a decent story in your mind, but you lack the skills to put it into a decent game?
Well, you end up with a game like this!
Without spoiling anything, the game seems to have a really decent plot... just a shame that there's only 2 episodes in this season, with little hope for a second one coming out anytime soon (this game was originally released on XBOX in 2014).
The season ends with a cliffhanger, and the epiloge hints that there was supposed to be a third episode. This makes me think that the developer was aiming at a second cash grab, by just ending the first season after 2 episodes (about 3 hours of gameplay).
So what about the content?
It's your typical adventure game... with tons of useless content...
Whoever thought it would be a good idea to put in costumes and all kinds of collectibles, should be punched in the face!
But that's nothing compared to the guy that thought it would have been a good idea to put in stamina, health and help system (vision) in a game like this. Basically in a game like this, you try to interact with as much stuff as possible (at least, that's what I do), but here, every interaction (opening doors, picking up objects,...) will cost you 'stamina', which you have to replenish by eating stuff or buying(!) it with points that get thrown around for every little thing you do.
It's nothing but annoying filler content, and it doesn't belong in this game.
Presentation...
The game looks... decent. Animations and graphics are smoother and more detailed than the stuff Telltale is releasing in 2016. However, backgrounds can look a bit dull in some scenes.
The voice acting is decent enough for most characters, but the main characters' voice is beyond bad! He seems to put on a different accent from time to time, and his voice doesn't seem to fit the character in the first place.
On a positive note, the music is pretty decent throughout the whole season.
Conclusion:
At this point, I wouldn't recommend buying the game. The story is anything but finished, there's no indication whether there will be a second season and the asking price of €15 is way to much for a game with this little content and quality.
If you are looking for an alternative, 'Life Is Strange' surpasses this game in every aspect, and will offer a much better overall experience. Quantic Dreams' games are also a big recommendation...

Want to prove to your family that gaming really _is_ an artistic sinkhole?  Play this game...and let them watch.
Mars: War Logs is a great third person brawler game marred by a middle school creative writing class-grade storyline and even worse voice acting.  No.  Seriously - Mars: War Logs' voice cast makes Elizabeth Berkley and Mark Wahlberg look like the principals of the Royal Shakespeare Company.  Forgetable characters, laughable script and a vision of the fourth planet that had me waiting for the Governator to jump out of the shadows and yell, "Get your a** to Mars!".  No...wait...Mars: War Logs makes the original Total Recall look like an art house film.
For all it gets wrong, though, Wars: War Logs has a truly enjoyable combat system and a skill-based character development tree that really allows you to play the game the way you want.  Want to go in guns blazing? No worries.  Prefer to sneak through the shadows and backstab?  You can do that, too!  Want to use "magic" and zap opponents from a distance.  Gotcha' covered. Just put your points in a different skill tree.  There are a lot of possibilities.  The game's crafting system is also fairly interesting and it feels like a nice extension to the skill tree, as you can tweak weapons and armor to match your play style.
Some of the environments have a lot of character, too, though the game very obviously divides larger areas up into smaller battle arenas to keep combat confined to relatively small spaces.  This is probably a memory management technique and, as such, points to this title's origins as a console game.  The problem here, is, which console?  The spaces are _so_ small, I assumed the target platform was the original XBOX or Playstation 2.
So: great combat, a few pretty (but small) spaces, nice crafting and skill systems, terrible storyline that telegraphs every dystopian scifi trope, 1-dimensional characters (to include your own) and voice acting so bad it screams for an MST3K voiceover?
And I'm *recommending* this?  Yes.  Because the combat is worth the $3.75 price of admission.  And because you'll cringe so much at the story that you'll find yourself laughing to relieve the shame.

This game reminds me of several titles: Dragon Age 2 (how the maps are confined), Witcher 2 (combat), and Mass Effect series (story/quest branching). For a traditional RPG it's got some things right, but it has its share of problems.
Pros:
1. Tactical combat. Combat gets even more challenging and fun at Extreme difficulty, but at a price...
2. Nice setting and atmosphere. Mars here is like a remnant of some former colony; a fresh change from those high-tech ones. Everything is rusty, red, and make-shift. Put it another way, it's more like an apocalyptic Mars.
3. Your choices matter. People may die/live, quests may be locked/opened, etc... If you like replaying for different endings then this is for you.
Cons:
1. At Extreme difficulty, a bad selection of skills will make the game almost impossible. There seems to be some skills that must be unlocked first, such as Evade, Sneak, etc.
2. No crowd AI. At hubs you may get invovled in battle, but civilians do not react at all, even when the fight is happening right under their noses. This hurts the sense of immersion.
3. Some quest are hidden inside branching conversations and are easily missed if you choose the wrong reply (but you have no idea of the difference). Choose between "just say it!" or "ok ok i got it"?
4. Characters and lore are rather under-developed. For an RPG of this length (30hr for me), you only get to know a few of the characters. Some just pop up with little background info. The romance here is merely a filler.
5. In combat you only have limited control on your companion (only 4 "states"), which sometimes is not that helpful.
Despite the cons, I still enjoy this game a lot, primarilly for its combat and story. If you aren't that picky about graphics and AI and just expect a down-to-earth action RPG, this shouldn't disappoint you.
