First off, let me say this:  If you're looking for a mindless, button-mashing type of game where you can vent your frustration on a hapless 12 year old kid (who is apparently also your father), this game is not for you.  If, on the other hand, you are looking for something to challenge your intellect both via in-game puzzles and through a touching story, then by all means, take my recommendation and play on, Restorer.
As this is an independently developed game, I was prepared to grant some leniency for in-game errors.  Imagine my surprise when none was needed.  Sure, you may have some slight clipping here or texture issues there, but I have personally experienced far worse from AAA-developed games.  Early in the game's release, bugs seemed to be relatively commonplace.  After my playthrough, I believe that the vast majority of them have been addressed in an adequate manner;  I experienced no faults throughout my time in the game.  That having been said, let's get into the categorical scores.
GRAPHICS:  8/10
Not terribly graphics-intensive, but then again that wasn't the emphasis of the game.  If I had to describe it, it would be Minecraft meets Fable meets Borderlands.  The effective use of cell-shading and traditional art styles really gives the game a unique look that oozes style and mystery while still being relatively believable.  As mentioned above, there were some slight graphics issues, but on the whole seemed really well polished.  I'm giving it 8/10 because I feel that with a bit more work they could have made the game just a *wee* bit more realistic, which would have added to the immersion factor.
ATMOSPHERE:  9/10
Very unique locations help the game's immersion.  Mines, lighthouses, harbor towns, industrial complexes, forests and laboratories; this game covers a wide variety of terrain, and does so well. The artwork helps blend them together into a seamless backdrop for the story.
GAMEPLAY:  9/10
Gameplay was smooth as silk.  The game ran fine on my laptop, which is by no means a dedicated or optimized gaming rig.  You should have no issue playing this on a desktop.
STORY:  10/10
Allow me to preface this by saying I wish I could give it 11/10.  Oh wait, I'm the author of this thing, so yeah, I CAN do that!  The story is brilliant.  The mechanic of dementia is not a common element in video games today, though if it is, it is most likely used in the horror genre.  The game sets you up on the path to unwinding the story and lets you go at your own pace.  There is no time limit, no pressure, nothing to compel you to complete it except for your own desire to know how the story ends.  I don't want to give anything away, but I will say this; the ending is well worth the time and frustration of figuring out the optional puzzles.
TL;DR
Great game, thoroughly enjoyed it.  Puzzles left me thinking about the game even after I quit playing, and the compelling story kept me enthralled.  Refreshing change of pace from my usual games.  If you're on the fence, I recommend going for it.

Tharsis has so many concepts working great for it, let me be clear on that. I love the core concept of a disasterous journey to mars, where the crew you have must survive through so many differing aspects of ship management.
I find myself continually playing the game, but always taking a severe beating (even on Easy)...And recently it's gotten to the point where my enjoyment is dwindling because the odds (dice random rolls) are just never in my favor and the difficulty is too steep.
Tharsis challenges the player to maintain their crew, ship, and many extra attributes to find a balance for surviving a journey to mars. The main problem I find is that there are too many choices, but given the immediate critical actions that are happening, most get left by the wayside as you fight to keep your ship intact even by turn 4. This leaves your crew suffering, hungry, and quickly out of dice for futher progression.
I want to love Tharsis and recommend it to others, I really do. I also want to say I've had a successful mission, but I haven't even got close. In fact i'm so far off that even getting halfway through the journey is an accomplishment for me. But I don't see how getting to Mars and getting a completed journey is even in the realm of possibility for the average player. It's just a game that's too punishing because of randomization via the dice system, and far too many reliant systems for those dice.
Pretty fun little game.  Worth picking up if it's cheap.

With a metactric score of 49 when writing this review I might have passed this one by, but my affinity for pixely graphics and throwback gameplay compelled me to give this game a shot.
In Bad Bots, you play as Sam McRae aboard the Titan Hauler in this side-scrolling 'metrovania' style shooter. With a plot right out of an Asimov novel, Sam McRae finds himself the only survivor of a robotic uprising incited by a malevolent AI; a story we are all familiar with, but maybe originality isn't what this game is going for.
I've spent just about a half-hour in game by the time of doing this review, maybe that's too short but in my opinion it was easy to see where the game was going. In either case, feel free to take my review with a grain of salt due to my lack of time in the game.
In a very crowded market of side-scrollers does Bad Bots have what it takes to stand a head taller than the rest? Personally, I don't think so. Maybe it's just my affinity for this sort of games but I feel like Bad Bots could have been a good game but the game's overall lack of polish and thoughtfulness hold it back. First of all, there's very little music in the game, I even thought the game was broken at first. I suspect it was aiming for a Half-Life vibe but I don't think it achieves this. In Half-life there are many other sound effects and visuals to occupy your attention, but with Bad Bots you're left with an aural void that doesn't feel particularly artistic and more like the developers trying to save money. I mentioned previously that this game lacked thoughtfulness; unlike a well thought out game of this genre where every room and enemy is placed with intention, rooms in this game seem to be thrown in arbitrarily and filled with rows of identical enemies. It's also nearly impossible to avoid being hit as enemies shoot with laser precision (hey, they're robots after all) through all manner of platforms and other obstetrical. To compensate the level is loaded with copious amounts of ammo and health and in my book this is a sign of weak level design.
In my first 30 minutes of gameplay I was able to make it to the first boss; they actually busted out the music for this battle. The boss quickly fell to my weapon in the matter of
. This lack of challenge doesn't inspire me to keep playing and leaves me with an empty gaming experience. I supect the challenge level would increase later on, but based on the previous gameplay how much of this challenge is derived from unavoidable damage taken from laser accurate gunfire.
Bad Bots appears to be a port of a Xbox game so it does support USB controllers. Conversely it seems they put minimal effort into doing a proper PC port as it lacks any options to rebind keys or even view what the keyboard controls art. Even the ingame control hits still show the Xbox buttons when you are using a keyboard/mouse. Playing with the keyboard and mouse literally required me to guess what the buttons are.
On the positive side, besides for the pixely graphics and retro gameplay (which is entirely subjective) the feel on destroying enemies is quite good. The game features storyboards that narrate the story and the overall presentation is decent but the previously mentioned flaws keep me from recommending this title. It's a shame as I feel this game did have potential.
Score: 5/10

In Bad Bots you're a mechanic who finds himself on a spaceship that's overrun by berserk robots. The story begins promisingly: you find yourself in a compactor akin to Star Wars and have to escape there with a portable AI who aids you on the way. Story advances in static cutscenes like a comic.
Then you meet the first knife bots. Their animation is annoyingly clunky. The bots will be armed with guns soon, thankfully with a better animation, and so are you: they will shoot you from behind boxes and will take cover if shot, which is cool. However, it is soon realized that their damage output is appalling: if faced with a single bot, it would take forever to die, for most attacks cause 1 HP of damage and you have 100 HP. Coupled with the fact the spaceship is full of health packs with 20 HP heal each, you probably won't die unintentionally during the story campaign except maybe to the final boss (or that death trap of a compactor along the way). You can effectively charge any non-boss enemy. To amend this, the game later throws at you tens or even hundreds of melee bots, electrocuting service droids and wall-crawling critter bots whose purpose is not explained.
These "waves" become easy when you start to understand the controls. Those are at times rather quirky. Jumping, you might hold on to a ledge you did not want to. Character defaults to climbing ladders, during which you cannot shoot, and you can't fall off the ladder except by jumping sideways upwards. At the top of the ladder the character might not take off the ladder at all to the direction you wanted, requiring awkward multiple tries to get it working.
There's no music except in the title screen. The game could have benefited from some eerie music, but now it's just awkward. Maybe you could put some scifi-style music on the background.
One thing that works is the spaceship interior design. The ship has everything a dreadnought is supposed to have from living quarters to storage to waste disposal, and it's used as well within the story. However the story, while beginning nicely, quickly proves to be rather stereotypic. And due to the bots' damage output being so low, it is implausible that the bots ever succeeded killing the rest of the crew.
As a basic platformer this game is okay. I would not call it a good platformer game though and can't recommend it. There's nothing new to the genre and it's otherwise too basic and simplistic to stand out. If you're still interested and/or just love platformers, I'd advice to get it on sale. For achievement hunters, it's quite alright, as it is fast to get them all: 4 to 5 hours should do it, unless you miss some on the first campaign run like I did.

is a game that combines luck and attending to problems in the correct order. You control a crew of 4 on a spaceship bound to mars. Each crew member has a maximum of 5 Health Points, and a maximum of 5 Dice Points. When ever a crew member rolls his dice, he will roll the amount of dice that is corresponding to his DP, while deducting one for the next turn. Each turn, some module  on the ship breaks downs. depending on luck, it can be something non critical, something that'll damage your ship at the end of the turn, damage the crew at the end of the turn and so on. In order to repair that module, one or more crew members can be assigned to a damaged module. The damaged module has a number above it, that indicated how many points it needs in order to be repaired. There are some aspects that I didn't include here, but this is enough to get the general idea of the game. Be warned, this is a pretty hard game, especially if you are not lucky.

I was at a Grateful Dead show one time, sitting out on the lawn seats, when some hippie sitting next to me asked me if I wanted any crunch berries.  It being a Dead show, we were like....an hour and a half into the first song of the concert and I knew it was going to be a long night so I figured I better eat.   Those were some crunch berries.
It didn't take long for whatever those things were laced with to kick in, before I knew it I was seeing all sorts of bizarre creatures and crazy stuff that I knew wasn't actually there. I mean hell.....the lawn section started to look like a dungeon and Jerry Garcia (RIP) started to look like a fat little devil with wings.  (That may not have been a hallucination.)  That was all well and good, it being The Dead and all, but it wasn't long before I started getting the munchies AND getting a wicked case of the munchies, so I figured I had to make my way to the concession stand.
As you can imagine, walking through a see of dirty hippies, tripping balls and hallucinating like a mofo is quite the adventure.
That's kind of what Giana Sisters feels like.  A crazy trip to the concession stand, with the pay off being a satisfying plate of greasy nachos that satisfies a case of the mary jane munchies like no other!
In addition to that great aesthetic, it's got some kick♥♥♥♥♥game play too.  I love platformers like a Dead Head loves crunch berries, and this has some of the tightest platformer controls in this modern era.
Did you stay up until the wee hours letting Mario crush your dreams as you made your way through the later levels, never giving up until you hit that flag at the end?  Did  you lean your first swear words at the hands of Kid Icarus?  Do you enjoy crazy♥♥♥♥♥trips at jam band music festivals?   You'll love Gianna Sisters: Twisted Dreams then!

I believe that adding a steam workshop to this game so you can customize rules, card sets and characters more easily would fix all my issues with this particular version. However as is, this is a literally waste of time and effort. Please games workshop give the community the chance to do what I know so many have done with your board game and let us make the game more fun as we see fit.

At first glance, Twisted Dreams seems like a rather simplistic (and somewhat nice-looking) platformer. You play as the sisters, controlling one but able to alternate between the two at any time. The two sisters each have an ability, one shoots straight in a ball of fire while the other jumps into a twirl, drifting slowly downward. And that is, for the most part, the extent of their abilities.
However, what makes this platformer very inventive is the change in the environment whenever you switch between the two sisters. Pathways may open and close, platforms may change directions, monsters will change form and possibly change their desire to attack you. And while this may sound plain, it really isn't. Unlike most other platformers, the world is not static. How the environment changes will in turn force you to change how you play. Ultimately, this makes the game engaging and challenging, as you're not only trying to control your character--but the world itself as well.

Won't take very long to beat if you're good at platformers, but there's a lot of replay value if you like collecting stuff and the levels are long and increasingly difficult.  Worth the 7 bucks I paid for it.

I thought I was a chosen one for this game, Hundreds of anime watched and some Telltales/Dontnod games completed. So what could possibly go wrong?
Problems start right in the beginning. The main character is restricted in movement, so he can only move like a train from station A to station B by following the guidelines. It feels awkward, but this is kind of person preferences, so you might like it, I guess, in parallel universe. Plus, add to this a stamina meter, which doesn't really feel needed and make the whole process of exploring uncomfortable. Its still not so bad, so let's go next.
The main problem comes with narrative and setting. I mean, Im totally ok with all of this Japanese weirdness. When its good, when there is a quality behind it. But here you get a total cliche western detectives combined with a most typical anime overreactive agressive unhuman girl in a bunny god**** costume. Such mix of heroes might sound intriguingly, but in reality it's just bad. Not so bad thats its good, but just bad and unimaginative.
But ok, it's still possible to overcome, The thing. which made me delete this game after 1.5 hours of playing are the dialogs. First of all its a narrative game, so the good dialogs could level the balance of good and evil, Unfortunetly, they turned into the dark side. Most of them or just too boring or absurdly stupid. Combine all this stuff and you'll get a lack of motivation for completing the game, The concept is there, but its not enough to make you seek for the answers,
In the end I must say one major thing, I've played only 1.5 hours of it, so the dialogs are might be better as narrative progresses, characters might show some "non cliche" depth to them and narrative get some more progression. At very end the game have a very positive score of reviews, so thats should mean something. But for all of this possible goodness you have to overcome the problems I've mentioned before and oh boy if it's not that easy.

Ignore my time on record, I played this on mobile before it came to Steam. This game is hilarious for all the wrong reasons. The premise is actually a decent one, but how they handle the relationships between you and these men is just beyond off-putting. I've never played a Japanese dating sim that didn't have a very dubcon feel, I expect that from their story telling style. However, this crosses that territory in to just plain creepiness and it feels totally unintentional. This game fails to understand how it comes across to a Western audience in particular. I played this game on mobile first and live blogged the entire thing and..the one thing that kept coming up was "are you sure this isn't secretly a horror game?". It would have succeeded far more as a thriller. I'm sorry but when you have three erotic scenes in one particular route and you're not even on a first name basis with the love interest by the end of the game, how am I supposed to take that? This entire office is INSANE. They are all crazy about you as if this were a frat house and they'd never actually encountered a woman before. Not only that but the way they ALL insult you and treat you as if your worth as a woman is limited to their cosmetics..it's baffling. With lines line "a goddess shouldn't ever have chapped lips, fix that" and "for someone who works for a cosmetic company you sure don't care about your appearance it's disapointing" and "I'm going to feed him like a pet, and train him to stay away from you." [in reference to a really sweet new guy wanting to have lunch with you], "Look at you using lip stick like a good girl!". Everyone in this story is emotionally abusive and manipulative. I expect that from our tsundere and glasses types, but literally, EVERYONE is like that in this story (even if they aren't a love interest). This game is baffling. Not as baffling as Secrets of Me--a game by this same company I really hope comes to Steam because you have to play it to believe it--but darn close. Nothing in this game is romantic or sweet. The only reason you should invest any money into it is a morbid curiosity of how deep the rabbit hole goes and how utterly psychotic everyone is. If you change your perception of the game and view it as a psychological thriller or a dark comedy or even a satire of this genre, you may enjoy it more, but as a romance novel it's laughably awful, insulting, and just degrading. If it were more self aware, maybe, but it clearly isn't.

Another solid port from the the Forbidden Romance mobile series.
As a huge fan of FR, I got this game in a heartbeat. I had actually downloaded it on mobile and tried the prologue + first free chapter of a few guys that interested me. Having everything neatly bundled up and with such a great discount is a must if you're interested!
On the positive side, the artwork is beautiful. The sprites have a lot of variations in expressions and the CGs are closeups/busts tht can be seen in their full glory in the gallery once unlocked. The backgrounds are okay and so is the music, few very chill track that aren't too distracting (special mention for the cheesy 'romance time' track).
The MC suffers from MC-ness, but is actually quite accomplished professionally, is passionate about her job and has great skills in Statistics, so I liked that she was competent and experienced.
Disclaimer: I was only interested in Kaido and Hyoga, and brute forced the rest of the routes via skipping, so I'll be talking briefly about those.
Disclaimer 2: given the theme of the game, I perhaps unfairly compared the two routes I played with the LEGENDARY Ebihara and Aiba routes in In Your Arms Tonight by Voltage. Both of the games share the similar Harlequin flavor, but Office Lovers is much more formulaic. The reader will immediately know what's happening, while the MC is confused.
Disclaimer 3: as another reviewer pointed out, the MC gets abused a lot. I mean A LOT. How and if she has comebacks depends on the route (she snapped back in Hyoga's, but in Kaido's she passively ate up the harrassment). All the love interests are on the jerk side.
So, Kaido. 50 Shades-lite. As someone in the scene, his route, which should portray S/M dynamics, reads as clumsy as best. Words like 'punishment, good girl, naughty' are thrown in there but don't really mean anything. He's also a jerk. The MC in his route is very proactive, puts effort in her work and actually works. She's put in charge of something different in every route, and in Kaido it was nailpolish. She came up with a neat idea, I thought, and I enjoyed the office bits.
I screenshotted very angrily Kaido's route, but in the end I found it entertaining and I overall liked it.
Hyoga was actually my first choice, as I liked him so much in Kaido's route (and I have a thing for foxy older guys). I thought he was mature, but oooh boy I was wrong. He's a manchild.
Heavy spoilers:
Weirdly enough, I also had a bit of trouble keeping up in his route because transitions from one scene to the other were non-existant or inconsistent. I think they're looking into that already.
If you like the setting, if you like FR games, if you like light, entertaining reads, this game is for you. It's nothing groundbreaking, but it deliver what it promises, and the love interests are many and different enough that I'm sure you'll like at least someone. Plus, each route takes about 3 hours, and sequels & date scenarios are included. For the price, it's a steal.
If you're unsure, you can check out the prologue and the first free chapter of each guy on mobile and if you like a couple, the Steam version is a better deal.
Edit: if you like the setting but find all the romance options insufferable jerks, you may want to check out My Famous Lover instead, by the same company (only on mobile at the moment). Haruki's route in particular was really sweet, Yuma's was good as well. I hope they will port it on Steam as well, I find it one of their best games! And the MC doesn't get abused in that one.

This is an excellent game, and is the current flagship game for the city building genre in my opinion. For my requirements, it is NEARLY perfect, save for a few drawbacks and gripes.
The Good:
- The main game is well-presented, stable and fun to play!
- Build restrictions are not noticable. You have a massive 25 lots to work with  and you're probably talking an area as big as say Liverpool, The Wirral and outlying suburbs (9 lots by default, mods unlock the rest).
- Mods: The community is active and talented. Everything from tiny props to reworks of key gameplay mechanics*.
- Good controls. Sometimes the grid snaps are a pain but they can be disabled/enabled quickly. Overall works well.
- Graphics are good for the genre. Not expecting AAA graphics here but certainly does not disappoint.
- Acceptable traffic simulation -> imo you need to download the mod, "Traffic Manager: Presidential Edition" to get the most out of this. This mod add some insane road config and traffic management options that will keep you occupied for hours and greatly improves the immersion for the game.
- MASS TRANSIT DLC: Get it! It adds a decent range of new transport options and contains core upgrades that certain mods need to work right.
- NATURAL DISASTERS DLC: Unusually fun! You can have disasters happen spontaniously or you can spawn them manually, from a selection made available to you in the options. Unobtrusive, so you still have a good chance of bulding a decent city**.
AFTER DARK DLC: Like Mass Transit, it adds to the dynamic of the game, this time by focusing on tourism. Great way of adding variety to your city.
- Collosal: The developer. They've made an excellent game and have been maintaining it well. Can't ask for much more.
Missed opportunities / weird things / things with potential:
- Districts: the feature works well enough to help split up your city into named areas but works weirdly. e.g. certain DLC features like "Organic markets and health shops" are set as spawnable as part of a district policy. This is weird, as generally such shops should be spawned based on the local demographics in the area.
- Traffic in general: This is not too bad as there are mods that fix it, but out of the box the Cims are a little dumb at driving. It's also difficult to truly optimise junctions as the stock game doesn't let you adjust traffic lights or, road priorities or even lanes.
- NATURAL DISASTERS DLC: **they missed a trick by not including nuclear and zombie based apocalypses. Nuclear may be a touchy one, given certain real life histories, and current events, but zombies would have been so cool! Both together would be epic. This DLC included bunkers that remind me of Vaults from Fallout. At the moment the facilities are automatically managed by the city but it would be so cool if you could build the vault (maybe an expansion to the underground view to let you add facilities and such like to each vault independently.
- GREEN CITIES DLC: It's ok. Get it on offer as it will add variety to the way your city looks, but I was really hoping for a bit of future-tech. Proper electric cars (maybe self-drive ones) with a gameplay "fuel" dynamic designed around them, so you get petrol/diesel stations as plopable buildings that offer folks the ability to refuel, and can leter upgrade to hydrogen and electric fuelling stations. Then perhaps a breakdown recovery service for folks that run out of fuel.
Forgettable stuff:
- All of the other DLC: It's the achilles heel of Collosal. Well-priced DLC is something that I think Collosal are still working out the balance for. Some are great, others are a waste of money.
Summary
For lazy folks that don't like reading:
- Base game = 8.1/10
- Base game with good DLCs and mods: 9.3/10
- Base game with all DLCs and mods: 9.42/10

Ether One is a very different game. On the "cover" it is a first person puzzle adventure game. But it is much deeper and darker, where it deals with dementia and its treatment, while delving deeper and deeper in hidden memories.
One particularly good aspect of Ether One is its puzzles. Most of them are tricky and difficult, but they make sense as long as you pay attention to details and explore well. There are no "how the hell was I supposed to know THIS" puzzles, and if you experience them, it means you missed a clue somewhere.
The game looks, sounds, and feels very immersive. Graphic style reminds of Borderlands and is very pretty. Ambient music and authentic sounds for all locations are varying from relaxing to unsettling. The movement of the player feels natural and interaction controls seem clunky only till you learn how to use them.
The story is written well. In games like these with unusual themes the story tends to become a mess, and even though there are points of it in Ether One that you have to think over to understand, it's a story that could be a well written novel where you need to use your brain to interpret parts of it in your own way. The game invites to this interpretation, while at the same time remaining logical and clear on the main parts of the story.
Keep in mind that there are a few bugs in Ether One, so some puzzles randomly may not be solvable. I am missing a certian part of a smaller story because of this. I hope there will be more patches fixing those.
The game is dark and emotional, and probably one of the most "grown up" games that exist out there. This was an experience I won't forget (hopefully no pun intended). Strongly recommended to anyone who is into psychology, thrillers, good puzzle solving, and anyone who likes getting immersed into atmosphere-filled environments.

David Young himself with his contant bubblegum chewing and Boston accent is delightfully charming in an industry full of 'serious' protagonists that wouldn't be caught dead making stupid faces at Chinese fortune cookies or piling on a literal pound of crackers in clam chowder. In a nutshell, the game is refreshingly silly while keeping its gameplay simple enough to be able to be easily picked up and played.

This is review for a game with criminally low sales.

D4 is a 3D adventure game that hits you with presentation right from the start and never lets you go till the end of the ride. It has cool characters, impressive directing, awesome dialogues, and really funny QTEs.

D4 is a detective story with murders, dangerous drugs, US marshals and undercover agents. One would think that protagonist is a clueless FBI agent working on a regular case, but no:
you are a private investigator, involved in all this mess only for your investigation's sake.

This game takes place in a super eccentric world, but everything feels very natural and you easily accept all the oddities, without noticing them. It takes a special skill to create an odd world which feels as normal as the world you are currently living in.

The best way to play this game — beer in one hand, mouse in the other. D4 is fully mouse-driven (or you can use a controller, it’s your choice, I’m not judging you), so it feels like classic point’n’clicks used to. It’s all implemented in a very convenient way — after a minute or so, you begin to move like a breeze and track items with ease. It is a good transition of classic point’n’click mechanics to a 3D era.

Core gameplay also has a very cool aspect: you have health, stamina and vision points. Health for hazardous actions, Vision for hints and Stamina for interactions with people and objects. So in this game you can literally exhaust yourself by talking to someone or looking at mirror. Because of this, you can’t just click everything in sight — you must mind the state of your character and make your priorities. As for “pixel-hunting”, lots of it has been made dynamic — you must spot something not at your own time, but during an interaction, a cutscene, etc, and be rewarded for success, sometimes even with bonus “Extra cases” — a type of side activity that D4 offers.

Graphics and overall visual aesthetics show that not every game with cell-shading should look awkward. You barely notice it.

Music is nice, but nothing you would listen to outside of the game. It really works within the game, though.

The only real problem this game has is right in its name — “Season 1”. So yes, it is not a full game, it is only the first part. And this is really a plague of this type of distribution: people don’t want to buy it before it’s complete, but it won’t be completed if people don’t buy it.

On the other hand, we have a game with deep investigations; cool aesthetics; a topic-based dialogue system that actually works; superb presentation and overall design. Made by developers of a Deadly Premonition, with every good part DP had left intact and every bad part tossed away.

If you’re still reading this, you definitely should try it out. It is super cool even for what it currently has to offer.

This is one of the rare games that gets your brain in motion, keeps it thinking for solutions when you are not playing, and makes you feel smarter after you've played it.
It's about making short simple programs, with very limited tools. For example, you can copy, paste, add or substract but you can't multiply or divide. At the beginning you just need to add 2 and 2, but this rapidly escalates to making divisions (still without a division tool!), sorting data in alphabetical order, and extracting prime numbers!
It will require quite some creativity, experimentation and debugging to achieve, but you will be surprised and amazed how simple the solution always is.
It's about programming and yet it's not actual programming. It just teaches you how how to "think" like a machine. If you actually have programming skills you will possibly find this game too easy, or frustrating.
Otherwise Human Resource Machine is a really challenging experience; it will require you to imagine and conceptualize your programs beyond what's displayed on the screen, until you find one of the solutions. There are many ways to solve each puzzle. Sometimes you think you've got it, and the game will throw an error message and then kindly feed you a different sequence to demonstrate how your program was flawed.
If this prospect doesn't scare you, go ahead and dive head in; I warmheartedly recommend Human Resource Machine!

A pretty simple and straightforward, yet classic board game about choosing whether to go right or left - and that statement really isn't that far from the truth. I don't mind it myself because it can be really enjoyable to play with your friends and in my opinion that's what's most important about these type of games.
But when you're making a video game adaptation of a board game, you have to somehow compensate for the lack of physical interaction between the players and the social part of it - by making the game experience much smoother, faster, more manageable (simplifying the things that the players have to do mechanically - taking away all of the mess with tokens and cards etc.) and approachable.
And this is the standard that I expect from every board game adaptation like this - this is something that is pretty much must be if there's any point in hoping that one would play it longer than 2 game sessions.
And this is where this title fails - the UI is really, really clunky, a lot of interactions seem not to work as expected; not to mention some pretty annoying bugs that we've tackled very early on into the game. These are the basic things that the game should provide, and while I find the existence of bots really helpful (when someone suddenly has to go somewhere or just got really tired of the game, he can leave without spoiling the fun for everyone), this is not really enough to compensate for the rest of the issues this game has.
The game itself is quite fun, as I said, but the board game original is the one that should be praised - the digital edition is very mediocre and is, as it seems to be, a superficial, hastily made, badly playtested piece of programming crap, and for that, thumbs down.

Ether One is a rather ambitious game that falls under the ever-popular "walking simulator" genre. On it's surface, Ether One seems like another stab at an Amnesia game, and whilst it does borrow alot of key features from them, it is something so much more different.
I have never quite played a game like Ether One, but it is one I have always dreamed of. A compelling narrative that can be enjoyed without the need of puzzles (but there are tons of optional ones) and a story that just makes you want to keep playing and playing until you reach that ending. Despite the core narrative being rather short, you can get well over 10 hours out of this game.
Whilst the game begins off rather tedious, Ether One quickly grabs you in with it's impressive story. Impressive is an understatement. It's been a long time since a game made me think, not just about the game itself, but about the value of human life, and just how fragile a thing like life is.
For an Indie title, this deserves the AAA treatment. Buy this. Right now.
+ Amazing narrative. One of the best I have experienced in years.

+ A very ambitious project. I'm glad it managed to produce something so inspiring.

This game's art design is gorgeous (effortlessly shifting the world from the cute and cuddly one dark Giana is in and the dark and sinister one cute Giana is in) and the soundtrack is perfect for a platformer - catchy and up-tempo.

Ah Ducktales Remastered. I'll admit this game had me unsure at first because I was already aware of some of its flaws but then again, its beautifully-rendered 2.5D graphics and the music tracks especially the Moon Theme drew me in and it was what convinced me to finally buy this game during a sale.
OK so what's great about it? The graphics are amazing as I've said. The animators worked so hard to recreate the Disney characters and they succeeded. They look like they leapt straight out of the cartoon and into the game. The music...good God it's beautiful. The Moon theme is great but the Mount Vesuvius theme ain't no slouch either. It's a new track and despite it being like this industrial dubstep/EDM sound, it strangely works. The gameplay itself is simple and straightforward but that doesn't mean it's easy. This is a remaster of an NES classic after all and that means a lot of platforming. Overshoot or undershoot your attacks or jumps and you lose health or die. Basically, it gives a decent challenge (for the most part).
Now what's bad? Notice the "for the most part" above referring to the game's challenge? Well this has more to do with the game design. The levels prior to the final level are fairly the same difficulty but the last level is like going from a 0 to a 100 in less than a second. I understand challenge but challenge should be given gradually to the player not just thrown around like a slap to the face. Another notable flaw I'm sure you already probably know of is the constant cutscenes throughout the level. It just disrupts the game too often. I wouldn't mind if they were before or after a level but the levels instead have a ton of cutscenes in between and it really kills the mood. Now if you say "Just skip the cutscene!" which you could but if you're following the game's story (like me), then cutscenes are necessary. Maybe if they cut them down some then it could have worked.
Overall, the game is still highly suggested. It may have the two prior flaws but it is still highly enjoyable. Plus, there are a lot of extras to get including the music, TV show concept art, video game concept art, the approved art sprites for the game and so much more. Again, it's not perfect but with what I got, I was still satisfied. It just felt so good to play Ducktales again after so long. If you can get past the two prior flaws, this will be a great game to add to your library especially if you grew up with the show. 3/4 stars.

This release is a mobile port from the extremely popular Timberman. On mobile it was free but it is it actually worth purchasing the game?
Timberman is an extremely basic game, but it is highly addictive and fun. All you have to do is chop on the left and right of the right avoiding the incoming branches. You have to try and get as high as possible and so get as high a score as possible. There is a system put into place to stop you going to slow also. A bar slowly runs down the slower you go but goes up if you chop really fast. If this bar reaches zero then you will loose.
The really reason to purchase this on steam instead of playing on mobile is the new multiplayer mode. It's a lot of fun. You could describe it as a kinda tug of war gamemode. It uses the deteriorating bar from the other mode but with a twist. You both use the same bar. So you have to try and go faster than the other person so you don't loose. This mode isn't on the mobile version and is steam exclusive.
That's about it for timberman. There is very little content but your playtime will come from repeating the game to try and beat your highscore. I think the multiplayer mode is enough to consider a purchase if you already play the mobile version. For the price of only £0.79 it is well worth it. But I do hope they update the game putting some other modes in it to have a bit of variety.
Disclaimer: I was provided with a free key by the developer to make this review.

Who would think that being doomed in space might by so entertaining?
"Tharsis" is a dice/tabletop game of space survival, where you lead the crew of 4 astronauts to reach Mars in a damaged spaceship. You make repairs, gather food for your crew, manage ther level of stress - all using dices.
Each round you are facing new dangers (damages to your ship) which, if not resolved, will destroy your ship or kill the crew. When you surive the round, you distribute food, which let your people function and perform tasks, and make tough decisions, which affect the odds of surivival for the group. You can even become a cannibal and feed upon your deceased crew members (or kill them to do so). It's a nice touch, and really builds the atmosphere of desperation in being doomed in space.
This is primarily risk/reward management game, but the luck factor is high (this is a dice game, after all), and may be frustrating to many players. This is why I prefer playing on "easy" mode, which give you decent chance of surival, but still offers a challenge to win the game.
"Tharsis" offers nice enough visuals and audio (screams and other unpleasant sounds can be creepy at times), and decent replayability, but after 5-10 hours you will probably move on to other games. I think the game is worth checking if you are into digital board and dice games.

I am an archer myself, so I was really interested in this title.
Before I bought the game on steam, I had already tried out the free version (with microtransactions) from the developers website to find out if I would enjoy this.
What is this game?
It is NOT a free ranging hunting sim like The Hunter. It is more like a very slow shooting gallery. You will not stalk any animals but wait for them to come towards your tree stand/ hide. Therefore this games requires quite a bit of patience. Slightly annoying is the fact that if you miss the deer, it is basically game over and you have to restart the level. This can get really frustrating. There is also some grinding involved of the easier levels to improve your gear.
The levels become more difficult the more you advance and add extra challenges, to spice up the shooting gallery.
I thought it was a nice touch that you can walk around the forest before the hunt and collect antler casts to earn extra money.
The graphics are serviceable but basic. Nothing to write home about, but at least the animals are nicely animated.
But, in some cases, the animals have slight pathfinding issues.
I also noticed some clipping and glitches.
In addition, the game crashed on me once while navigating the menu.
Positives- very relaxing game. The forest sounds are nice and add to the soothing atmosphere. The game runs fine on my old labtop (even if I had one crash) and controls are straightforward. The animals are nicely animated.
Negatives- gameplay can get repetitive. It also requires a lot of patience.
If you are looking for a open world hunting sim, go with The Hunter (which has the downside of being very expensive in the long run). If you want more action, maybe try hunting in Skyrim or try out Carnivores Dinosaur Hunter (which is great for the price).
If you are looking for a nice slow relaxing game, this might be it.
My only criticism is that it is a bit overpriced for what you get. The price is a bit steep for a shooting gallery that does not allow you to shoot more than one deer and where you have to restart the level when you miss a deer.
I also hope the developer works a bit more on improving the pathfinding of the animals and solves some of the glitches (when my character holds the GPS unit, my fingers poke through the GPS screen). Also, I had a crash when navigating the menu. If the developer fixes these issues and adds some more content (I would love to see a hunting recurve bow), the game might become worth it for the price.
So yes, I recommend the game, with some restrictions. I especially hope for some updates and more content from the developers.
If you want something slow and relaxing, this game would be worth picking up on a discount.

For veteran players like myself, having grew up with C&C and Starcraft amongst others, it currently lacks a little depth in variety of units.
Graphically the game has a charming appeal, and the soundtrack and sound design is well done, as you'd expect from Frank Klepacki.
Petroglyph have always been leaders in the RTS realm, and coupled with Grey Goo last year I'm really hoping we see a revival of this sort of game from AAA studios and indie developers alike. There's nothing like steamrollering an enemy base with an expensive arsenal of weaponry!

For its price well worth the investment, very reasonable and it looks like Petroglyph are looking to add more content should the game be well received and should the players request it. I'm really looking forward to this game's evolution!

One of my favorite ways to relax with my husband.  The controls are responsive, the enviroment is stunning.  The story, while easily skipped over, is well written.  Voice actors kinda suck, but that doesn't ruin the game for me.

There are certain race/gender locked classes that are fun to play, but if you want to be a male gunner (or a male for any of the special classes), you're outta luck.  My husband and I both always play female characters, so it's not a huge problem for us.
Can pay to play, or work for it.  I never feel the need to spend money on this game unless I want another character slot, but they're about $5, so I justify the purchase as supporting a game that I can accidentally play 30 hours in a single week...
All of that being said, I could very likely have rose colored glasses for this game, as all other MMO's I've played have looked like fecal excrement to me, and enticing visuals really does it for me.  So! read more reviews, watch gameplay videos, then decide if it's worth a try.  Don't spend money on it until you know it's something you really like.

The minute this game starts and the familiar sounds of the Ducktales theme begins to play, I knew I was in for a delight. If you're a fan of the old tv show, and platforming type of games, then Ducktales is definitely for you. All of the right nostalgia notes are hit perfectly. The sounds. The looks. The original voice actors doing the work. It's fantastic. I felt like I was watching a lost episode as I played through it.
I've heard complaints that there is too much dialogue and too many cut scenes, and maybe there is, if you hate a game to have a story. But me? I absolutely loved it, and was always curious to see what would happen next. No, this isn't a note for note remake of the old Nintendo classic, but then what would the point of that be? If you want the old game, play the old game. The remaster aims high, trying to be true to the source material, while also doing its own thing. I think it succeeds. This is a really fun game to play.
The platforming controls well, and the puzzle aspects of the game aren't too difficult. I will say that the challenge does ramp up a bit towards the end, but it's nowhere near as tough as the old 8 bit games of yesteryear. Ducktales isn't a super long game, and can be played through in a few hours your first time, but there are achievements, leaderboards, and plenty of things to collect that provide replay value.
I recommend this game to anyone who likes platformers, or the old Ducktales cartoon, and give it not pony tails or cotton tails, just a big thumps up. Woo Hoo!

D4 : Dark Dreams Don't Die is an episodic detective game in the tradition of tv shows like Twin Peaks or Lost.
The gameplay is typically point and click stuff.  Find objects and interact with them. The question that remains is if it is always meaningful, e.g. you can click on a flower, squirrels, newspapers, the cat, and furniture, almost anything and are also able to interact with it. Which is kind of fun. But....you lose stamina. For every action you take, you lose some, which has to be refreshed by eating something. You also possess a detective 6th sense, which when activated, trigger a vision of meaningful items in the vicinity. But this also uses up the "vision" bar. If you need more vision you need to drink a coffee, tequila or something. Very neat.
I recommend you play the game with a gamepad, rather than with the keyboard. Because there are times where there are some seriously difficult and time controlled quick time events, where playing with a keyboard will fail you.
The graphics are comic-style and have a very unique and distinct style. You can interact with various objects and the surrounding is very detailed.  I would rate it a solid 7.5.
The sound is very sparsely and only sometimes there are complete musical score played. It’s okayish. Was not that impressive, yet did not disappoint at all.
The story is where this game really shines. Starting out just as another "traditional" detective game, where you, David Young, are looking for the killer of you wife "Little" Peggy. But the more you play you realize there is something wrong with the story. Because some facts are not adding up. Why can David travel through time and space? What's the meaning of the house cat and why can only David see a mysterious gigantic doctor. I won't spoil anything, but it's one of a kind story and something really unique in pc games.
I can truly recommend this game for all gamers of detective games and if you liked Twin Peaks as well you will like this one for sure.

Stamina doesn't make much sense here (is turning a door handle really that exhausting, David?), especially given the short time span the game covers, the amount of food you need to wolf down to make it to the end (how can you still walk, David?), and the mechanic's utter lack of any contribution to game balance.  You'll never need to worry about running ot of Vision, either.  New to
, Access have even added achievements for shoving as many things as you can.  No, really.  There's no rhyme or reason to it, although I suppose it does add somewhat to the game's quirky charm.  Incidentally, much of the DLC is just for unlocking items that can be found in-game, or adding yet more character outfits, and all of it can be safely ignored.
Don't get me wrong; I still recommend
, despite its numerous flaws.  It's just so freakishly bizarre, I can't help but like it.  It's pants-on-head insane, in a good way, and must be experienced to be believed - but you ought to have some idea of what you're getting yourself into before you buy it.

Maybe a hint system that gave you a bit more info would have helped. Letting the player adjust their own difficulty.
To sum it up, this game is a great teaching tool and refresher for computer scientists and people wanting to be, however do not give this to your friends and expect them to finish it on their own without previous programming experience.

Ether One is an interesting first-person adventure that explores human mind and the causes of dementia in a very original way. Technically surprising, considering the low-budget nature of the title, it deserves to be tried, albeit slow pace could distance action-oriented players.

Ether One is a pretty decent puzzle game/interactive story, offering a beeline to the very end for those who don't have the patience to finish the real puzzles of the game (filthy scrubs). Those who enjoy puzzle games such as Riven or Schizm, this game is sure to impress. It'll encourage you to explore the detailed enviroments in depth to uncover deeper parts of the plot. The music, area design and voice acting are fantastic and the story is enough to get atleast two playthroughs out of you.
The controls are somewhat sluggish however and it'll chew your ram and gpu to pieces. It's probably unreal engines fault more than anything. Ether One also requires a lot of back tracking and sifting through large areas to progress, so clipping on every single clutter object and shin high fence does get annoying. My pinky is tired from holding shift the whole time. As for the difficulty of the puzzles, I can't complain. Some were tougher than others, but the solutions were always surprisingly fair. I suppose going on treasure hunts for smaller items in random seemingly unrelated houses was a let down though.
Completionists beware, this game has other problems. Many of the puzzles are currently pretty buggy which is a real shame, considering their difficulty and general time consumption factor. These are very much game breaking ones that'll either reset completed areas or lock you out of them by having a moving object in the wrong place on loading the area. It's a save file related problem, most likely. If these are ever fully patched out, this'll sit as one of the better puzzle games on the market.
All in all Ether One is a real good package with a really solid story and world to immerse yourself in. Bugs let it down heavily.

Ether One is a first-person, story-focused, no-combat exploration game.  Gameplay includes walking around in four different areas, reading things, finding specific objects to progress the story, and completing optional puzzles that reward you with more bits of story.
Though not a horror game, many parts of Ether One are unnerving, perhaps unintentionally.
I felt that many of the puzzles were arbitrary and I was not motivated to complete many of them during the game.  However, after beating the game, I found that the story was good enough to tempt me to go back and complete those puzzles to uncover more of the story.
The game's audio and music is minimalistic and sets the mood well.  The game's graphics appear to be cel-shaded, and although I was initially disappointed by the graphics, I got used to them and they hold up well.  Because of the game's descriptive subtitles, it can be fully enjoyed by the deaf.
Although the game's writing is good, there is a bizarre amount of repeated grammatical errors that turned me off at times.
I beat the game in 4 hours, but I skipped most of the puzzles.  Virtually all of the puzzles in the game can be skipped.
I recommend this game to anyone with patience, as I initially found the game boring and the story too vague to appreciate, but the ending (which I liked) makes me want to replay the game now that I have a better understanding of what it's all about.
I do not recommend this game to those who are not willing to read or to immerse themselves in the game.  This is a game that should be played with headphones on, lights off, and in a relaxed state.

As someone else has mentioned, you could almost certainly rush your way through the game in a couple of hours, but you would be completely missing the point if you did. I never felt the inclination to rush through any part of it as the entire experience was packed out with extra details of both the main story as well as other sub-stories that you can piece together. The desire to know every possible part of these stories mean there was no way I was going to skip any of the puzzles which, other than 1 or 2 towards the end, were some of the best in an adventure game for quite some time and at times genuinely made you feel fairly smart for solving them.
As a side note, the ability to use the Oculus Rift was rather nice and this is exactly the kind of experience which I was hoping would become available for it. However, it isn't really possible to fully enjoy the game that way as there are too many pieces of text that are either uncomfortable or impossible to read using the Rift.
Overall, a definite recommendation from me.

A beautiful and fun throwback to challenging old-school 8/16-bit platformers. Same goes for the sountrack, which is solid but gets a bit stale after the first couple hours.
Gamepad controls are precise and responsive, and considering how difficult Giana Sisters is, you'll need them to be. Enemies and traps can take you out with one hit and some sequences tend to feel like trial-and-error. Overall, a gorgeous, fun and fresh 2D platformer. It has a traditional old-school feel that's both welcoming and comforting, but also offers some unique mechanics to shake things up and keep you interested.

A nice amount of strategy packed into a small amount of time. I found each playthrough to be generally no more than an hour (sometimes two hours on hard) and I spent most of my time thinking. I found that Medium took three times as many tries to beat as Easy, and Hard took four times as many as Medium.
Strategic decisions come from the fact that you can control which people to include in your crew (after unlocking some extras), the order that your people act (and some abilities say "each person in the room gets this bonus"), which dice get thrown away to power special auxiliary abilities, how you want to power up your people, and which disasters you want to handle and when. The fact that there are die rolls is no different than many other games, and the fact that the dice are visible is a nice touch.
I definitely recommend this game if you don't mind its shortness.
The main cons of this game for me:
I wish that there was more content. I got 17 (split amongst the 3 difficulty levels) hours of great gameplay out of the main game. I tried a couple of missions and found they were too easy to be interesting. It'd be nice for there to be 10-turn long missions  with adjustable difficulty and some minor restriction on the starting criteria, for example possibly requiring a certain set of crewmembers for that mission. I also recommend that there be additional ship layouts where the different rooms have different stats.
I found that even on Hard, the crew stress levels were mostly irrelevant. I think I once had to spend a couple dice to lower everyone's stress levels slightly. I'd like for it to be made more relevant, probably by increasing the consequences of high stress (I think that high stress worsens the once-per-turn decision that you get, but I'm not sure because it was so easy to avoid). I also found that Ops's stress reduction wasn't important.

Spiders made a cyberpunk RPG borrowing the best elements of the Mass Effect franchise. Too bad the game offers only a short adventure. Although a complete walkthrough can be done under a dozen hours with all sidequests accounted for, War Logs offers replayability thanks to the variety of specialisation it offers along with the choices the player can make during dialogues.
Pros:
-- An interesting story that puts our protagonist, Roy, in the centre of a guild war. Two guilds are battling for the power on Mars where the most valuable source is water. Roy is a prisoner of war who desperately tries to escape the camp he's sent to by joining forces with others to plan the great escape.
-- Techromancy: The manipulation of electricity. Technomancers are the mages of this RPG. Roy later on obtains this ability and along with combat and stealth the door is open to the 3rd gameplay style.
Cons:
-- Horrid voice acting: Some of the voice acting is just awful. One particular example was when I needed to get rid of someone bothering a farmer. Intimidation was a good way to do that instead of a fight but the actor was so awful that I really felt like loading the last checkpoint and going for a fight. Also, sometimes the texts do not correspond to the sentences uttered. An example of why War Logs feels a rushed development.
-- Shortness: See the first section. The game is quite short considering it's an RPG. They could have included a couple of more missions and one or two extra chapters. The ending also felt rushed and while the epilogue was satisfying I thought the game could have offered a better antagonist.
-- Companions: Just like in Mass Effect you have companions. Sometimes one and sometimes two. The problem with them is that they die. All the time. I played the game on normal difficulty and a couple of hours into the game the enemies were so strong that they immediately took out my companion.
-- Taking sides: Again, a similarity with Mass Effect. You can take the good or the bad path. But what exactly is the result of this? I could not really find out as I became good but did something at one point that immediately rendered me neutral. This could have been more refined.
Well, I have more negative bulletpoints but make no mistake War Logs is an entertaining RPG. Coming from an indie developer it is a plus. Do give it a try if it has a discounted price.

Compelling concept behind its message: uninvolved execution.
The reason this review is
is a response to the overwhelming praise this product has received. To be clear, the idea alone is worthy of a positive review in a Steam Store flooded with indulgent dating sims, but the only
aspect
of the product are meerly conceptual. I hope the author revisits this concept, as it is very worthy of further exploration... (...and if you, Eyzi, happen to be reading this, don't let the big red thumbs-down deter you. XO XO XO)

I like the message, at least its concept (that is, a big middle figure to those living their unexamined lives in virtual worlds to escape the torture of critical introspection: sad, pathetic, and heartbreaking), but the concept is the only worthwhile 'thing' in this product—and even then, the concept isn't taken to its full potential, as it is bogged down by its unnecessary attachment to traditional narrative elements after the "twist" occurs, lessening its potential for impact—e.g.
Jung programmed Ai, adding a degree of separation between the player and Jung (ideally Jung would be playing a dating sim, just like the player himself or herself);
the Turing Test is unnecessarilly included because
and Hey, I've seen that term!—and, it must be mentioned, the lack of visual and audio diversity, so get used to the same images and music! They're nice at first, but soon become grating like everything else when it lacks variety! The writing could have been a bit darker, with a few more jabs at the proverbial player through Jung, I only counted one (he only eats ready-made food), but granted, I only explored one of the three narrative branches...though they all end the same, so I felt no need to explore the other two.
Oh, I like how its message is sending existential crises through the discussion page. Maybe I'm a sadist but that alone deserves bonus points.

I've been able to play many matches of this game now and I can safely say this is a great addition to the Free-to-Play category.  This game feels like I’m playing Mordheim.  You will pick a starting war band from one of the three factions and you'll hit play.  You set up the match you are looking for and you get put with a real person and engage in some great PvP turn based tactical gameplay.
You can also train and play some PvE matches/scenarios.  There is a list of PvE matches to play and have fun with.
When you are done with the matches you can send your units on missions. (Kind of like in Mordheim)  You send one of your units off on a mission to gain you ducats (in-game money) and there is a chance of success or failure (unit injured).
The game is NOT pay-to-win.  I have played under 20 matches and I've already purchased 3 or 4 figures with in-game money I earned from the matches I played.  You buy more figures so that you can draft a higher point army.  They give you a standard 200 point army and you build from there.
If you are a table top war game fan you have nothing to lose here.  It's free, give it a try.  I think you'll like what you find.

Good idea for a game but balance is horrible. Like most table top games it has units that are over powering unless countered with the same type of units. Trouble is unlike table top games this game has no concept of mass combat (one unit fighting multipe units at once). There seems to be bonuses to units if you surround them but either they are way to small or don't actually work.
The different factions are seriously unbalanced. Wolves get double attacks and triple counters but still have etremely high health compared to other factions. Holy factions get strong heals and improved accuracy. Undead get debuffs that take three turns to power up and unit costs as high as the other so there is no way to offset their poor accuarcy by fielding more units than the enemy.
All in all the game shows promise but balancing issues must be addressed before they even think of getting out of beta.

I knew I'd love this game from the moment my wife pointed it out to me on Steam, and I was right. The art style and mood of the game is equal parts Nightmare Before Christmas and Paper Mario. It's amusing and friendly, and makes assembly language programming really accessible. And that last point is really what makes this game great. As a professional programmer, I'm always happy to see new pathways for entering the field.
One of my most memorable childhood experiences that led to my love of programming was an exerise we did in school where the students gave the teacher step-by-step instructions to make a peanut butter & jelly sandwich. For example, a student might say, put the knife in the peanut butter jar, but if the lid was closed, the teacher would just bang the knife against the lid a bit to the sounds of raucus laughter.
Human Resource Machine is probably the best embodiment of those ideas I've ever seen, and you'd be forgiven if you thought it was just another puzzle game at first. However, the puzzles can get pretty challenging, especially if you are going towards the optimization goals.
Any programmers who don't have much exposure to low level coding should get this game. It will give you a much better intuition of what's going on under the hood in your programs. This is especially true with the way the animations play out. Watching your toon wander around the play space, picking up data from boxes, moving them to other boxes, etc. helps you identify unnecessary/duplicate work, and other possibilities for optimization.
As a final point to drive this home, I spent last April and May doing a job search. At least 50% of my interviews/code tests involved problems with the exact same structure as many of these puzzles. If you can do well at this game and haven't done any programming before, you might want to consider a career change. ;)
THAT SAID

Logic is a core part of human education that was pulled out of the norm, you are doing yourself a favor when you purchase this game.

The beauty does not entirely come across quickly unless you realize the game is showing you ways to see the universe early on, even though it is still fun.
Later on, both in class and in the game, if you do not think mechanically enough or fully understand a conjunction then you can spend a few minutes or hours looking for a ray of hope.  This can either be calming or boring, depending on your mindset.

If you learn from the experience (eventually), then you will benefit even if it was not fun, so I recommend the game anyway.
If you have an oppurtunity to learn First Order Logic from a person with a background in Philosophy, I recommend it, since they will likely spend more time with what some proofs and conjunctions mean about our world.
This game was made by game developers, and uses a system that works best on computers even if it is harder for people to read, so there is another reason to supplement.

As part of a Disney-loving family, I watched DuckTales reruns growing up until some older siblings got me the first season on DVD. Some would say it's one of Disneys better animated shows, and I'd agree with them. The original DuckTales game for the NES was also one of the only games I ever played on the NES.
But enough about my backstory...let me tell you why I like this game.
The gameplay is incredibly smooth. The controls are basically the same as that of the original NES game, said controls being Left, Right, Jump, Duck, Pogo Cane, and Menu Access (unless you play the game with Hard Pogo on, then you need to press Pogo Cane and Down at the same time in midair).
Due to this, it's most likely best to play this game with some sort of controller instead of the keyboard.
On top of that, you stop where you think you should stop when you stop, which is a great mechanic for me due to some past experiences in games (curse you past experiences).
The gameplay itself is as simple as the original; collect the diamonds, defeat the enemies, fight the boss, get the treasure.
Some elements have been added to this remastered version, such as completing set tasks before progressing in the level, less or more items being available on different difficulties, and a few mini bosses to name a few.
This game is filled with story while also being true to the story of the original game. Basically, there's 3x more story. I'm also someone who just loves a good story. It's not great, perhaps, but definitely good.
You might as well be watching a DuckTales episode instead of playing a game because this game has voice acting and animated 2D sprites. With subtitles...if you want.
The voice acting was done by all members of the original voice acting cast of the TV show that were still alive at the time the game was made. It's quite nostalgic, to be honest.
It all makes it feel so much like the TV show, all the way from Scrooge and Glomgolds rivalry to Launchpads strangely stupid antics.
If theres one thing that's the most like the original NES DuckTales game, it's the recreation of the levels. Almost every aspect of the levels have been faithfully redesigned into the game.
They're in 3D...which is nice.
The enemies, items, bosses, obstacles, etc. are in the same places as they were in the original,  with a little bit of rearrangement (well, as much as I can remember anyway).
The remastered levels are also very pleasing to the eye. They're just so beautiful and colorful...
Some things have been changed, like how to leave levels, for example. Launchpad isn't in his usual spot to give you a lift back home. Instead, you can leave a level whenever you want via the pause menu. Along with this, their's cutscenes and dialogue in various places throughout the game that replace walking up to a sprite and reading the text box that follows.
Secret areas and hidden diamond locations remain the same...I think. It's pretty simple to tell where diamonds might be after a level or two, especially if you've played the NES version before.
There are also two new levels added to this game. The Money Bin, which is a tutorial level, and Mount Vesuvius, which replaces your returning trip to Translyvania to fight the final boss.
The game is a bit time consuming on the harder difficulties. I'd say it takes about 15-20 minutes per level on easier difficulties and 30-40 minutes on harder difficulties and that's if you're not speeding through it.
Music...one of my favorite parts of a game.
The main menu theme, the redesigned levels, the new levels...I love it all...which means I'm not the best person to tell you how good the music is. I don't trust myself enough with scrutinizing music because I like it too much.
The remastered versions are basically the same as the 8-bit ones but with less 8-bit electronic sounds and more...well...modern electronic sounds. The Translyvania level music even has some dubstep in it. You can switch between the two soundtracks at any time you want.
I, for one, do not care much about graphics. I'd rather have a fun time rather than concern myself with how the game looks.
I will tell you that it's a MAJOR improvement from the NES version from 1989-1990...because 2.5D is better than 8-bit as far as games based off of TV shows go.
So colorful...so animated...
A little bit of extra stuff that doesn't really fit into any other category...
DuckTales: Remastered is a throwback to the early 90's for those who were alive at that time (myself not included) and to those who grew up with Disney and an NES (myself included).
It is an incredibly faithful recreation of the original game and a great homage to the television series, which, coincidentally, is being rebooted in the Summer of 2017.
I hear David Tennant is playing Scrooge McDuck. My life is complete.
It's a very enjoyable, short-ish game meant for children, but is still fun for older Disney kids and avid NES lovers nonetheless with difficulties tailored to all ages.
Now where are the DuckTales 2 and Darkwing Duck remastered versions? I mean, really...they should be things.

A visually stunning 2.5D throwback to a simpler time of both television animation and console gaming, Ducktales: Remastered is perhaps the best remake of a game I've ever played, bar none. The visual overhaul from the original 8-bit classic is almost immediately noticeable, due in no small part to the 2.5-D approach of the faithfully-recreated level designs and wonderfully hand-drawn in-game sprites contributed by actual Disney artists. The controls, while inherently still the same whether playing on a keyboard or with a game controller, are simple to master, but the relentless barrage of colorful foes and classic platforming pitfalls will throw you one quack-a-roonie of a learning curve. The soundtrack, a masterful blend of both orchestral scores and chiptuned instruments create a symphony that's at part times epic, and other times overflowing with nostalgia. The story, as simple as it is, is a cute and entertaining gimmick, and with the bonus of having a majority of the original voice cast that were alive at the time to reprise their roles, what once felt like a slog to get through to just play the levels now feels like you're playing a natural extension of the television series. Sure it is a bit cumbersome to skip them, but I've played games where you couldn't or you had to press one or more button to skip them than in here. All in all, I CANNOT reccomend this game enough. Give it a chance and see why life is like a hurricane, here in, Duck-berg!

A lot of people will complain about the difficulty, let them complain while clutching their participation trophies and crying in a dark corner of their closet after Tharsis destroyed their ego. This game does not hold your hand nor does it give you a pat on the back each time you click the mouse. It isn't a lazy Saturday at the beach, it's a full marathon through the seventh circle of hell, not unlike a crippled spacecraft hurtling through interplanetary space... But the euphoria and elation from completing this game through cleverness and skill is second to none. Tharsis appears on the surface to be a simple game, but the depth of the story and strategy are unparalleled by many larger titles. I enjoy a story that isn't a simple trope force fed to us with a Dr. Seuss narrative. A little ambiguity and mystery goes a long way to ignite the imagination. Reading through the negative reviews, it's clear many players view of the game play is very short-sighted. Using the dice directly in repairs isn't the only way to solve an event. They'd like to believe their failure is up to the RNG elements of the game, but it's truly their choices that result in failure. The game is tuned to near perfection. Each start has roughly the same chance for success, but make a series of key bad choices, and you will be put under a pile of events that cannot be overcome. While there is little margin for error, proper thoughtful planning, skill, and a bit of luck, you can put all of your crew on Mars. The harmony of a great Tharsis is like that of an orchestra, carrying you to victory upon the music of the heavens. Buy it. Play it. Get your♥♥♥♥♥to Mars.

Giana Sisters is a platformer where you play as two sisters.  Each sister has a special ability (fireball and twirl) that you have to use to make your way through levels.  You will find checkpoints along the way that you will return to after dying, which you will do a lot.  There's plenty of secret areas to find and lots of little crystals to collect, though their only purpose is to determine how many stars you are rewarded for completing the level (the purpose of which is to unlock the boss levels and if you score high enough on every level, hardcore mode.  Good luck with that.)
This game has a wonderful aesthetic.  When you switch characters, the world around to morphs to match the personality of the sister you are currently controlling and the music changes with it.  The music is really well done and switches seamlessly between styles.  Unfortunately that's really the only good thing about the game.
Giana Sisters starts out fun and fresh introducing you to the world.  You'll quickly discover the controls leave something to be desired, especially the fireball which has a habit of rocketing you towards an enemy just slightly out of range, then ending one pixel before hitting it so you instantly die.  Puzzles rapidly become more complex and deathtraps start appearing everywhere while the checkpoints get further apart and before you know it the game has become a trial-and-error exercise in frustration.  I stopped enjoying the game about halfway through but I slogged through the rest to see if it got any better.  It didn't.
I find it hard to recommend this game since there's a lot of better platformers out there that aren't nearly as frustrating.

A worthy follow up to the iconic cult hit Deadly Premonition. D4 is filled with joyously insane characters and situations and like Deadly Premonition is one of those games you simply have to show someone else (just to verify that you didn't dream it happening). If Deadly Premonition was a mad scientist vision hiding inside a largely broken game then D4 is a great step in the right direction. It's largely playable for one thing and simple gameplay mechanics hid a surprisingly complexity that at times equals or even surpasses Telltale's best work.
Sadly, despite being a so-called "first season" D4 doesn't even come close to providing anything close to resolution to it's numerous plot threads. This is like if the first season of a TV show amounts to a couple of episodes because a network realised it's creator was insane, so they cancelled it part way through. Given that much of what made Deadly Premonition such a special game was it's surprisingly masterful conclusion, it's a shame that D4 will probably never recieve an ending.
Also, while the prologue humously sets up it's main characters, and episode one is an inventive and insane time travel adventure on board a plane, episode two sadly lacks much in the way of memorable situations or characters and despite a rushed and bonkers ending, largely leaves D4 on a bit of a downer note.
Still, true gamer auteur's like Swery should be encouraged with your money! The modest asking price is well worth the joy of playing a truly unique gaming experience.
So if you're looking for an inventive and completely insane point and click drug trip through the mind of a mad genius of gaming, you should totally buy D4! 8/10
