An episodic, point-and-click adventure game in the same vein as the works of Telltale. However director Swery's special brand of weirdness that made "Deadly Premonition" such a cult hit gives this game an identity all it's own. His unique style pervades through every part of it.
The story is instantly gripping. Unique themes are prevalent throughout and the tone is constantly shifting. Moments can range from serious and emotional, to goofy or downright odd. An interesting and compelling world has been crafted and I can't wait to see where the tale goes from here. The only thing I would like to see improved are the graphics. I get that they were going for a graphic novel style with the cell-shaded graphics, but other games have shown how to do it better.
Gameplay is also on the very solid side. As typical with the genre you'll be exploring the environments and solving some great puzzles, but Access Games has thrown in some great scenarios. Plenty of side-quests are made available by the characters you'll meet and they usually offer some goofy thrills. Quick-time events are fun, mostly because of the crazy stuff that's happening on-screen. It's just a shame that you have to put so much emphasis on watching the inputs, because you miss some of the entertaining stuff that's being caused by them.
"D4" is a real treat that takes the oddball charm that I loved so much in "Deadly Premonition" and applies it to a compelling episodic adventure. With so much mystery in it's story and such a delightfully weird cast of characters the wait for season 2 is going to be grueling. Luckily there are plenty of reasons for me to dive back in to 100% percent this while I wait. These first two episodes can provide a unique experience for adventure game fans and I recommend you give it a look. My total score is an 8/10

The graphics options are limited to only the resolution (which are incredibly limited in options as well), window mode, vsync, and dynamic shadows.
Control is very limited to the QTEs themselves during cutscenes and outside of cutscenes it's just clicking to designated marks to move around. You can play with a controller or a mouse but I found the mouse to just be crazy faster with most everything here.
It's incredibly short especially since all you get is a prologue and two episodes which are the entire first season. It's got very little replayability and far less so since the story is linear despite having some different dialogue options. The different dialogue options are there just so you can "synch up" with the character, like choosing the right thing he'd say in the situation only it doesn't matter because the story just goes one way and it doesn't really change anything practical.
If you want to replay a scene you have to go through an entire episode from the start. If you're replaying an episode from the "Replay Episode" menu then only your "collection" progress is saved and not your actual progress in that particular episode, meaning that if you were to leave the current game you'd have to start it over.
The cel-shading doesn't look entirely great here and I don't know if that's just because something was off with this port. The outlines for the characters up close look like they were badly rendered out of something so it comes out all jagged looking.
I don't know for sure what to say about the story for sure on whether or not it's good or bad (at the very least the concept and how it goes about is interesting I thought) but its charm sold it to me with its sometimes cheesy dialogue and the characters having character with some more unique & overzealous than others.

This game had potential and it was a great idea, but like most free to play games, it was a complete disappointment. The tutorial is also horrendous and the way that they word the tooltips for abilities is so overly complicated. I do not recommend this game, let it die off like the rest of the P2W games.

3.) Matchmaking is based on so called Armypoints: The stronger the unit - The more AP you have. Thus, anyone can meet anyone, depending on troops ofcourse. Which is certainly a grave mistake: Experienced players can and will easily outplay any newcomer.

I'd claim: Give the game more time to evolve. It's good, but not good enough - for now.

Short but interesting game about "ghost hunting",the aim is to search for evidence using (your selection of three) "typical" paranormal investigation tools:  a camera, camcorder, thermometer, voice recorder, pendulum, and an EMF (electro magnetic field) detector. This is a point and click adventure that utilises, full motion video scenes throughout the game. The story was interesting  but could have been fleshed out a bit more, the ghost video and audio recording were very good and will prove interesting for those interested in paranormal investigation. A bit buggy, the  game crashed for me several times during FMV sequences.

STATIC: Investigator Training is a quite easy, casual approach on the point and click genre - it's really short, finishable in 1-1-1.5 hours. The game's about ghost hunting, so if you adamantly believe that ghost hunter shows are a fake thing and you're annoyed by them, I suggest you not playing the game, because you won't enjoy it's story.
Also, 8€ at full price is a lot for the quite amateur quality and short, unoriginal story - I don't like to lowball creators of intresting (and actually working) indie games, but I can't recommend to get this game for more than 1-2€, sorry. (Another FMV, Tesla Effect: A Tex Murphy Adventure has 10++  hours of content for 20€ while having much better quality.)
I still give a recommendation for it, because it's already a quite niche-genre - lovers of FMV probably will like it for a fair price, and people who doesn't like FMV won't need reviews to realize this is not their jam.
The game is an FMV, Full Motion Video one - meaning the actors are real actors, filmed before greenscreen.  I like the genre, so I was looking forward the game. I don't say I was disappointed, but neither was is great - it was an okay indie game, and this time indie also means low budget and experimental from the developer's side, as there are many weirdly done things are in the game. Current 8-to-5 (61%) rating qualifies this game as a mixed, and I also had mixed feelings about it.
FMV is most definitely a plus in my book, as I still find the genre a really intresting one.  But I can not comprehend why they animated the little popup-dialogue faces instead of capturing it by camera - or maybe they were using a low-frame recording camera. At the end, it doesn't matter why, but during the dialogues the character's face is totally static, only their mouth moves in a really weird, and not too life-like way. Uncanny valley all the way (Looks life-like, but the way it works/moves kind of creeps you out).  Also, there's only one pace of walking in animation, yet at least 3 different speed at generally moving - meaning that sometimes the lady steps one and slides 3-4 metres during that time
Voice acting is inbetween terrible and acceptable - the actual lines are not bad, but for some reason the actress reads every single line as it's written and takes a huge ........  pause after each line and before she starts the new one. I don't know if it was her fault, or they recorded the story in segments, but when there's two line of text on the screen, she reads/tells it perfectly. If the sentence is presented on two screens, then there's the huge pause after the first screen's text ended. It won't make the game bad, but a really amateurish / unexplained thing in the game.
(And I managed to froze the game up by initiating a cinematic few minutes before the game's end, and for some reason I still went to the next room - the cinematic couldn't play because I was in a wrong place, and couldn't move/save/load because the cinematic wanted to play, so the game just froze up)

The Sign Painter is no more (I presume; your supervisors now deliver those strange, cryptic messages), and you have moved to an office building where you manipulate inputs and control the outputs. I love it and I've played it as much as I can in my spare time.
Once you've beaten the game, (I'm not even halfway yet, coming up on 10 hours) there is tremendous replay value. As with most puzzle games, you may solve one problem in tons of different ways. You might replay a puzzle to fulfill a Size Challenge or Efficiency Challenge, or to snag a Steam Achievement. To design your solutions, you are given extra documents to create these workflows on, and to test different prototypes.
Would I recommend this game? Ohhhh yes. If you loved World of Goo, you owe it to yourself to play this.
The only thing I would ask for, Tomorrow Corporation, is a sandbox!
(PS. Play World of Goo!)

This is actually a pretty cool little game for people who love logic puzzles.  You are given an extremely limited set of commands to perform complicated tasks with, such as multiply two numbers together using only addition (that's one of the earlier, easier puzzles).  Each puzzle is also ranked on the number of program commands you use, and how many steps the program performs before completion.  It starts out easy, but some of the puzzles become wickedly hard, and because of your limited command pool, programs can quickly become a tangled mess with all the "jump," "jump if 0," and "jump if negative" commands.
Definitely worth playing for anyone interested in math, logic, or programming...

HRM is programming/coding puzzle. You write in assembly-like language (very simple instructions) programs that manipulate data in input, and generate some data in output. Task vary from doubling the input values, to sorting the input values.
Pros:
- easy to learn, good for young learners
- good learning curve: instructions are introduced when needed
- simple UI: instructions dragged and dropped as blocks
Cons:
- if you don't like coding/puzzles stay away from this
- Not many instructions are visible at a time
- Too easy if you mastered TIS-100.
The pros are pretty much self-explanatory. The instructions as blocks are especially good for novices.
About the cons, I found the puzzles too easy compared to the ones from TIS-100. Each puzzle has challenges on writing short or fast enough programs. Those are not always that easy, but personally they extended my play time from 5 to 7-8 hours. Not much.
About TIS-100, I believe a comparison is needed. In TIS-100 you need to code a grid of processors that 1) can only run short programs and 2) have no memory. This made TIS-100 puzzles extremely hard. This game, instead, is about more traditional (simpler) coding because 1) there is only one processor, 2) programs can be indefinitely long, and 3) there is random-access memory (except for the first, very easy puzzles). The most obvious limitation of the processor is that you can't load an arbitrary value (say 4) in its register/tile, unless it is in a memory cell you can copy the value from.
Overall, a nice puzzle game for people who like the genre or they want to learn what coding means. A little too easy for people who mastered TIS-100.

Story - I could not care. I just could not care. I'm sorry, the tragedy story is tragic and everything, but I could not care.
So yeah, remember how everyone fell in love with the Ezio trilogy? There was so much to care about, like his love interests, his character, his personality, the flirt that he was with the ladies, and the fact that he used his time at the brothels to learn French... there was so much to care about Ezio, and it gave us a reason to care about him as a person, starting from his tragedy with his family all the way to Embers. Take all of that magic, all that personality, the memorable characters, the soundtracks, and everything else... and just toss that out the window.
Yeah, just... tear up those memories and just burn them, cuz you won't need them here. The story just DRAGS ON FOREVER. Jesus. Like, the beginning was tragic and everything, but after 50 cutscenes of just him doing assassin-like things while not exactly being an assassin yet made the pacing akin to molasses, and I only stuck through with it thus far just to see what would happen, as I'm a diehard Assassin's Creed fan. I've been there for all of the stories, even Liberation and Rogue, which are spin offs, if anything. Everything feels shoehorned in, like the explanation for the ring finger ritual that the Assassins later on performed during Altair's time, and other nonsense. There was one side quest where an NPC mentions the "Nothing is true, Everything is permitted" quote, but it felt like more of an easter egg than an explanation of anything.
Almost nothing drove the story forward. There was almost NO momentum. It was just Cleopatra telling me to go kill people, and I went and killed people.
There was one story that I cared about, and it involved a little girl. ONE. Out of the entire game, ONE STORY MOVED ME to go do things. ONE.
The rest of the story kinda  just drags on and on and on and on and on FOREEEEEEVVVVEEEERRRRRR.
Also, you would think that since the romance in Unity was a flop, that they'd fix it in Origins. No. I don't know why Bayek was in love with Aya, and I ultimately didn't care at some points. I read the book that was associated with AC Unity, and there, I found the reasons and motivations of why Arno and Elise were in love. That **** was cut out of Unity, and it felt like a formatted cut version of the book, so I thought I'd see it be made better in Origins. LOL NO.
No.

Combat/Stealth - The combat was ATROCIOUS. A-****ING. TROCIOUS.
Ubisoft is the company behind Splinter Cell Blacklist, so I know damn well that they damn well know how to make a proper stealth vs assault branching skill tree that encourages either gameplay. YOU WOULD THINK that stealth gameplay encourages STEALTH equipment and STEALTH exp to level up STEALTH skills to encourage more STEALTH gameplay.
Nope.
Sure, you can use your UAV bird to go track all the enemies, and scan the area, and plan your attack, and surgically take down one enemy at a time for the bonus exp... or you can just rush the base, and just kill everyone and complete the objective in like, 2 seconds because the bonus exp is almost negligible. Like, long term, you would probably get more exp out of just rushing everything than you would with precision stealth kills.
The combat is atrocious, too, however, did I mention that? So since they made the combat style in Unity and Syndicate a certain way, you would think they could only build upon it or make it better, right? Yeah, no, **** that, that'd be too ****ing easy, ya ****wads. I can't tell you how many times I got s**tstomped by enemies just because you can't interrupt moves to counter, or because the counter didn't work consecutively. I like city builders. But this is not one. It is actually a puzzle to find how to play the game.
At the beginning, there is a square area and a road connected to it.
What do I am expected to do? That was not very hard to figure out that I need to build a road.
Zoning was also easy. Next, game citizens started to ask for water, sewer and electricity.
It took QUITE SOME TIME to figure out that you do not need to build set of pipes for water and sewer separately.
I had to search the web for this!
Next, I spend some time trying to figure out how to connect my power stations to houses.
After a while I realized that there's no need - you just need to have electricity in general area.
Was it so hard to tell that at the first game play?
Ok, I am building my city and it is growing. Suddenly, some areas are out of electricity. At least, this is I think what the icon meant. Deciphering these icons is a separate problem! This game is like a map without a legend. You can guess what the icons mean. There is no help, you are on your own.
So, part of my city is out of electricity. WHY? I produce enough, my production is well more than consumption. That area is totally connected to the grid. Any hints? No hints, just the blinking icons.
AND THERE IS NO WAY TO CLICK ON THE ICON. I tried everything - switching views, randomly closing and opening various windows - NO USE. The web didn't help - they  just tell to 'click on the  building'.
I got tired of fighting with these obstacles. I just want to play city builder, not  search the web and youtube for answers and tutorials. Horrible UI. Not recommended.
EDIT: And don't forget the night! All of a sudden, somebody turned the lights off! I freaked out, trying to find out what happened. Is it a bug, is it a problem with my PC? No, it's 'day-night cycle'. Had to check the web for this as well.

This is one of those games where I don't even know how to describe what happened over the course of playing it.  It certainly does not take itself seriously or limit itself to silly concepts like physical reality.  A series of unexpected and entirely bizarre things happen  over the course of the three chapters making up this game.  Unfortunately, the last chapter ends on a cliff hanger and the story remains incomplete.  It still is worth a look because something this strange deserves to be looked at.
Just to say how something average in this looks like would be to describe how it starts - After a tutorial scene, you wake up in a bath tub, walk out of the bathroom and are attacked by what is either a woman who thinks she is a cat, or your cat who your entirely mad mind decides is a woman.  After fighting off the cat? a portly man arrives and tells you to use your weird power to go back in time and find some info on the guy who may know something about the guy who killed your wife.  He then drinks a bucket of clam chowder, stacks several slices of pizza together, disjoins his jaw and eats them all in three bites.
All of this is played seriously and without an eyebrow being raised by the characters.  It lends to the game's charm alongside the strange cast of characters series of bizarre events you wind up in.
Gameplay is nothing spectacular for an adventure game.  The gameplay is done through dialogues, item searches, quick time events, and mini games.  You have a set amount of endurance which limits the amount of things you can look at and how many times you can speak to people.  There is a highlight hotkey showing all the interactables, but you can only do that so many times before needing coffee.  There is enough food laying around so I never had any problems looking at everything in an area at least once.
Puzzles are served fewer in quantity and in smaller areas than what you may see in other adventure games.  It does set the pacing and focus on one event at a time.  None of the puzzles can be considered particularly difficult, the hardest part may be finding the point on the screen where that one item your looking for is before bringing it back to the character who wants it.  Transitioning to the mini games can be jarring as you don't expect it and they have nowhere near the polish as the core game.
You get currency for doing well, searching out-of-the-way areas, accomplishing goals, doing well at a mini game.  These are then either  wasted on coffee and food so you can inspect more objects or spent on outfits for the characters you can dress them in as you go through the game.  I honestly thought this form of reward was weak and artificially encouraged replayability - when the game stands fine on its own for replayability - and also seemed like the designer wanted to reward the player but didn't quite know what to give them or do with the currency system he made up.
In all, I'd say this is different enough from most other adventure games in sheer weird value to give it a go if you enjoy adventure games in general.

Being a fan of Swery, I'm quite biased towards this game. But even for those who aren't familiar with this video game director, I still wholly reccomend this game.
This experience is split in to two types of gameplay; Exploration, and action scenes.
-Being a port of a kinect game, you aren't given direct control in the exploration sections. You point yourself in a direction, and click on a movement icon to walk to that specific point. It's very intuitive and easy to learn.
But one mechanic mixes up the usual point-and-click formula: A stamina meter. Everything you do, from opening a door, to walking across the room uses a little bit of stamina. Stamina is replenished by eating food you find in the enviroment. It's an interesting inclusion, and subtly adds to the quirky nature of the game.
-The action scenes control quite differently though. Usually, a direction is displayed on screen, and you move your mouse along its path. These scenes are full of energy, and fun to play.
While the game is short, it has tons of replay value, with hundreds of interactable items, each with unique flavor text. Every single action you perform gives you credits, which can be spent on clothing items, music tracks, and more food for your stamina.
-So far the game consists of a prologue and two episodes, each about 30 minutes to an hour depending on how you play.
-It has plenty of sidequests and collectibles to find, to encourage subsequent playthroughs.
But while I love this game to death, I do have a couple complaints about it.
-Sometimes it is unclear on what will progress the story with no point of return.
A couple times I performed an action, without knowing it would continue the story. Because of this, I missed sidequests and items, having to replay the whole episode.
-No chapter select.
Granted, while the epsodes are short, (about the length of a television episode,) it can be annoying having to replay parts you've gone through multiple times to get to a perticular section. Thankfully, you can start a new save with all your collectibles once you complete the game.
-Very short length.
This is probably the biggest issue with this game. It's incredible short. I've gotten about seven hours at the time of writing, after replaying the first two episodes multiple times. Unfortunately, being a stealth release, this game got almost no attention on launch. Since then, it's sold only about 150,000 copies worldwide. We're probably not going to get more episodes, but we'll just have to wait, as Swery is (at the time) facing medical issues.
Despite these issues, this game is probably my favorite game of 2014, as well as the past several years. There is nothing else like it, and any fan of TellTale or David Cage games would feel right at home. It's funny, well written, and full of genuine love for the project. I would reccomend this game at full price.

Complaints about the Wolfen should be mostly disregarded.  Predator of Blood is overpowered but manageable.  Everything else is strong but balanced for its price.  The 200 AP bracket isn't well-balanced and if you plan to stay there (not recommended, 300+ is much more fun) it's a good idea to specialize to take down the ubiquitous dogs.  Necromancer, Skull Warrior, and two Skeleton Swordsman will make short work of most wolfen with good tactics.  Play defensively.  Keep your swordsmen up front and when the dogs engage surround them with morbid puppets (don't put puppets up front, they'll get one-shotted and allow a pursuit attack) and bring in the skull warrior to put them down.
Past 200AP the game is much more balanced. Wolfen are still strong but soon become heavily outnumbered with their high AP costs and encirclement negates most of their stat advantages.  When you add in the "dogs are op" popular opinion and the kinds of players that brings in, wolfen are no big deal. For the price it seems like a capable-enough video editing program. Of particular note is that unlike some other programs which cost more, SMS' GPU accelaration works. It's not as fast as CyberLink's PowerDirector's, but at the same time that software costs more and more importantly to me has a comparatively ridiculously-limited range of settings to customize with regards to video renders' output quality. It (PowerDirector) may be able to output a 1080p48 video in half the time using my GPU, but the quality is very noticably worse all while yielding slightly-larger filesizes.
Beware that if you intend on using this software for non-game-footage editing and encodes, it lacks a built-in video-footage denoise function. It may be possible to do so using manual compositing, but it's going to take me some time to figure that out myself adapting it from what's possible in other software (like After Effects). Also know that unlike Davinci Resolve you have no control over the automatic video stabilization. You may be able to manually create your own stabilization tracks using the pan&crop function, however.
If you're looking for an intuitive, easy-to-use video editing program which can render relatively/very quickly with GPU accel, I recommend this; in particular, for videogame stream encoding I highly recommend SMS. If you're looking for something more advanced in terms of editing functionality then pricier software may be better suited to your requirements. You can get a 30-day trial for SMS and PD, so I recommend trying both those and other software out to see what suits your needs.

There are many problems I have with this game that in my opinion make the experience have many, many lows. I will say right now at best it is a fun game to play with friends, but nowadays what isn't? There are many classes (just referred to as an Operator, to give it that Tom Clancy feel), and different weaponry and equipment for each Operator depending on what agency/military they are from. For me, this introduces a lot of problems with balance, usage and pure happenstance.
ISSUE #1: WAY TOO MUCH♥♥♥♥♥♥TO KEEP TRACK OF
In a 5v5 game, there are many things to be aware of. Mainly positioning, equipment and general information about the two teams are of some of the highest on the priority list. This game actually does a great job at letting people get intel on other players. BUT WAIT! In Siege, you can barely tell what equipment your enemy has, not to mention most of the walls are destructable. I'm going to say this right now, destructable walls should never be and will never be a selling point for me. More into this later. Anyways, if you're defending, you have to deal with at the very least five but at the very most 10 drones with cameras, plentiful breaches, and spawns. You could pick an operator that specializes and has kevlar barricades, but this doesn't matter when the room you have to defend has 5/6 windows and two doorways. You are given two metal barricades to block walls, but some rooms you have to worry about people blowing holes in the ceiling, and I've even run into people blowing up floors to throw♥♥♥♥♥♥upwards at you. How do you plan for something like that if you can't see what you're defending before you pick an Operator? And this is only defense. Offense is an entirely different beast. People can use the breakable walls to give themselves a small window to shoot you from. I'm talking pixel tiny. The best way to describe it is if you've ever played CS:GO on de_train and someone AWPs you from a specific angle where you can barely see them. Imagine that angle
when clearing a room. If it comes down to "oh, I would've been able to hit him through that hole if I picked Glaz" or "oh that trap wouldn't have worked if I EMP naded it", you're not playing a game that rewards skill, you're playing a game that rewards you if you would have clicked on the dude with the EMP grenades over the girl that breaches♥♥♥♥♥♥during character select. And holes in the wall only scratch the surface of another issue I have with this game.
ISSUE #2: VISIBILITY
Coming from CS, I have a panic attack if a playermodel shares a same color as any background in the map. How do you think I reacted when I saw, well, nothing but the holes in someone's balaclava against a dark-ish wall? How about when I'm using a longer range weapon and the attackers blew a hole in a garage so the sun is beating down on them and I'm in a place without any light? Not to mention the cosmetics in this game can be really distracting and over the top at times. ♥♥♥♥, there's an exploit where you can hide below a shelf and use a box to cover you. Sometimes you can't see camera drones in bushes or other tall foliage, which means you best be feeling lucky with your spray. Outdoor cameras can still ID you through trees at 50+ meters away. Half the time you lay down and move a couple feet left or right your legs suddenly shift position. I haven't even factored in dumb♥♥♥♥♥♥like q+e swaying to duck in and out of cover and away from shots, operators that have abilities that are essentially made to give their teammates pseudo-wallhacks, really bad spawns that can be unsafe from someone looking out of a 2 foot hole in a window. It's all there and it's all annoying as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Maybe I would be better equipped to go against things like this, but...
ISSUE #3: YOU CAN'T CHOOSE WHAT MAP/MODE YOU PLAY.
This one is a little less annoying for some but still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for me. How am I suppose to get better at the game if I can't freely look around and learn a bit about the map? Every time I play it's pretty much a nearly different scenario and I would like to be better equipped for that. And you could argue that I could play the single player scenarios to learn the maps, but that's still not as free as straight up being able to run around the map. It's even worse that I can't choose what gamemode to play, since some gamemodes are pure trash on certain maps. I didn't even see any community servers that only run certain modes, it's pretty much just all "hope you have nine friends because if not get ♥♥♥♥ed idiot" (for all I know, those are there). Everyone knows I don't have friends, not that many anyway.
ISSUE #4: WORLD RENOWNED CURRENCY SYSTEM
Now this one I'm a little bit lenient on given the fact that you can get a good portion of the characters pretty easily. However, I am locked behind two walls, one's a wall with some of those rock climbing extrusions spraypained "grindwall" and the other is a magnificent golden Trump border wall with a gate with the sign "paywall" over it when it comes to Year X characters. And some of these characters have really nuts abilities. This is due probably to the fact that these characters had to have some spice to be rationally offered to players at a price. Or they came up with some crazy♥♥♥♥♥ideas like "dude what if we have some Korean chick that made peoples' phones go off" or "dude what if we had a Chinese guy with needle grenades". Who the ♥♥♥♥ brings a phone to a bomb planting anyways? Anyways, the currency system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. So that's pretty much how I feel about this game. In my point of view, there are at least three things I could be. Ah yes, Rainbow Six: Siege. It's a totally unique experience playing this game, as you have all kinds of emotions playing it.
When i first bought the game, i was madly in love with it. It is unlike any other FPS in the market, and has a big variety of playstyles to get comfortable with.
But as the months passed, i started to notice the defects of the game and why many players are disappointed with it. The game as a concept is on a league of it's own, but the stability of it is very poor. New updates cause tons of bugs to pop up, servers are broken, hit registry is broken, and matchmaking may sometimes take more than 20 minutes depending on your rank.
Excluding the cons that i mentioned above, the game is very addictive and fun to play with friends. It is super competitive but you can also mess around in casual if you want to. The community is not as good as it used to be, but you can't blame Siege for getting more popular over the years (bigger community=more toxicity).
So would i recommend this game? Absolutely. I met some amazing people through this game, and in general it was all a 'thrilling' experience. Sure the broken hit registry is a big frustration especially considering it's a AAA title, but with Ubisoft games I never expect everything to work out smoothly.
TL:DR- Siege is like that drunk uncle who is pretty cool to hang out with but won't fit into society as he has a lot of issues in his life.

I don't normally write reviews, but I absolutely adore this game, so I'm making an exception.  As much as I love it, I'm still not sure I would pay $15.00 for it, though with the time I have put in I suppose even that's not really fair (a lot of the playtime showing for me is time recorded when I left the game running on my computer and went to bed).  I got mine in a Humble Bundle recently and would suggest that you look for it on sale unless you are certain you'll be as hooked on it as I am.
I don't find the RNG to be at all unfair as some have said.  Random is random...sometimes I get exactly what I need, sometimes I get exactly what I need to drop dead and am given a pile of cannibal chow in exchange for it.
While the game can feel quite difficult when you first start, the learning curve for it is about average.  You just need to put a little bit of thought into your various moves and the other options available to you.  After a bit of playing easy quickly becomes too easy, as it should.  Normal mode feels like a huge leap from easy mode, but is also fairly easy to become proficient in after you put some time and effort into it.  Hard mode...I'm just starting on it, and thus far it doesn't feel a LOT more difficult than normal mode.  Though I may have just gotten lucky on my first couple of scenarios.
I do hope that they will add more missions in the future as I feel they add a lot more interest to the game.  I also wish that the main mission screen showed when you had beat each mission on easy, normal, and hard modes instead of simply giving you a star for completion in general.
In short, it's a great little game for people who like to roll dice and are willing to take the time to think through their options before acting.  It's less likely to be enjoyable to players who prefer fast paced action, shooters, etc.

When a RPG or action-RPG is smaller, simpler and humbler than "monsters" as Morrowind or Mass Effect it doesn't mean that it's a bad game; it depends of their potential and the better or worse development of its own scope and capabilities.
The stealth subject is, by far, the worst implemented part of the game. You cannot exploit all of its hidden potential despite you upgrade al your stealh related skills (for not mentioning that you're the one alerting a gang of idle/patrolling foes, but your partners are blessed with "feather feet" and won't alert them even when they run in front of them -that makes a bad and very ugly impression-). But the rest of the game features goes from the good implemented to the very well implemented. All the RPG part in this game is very simple, but you won't find any lack of fun for it.
Visuals in this game are always good and, sometimes, they're stunning. Its atmosphere is well implemented (in the line of Mad Max, Chronichles of Riddick or Borderlands).
Combats are tremendous, almost a matter of button twitching but, again, fun and addictive (the fact of almost stopping the time -but not completely- for determining an action or give an order to your partner gives a chance for you to not think only about twitching).
Sounds and ambient music make its role, and voice are pretty well (at least the voices in english, I can't understand some comments regarding to the awful voice acting but to refering to other languages, or it's me that I ain't so demanding on this term -but I don't think so-). :P
Throwing sand to the eyes of human enemies not protected with Riddick-style-sunglasses is a feature I'd never seen before in a game, and useful a lot.
History is fragmented, there's not a clearly central plot involved as their tittle ("War Logs") suggests, and mainly focused in the friendship between the two protagonists and their fight for survival.
In resume, a well planned game (and well executed almost all the time) that is absolutely worthing of a try. Just don't expect a complex and big "monster" as the above mentioned (which they're not games, they're UNIVERSES) with a rich amount of player statistics.

A French RPG that combines 3rd-person action with questing and crafting. It is really an indie game and tries to depict its large ambitions with quite limited means, leading to an uncanny feeling of discrepancy.
Pros
* Fun combat system once you get enough tools in your arsenal, a bit frustrating otherwise
* A good art direction for characters and enemies, but the decors are too linear and empty
* A cheap price for a reasonable amount of content
Cons
* The lack of polish is frustrating considering Mars: War Logs looks and play like an AA product rather than your standard indie game

Very bare bones at the moment, I bought this way back in 2014 so I have a lot more hours than the steam version shows here & there's been a few cool changes here & there but nothing substantial enough to make me want to recommend this game based on content alone, but if you're looking for a small indie space romp then this is certainly a promising game that hopefully will have much more in the way of content in future itterations.
Pros:
-Space exploration & massive planets to land & explore
-While still bare bones the flight mechanics are fairly solid
-Customizable ship interiors (not a lot of useful stuff to add from what I've seen, but it's a nice touch)
-Awesome soundtrack makes exploration a soothing experience
-Pretty cool sci-fi vibes, especially when landing in massive planetary vistas & seeing just how small you are
-Pressurized ship interior (not exactly space engineers level of cool, but still makes you be sure you closed the airlock...)
-Space physics (IE Asteroids spinning about as you try to land on them)
-Interesting graphical style, though feels somewhat dated in places (see cons for elaboration)
-1:1 planetary scales, you literally can get lost for months on these truly massive celestial bodies, and this really becomes apparent as you approach geological features such as mountains & valleys.
Cons:
-Both ground & ship combat feels unfinished & sluggish (I've heard of people who enjoy the combat in this game, so
different strokes for different folks I guess)
-General lack of content to engage players for long periods of time (though obviously a lot more is planned for the future, so I'd say it's worth waiting)
-Feels limited being set in only 1 solar system. While the scale is large enough on it's own, I feel that there wasn't enough variety of planets to warrant further exploration (Was my experience a while ago I'm going off, so if I'm wrong here let me know & I'll correct the review)
-Poor lighting on models in certain situations & occaisonal muddy graphics (Can't help but feel that when I land a ship on a planet, that nothing is being reflected off or onto my ship, and the same goes for weapons too) although being an indie title going for a more primitive graphical style I can't hark on about this too much)
-Bugs aplenty! But this goes for most Early Access games, so it's not really worth mentioning them outside of a bug report.
In summary this is an interesting little game if you're into that cool sci-fi "one man & his ship" setting, and the gameplay is (supposedly) intended to flow a little similar to older Elder Scrolls games, so this is definitely a unique title to keep your eye on, or purchase if you wish to support the developer (Who's just 1 guy on his own, and a pretty cool guy going off my interactions with him in the past)
If I got something wrong in the review, feel free to let me know & I'll make corrections according.

D4 is an interesting, amusing piece of interactive entertainment that revels in fetishization of the american way of life, food, culture and sports. The game is "episodic" but more in the sense that it mimics the look and structure of a TV series, something that its creator SWERY has intentionally pursued. Full of oddball characters, overwritten and acted dialogue and lots and lots of detail, it is a very unique experience.
The game plays as a point and click adventure game with QTE trials. Player explores limited environments searching for clues, with progress being made whenever a relevant hotspot is examined. However, there's also a lot of detail in every area that entices player to explore in order to collect text files, collectable clothes and credits that are used to unlock more clothes for game characters.
It is difficult to recommend this game at its current full price. If you can pick this up from a bundle or otherwise at a reduced price it is well worth its ~4 hours of playtime.

This is a review from a person who has collected and played the Talisman board game since its 2nd edition (Steam uses 4th ed).
Talisman, the board game, is a game of funstration.  It is enjoyable enough to play, but you cannot take it too seriously.  It will delight you as many times as it will break you.  Talisman:  Digital Edition emulates this experience precisely.  I know some people have an issue with the RNG of this game, but when it comes to simulating the physical board game, I can say that it is spot on.  You will rarely roll the number you need to survive and you will often draw the worst possible card at any given time - just like the real board game!
My advice to anyone playing this game is to play without the expectation of winning.  Play it as if it's a rogue-like, choose-your-own-adventure fantasy story represented by a board, some cards, and miniatures.  I guarantee that once you lighten your expectations, your playing experience will be much more enjoyable.  It is the very same mindset that my friends and I discovered when playing the physical board game.

I picked this game up in a shop for £5 just because it was there, not expecting much to come of it. Since then, I've bought all of the expansions and many of the additional characters. This game is a must-have for anyone that enjoys fantasy board games and I would recommend the physical version as well.

At first i worte a negative review, but I like to change it.
Well as you already know you have to survive your journey to mars.
Every turn you will be hit by 2-3 different random failures that you need your crew to fix.
You use dices that you roll and use to repair things.. But what you might not know is that your crews health and such things will all effect how many dieces you have, and special rules can make dices worthless or stadic so you cannot roll your dice again.
What this mean is that things very fast can become rather complicated and you will have problems you cannot fix and this will effect your ship and crew all the way to mars.
The game is NOT EASY, not even on EASY mode. Actual it tooke me more htan 15+ tries to reach mars. ( bye the way at the end turn all crew need to be in the command capsul and your ship need to survive all the failures at the end of the round ).
But here are some small advice that will make your journey to become more successfull.
First of all you need food, so try to role 2 or 3 of the same dices in the food section when you can. Next you need to pay special attention to the ships hull. meaning the events that damage the hull are your priority. To make the game a bit more easy you can use unspend dices for research/bonus things such as extra dice, or repair 7-20 damage or other stuff.. Use this without it you will have problems.  All in all the game is easy to play, but difficult to master, and often you just have bad luck regarding the dices or damage to the ship that you fail and fail and fail again.
But once you actual complete the game its like, ohhh that is how you are supposed to play it, or this worked i will try that again.. that is also why i change my review from negative to positive since I was under the impression game was just impossible to win.

Don't be mislead by the game's presentation: It's a less-than-deep sequence of randomized logic puzzles pretending to be a dice game. Seemingly random events aren't really that random. The mechanic of rolling the dice -- which is presented as a core part of the gameplay -- is largely there to give you something to click on. Most of what the game presents itself as is little more than window dressing.
Once you master the basics of the logic puzzles (it's a bit much to call this "strategy"), there's really not much to it. It's an exceptionally frustrating experience if you try to take the gameplay at face value (like thinking the dice results actually matter), and a completely underwhelming experience once you figure out how it actually works. Read the forums about the optimial strategies for each turn, and the challenge largely evaporates. Unless you like replaying the same-ish puzzles over and over, I recommend that you find another game.
The devs did a fine job with the presentation, but it's ultimately much less of a game than the one you're probably imagining it to be. The seeming unfairnes of the random event and the dice rolls -- which everyone is understandably hung up on (including me, for a time) -- is actually just misdirection. I do appreciate that the devs have tried to add some variety to the gameplay with various scenarios, but these are really just variations on the same theme.
Those people who gave up on the game after an hour? They were right. I liked this game so much more when I thought it actually was the hardcore, slightly unfair, randomized, dice-based survival board game it pretends to be. If you're going to pick this game up because it sounds interesting -- as I did -- do it on a steep sale or in a bundle. It's definitely not something I'd recommend buying at $15.

The game is a really good idea. I love the concept, but the game is too difficult to be enjoyable, even on easy mode. To put it this way, i've died 10 times in a row in the 2nd training mission on easy mode. The strategic element to the game is so thin, it's often hard to see a distinct strategy at all.
The game needs strategic adjustments to allow a balance.
Played it some more, but it's no better. I got past the second training mission. So my mistake was, that i read the instructions which suggested i should go after the most serious issue. There were two issues, a Windows BSOD and a airlock breach that was leaking out into space. Apparently the trick is to fix the BSOD and ignore the fact that oxygen is venting into space, because BSODs damage the ship 1 hitpoint a turn and airlocks do not. I did not realise this because I didn't see the red line on the danger alerts. In part because my eyes aren't as good as they used to be, in part because i am mildly colour blind, and in part because i didn't see it mentioned in the tutorial.
Suggestions for how this game could be improved:
Injuries when you roll, sure you can get assists, but in my opinion hand of fate did assists better. See in hand of fate, they allowed you to reroll, before they injured you, so if you couldn't get a good result on the reroll, then you were screwed. It felt much more reasonable, than, you can have a reroll, but everytime you reroll you must die a bit. That frankly sucks and doesn't feel like you have any control over the strategy.
Also I think an injury for every single roll of the die with a special number is harsh, if the injury number is 2 and you roll 5 twos, then you're dead, even if you start from full health. It's even more harsh when something like that happens in a training mission and teh death wasn't scripted.
I don't think that fire should spread simultaneously throughout the ship instantly, i think it should spread section by section, that's a lot more realistic.
The tutorial despite being longer than charlie manson's jail sentence, doesn't cover how things like research works. It should be made shorter, and more optional, and should at least give you basic information about the game.
Other things the tutorial doesn't mention is the health bar, the fact that system failure is non-critical issue that can be indefinitely ignored (huh?), what the red lines are in the disasters, what the dice and the stress meters were. - this is something that might be useful to display in a diagram along with the other stuff.
The game would benefit from having some kind of dice crafting system where you can make permanent items to improve your luck, rather than just next turn fixes for issues that expire the turn after. It creates a feeling of helplessness over the strategy and there's not enough weighing up short term survival against long term benefit because of this.
It also feels like it's missing some kind of experience ranking system for the crew, like it feels like with experience the crew should become more specialist in particular areas. That's something that could be massively expanded on within the game and make the game far more interesting and engaging.
It would be pretty cool if you could click on the faults and get some kind of feel for the severity of the issue, what the issue is, the longevity of the fault, if there's any latency before things get more serious. That kind of thing.
All of the faults I found so far affect the gameplay now... it would be cool if some things didn't become serious until later.
If would be nice to see some totally different mechanics of fixing different faults, that breaks away from the samey feeling of fixing issues on the ship.
Respite periods in the gameplay between disasters would be welcome too, so that you could do things to consolidate your strategy / resources / etc.
The introduction of choice would be cool. For example when dealing with fire, do you vent air off into space to kill the fire, or do you go in with fire extinguishers? or do you seal off the unit and let the flames burn themselves out ? Choices like this could have far reaching consequences into future gameplay.
Luck should rarely kill you unless you make a strategic mistake.
I really hope that a sequel to this game is made which a lot more depth to the gameplay and balance to the luck, because it could be a really good game if these issues were addressed. Right now, the game feels frustratingly limited, and i think that's reflected in the reviews that some people have left.
Given that I could write a game like this in wxWidgets admittedly without such good graphics, but just the raw gameplay, in about a week, I don't think that 10.99 is a good price for this game as it stands.

A fun programming game, more accessible than something like TIS-100, but with enough complexity to make it worthwhile. The theme is applied pretty well, and adds something to the game.
It isn't particularly long, if you are familiar with programming you could get through the whole thing in a day with both length and speed challenges beaten, but that seems reasonable for the price asked.
Unlike TIS-100, the challenge limits seem to be fixed, rather than based on what users have actually achieved, and many are not the best achievable, so you never know if you could push slightly harder to get an even better result. I'd like it if they added that sort of global leaderboard aspect, so you knew what to aim for.
One downside is that because there is no limit on program length, beating the speed challenges is often simply a matter of applying loop unrolling, which while a very useful optimisation technique, isn't very ... elegant.

A must to anyone trying to understand and learn the logic behind programming.
It did help me understand some very basic and crude concepts, that are the foundation to the carrer.

Although the game still isn't properly optimized for the PC platform, I'm having a great time playing it. It's very stable, at least in my rig, although CPU usage really is suspiciously high (even for a game this complex); the most probable culprits are the anti-piracy measures, though the publisher will never admit to it.
The quests are interesting, though not as handcrafted as the Witcher's ones. And there also doesn't seem to be branching paths to the storyline.
Now the graphics are really beautiful, I never thought ancient Egypt would have such a breadth of vistas! Though it doesn't run as well as my machine should be capable of running it, I have an almost locked 60fps 1080p experience, with max settings.
The gameplay has changed some elements:
- The combat, which is more "Souls"esque now, though it's much much easier.. But it's a nice change from previous versions.
- Now there's an RPG progression system (level up and gain points to choose abilities), and also a loot system in the likes of Diablo (normal, rare and legendary items).
- There's also the now obligatory crafting, but it's used for improving your character only (better health, better weapon damage, better long range damage, and more space to hold items), and it's well implemented.
- The free running is GREATLY improved from previous versions. This alone makes the game worth it for me... Traversing the world on foot, on a vehicle or animal, and swimming, all feel very natural.
- "Loot Boxes" - the game has it's version of a loot box, and has a store where you can buy in-game currency for real money. But I haven't been compelled to use the store at all while playing the game. This one really is fairly balanced in this aspect.
and lastly, this game is BIG... I'm almost 50 hours in and I'm about half way yet...
If you don't think it's worth full price, you should at least consider it during a sale :-)

Dogs of war online is a free to play online tactical turn based strategy game developed by Cyanide studios. Cyanide studios themselves are a French developer based in Paris France and are some what of a hit or miss company in my opinion. While they have developed great games like blood bowl, confrontation and the highly underrated of Orcs and Men. They are also the ones responsible for the terrible game of thrones game. Please note a the time of making this review, the game although mostly complete is in open BETA and as such there are quite the few bugs and glitches to be had.
Dogs of war is heavily inspired by the confrontation boardgame by Rackham, as was their previous confrontation game. The game is set in the world of Aarklash which as you can imagine is in a state of war. Three factions vie for power, the forces of light, darkness and destiny. Seeing this as a grand opportunity mercenary companies have started to spring up and as you can imagine your going to set of these companies up.
Each of your units has a number of attributes such as attack, damage and parry as well as a AP value. AP stands for Army points, the way that battles work in Dogs of war is similar to popular table top games. Each battle has an AP limit value for example a death match battle with a limit of 200 AP. This means you can you'll only be able to deploy units that match or go under that score collectively. For example I can deploy my predator of blood, a Wolfen crossbowmen and a lone wolf-man unit which adds up to 167, however I cannot deploy my fang warrior as adding him to the selection goes over the 200 AP limit
So lets get down to the main focus of the game which is its combat. There are currently three types of player vs player game mode available. You have your straight up death match mode, Elimination VIP which is where you are given a unit to protect while trying to kill the enemies VIP and last is king of the hill, where you need to place units in a selected area and hold it until the timer runs out. When your not killing real peoples mercenaries, you have the option of training missions. These training missions have varying difficulties and place you against an AI.
The combat itself is your very traditional turn based strategy, the movement grid is a hexed grid and  the game shows you your movement options clearly. The green area around a unit is where you can move and still do actions like attack, you also have the option to move further by going into the orange highlighted area at the expense of any form of attacking action.
Attacking works on a basic formula, your units accuracy versus the enemies parry. Should you succeed damage is then worked out by your units damage versus the enemies toughness rating. There are a variety of factors governing your units attributes in a battle, things like terrain, cover, injuries, and other status' can affect the rolls.
Speaking of terrain and cover, the maps are beautifully crafted. You can make use of walls, hedges and more to take cover from ranged enemies or shoot from hedges thus making your character covered while attacking. There are also blocks of terrain that have rubble on them, these areas are classed as heavy terrain and units standing on them incur defensive penalties.
Two really useful mechanics in combat are the charge and pursuit movement mechanics. Charge is exactly as it sounds, your unit can charge an enemy. A successful charge will not only engage the enemy in close combat but also inflict a stun state which incurs a -1 to all their attributes. Pursuit movement occurs when a unit defeats an enemy, your able to take another action be it movement or attack another close enemy.
You also have orders at your disposal in combat, orders are essentially consumable abilities that you can use on any of your units. Some orders are faction specific for example as you can see I play as the Wolfen, their faction specific order is natural selection which gives a +2 to damage to the unit for the rest of the turn. Orders are crucial to victory in Dogs of war and can be the difference between a win or a loss.
Any fan of turn based strategy will be straight at home with dogs of war, even newcomers to the genre will pick up the mechanics of the game quickly and without much pain. The games tutorial explains everything nicely by actually letting you play the mechanics rather than just show you.
Dogs of war is no where near perfect, Cyanide still have a lot of work to do to not only bug fix but to also ensure the correct balancing for the units as some currently do feel over powered. Combat is solid and it is a good framework for cyanide to build on as the game progresses, luckily it is a completely self published title and cyanide own the IP meaning they can tweak to their hearts content. If your a big turn based strategy fan, you'll find real enjoyment here as I did. It is also a good place for newcomers to the genre to find their bearings as the game is not too difficult and you can just play with friends until you feel ready for more challenging foes.
As free to play games go, Dogs of war is by no means pay to win, though progression solely through ducats is slow and sometimes tedious, its easily done. While its a definite work in progress, there is certainly potential to build upon and I'd have no qualms about recommending this to anyone looking to play a turn based strategy.

It was difficult to decide whether to recommend this game or not. As a summary, I would say this is a game for sci-fi fans that prioritize story over game play and are not afraid to sacrifise game-play and graphic looks to delve into a slightly unusual universe and an OK story.
What was good in this game: a) The story was in addition to dialogue and cut scenes told through diary entries, which helped keep up with what is going on. b) Good character and location descriptions. c) Technomancy replaced magic here, which is an interesting skill to master and play with.
What could have been better: a) The game's graphics are very outdated, there are not many details to look at both when it comes to pure graphical looks, and immersive details. b) Almost all side-quests involve doing something and returning for reward: there is simply too much running from A to B, back to A and B again. If the world was more immersive, it might be more fun this way, but now it can be a little bit boring. A good thing is it doesn't take too much time to run like that. c) Voice acting could have been better in certain places to make the story more immersive.
Neutral points to note: a) The game is majorly linnear, with a few exceptions. b) Fighting is basic and not very complex, but made more fun through Technomancy skill tree. c) The world is limited to the player, there are invisible borders here and there, but mostly there is walking in corridors between structures and rock walls.
I chose to recommend this game, mostly because of the story and the way it was presented through diary entries and descriptions. Although the story itself isn't very immersive or more than averagely engaging, it kept me interested enough to finish the game. However, I would like to note that the story and universe they built in this game had several parts which would have been very interesting to learn more about. Simply put, there are some pretty interesting ideas, but it is a pity the game never explores them (more deeply).
So try this if you aren't bothered by above mentioned negative and neutral points.

I've used this software and some of its alternatives. It happily plows through even the most intense 1080P-60 video even after lots of effects, and its greenscreening works brilliantly, there's no "Green Edge" around anything.
If you do gaming videos with OBS or some other high-performance recording software, this is the editing software to use it for, and it's only the cost of a triple-A title!
For most intents and purposes, it's Sony Vegas for $60.
Now for what I can complain about:
Adding objects on top of your video is counter-intuitive at best. You need to resize and move the video frame instead of the object itself, so everything you need to do to move that object is reversed. You can't easily stretch objects, either, aside from just making them bigger or smaller.
THERE IS NO MASKING HERE! You need Vegas for that, it's on Steam, too. Not a big deal for me, I don't do masking for my videos, so I don't need the premium software for it. MovieStudio will still do greenscreen, though, so you can make custom masks in Paint or something.
For me, if my Internet goes down while I'm using MovieStudio, it immediately crashes. Again, not much of an issue unless you have unreliable Internet. In that case, run Steam in offiine mode and start if from there, it will still work in offline mode.
Other than those minor issues, though, this is great software for a great price!

As a fan of Deadly Premonition with its weird characters and plot, and narrative driven adventure games in general: I highly recommend this game.
The story is fascinating and keeps you wondering what's going to happen next while you get attached to all these bizarre characters that you can't do anything but love because of how bizarre they are.
The interactions with the environment are goofy and they encourage the player to literally touch everything there is on the screen because they reward you with points if you do so, even the characters can be touched and they react accordingly: it's funny and I love it.
There are also a bunch of QTEs during the story, but don't worry because these are actually entertaining and fun to do unlike some other games where they are just annoying to get through. I actually think the quicktime events in this game are some of the best in all of videogames.
Unfortunately the real bummer is that the story ends on a cliffhanger, but they're already making a second season that I hope it'll get released soon enough. I want this game to sell well so we can get one step closer to getting that sequel!

was one of my favorite games of 2010. Actually that statement isn't entirely accurate. My favorite "experience" of 2010? Hmm... Well the long and short of it is that Swery65 and his team at Access Games are exceptional talents in some respects, much less so in others. The strongest elements of
were the character interactions, the story, and those absurd, surrealistic, and also strangely subtle moments that held everything together. The actual game portions (particularly the "action" stages where you shoot the enemies) weren't anything to crow about.
The recipe for D4's success is Access Games focusing on their strengths. Rather than attempt another low-budget
, what we have is an adventure game, filled mostly with quirky character moments. The main plot is certainly interesting, but the real charm is in how everyone plays off each other, as well as the limited interactions you have with their world.
It's fair to say that the bulk of the game is spent "goofing around". When you're not piecing together the events of a mysterious incident on an airliner, you're seeing what's on TV, pushing objects (and people) around, and drinking heavy. Most of the conversations that take place in this game, have nothing to do with anything. Still, they are what makes the game all the more entertaining. It reminds me of the earlier Metal Gear Solid games. Yes, Snake is on an important mission, the world is at stake, but is that any excuse to miss out on discussing James Bond's gadgets? I think not.
Most of the actual game-playing is investigating objects. A lot of the text is flavor, but there are those rare times, where you'll feel a brush of emotion. This is what makes attention of detail such an underrated aspect of videogames. David Young's house is filled with reminders of his recently-deceased wife. He recalls the simplest things, like notes on a fridge, or the time a cabinet is purchased. It reminds me a little of a hat I purchased for my grandfather. He passed away several years ago, and I still have the hat as a memento. It's odd how I can recall when the hat was bought, the store, and how I felt at the time. Sometimes I wonder how David can stand it. He's living in an apartment where he's literally surrounded by mementos of his wife. After awhile it really has to... eh well perhaps this review is overdue for a change of subject.
As far as the QTEs go, this is one of the few games where I actually like how they work. All of them are handled through various mouse gestures, and they're very lenient. I suppose they'd have to be, considering that the game was originally designed for the Xbox One's Kinect. There are only a handful in the game, and half of them involve fights with a cat-girl. Did I mention D4 is weird?
D4 is a difficult title to recommend. It has all the charm and personality of Swery65's last game, but it is definitely incomplete. It's possible that we might never see a Season Two. It's also entirely possible that you simply won't like Season One. This is the part where I throw in "Not for everyone" right? That's usually the case for these games. Still, it could be worse. At least this game didn't recieve a garbage PC port like
did.

The game takes place on randomly generated terrain for increased replay value, but there is only one saved game allowed at a time. The translation shortcomings and lack of tool-tips make learning the game more difficult. The objective is to build a town and defend against nightly goblin attacks. Resource producing structures are placed and allow for citizens to collect specific items from the world, such as wood, straw, fruit, and stone. Buildings need to be placed on a road (but the road doesn’t need to be connected to any other roads), and houses can be built to increase the population. Town limits can be expanded using gold, which can be traded for using spare resources. Citizens have an assigned job, and need milk and fruit to survive. Defenses can be placed to fend off goblin attacks, or an army can be recruited to invade the goblin castles in a platformer-like setting. Carton is full of good ideas for a management game (random worlds, resource production, defending against nightly attacks, action platform mini-game), but it’s not polished enough to be totally engaging.

It would be quite a stretch to call Mars: War Logs  cyperpunk; though, that is what it is billed as. Once you get passed that and the voice acting (which vascillates between pretty decent and far less than stellar), you will find a very solid story about a hard♥♥♥♥♥that gains a following of broken people. Unlike many so-called RPGs and like many of the greats, your actions actually have meaningful impact on the story, not just in the way merchants may react to you, but in what quests will be open and who survives.
The character growth is full of fiddly bits very similar to the Witcher series, but you can usually get a grasp on it. The combat has issues in terms of targetting, but the other mechanics they give you to work with play out quite well. Learn to evade and throw dirt, and you will likely do alright.

Simply looking at Mars: War Logs for what it is, I found a very enjoyable, fun and slightly different RPG that has a really interesting world and some promising game concepts. I really enjoyed my time with the game and played it twice to try different builds, difficulties and to see all of the story.
I do recognise that there are limitations in things like the size and variety of the game world, limited weapon and armor choices, some voice acting etc but this is also a title by an indie developer so you expect some compromises compared to big devs. As a first effort in a new game universe I think it has potential for a sequel where the good parts of the game like the combat, character development, quest choices, crafting and the world itself could be fleshed out some more to make a top notch title.

A surprisingly cute and effective way to teach someone programming concepts, albeit low-level programming. I honestly can't recommend it to everyone, as it requires a very specific way of thinking. But if you have any knowledge in coding, or want to get into coding, this is a fun set of challenges to tease your brain.
As far as level of difficulty, it's nothing you won't find in assembly language homework assignments, so if you have that background, things will just be a matter of implementing the solution. However, for someone who hasn't dealt with this kind of stuff before, the commands can seem very limited and confusing, so I do warn anyone who doesn't want to do some heavy thinking to stay away.
For those who are experienced programmers, the game does grade you on optimization after the first few levels, which does get interesting for some of the later levels where you can optimize a solution for either number of instructions, or actual runtime, but not both with the same solution.
The story is very minimal, so if you're not into coding and just want to see the story, you'll be disappointed. However, for the specific niche of people who would enjoy the gameplay, it's a very solid experience in a neat little package.
Suprisingly challenging, fun, and a great overall coding game for a begginner or experienced programmer!

is the first part of a planned episodic adventure games series developed by Access Games in the same vein as Telltale's cinematic titles.
is a crazy story filled with wacky characters and ridiculous situations somehow fittingly wrapped into a serious, moody detective crime story.
follows the tale of David Young, middle-aged ex-cop and widower turned private detective in order to find D, a mysterious individual whose only known initial was Little Peggy's (Young's wife) dying breath.
If the plot I described above sounds super cliché, I can assure you that this is where any parallel resemblances to other detective stories end. David Young has developed a special power that allows him to find the truth about the past through objects he finds. This allows him to manipulate and learn about the past, convinced that his power can bring back his wife if he can find the right clues.
The story manages to remain entertaining in large part due to the extremely strange characters that David encounters, including his gluttonous, Bostonian buddy called Forrest Kaysen and a crazy half-human, half-cat freeloader called Amanda.
The game plays exactly like any other episodic adventure game the likes of Telltale Games' titles but manages to add some variety to the mixture. A huge variety of objects can be inspected, picked up and collected throughout the game and multiple optional character dialogues, mini-games or side quests can be triggered (or missed) at certain times.
You'll spend a lot of time pointing and clicking, dragging and rapidly executing action-driven QTE sequences but it feels natural and is an enjoyable accompaniment to the pace of the game. The only downside to the game is that it is easy to miss certain events or collectibles and, with the game sectionned into only three chapters, it can take some time to progress through previously-played chapters in order to find what you missed.
has a gritty cell-shaded appearance, leaving many visual imperfections (such as character outlines overlapping each other) that yet somehow appears intentional and could be considered artistic design.

I've had every single version of this game (original PC retail, GOG re-release, Steam re-release, mobile port, and original PS1 release), and there's even a mobile version, which was given an art revamp with a new UI and easier controls.  However, the PC version is a lot better for mods.  It has a pretty easy to figure out level editor, and while it's very limited in scope, there are some mods for this game.  You just have to hunt them down.
I find this game insanely fun, but it doesn't stand the test of time at all.  It's difficult to deal with the game in later versions of Windows, and the visuals are too poor quality to deal with on a regular basis.  The music is good, hell, it's some of the best I've seen in a dungeon crawler.  However, I don't care for the sound effects.  You can turn sound effects down, but they're unfortunately necessary to cue danger and things like that.
Ultimately, I think my favorite version of this game is still the PlayStation release and not the mobile version.  It doesn't offer multiplayer, and it has less content with no mod support, but the controls are way more comfortable than even the mobile version, and you get a better initial experience with a legit intro song, the vocal version of the town theme.  If you don't mind playing by yourself, it's easily the better experience in a lot of ways.  Plus, it can be played on a phone if you get an emulator.
However, the Steam/GOG/PC version is pretty good, and I highly recommend buying it on sale.  It can be a lot of fun with friends, but it's a LAN-only game with no real communication structure.  You'll want to be in the same room as your friends... or just play by yourself, of course!

Usually I don't bother to review games which I bought on humble bundle for a buck but the amount of misinformation I got from negative reviews before I've launched the game made me take a stand and support it with my positive at least.
Its funny how people don't mind when there's plenty of hidden RNG in other games like XCOM or FTL, but make it apparent by actually showing the dice roll and they go crazy about how the game is RNG-only.
Like it was said in other positive reviews - there's a lot of planning and decision making involved and player has a lot of options to mitigate or take advantage of low dice rolls. So it's not like You need a streak of 5 and 6 all the time to win, the brilliance of the game mechanic is that any roll can be put to use and most hazards can be nullified by the options player has.
Many negatives go like this "hurr durr I've got a disaster which needed 30+ score on dices with 4,5 and 6 causing injury I've lost there my crew members and lost the game hurr durr bad game 0/10, I prefer dying in Dark Souls a lot". What they don't say is this:
- game lets you use any rolls from 1 to 6 to get research points which let you have super boosts like total immunity to said injury or automatically fix the disaster for 17 or 26 points
- you can totally ignore said disaster go to one of ship rooms and regenerate ships health to counter the damage done by the disaster
- you can use another of the rooms to charge so called 'assists' which protect you from injuries caused by rolling 4,5 or 6
- you can use your crew skills like the mechanic which heals your ship a bit when you roll 5 which can lessen or totally counter the damage
- nobody says you should fix everything on every turn so you can slowly chip away needed score points by using crew with less dice and/or rerolling only some of your dice to avoid rolls which trigger hazards (I fixed one of my bigger disasters after 3 or 4 turns with 1 guy using only some of his rolls on fixes and the rest to boost research and use skills)
I'd say that's a lot of options for RNG-only game.
I've played dark souls and I remember that when you're about to get whacked with an axe size of a house you dodge, people sending their crew to disaster which butchers them on half of the rolls apparently don't dodge.
Proper managing is needed to keep your crew healthy and operational. Many skills and room abilities need 5+ roll to be usable which sounds like RNG fest but mind this - your crew members can have 5 dice max each, after every roll you can have 1 reroll of all 5 dices, which basically means you won't have problem getting that one 5 and use other rolls on whatever comes next. Some ship abilities trigger only when you roll the same score with 2 dice (3 for bigger bonus) which can be two 1s for example so you can use 'waste' rolls to get buffs, one of ship abilities which regains dice for your crew actually works on every single roll (second similiar roll doubles the effect).
That being said:
Tharsis lacks replayability - I don't feel that much reason to beat the game again because unlocks are very few.
15 euro price tag is to high for a game which you can finish in 30 minutes with no replayability as stated before.
Tutorial is lacking and it won't change since game isn't developed anymore.
TL,DR:

The majority of the games that I play are open-world. This is likely the case for many people; to see a particularly eye-catching landmark or building in the distance and not be able to go there is a grave sin in my eyes, especially in this day and age, where advances in technology have made an expansive, vibrant world expected.
But no game I have ever played truly compares to the vastness of Rodina. True, the planets are anything but vibrant at this point, and the same enemy ships appear over and over, but all that pales in comparison to what can be seen in the game now: potential for something truly great. The developer has confirmed that alien structures will be implemented, and I can only imagine how the story will progress from its current, unfinished state.
There is something done completely right, though, and that is the sheer size of the Zorica system. In making it the developer has created something fantastical, but what is, beyond the rapid and brutal orbital dogfights, faster-than-light transit, and speeding over the flats of an alien world on an anti-gravity bike, a very accurate representation of something that could very well be in our own cosmos. This is the universe we live in: a realm of terrifying distances, which can normally only be traversed slowly and with great care. Were the aliens and salvage sites removed, this would be something close to a spaceflight simulator.
Explore a star system. Fight aliens. Recover snippets of data, pieces of a story of an Earth that has fallen into opulence and eschewed progress for the sake of comfort, and a hopeful few who dare to venture to the stars to escape that grim reality.
Welcome to the Zorica system.
