"Final Fantasy IV" was the first Final Fantasy game to release for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). When it was released in 1991 it was very well received by fans of the series and newcomers alike and it was the first game in the franchise to use what's called Active Time Battles (ATB) which was used for most of the Final Fantasy games following this one. Fast forward 16 years and a 3D remake is released with voice acting and improved graphics. The question is, is it still any good?
Just to clarify, this review is about the 3D remake (which is the version that can be found here on steam).
This game is a JRPG that focuses on the story of Cecil, a Dark Knight who is the Captain of the Red Wings from the Kingdom of Baron. The game starts with Cecil being on an airship carrying out the king's orders. He goes with the Red Wings to Mysidia to seize the Water Crystal. Cecil takes the crystal back to Baron thinking about his action and deeming his actions as being wrong. With this on his mind he confronts the king about the reasoning behind the orders. When the king hears of this he strips Cecil of his rank and sends him and his friend Kain as messengers to the town of Mist. From there starts an epic journey about friendship, love, war, and betrayal.

This game is the game that introduced the mechanic called Active Time Battles (ATB) to the series. The ATB system has been used for most of the Final Fantasy games after this one and it has given the battles of these games a depth that was previously impossible to give them due to the turn based battle system where everyone would get the chance to attack once without any cast time every turn and then it would just loop this process. With the ATB system you can use tactics that just wasn't possible in the same way without the speed factor.
Yes, this game is very good! The game always keeps a good pace and you get introduced to new characters along the way. A minor issue that was present before this remake was that the difficulty was either too low (like in the GBA version) or too high (like in the DS version). This game, however, let's you choose between Hard (The DS difficulty) and Normal (Easier than the DS version but not as easy as the GBA version). The only other problem I had with the game was with the augment system, there is no way you'll know how to get the better augments unless you either google it or play it multiple times. And trust me, you definitely want the better augments, some of them are really cool. An example of one such augment is the Omnicast augment which gives you the ability to use single target spells as an AOE spell. That means that you can either A) Buff your party with a lot of defensive stats rather quickly, or B) You can deal very high amounts of damage with expensive high level spells to a group of enemies. It's really cool but it's rather tricky to just figure out how to get it. You might just get lucky and get some of the augments but if you don't look it up you're generally going to miss out on a lot of the augments. Apart from that the game is very good. I really liked the story, I liked the characters, I liked the voice acting. I don't know what more to say, it's simply a good game.
Yes, I really think you should. This game is great and I would absolutely recommend it for any Final Fantasy fan out there if you somehow missed this entry in the series. Also, luckily, if you're new to the series this game is a great starting point along with "Final Fantasy VI", and "Final Fantasy VII".

D4 is about David Young, a detective whose wife was murdered. Now he is trying to solve the case behind his wife's murder  and find the murderer with his only real clue being his wife's last words, "Look for D." Now, this sounds like something you have seen before doesn't it? Well, that's hardly surprising. The setting is very generic and by now a cliché. However, with D4 that is hardly a problem. The way D4 is executed is done in such a ridiculous and unique way I have only seen D4 pull off in a video game that I just couldn't help have a really good time with it. D4 is like those B movies you sometimes watch with your friend just have a laugh at how terrible they are, except that it's not terrible. It's like a detective story Tenacious D.
That doesn't mean that the story of D4 would be terrible either. It's not, but it's not the strong point of the title.
D4 is a point & click game similar to, for example, Telltale games or Life is Strange, except that it turns the whole thing up to eleven. Almost every little thing in D4 has a QTE for it, and by that I do mean almost everything, like raising a toilet seat for example. That might sound quite annoying but it really takes only just a quick movement of mouse and you get used to it very quickly. The game also has some longer QTE action scenes that are so ridiculously over the top that despite my general dislike towards QTEs, I couldn't help but love them. They are just so well executed in D4. Aside from QTEs, gameplay of D4 involves searching clues from the environment that will allow you to progress with the story. It is also played with only your mouse, or a controller if you choose to use one.
Characters in D4 are not any less over the top or cheesy either. The main protagonist, David Young, is your typical gloomy detective type, except that sometimes the things he says or the way he acts is so cheesy that it is impossible to take him seriously, and with each new character the game introduces, it gets worse. And when I say worse, I mean better. Each character in D4 feels more like an exaggerated caricature than a proper video game character, and I really enjoyed that.
Voice acting, again, was not very good in D4. In fact, on few occassions it was so bad that as I was playing, I looked up few of the voice actors and it turned out that the game uses English voice actors who have mostly worked on English anime dubs. That might tell you quite a lot about what kind of voice acting you should expect. However, this never bothered me while playing the game. I think somewhat cheesy voice acting that was bit on the poor side actually contributes to the overall mood of D4, but I'm sure this is something that can bother other people.
Soundtrack of the game on the other hand is very good. It is mostly composed by MANYO (aka Tomomi Teratani), whom visual novel fans might recognize from Sharin no Kuni, Himawari no Shoujo and Kara no Shoujo.
What about the PC port? Well, it is very bare bones but does the job. The game runs at 60 fps, there's some resolution options (not much), and an option for VSync and dynamic shadows. It also seems to be fairly poorly optimized with frequent fps drops and long load times. So yeah, it's not great, but it's perfectly playable. At the very least it's not so bad that you should not play the game because of it.
Now then, while I greatly enjoyed D4: Dark Dreams Don't Die, I won't claim that it's flawless. Story is not particularly amazing, setting and characters are arguably cheesy, the game is pretty short, and the voice acting is not very good. However, what is most likely the biggest flaw of the D4 is the ending. The game ends in an annoying in cliffhanger, one that is so ridiculous and over the top I actually laughed a little, but also one that's probably the worst kind of cliffhanger you can have. What makes it particularly annoying is that there is no confirmation of a second season for D4. That is not to say it won't happen, but it really is up to how well the PC release will do. Either way, you should buy this first season of D4 for the content it offers and not while expecting that the game will get its conclusion later down the line. Of course, I really hope this happens.
In the end, it comes down to does this kind of ridiculous B movie styled nonsense D4: Dark Dreams Don't Die offers sound like something you would enjoy. I personally had a blast with it.

A decent game overall I would say. First off, people with basic programming skills will probably whiz though this game fairly quickly, I managed to finish 90% of the puzzles in one 5 hour sitting. Any real issues you'll end up facing is using your programming knowledge and implementing it into this games ui, which can be a little cumbersome at times.
However, this game seems to be quite welcome to people who have never coded in their life. It teaches the basics steadily and in an easily understandable way, but I found the puzzle difficulty to ramp up maybe a little too fast. I watched a LPer have a crack at this game and started to really struggle at year 5, and just ended up quiting :C
Each year has extra challenges too, and these are aimed at the highly skilled (at least the later years). It presents some extra diffculty to a puzzle if you're up for it. But as I said and the game itself states, this challenges are very hard, maybe a little too hard; as they require a very specific solution in a very flexible enviroment. It's quite difficult to "trim the fat" from coding normally, this game makes it an even more tedious task.
One other downside is the story. Normally I wouldn't complain about this as I prefer games with interesting mechanics over games with a detailed story (not that I don't enjoy them). But Human Resource Machine hasn't really tried all that hard. All you really get for story are brief cutscenes which most point to the "robots will replace humans" trope. While a fitting story for this game, it's not explored.... at all...
Other than that, I nothing but good things to say about this game, awesome music, the "tomorrow corporation" artstyle and I've not encoutered any performance issues or crashes playing.
tl;dr
+ Interesting puzzle mechanic implemented well
+ Awesome music (where's my downloadable soundtrack?)
+ Great introduction to programming, or just to test your current skills in a neato enviroement
- Lackluster story
- UI can be cumbersome at times
- Challenge requirements are too specific

At the $10 price point it's definitely worth a purchase. If it were more than $10, it would not be worth a purchase. But it isn't, so it is.

PROS:
A fun programming puzzle game for those who are into that sort of thing.  The game does a decent job of introducing instructions (the gameplay mechanics), but does get quite challenging later on.  I like that they include some background information about the programming principles that the challenges are built on (enough to turn around and then Google the concept; indeed, some in-game dialogue even encourages you to do so, but not necessary).  Optional levels and optimization challenges provide something for those who want more (and I do recommend taking them on).  The tone and style of the presentation and narrative will be familiar to fans of the team's previous games ;).  The option to edit your code in an external editor is nice as well, and proves useful for the motivated.
NITPICKS:
I would call these more nitpicks, as opposed to true "cons", as they seem to be mostly design choices.  For example, the UI is a bit blown-up -- likely to make it easier for touch screens, and perhaps to give it a wider appeal (which I think is great, so ultimately a worthy concession).  Working with many lines of code can get a but cumbersome when not working externally (perhaps there could be options for collapsing/moving the instructions for each level).
TL;DR:
Definitely recommended for fans of the genre, but do be aware it's core gameplay is very different from Little Inferno or World of Goo, despite the somewhat cutesy signature art style.  If you're not sure about the genre, this is probably one of the most accessible and beginner-friendly I've seen.

Mars: War Logs is a bit of an enigma. Some have deemed it the "poor man's Mass Effect" but this is incredibly misleading as the similarities between the two games stop at the sci-fi setting.
When I finished the game I found myself wondering how I made it from start to finish without utterly giving up on it. If it wasn't because the game is only 10 - 15 hours long then the only other reason I could come up with is that the game really makes you ponder what it could've been if it had come from a more experienced developer with a bigger budget.
All the usual trappings of an RPG are present but none of them feel particularly fleshed out or provide any kind of depth. The combat harks back to the "old school" style of pause-and-play (ala Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age: Origins, etc) but beyond the fact that you can pause and then choose an ability none of the other aspects of the style are there. On top of this, while the game allows you to have a companion character you can't choose their attacks, outfit them with weapons/armor, or even take control of them in any way other than choosing their "stance".
A dialogue system is also in place but a lot gets lost in translation - literally. Since the developer is French the game is localized for anything else and it's terribly done. You'll find countless examples of this when your character says something that doesn't even kind of sound like your selection and/or when another character reacts to you in a seemingly opposite or confusing manner. Additionally it doesn't help that the voice actors bring disgustingly wooden performances to the table as well.
The inventory system is barebones (perhaps 4 different sets of "armor" and maybe 6 weapons), the crafting/upgrading system is totally out of whack, despite having skill trees to that branch into RPG archetypes (rogue, warrior, magic user) the game almost seems to want you to max out everything and use everything in one playthrough, a romance system is there but is so poorly done it's easy to find yourself not knowing it's even there at all or glitching it/breaking it yourself, and finally the story (while pretty unique) is at times confusing, ill-paced, and withholding.
How/why did I finish this game? In the end perhaps it was it was a strange desire to see a good idea shoot itself in the foot with poor development and virtually no QA. Mars: War Logs is a yet another example of something that could've been great, that wanted to be great, but just couldn't.

Do you love watching paint dry? Enjoy the frenzied excitement of watching a snail move? Leave your life to the whims of the fickle winds of fate? Then this is the game for you! If not, read on.
If you do buy this game or have received it for free, then by all means enjoy it with the friend/enemy who gave it to you and never ever play with the AI. This game mimics the classic board game well but it\'s a vastly different experience when you play with a physical board, miniatures and a jolly group of friends in front of you. With the digital game, it just feels hollow without the expressions and emotions involved when a plan comes together or falls apart.
The game itself is quite easy to pick up but expect to spend at least 2 hours per playthrough depending on how many players in a match. There\'s a lot of downtime as to be expected with most board games while waiting for your turn to roll around and the mechanics are pretty rudimentary and very RNG dependent. Imagine your delight as you reach the very anticlimatic finale which is the Crown of Command. While there, expect to spend the remainder of your turns and probably 45 mins of your life just constantly failing a 50-50 chance a zillion times just to ATTEMPT to end the game while other players counterspell you, heal back up or just try to reach you.
Aside from destroying my mouse on multiple clicks to try to speed things up in frustration, the worst came when another player finally reached the Crown too then promptly died and left all his junk on the same tile which prompts an encounter at the start of each turn asking if you\'d like to pick up their stuff even when your own inventory is full thus adding more time to the excruciating endeavour.
If you must play the game, then I whole heartedly suggest playing the physical tabletop version with some good friends instead of the digital one.

After putting +100 hours in this game, i decided to write my first review, to hopefully raise awareness to this amazing tabletop.
Talisman is great for fantasy lovers and offers lots of diferent heroes with different abilities to play as, which is one of my favourite features in a game. All the heroes are fun, some more powerful than others, but every one of them can win if you manage to use their abilities to their full potential.
Although there is some skill involved in this game, most of the player's performance is driven by luck. Preety much all actions (movement, combat, encounters) are defined/influenced by the dice rolls. This means that no matter how experienced you are, you can get destroyed by a noob who installed the game 10 minutes prier, which can be frustrating at times.
Another thing worth noting is that there are lots of possibilities for turning the tide in the middle of the game. This means that even if you're losing completely and the other players have much better stats than you, there's always a chance one of them will suddenly turn into a toad (and therefore leaving all objects/followers available to pickup) and allowing you to get all his stuff. Or maybe someone is about to enter the Crown of Comand (the place you need to reach to win the game) and you cast a spell on them and force him to loose his Talisman, the one object that allows them to get there. This triggers a lot of people, but I personally think it adds a lot to the game, and even though this stuff has happened to me numerous times, I end up having a laugh about it because at the end of the day, the game is fun. Just note that there's never a guaranteed win/loss, and you can always hope for a comeback or fear your demise!
Expansions make the game a whole lot better, and the more you have, the more complex the game becomes and the more ways there are to make your way up to the top!
Overall, I definetely recommend this game. A must-buy if it's on sale!

Final Fantasy IV on PC is a port of a phone game that in turn is a port of a DS game, which is a remake of an SNES game. Confused yet?
Final Fantasy IV is one of those classic, almost genre defining games, that made a big splash when it was first released, and which helped cement the Final Fantasy series position as THE JRPG series in the west (Dragon Warrior/Quest was not as popular over here as Final Fantasy, while both series were huge in Japan). Despite a questionable translation, the game captured the imagination of a lot of people, and remains to this day the favourite for a lot of people.
I did not play it on the SNES, and apart from getting to the first real boss on the GBA version, this was my very first experience with it, so there's no nostalgia involved here. From what I've gathered, this is supposedly a slightly harder game than the western SNES release, but I don't know what makes it harder, if they just fixed some exploits, or if we're actually playing a remake of the Japanese SNES version (which was harder than the SNES version).
You can tell that this game was made for a system with relatively weak hardware, as the models are blocky, and the textures are low res. Very little seems to have been done to improve the graphics over the DS version. Personally, I prefer the look of the SNES version, even if that game had relatively poor graphics for an SNES game, but that's a matter of taste. Neither version is a graphical powerhouse. At least the enemy design is strong, and despite their low-fi look, most enemies look intimidating and distinct. So while the graphics is technically weak, the art style is good.
But where the graphics is nothing to write home about, the sound is pretty good. You've got Nobuo Uematsu's legendary score, and it fits really well with this game. Nothing feels weak or out of place here. The sound effects are also pretty good, and you can often easily tell what's going on by sound alone.
You can tell that this game is old by the way its story is structured, and how its setting seems to be a smattering of different ideas that don't quite come together. Don't get me wrong, I do have a soft spot for these 80's & early 90's type game settings, in fact I find them very charming, and I liked the setting in Final Fantasy IV, but it's not as coherent as you would expect from a more modern game. You've got a mix of sci-fi elements in a classic medievalish setting, and nobody seems to really be bothered by it. And no, not just the typical Final Fantasy steampunk-esque things, like steam powered blimps, but full on killer robots shooting lasers, spaceships and that type of stuff, mixed in with dragons and medieval knights.
You're playing as Cecil, a Dark Knight and commander of the airship fleet "The Red Wings". You've just returned from a mission that the king sent you out on, where you stole a magical crystal from an innocent group of people, and you're feeling guilty about it. The king then sends you out a mission to deliver an item to a village, but the item turns out to be something that ends up destroying the village, and this is where the story really starts. How could the king, a man you once respected, make you do such a horrible thing? And how come the king is evil, and there's not an evil emperor that wants to do something bad to the good king, like in pretty much every other classic Final Fantasy game?
Over the course of the game you get to learn what's really going on, meet a varied cast of characters and kill hundreds of monsters while you're at it. The story is mostly well paced, although it does go off on tangents that feel like they're padding rather than important plot elements. If there's one area where I think the game falters, it's the world building, they really should have spent a bit more time on it, introducing elements of the setting to the player and giving you a more coherent understanding of the world. As it stands we mostly get what's important to the story itself, with relatively little "fluff" outside of that. The characters also feel a bit less well developed than those of later Final Fantasy games, with some of the party members being little more than stereotypes. At the time of release, at least for a console RPG, this was still more characterization than most got, but compared to more modern games it falls a bit flat in this regard.
Final Fantasy IV introduced the "active time battle" system to the final fantasy series. Rather than taking turns, like in the games that came before, you've got a bar that fills up, and when it's full, you get to perform an action. Unlike  many other games using a similar system, there's also a windup time for most abilities, which means that casting something like a high level spell might end up nearly twice as long as casting a low level spell, and you can't cancel this windup once initiated. This hurts casters pretty badly towards the late game, as physical fighters end up dealing more damage than them, because they can attack more often. It does make it more of a strategic choice on what ability to use though, something that becomes extra important to consider when it comes to healing and protection spells. Can you afford to wait for a big heal, or will you be better off casting a quick heal? Will you waste a quicker "phoenix down" to resurrect your fallen party member, or cast a slower spell, which just costs mp?
Most of the game is pretty easy, but it feels like there are some "grind gates" along the way, places where enemies deal so much damage that you simply don't have time to respond before they kill your party, so you need to grind a bit to reach a level where you can actually fight the enemy. These grind gates are mostly the regular trash enemies, with bosses being stronger, but also more predictable, so you can get by with more strategy against them. For an example, in the final dungeon there were some enemies I simply could not beat, yet the final boss was a bit of a pushover once I had figured out how it worked, and the same thing was true for many of the other bosses during the second half of the game. If you can survive the first two attacks the boss throws at you, you're good to go, while the more unpredictable regular enemies can be far more challenging/unfair.
You can tell that Final Fantasy IV is based on an old game, and without any nostalgic attachment to the original, I don't consider it one of the best Final Fantasy games. But it's not a bad game, just one that's a bit rough around the edges, and a bit underdeveloped in some regards. Fans of JRPGs should check this one out, but those new to the genre, or who only play one once in a blue moon should probably go with Final Fantasy IX, VI, V & VII  first (I've not played any of the PS2 games, so I can't comment on how good they are).

Final Fantasy IV is easiliy remembered as one of the most classical JRPG games ever made and for several reasons. Let's take a look at them.
While this version takes away the charm the 2D sprites had for DS-level 3D designs, it will still make you fall in love with its strongest point: characters and story.
While most plot twists and remarks games like FFIV has to offer have become cliche by these days, they are still very enjoyable and quite a breakthrough by the time this game got released. This version dig deeper into the story by adding more scenes and content, reinforcing what may be the greatest point of this game: all the story in regards to the tale of Dark Knight Cecil and his redemption to become a paladin and attone for his sins. While he may be the protagonist, he is not the only character with charm in this game: the lonely and tormented Kain, the mysterious villain Golbez and his Archfiend Elementals, the gaudy Edge, the lovely Rosa, the cheerful Rydia and many others will submerge you in the rich story of FFIV.
As for gameplay goes, this entry of the FF series was the first on to use the Active Battle System (ATB), making your fights more pacy and tense than ever before in the series (I'm looking at you, Demon Wall). The job system that was one of the strongest points in FFIII has been completely erased to focus in each of the charatcers traits. In stead of this, throughout the story you will find "Augments" that will allow you to custom your characters with active or passive abilities.
As for duration goes, completing the main story + side quests will take about 30-35h. But be warned completionists, in order to defeat the two superbosses contained in this game, you will have to go through a second playthrough.
All in all, and despite not being at the level of the top Final Fantasy entries, FFIV offers a very enjoyable experience and I would recommend it to any JRPG fan. In addition to that, if you are looking to get inot the Fina Fantasy series or the JRPG genre, this is a great place to start.

I can only recommend this game for certain types of people.  Think of it less like a strategy game and more like a punishment simulator.  You manage a crew of desperate astronauts trying to complete their mission to reach mars.  The game starts with an unfortunate accident that leaves two of your crew members dead, so you take charge of the remaining 4.  Each around, various systems will malfunction on your spaceship and you have to triage the crew to resolve them (or tactically choose not to).  You have to manage the Health, sanity, and ability points (dice) for each crew member.  Taking an action involves rolling and deciding what to do with the outcome.
Where Tharsis diverges from other dice games, there's a very heavy element of randomness that can be frustrating.  You're only allowed essentially one-reroll (maybe 2 on a particular character).  Certain events could be in play that prevent your dice from being re-rolled, eliminate them, or do damage when certain numbers come up.  There's a lot of chaos and hazardous elements to remove your control of the game, but not that many elements to build it back up.  This is a game of subtractive progression where you often will become weaker as the game goes on, fighting a war of attrition.
It's punishing, and clearly not for everyone.  Most games follow the opposite model and allow you to feel like you're becoming progressively more powerful over time. It's clear that a lot of thoughtful work went into this game, though, and it's worth a couple of re-plays to unlock the additional characters and try on harder modes.  The missions also add some variety.
I wouldn't expect many people to get more than 20 hours out of a game like this though.  Each play session exists in isolation and doesn't really contribute to an overall end-goal, except maybe unlocking a few extra characters.

Tharsis is based on dice rolling and a random number generator. Most people will pass up the game after hearing this, and usually I would to but I'm glad I gave it a go. Despite (presumably) very simple code and ideas, it still manages to be fun. The game challenges your ability to make difficult decisions, manage multiple problems and prepare for worse problems to arise. At first it seems very complicated, but once you learn all the core concepts the game becomes about developing a strategy which you will inevitibly have to adapt in future. When people say the game is too hard, they've most likely repeated the same mistakes or put no thought into their actions. The game is a lot like FTL: Faster Than Light, and if you've played that you've most likely failed far more than you've succeeded; Tharsis is very similar but you can't avoid problems. Sometimes you need to know what to fix and make priorities while not neglecting what needs to be done. Tharsis is a great game to play casually or hardcore, everywhere from your lunch break to Saturday nights while drunk and listening to Wolfmother. Absolutely worth picking up on sale, or even at full price if you're interested in this sort of game.

This game places you as the leader of a crew sent to Mars, your ship encounters some mild technical difficulties leaving you with limited resources and crew to try and survive the rest of the trip.
The core mechanic is dice rolling, so there is a lot of screeching and flailing as you roll the exact number you did not want to roll somehow every single time because dice are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, it appears to use a physics modelled solution for the dice rolls which I always appreciate and seems to work quite well.  Beyond the dice rolling you have tactical choices which in some ways boil down to which dice to roll when, and some more strategic choices which generally relate to resource management and use, including hull durability, food, stress, and crew health.
The tutorial was good, but it still took me a few losses to feel like I had any real grip on the game, and given the challenging / not-quite-roguelike nature of the game you should definitely go in prepared to lose, a lot.
I would compare some aspects to games like Zombie Dice, or possibly Elder Sign, there's an element of press your luck and limited numbers of dice that you can roll for each crew member, do you keep the 3 or risk a bad thing happening when you roll again while hoping for the elusive 6?
All of this is wrapped up in a lovely thematic bundle, slightly spooky at points (as space should be, really) and with a rather gorgeous soundtrack.

I just noticed Duck Tales: Remastered was on sale for $5.  That is the most I would recommend that you pay for this game.  In terms of what you are getting, there are two aspects to this game: (1) a very simple 2-button side-scroller kids game and (2) nostalgia.  Some gamers will value one more than the other; some will want both.  I value DuckTales: Remastered at about $2.50 for the genre and $2.50 for the nostalgia, in comparison to other games out there on Steam.
The emulated version of the original Duck Tales game for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) back in the late 1980s is available for free on the internet and is legal to download, own, copy, etc.  You can play the 8-bit version and compare it to this one.
The obvious differences you'll notice in this version offered here on Steam are the upgrades to the graphics and sound.  Hence, for a very simple 2-button side-scroller kids game, you will be able to expend a few hours of your life hopping around and trying not to get hit by things or to fall into pits.  However, this genre of 2-D, 2-button, side-scrolling kids action means that you won't be developing your character (such as "leveling up"), or carrying around an inventory of various items, or solving challenging puzzles.  Instead, you will simply be jumping and bouncing on top of bad guys, occasionally golf-shotting less than 20 rocks all game.  Very straightforward; very simple; not a bad way to spend your time, especially for $2.50.
In terms of nostalgia, this particular game (the "Remastered" version) is unique for a few different reasons when compared to other games on the market, especially of the same genre.  For starters, it's based on a wildly popular Disney cartoon series from about 30 years ago, and they even brought back the voice actors of the popular series to do some voice-overs for this game (during the cut scenes between stages).  Also, Duck Tales: Remastered is a faithful rendition of the original NES game, which itself was a smash hit.  The familiarity of the simple gameplay and kids action genre will remind you of what it was like to play games as a younger person.  Essentially, playing Duck Tales (the original or the Remastered versions) will make you feel like you are participating in a Duck Tales cartoon episode.  For $2.50, that's pretty cool for a few hours of your life.  I analogize this to buying six episodes of the show on DVD, for example.
So if you only prefer simple kids games but don't care about the popular Disney cartoon series or the original NES version, then I'd recommend that you get this game when it finally goes on sale for $2.99 or less.  If you are nothing but a lover of popular Disney stuff (especially Duck Tales) and/or love remakes of great old-school video games, then I'd recommend that you get this game when it finally goes on sale for $2.99 or less.  If you are a diehard fan of both the genre and the associated nostalgia, then I'd recommend you pay no more than $4.99 for Duck Tales: Remastered.  (And I'd also recommend that you legally obtain an emulated version of the NES version in either case.)

Many people have compared D4 to Deadly Premonition and it is an apt comparison. Much like that game, D4 is the kind of energetically confusing adventure that one needs to play to fully grasp exactly what it is and why it is so fun. Unlike Deadly Premonition though, where the game as a whole was “so bad it’s good,” D4 is “so good it’s good.” It’s clear that Access Games knew exactly what made it’s previous title so great, and poured it into a better constructed frame. More importantly, Access Games has created undeniable proof that more can be done with the genre as a whole, and I look forward to seeing what else they can do in future installments. There are two episodes and the prologue out for D4 currently, but more may be on the way, and what is currently there is well worth the fifteen dollar price tag. If you enjoy adventure games, then you will no doubt love D4, and if you’re not keen on those kinds of games, I still recommend you check out D4 as it really does set itself apart from anything else I’ve ever played.

My reason I'm so torn is due to the fact that Season One offers no resolution to ANY questions. Personally, season one feels like that intro to a great game and just as it's about to pick up steam and get to the good stuff BAM it's over. It truly stops right before an action scene, leaving you confused as to why there is no episode 3.
Season one just feels like a 5hr or less demo♥♥♥♥♥♥tease for a spectacular game. I would still find the game worth my $15 if I knew there would be more, if I could expect a continuation and explanation for at least SOME of the questions I have. At this moment, however, there is no solid news on if or when D4 will continue.
For that fact alone I want to implore everyone who is interested to support it and speak out on your desire to see more. I admit they went about having an episodic series pretty badly. They should have taken a page out of TTG's book on how they do their seasons. For a game season you want to present the story, present questions, but you also really want to resolve SOME and have what feels like a season conclusion. If you are unsure if you will get a continuation in the future, you'd damn sure want to make it so your customers don't get a lack of a finale for a season. You want people to feel satisfied, but also eager to come back. The current 'ending' to this season may do more harm than good to the series as a whole. As an example, I was so close to just telling people to avoid it til news of a continuation arises, but that very well might spell the series' doom.
All in all, be aware of what you're getting into BUT the experience of playing this, the characters, and the story that's being built is all very much worth $15.

If you're a non-programmer with an affinity for logic and maths and want to learn in a fun way how computers work at one of the lowest level (that is assembly), go for it! You will learn interesting stuff. If you're grossed out by the thought of having to figure out how to find the rest of a division of two random numbers using only addition and substraction and basic logic, you should probably pass because you're not going to enjoy this game.
If you're a programmer and want to remember your old school days of learning basic sorting algorithms and/or assembly -> go for it! The levels aren't that hard to complete, but the challenges (code size requirements and execution time requirements for each level) will definitely have you rethink your solution and pull your hair trying to optimize as much as you can.
The only subjective thing is how much "fun" can you have writing programs and optimizing them within a game? There is nothing to "cover up" the fact that you are indeed sorting number chains and character strings, so if you're not having fun doing this, what's the point? The game atmosphere is very similar to other games from the same studio (world of goo, little infermo) and by that I mean that the story is very minimalistic and mysterious, and the humour is very cynical (you're basically working within the game).
It took me approx. 6 hours to complete the game and various challenges (I´m missing 30% of the latest levels challenges to be 100%), but it was definitely a fun experience that made me think back about basic logic and how difficult it is to perform operations like sorting that are very easy to do with higher level programming languages. Recommend!

Mars: Wars Logs was a real surprise for me. Being only $20 on release and being from an unknown developer, I went in not expecting much, but I'm happy to say this game was worth it beyond expectation. Fans of good RPG's shouldn't be disappointed. You'll get an interesting story, great graphics, talent/skill upgrade paths and a really decent equipment upgrade/crafting system.
Also the combat in this game is really well done IMO. At first it looks like a bit of a button masher, but once you get the hang of evading attacked, using skills/weapons during the fight and even throwing sand in your opponents eyes, it gets really fun. IMO its similar to the combat in the Batman: Arkham games, but maybe not quite as fluid or seamless.
Oh and Technomancy is too much fun. Throwing chain lightning into a mob of guards never gets old!
Only downside is there wasn't much to spend Serum (money) on in the end, and I wish there were more outfit options discovered along the way, but those are only minor faults.
Fingers crossed we get a sequel before too long.
Story  and gameplay are up there with the big block buster games. A bit short and a little too linear but other then that a great game. If you like Sci-fi RPG games, definitely check this game out.

Another fine example of "Good idea, terrible execution."
The core of the game is learning about the concept of triage, but with dicerolls added on top to determine the success rate. Add in an alluring story and wonderful atmospherics, and one would think that this game is a winner.
Except the game is rigged. If you do well, at all, at any time, the game punishes you by dogpiling you with harder tasks. It's only recently that I've been playing this game myself, but I've seen and heard enough from others playing it that the dice are ALWAYS stacked against you.
You manage to clear the ship of all threats 2 weeks in a row? Watch as you get problems in the 30+ range with every number above 4 being marked as VOID - meaning any dice showing those numbers get removed from play if you roll them. Games are meant to be challenging, not "Impossible, and sucks to be you for even trying." Nobody plays the Kobiyashi Maru for kicks.
What's that, you say? This game has an Easy mode for all you crybabies? My time with Tharsis is ALL on Easy mode...and the above example is what I get for managing to stay on top of things. If it happened once, I'd curse my bad luck. But this "bad luck" is consistent. I know the game mechanics, I know what I'm doing...but I can't fight the impossible. The game is really out to get you, by any and all means possible.
As a result the game is nothing more than an exercise in futility, only suitable to masochists.
Avoid like the plague.

As an AC series fan since II to Black Flag, I'm not so enthusiastic as before (well, Unity get me sick, then I bought Syndicate through but never have a passion and time actually to play it). I even didn't track the news of a new AC game in this year (but I have a sense that 'it's time'). I used to be a loyal customer of the physical deluxe edition (in practical, 3 to Syndicate), but this time I just purchase a digital edition on Steam, thinking about to give it 'a try'. Another reason is that I also want to have a taste that what's the feeling of playing a game like this on my new PC (i7700, gtx1060 6GB).
And this becomes my favourite game in the last of the year.
Overall, the technical skill -- Ubi's landscape rendering on every AC game is their best strength. I trust them, and I have an expectation. Different from the previous AC games that most story stages still exist in the modern age (like Jerusalem, Venice, Rome, Istanbul, New York, Paris and London), the Egyptian landscape of Origins last noting at now but several faded ruins. So I know it's a challenge to create a realistic, convincing ancient Eygpt in the late Ptolemaic dynasty.
But this time I still get impressed. The ancient Egypt where is a mystic to me now looks so real and colourful in this AC: Origins. You can find out that at that age, Egypt was in an ethnic conflict among Greek, Roman and Aboriginal Egyptian. You can be surprised that the Sphinx was not so large as our imagination. You can row a boat in the magnificent view of Nile and understand the Egyptian's proud of it. And most important one, climb on the top of the Great Pyramid of Giza -- then ski down from it!!!)
Plot: 3/5. Even the main plot is surprisingly short, but at least it explains the origin of Assassin Brotherhood. It makes me sad to experience the struggle of the protagonist in the main plot. Good to see him became relieved in the last. The determination and perspective of Aya surprised me (and controlling her in the primary ending quest is another one).
Battle: 5/5. Compared to the previous games that focus on assassination, Origin gives players more choices. You can become a battle master who deals an army in front, can sniper everyone without a sound in a bow, or be a pain in every soldier's♥♥♥♥♥by mastering tricks of fire, poison and smoke. A traditional assassin player (like me) can also be satisfied with a new foe-tracking system (with your eagle), more challenging, but more rewarding to achieve every perfect assassination.
Quest: 4/5. Side quests seem trivial, but they are in fact enjoyable to play. The number of them is reasonable -- not too many nor too less. Beside from a crucial step of levelling up, they provide the opportunity to understand the culture of ancient Egypt and shape the character of Bayek more vividly.
UI design: 4/5. Seems like largely improved. Never got a time lost by changing item or checking map, and overall looks more beautiful than before.
Rendering: 4/5. Sometimes there can be slight rendering issue on texture, mostly at the start of plot animation. But it doesn't cost a lot to an overall outstanding display expression on my PC. Everything looks so real and adorable.
Exploring: 5/5. No need to explain a lot. If you even got a time bored in travelling on the ground, you can call your Eagle to see everything from the sky, or just sit on a boat, let the boatman carry you across the Nile. Being a 'tomb raider' is also an amusing experience and the most rewarding one.
Socialising, and after-time playing after completion:
3/5. Origin doesn't feature a multiplayer, but it proves that multiplayer is unnecessary to make online socialising and keep players to play the game even after completed the main plot. You can compete with your friend with the score of racing and arena, the quickest completion of trials, even whose photos are better-looking. I know there is a possibility of the multiplayer mode to be add in future DLCs, but now I don't see any necessity of it. To me, the game itself is completed enough.
Overall:
If you are an AC fan, play it for your love of series.
If you just know AC recently (maybe by the movie), play it as it will make you surprised by the charm of the series. Oh, remember to at least play Ezio trilogy as well.
If you don't know what the h#*l AC is, play it as it can be the first game that descript the scenery of ancient Egypt so vividly. You won't be disappointed!

OK, I'm 15 hours in and although the game had a slow start (including a strangely disjointed prologue section), once I got to Alexandria things really started to pick up. Now I'm finding it to be one of my favorite AC games (alongside AC2 and Black Flag). I like the new RPG features and the immersion factor of seeing life in Ptolemiac Egypt is very cool. I have some complaints: 1) the beginning (which I already discussed), 2) a few sparse areas (especially before you get to Alexandra), and 3) some slowdowns that required me to dial back a few settings, which probably shouldn't happen on my system (I7 7770K 4.2, GTX 1080, 16 GB RAM). It IS a very pretty game and perhaps the Ultra settings are meant to future-proof the game a bit, but the game (and Nvidia) did recommend Ultra settings, so maybe a few patches are in order.
All in all, if you like AC, this is a very good AC game!

While it may be good value for money, Bus Driver is a very basic bus simulator with very random locations and bus routes.
The world map contains different areas for the bus routes to be taking place in. Their names are very random, as for whatever reason, SCS Software has named bus stops as towns in Greater London, and as a Londoner, it is a negative, as they look nothing like their real life counterpart. For instance, a bus route has Beckton a bus stop away from Eltham which realistically, they are on either side of the River Thames
Most bus routes are short or are long distance with routes having only 5 stops or long distances with no stops. Many buses have similar routes as there are 5 routes that operate around the Grove Park and Hounslow/ Ewell area.
You can only operate a bus route in one direction, with no variation of passengers, weather or traffic, making each playthrough of a bus route the same.
The game includes 5 different buses with two buses having a different colour scheme. They are, except for the double decker, American buses, so you'll be driving in the right side od the road. They look ok, but there isn't a cab view or the ability of exit the bus or free roam, so the game is very linear. There are also two coaches, school bus and a prison bus.
The game was originally released in 2007 with 5 tiers. There are 6 routes for each tier, making this Bus Driver include 36 routes. You could fly through the game in less than an hour, as to pass a teir, 4 routes need to be completed.
Graphically, there has been alot of backlash and nowadays, it looks quite poor, but for 2007, it's good.
The game overall is very basic, geographically incorrect and very short. I'd still recommend it as it was my first bus simulatior almost 10 years ago and is good for beginners and value.

Dissapointed by No Man's Sky and need something to scratch your space exploration itch? Rodina might be the game for you.
In Rodina you explore a vast solar system with 4 massive planets all roughly the size earth and tens of thousands of asteroids. You will need to scavenge items and fight off hostile xenos to uncover the storyline. The feeling of loneliness surrounds you and the amazing soundtrack enchances the feeling of solitude.
The storyline is absolutely amazing even when it's purely made of text. Be prepared to read. It will keep you engaged and it will surprise you.
The combat happens in air and on land. The land battles FPS battles against xenos with different kind of weaponry. The air/space battles are fought with space ships and different kind of weaponry which you can easily equip to your spaceship. My only problem with the combat is that the guns you get to currently use in land combat feel like peashooters, so it's a lot easier to just kill everyone with your spaceship.
The spaceship has a fully customisable interior, which I have spent a lot of time on making it fit me. It really adds to the homeliness of the spaceship. While the exterior can't be changed in the current version in vanilla, modding the game is pretty easy so you can go download exteriors for Nexus Mods. So with mods you can fully customize the ship to your liking.
There is basically only one type of thing you do to get forward in the game. Fly into a plus sign in an object, kill all enemies on the site, and salvage the items left there. It might sound lame but I have had a lot of fun with it so far, purely because the atmosphere engrosses me in the world.
This game is still in early access, but it still manages to do what many other games will never achieve. Best part is... It keeps getting updated and in the coming year the game will advance a lot. I recommend looking the roadmap at the Elliptic Games site.
Basically this game is worth your money in it's current state and it will only get better from now. Buy it.

Final Fantasy IV, how do I even begin to explain how amazing this game is.
Final Fantasy IV was the game that introduced me to the Final Fantasy series. It's truly an excellent game and definitely worth playing. I love the game so much I actually went ahead and got all the achievements in the game. But that's not at all convincing, so I'll go into more detail as to what makes this game truly spectacular.
Story: The story is incredible for a game made originally on the SNES. The story's main protagonist is Cecil, a dark knight, who is leader of the Red Wings of Baron. The main goal of this game is to hunt down Golbez, who is planning to seize the world's crystals and use their power to destroy the world. During your quest, your party will frequently be changing, meaning your battle strategies will have to change, but I don't want to go too in depth about that to avoid spoilers.
Gameplay: This is where the game gets very interesting. In this version of the game, there are things called augments, where if you use them on a character, they can be taught abilities, such as Dualcast for double spell casting, or Omnicast for casting any magic on all allies or all enemies. This makes for some really interesting and customizable gameplay that you won't find in any other version of this game.
Music: This is in the top 3 soundtracks in final fantasy in my opinion, can't say it's the best because it does get repetitive, especially if you grind for many hours straight as I did.
*Fun Fact* This Final Fantasy was the first to introduce the ATB (Active Time Battle) system in its SNES version which was a staple in many of the subsequent Final Fantasy games we know and love.
Do I recommend this game to people who have never played Final Fantasy before? ABSOLUTELY! It's a great way to introduce the core mechanics of Final Fantasy games to someone who's never experienced them before. Ever since I first played FF4 I haven't had enough of the Final Fantasy series.
One final note: If you decide to do tail farming for achievement purposes like me, expect to be at each tail for many hours. 0.4% drop rate!

I'll start with the tl;dr version:
It's kind of a fun game, but know that
--a very literally shiny, well made, physics intensive game where you try to reach the doors at the end of each room faster than the people on the leaderboards. That's it. Nothing more, nothing less.
The game feels like a solidly finished, 3D platforming framework for somebody to fill in with substance, except somebody forgot to expose the API. Whoops.
Now for the longform:
It's my fault for making assumptions. For some reason, maybe the people mentioning Portal when talking about the game, I just figured there'd be a little more to it once you got going a bit. You know, some sort of further interaction between the character and the disembodied voice of the researcher that initializes them, or maybe a backstory. A plot thing to keep me interested.
To be honest, this game was kind of an impulse buy for me because I liked how shiny it was and I wanted to listen to the music and see the rooms designs, what have you. Plus it was on sale.
My experience so far has been that the chambers, and therefore the game itself, are little more than a novelty. They're 3D obstacle courses with fancy mechanics (and some not so fancy, like basic platforms) that have you racing against the clock to figure out how the chamber works.
These chambers are indeed quite challenging as you progress. It's mostly because the basic physics of the game itself are just
particular, which is good. However once a chamber's novelty wears off, they just grow tiresome due to the
required to complete most chambers. That means that when I screw up I have to start
in chambers that just seem to keep getting longer and longer. It's just arbitrarily time-consuming, and that leads me to the real problem.
The problem is that the devs dangle no carrots to keep me on the hamster wheel. There's no cheese at the end of the tunnel.
I get virtually no satisfaction from completing a chamber other than being glad that I've finally gotten it out of the way. All of the chambers are just disconnected rooms with no purpose or structure, no story.
As shiny as the game is, there isn't even anything pretty to look at due to their choice of visual aesthetics. (All the chambers look exactly the same as you see in the trailer.) I'm not progressing toward any sort of goals other than to complete the entire list of chambers, but I'm so bored now that I don't even have enough curiosity left to manage that. Scoring diamond on the leaderboards may mean a lot to some people, but I don't personally give a damn.
If you want a better game of the same type, I highly recommend
instead. Sadly it's not nearly as shiny, but it's a much more engaging experience overall. Not to mention it's cheaper

Thus far, the developers have not done anything to address this issue. I haven't seen one post on the Forums about it and it is unclear if they are even working on a fix. My gut tells me they are not, yet they do not hesitate to put this game out on sale.
There are supposed fixes around, but they require a lot of work and I simply can not be bothered to fix something that is not my fault as a customer.
If they ever fix the bug I will happily change this review.

A set of cumputing tasks you have to solve with a very basic set of micro-instructions, and a very limited amount of memory.
Each task stands on its own and there is very little in terms of overarching story or plot. The game sets a thematic mood, and runs with it.
There are 41 challanges, some 10 of which are meant to be tutorials introducing the way the machine operates or getting to use new instructions.
Leaves ~ 30 challanges to solve in "mini-assembler".
If you're familiar with this kind of programming, you're going to find working solutions to the puzzles pretty quickly. There might be a few challanges late-game that require a not-entirely-trivial algorithm to work: sorting and integer factorization. The easier ones will be done in anywhere from 30 seconds to 10 mins, the hard ones maybe in 20 (you still have to try your algorithm and fix all these off-by-one bugs, right?).
If you're not familiar with programming at all, the learning curve will take its toll in terms of time spent, but you'll learn how computers work at the fundamental level. Modern ones, and not so modern ones. I promise you, after you're halfway through the game, you'd be able to look at an article like
and have a basic understanding of what the author is talking about. The learning curve is quite enjoyable, and the pacing is pretty good. New instructions are made available every couple of levels, the challanges gradually increase in complexity.
There are two optional challanges attached to every level.
Like in many real life scenarios where micro-instructions are involved you're to preserve memory and optimize runtime speed. And you're going to realize that you usually can't have both at the same time.
These challanges can be hard if you've not programmed before. They will be easier if you have programming experience at any level.  They will be much easier if you've programmed with micro-instructions before and are familiar with low-level optimization concepts like loop-unrolling. Often you'll be able to solve the speed challenge by just taking your unoptimized solution and "being the compiler". You'll start unrolling loops, reordering instructions to save memory accesses etc.
Sometimes you'll have to change the idea behind your solution to pass a challenge. Usually that would happen with the size challenge, and usually late game, where there are real choices for algorithms. There's several ways to deal with sorting for example, and once you googled the simple approaches, you pick one and implement it. Might want to
how they work first. And for the size challenge you'll always want to go with the simplest idea. Simple ideas usually need fewer instructions.

One thing that I found could be improved upon is that, especially end-game, there's not enough high level instructions and/or space on screen to lay out your program. Either give us a div/mult instruction or make the screen-space for the program bigger. Writing division loops in assembler takes space you know, and seeing more of the program at a time would help staying organized.

Also, there's no code block copying and you can only save 3 solutions to any puzzle - both problems can be overcome by copying your solutions into text files, but you shouldn't have to do that.
Finally, I found it boring that many programs could be speed-optimized by merely unrolling loops. I know that's a real technique, but it just isn't that interesting. Maybe you could make unconditional jumps free? Just a thought.
Still, this is a very good game and I can easily recommend it regardless of programming experience.

Shame, this novel concept could have been "The Oregon Trail in Space," but someone started overthinking it, adding more and more features as they went, oblivious to the exponential levels of complication they were introducing. Even if you're dedicated enough to grok the underlying mechanics, you'll find yourself repeatedly failing thanks to the ruthlessly randomized dice rolls that determine the results of every action. The final product is an already difficult game made nearly impenetrable to anyone except diehard fans of the concept. To the average gamer it's just hatefully unapproachable.

The game is short ("lucky" playthrough would last maybe 30 minutes max), with only a few mechanics and quickly gets quite repetitive. Not really worth the prive tag IMO
But my biggest issue with it is how largely it's based on RNG. Depending how the dice roll (yes, the main mechanic is about rolling actual dice) you get either totally screwed or get to live on. The luck factor plays too big role in this game.

Nevermind the negative reviews. If you read them, you will realize that they do not understand this game.
This game is about one thing. DAMAGE CONTROL.
To further elaborate. It is a game about managing bad incidents. It's not a game about luck or a game about winning. It is a game that makes you think very very hard on how to survive when you-know-what hits the fan.
The purpose of the game is to try and make the best out of an insanely BAD situation. That's it. If you don't find this idea intruiging or if you are a person who can't stand to lose then simply this game is not for you.
For what this game is, it is very good and the execution of the concept is great. It has a somewhat steep learning curve in regards to what station module has what effect etc etc but once you get the hang of it then it's all about strategy and damage control. The info buttons help a lot at first. Use them.
Is it brutal and unforgiving? YES and YES. With capital letters for emphasis. Can things go south very very fast? YES. But that is a good thing. When playing Tharsis you should always anticipate disaster. Even when things are seemingly going your way.
If you have ever played Elder Sign on Android, Tharsis is similar in concept and brutality :)

Tharsis is a good looking and simple board games. Don't be fooled though. Only rules are simple. Game itself presents sometimes quite a challenge. You have to be aware that it's based on dice throwing, but again - don't be fooled by that. There are many ways to counter bad outcomes and to plan ahead. Simpleness is starting to become boring after a couple of hours though and that seems to be the only true con of the game and that's becouse of lack of content. Still, I believe it to be a very good game to play once in a while.

AT the 17CAD price Steam is asking, definitely not - for the part-of-a-dollar it costs you from Humble Bundle, sure
It's a dice game, to boil it down - it sure looks like a strategy game at first, and there's certainly little decisions you can make to improve your odds, but to be entirely honest you essentially sit in front of the screen and click "roll" until either a "game over" or "you win" screen pops up. Aside from that and the dinky little CG heads bobbing around I still enjoyed myself.

If you're the kind of person who's put off by dying every single game... Tharsis may not be for you. However, if you're willing to work through the constant dying, screams of agony, and suffocation, and figure out a strategy that gets (at least some) of your astronauts to Mars, then I would highly recommend this game. The gameplay balances ease and simplicity with complex strategic planning, the story (which has multiple endings) captures it's audiences curiousity, and the "70's Sci-Fi" style in this game is really nice to look at. Tharsis is an overall great game, and I'm sure anyone who picks it up will have great fun replaying it for hours.

The game is full of horrible decisions, and sometimes you get♥♥♥♥♥♥on. But that just makes winning that much sweeter.
All that said, I wouldn't pay $15 for it. Pick it up on a sale though, it's good.

Mechanically a very standard, but very solid Final Fantasy game.  The drive to keep playing comes from the characters.  The protagonist Cecil and his supporting characters are well established, with refreshingly relevant reasons for being in the plot.
The story isn't afraid to get dark either, as the Hero begins obstensibly as a hired thug that invades weaker kingdoms on orders of his king.  Characters die and the protagonist has to learn to live with his actions and atone.  It isn't all dark either, as there are lighter moments and levity throughout.
There is a bit of an unfortunate turn around towards the end, and things get very 'standard' in the fantasy/hero sense.  But for the majority of my 40 or so hours I remained engaged and happy with my time with FFIV.

If I were to select a handful of early RPG characters that stand out for me even now, years after playing them, Rand, the swole as hell armadillo-man from Breath of Fire II, would hold one of the top spots.  However, since this review is in regard to Final Fantasy IV and not Breath of Fire II, I should mention that Cecil, the dark knight, would also be a strong contender.  Although much of Final Fantasy IV is outdated by modern standards, the game is still very fun and a great trip down Nostalgia Lane for those who enjoy early JRPGs.
The story is well-written, but it certainly does fall into the cliche trap that all of the early Final Fantasy games fall into.  The story revolves around the same crystals as all of the games before it, however, the character development is exponentially superior to the previous titles.  By the end of the game I actually felt attached to the characters as opposed to just seeing them as vessels for the the stats that I had built up over the previous twenty-five hours of playing.
Final Fantasy IV is also the point in the series where the mechanical aspects of the characters became far more fleshed out.  The job system that was previously used was scrapped and replaced with a system that made each character their own class with their own abilities.  Although this may disappoint some, there is not arguing that the system is far smoother than that of Final Fantasy III.  Augments were also added into the game.  These consumable items are used to teach a character a new type of skill that they could not have learned otherwise.  Characters also join and quit your party throughout the game, allowing you to play with over twice as many characters as you had in any of the previous Final Fantasy games, and adding diversity and a dynamic environment to your party.
Overall, a strong entry of the early Final Fantasy games that shows a significant evolution from the previous titles.  As you play you'll notice the seeds of many aspects of the universe that will later become the unique Final Fantasy tropes that we know of the franchise today.  Although I recommend Final Fantasy IV to all JRPG and Final Fantasy fans, I consider it a must-play for those nostalgic for the simpler RPGs of the old days.  You won't be disappointed.

I fell in love with this game immediately after playing a demo at the 2015 SXSW Gaming Expo. While it does resemble Portal at first glance, its gameplay is more reminiscient of games like Super Meat Boy where precision and timing are everything. The game teaches you the basics and then leaves you to figure out more complex manuevers as you play. The ranking system amplifies this as certain ranks can only be achieved through specific paths and more complex moves (See the Gold vs Diamond video above).
At the moment, there are 29 levels, not including the tutorial and the several bonus challenges like the Creator's Challenge. There is a checkpoint system if you desire and after the tutorial cutscenes, there is very little downtime, leaving you to focus on perfecting your runs for that elusive Diamond ranking. All in all, this is a game for people who enjoy a fast-paced, challenging, first-person 3D puzzle platformer that allows them to get in quickly and game.

Like others have said, this game is a puzzle platformer, somewhat in the vein of Portal.
Like Portal, it has an understated graphical polish that reinforces the central theme of the game -- a kind of apathetic hostility evoked by the sterile test chamber setting that jives well with a game that's hard for the sake of hard. Also like Portal, APT's deceptively simple mechanics unfold to reveal a real depth of gameplay hidden within just a few straightforward actions. Coupled with the visual minimalism, the core simplicity of this game is the perfect setting to showcase the punishingly well-crafted level design.
Unlike Portal, the difficulty in this game is the kind that requires quick reflexes, adroit handling of the controls, and a quick, intuitive sense of the physics in order to do well. It's not the kind of thing that will appeal to everyone, but for many -- myself included -- the merciless, impersonal taunting of a tightly-tuned ranking system is the kind of thing that engenders a genuine sense of satisfaction when you finally shave a few thousandths of a second off your best time to eke out diamond rank on a particularly challenging stage, hours later.

My wrists are super sore and my fingers hurt because I've been mashing the keys so hard for three hours. This is WAY more difficult than Portal, and takes things a step beyond. Split-second timing is the difference between success and failure, and you'll have to use superhuman reflexes to beat the best times and top the leaderboards.
The gravity mechanics are fantastic and force you to plan your routes in advance. Tethering balls and double-jumps help you navigate this first-person puzzler and it gets EXTREMELY difficult as the game progresses. This is not for the casual gamer, it's for challenging yourself.

APT is a Portal-like aesthetically looking game where you solve puzzles in a closed set of room(s), but instead of a Portal gun, you have Jets, Tethers and Switches. If you thought Portal wasn't a very challenging game, APT will be right up your alley, Portal's level design focused more on figuring out where to go and what to do, while APT is more about fundimentals and execution, and still finding out what to do.  So this game is for the bit more hardcore puzzle platformer than others. Each Level/Trial has it's own little puzzle that can be solved in most cases, more than 1 way. The game keeps a good balance between really hard levels to easy ones, sometimes you'll come across a really hard level that might take you an hour to get Diamond or top score in, while the next couple preceding it only take 5-10 minutes doing the same. There is a ton of satisfication to beating the trials and getting that Diamond Rank and that's where it gets addicting.
So to Sum it up, It's like Portal but harder, Level design is on point, and if you're really into being the best at this game you'll easily get your mone back on this purchase.

APT is a cool puzzle platformer with a nice feeling of achievement when you perfect levels.
The game's puzzles mostly revolve around momentum, and traversing around the map as fast as possible.
After your first jump, you can launch yourself incredibly far with a jet boost, and swing from floating balls with a tether tool.  Both of these actions require a small cool-down in between uses, which forces you to perfect your timing. You've also got another action, with which you can press distant buttons in order to activate objects like platforms.
The game has a good replay value due to the medal ranking system, which will most likely tempt some people to retry and perfect certain levels. There's a good variety of levels with different types of skills needed, which keeps the game fresh.
Overall, I think the game is quite fun if you're into this genre!

Rodina, for having a story that plays out entirely by text, has one of the best stories I've read/played/experienced in a long time. The story combined with the stunning star system the game takes place in really make Rodina a great experience despite not being so early in it's development. The updates to the stable branch are few and far between but when they come out you can always tell how much the developer cares about the game he's creating. Truly a gem in the Early Access scene.
As far as the game itself goes, the combat is challenging and fun, it doesn't feel at all boring or cookie cutter. The music is probably some of the best I've heard out of a small indie title like this, and the planets are properly massive and breath taking. The models are for the most part very primitive, yes, but you'll hardly notice that as you're trying to put out fires and shoot down enemy ships.
I could probably go on for a while longer about all the things I love about this game, but my favorite thing by far are the organic movie-esque scenes that happen on a regular basis. Watching enemy ships fall to the planet below in a ball of flame is probably one of my favorite things in the world.

What is more frightening than a God?
This question was posed to me upon completing Rodina's main story, as well as the answer, in quick succession.  Not literally, of course, but thematically; I felt that this was the underlying thesis of the entire work.  My interpretation, anyway.
That's probably a pretentious way to start.  Okay!  I'll talk about the game now in more literal terms.
Short version:
Do I recommend?  That depends.  Rodina is quickly becoming one of my favorite games, but that's because it's both a fun  activity that revolves around interesting exploration in a vast, vast world and a vehicle for philosophical quandaring through some pretty excellent writing.  If this does not appeal to you, then no, I don't recommend.  If it sounds remotely intriguing, then yes, I whole-heartedly recommend.  Do it.  Play the demo.  Then pay the 250 that this company sorely deserves (if I had that on hand I would do so in a heart-beat).
Long version:
I'll describe the game by listing and explaining each facet any game would typically have.
Graphics:
Subpar.  I find the visuals to be charming, reminding me of a few games I used to play when I was a kid fiddling around with my parents' bulky Macintosh.  Honestly I never cared about the graphical style of a game I'm playing, so long as it doesn't hamper the overall experience (I like Minecraft, for example).  Compared to some AAA games out there, it'd get trampled in this department.  However, I think the initially unappealing look of the game works to the game's advantage, in what I think the game attempts to portray.  I won't spoil, however.
(I saw that there was a separate artist for this game, so don't take this as me dissing you - I'm only comparing it to games that have like a zillion dollars backing it and pretty much nothing else, and also I can barely draw a stick figure so take that what its worth.)
Gameplay:
The actual, full-on, no BS reason I bought this game in the first place was because I read you can walk around in your own ship.  Seriously.  After playing Starbound and finding great satisfaction in essentially piloting a flying house, not being tethered to anything anywhere else, I was greeted with a great sense of freedom I don't find in any other game.  Alas, Starbound was still limited (2D notwithstanding), and I longed for even greater freedom.  Rodina, then, heard my call, burst into my living room, stripped itself of all clothing articles, and demanded that I make love with it.  Of course with the graphics I was mostly aversive but I at least complimented its hair.
Okay, okay.  So yes.  Walking around in your own ship - a ship whose interior you can design AND walk around in whilst mid-flight - was just really fun for me.  As was the difficult control scheme.  Learning to fly took a lot of effort, but it made it worth it.  Same with dog-fighting.  I've seen complaints for this, but honestly, I found the hectic nature of the space battles riveting.  Especially when you're in the atmosphere of a planet, having to pay attention to where you are so you don't burn up while also keeping track of the swarm of enemies trying to practice their anti-protagonist agenda.
In addition to movement and such, I am also continuously amazed at the size of this world.  It's merely a solar system, yes, but holy cow is it gigantic.  The planets feel collosal, in a way that makes you quickly realize that you're just a speck.  Likewise with the distance between planets and asteroids.  There's just a scope here that I'm still wrapping my head around.  If nothing else, this game seriously hammers in the idea that, hey, space is really big.  Like, bigger than the biggest thing you can think of.  Yes, THAT big.  Some kind of space scientist would be proud.
If I had one minor complaint, though, it's that I think the Xenos' weapons are a bit over-powered.  Not against your character, mind - that's just fine.  I expect a rocket to blow your face off.  However, how come a few pew pew bullets can down your entire space-craft?  Especially those homing thingies.  Two of those and you're gone.  Feels kind of uneven to me, but what do I know?
Story:
And this is where we rub up on the reason I think this game works as well as it does.  I'll get this out of the way, first, though - the writing is excellent.  Delegated to out-of-the-way documents that you can collect, each contain a small part of a short story that interconnects with the greater context of the universe.  It is not required that you read any of them in order to get any enjoyment out of the game, but doing so will deepen the world you inhabit while you murder those poor green men.
That is, until you rip through the story without reading anything and get to the end, where you should be thoroughly confused by what happens.  And this is where I fell in love with the game.
It's not visibly enormous or spectacular by any means, no.  It'd just generate a small bit of confusion that may compel you to read why it happened.  But for me, this created a thrust that I just haven't seen anywhere else.  A context was created that perfectly married the graphics, game, and story into a single entity - you.  The player.  A trajectory is set at that moment, one that I'm unsure could be stopped, and I think the understanding of that is what propels this game into the profound.  In the end, it made me realize that with the scope of the game's world, the abilities I possessed, and the enemies I've mowed down, I realized what exactly this protagonist was capable of now, and will be capable of in the future.
The game at this point asks, what is more frightening than a God?  And you get the answer to that as quick as the question is asked.  And this, Mr. Ebert, is why you're wrong - this video game IS art, and it's art in a way that no other form of media would be able to accomplish.  Or I could just be talking out of my♥♥♥♥♥like some pretentious hipster.
Anyway, to all those involved in this wonderful work's creation, thank you.
