Human Resource Machine is a game about programmatically sorting tiles, and about climbing the corporate ladder. As you progress, business conditions will change, and your character will gain seniority. You will gain access to greater sorting functionality, and you will be entrusted with more sophisticated sorting tasks. Optional side content exists for those seeking greater difficulty. Those seeking to extend their playtime may choose to optimize their sorting methods. I recommend this game for people who enjoy puzzles of moderate difficulty.

By simply taking a look at the screenshots you’ll know exactly who is behind this seemingly-casual-but-still-harder-than-expected puzzle/programming game: the Tomorrow Corporation! Better known as the developers of Little Inferno and World Of Goo. Is Human Resource Machine (HRM) just as brilliant as those games or is it maybe even better? Or, God forbid…*gulp* worse?
Let me reassure you: HRM is absolutely great. It might not necessarily be better than their previous games, but I enjoyed this just as much (and at times even a bit more), but it’s still a unique game that tries to teach you the basics of programming. It can be fun for actual programmers and people who have never even attempted it before, although it speaks for itself that it will be more challenging for this group.
You start at the bottom of the company, where the level number is relative to your years in service of the company. It starts off rather linear with only one way to go up, but after level six you can choose to play more advanced puzzles, and these branch off the otherwise linear path. These are usually more difficult versions of the levels you’ve already played and they are entirely optional.
There seem to be 33 levels, by the way, and this is excluding the optional puzzles. In total there are around 44 levels.
The first few puzzles can be solved with relative ease, but the game always wants you to use your brain. You might make some progress by just trying things. You might even be able to finish a few levels this way, but ultimately things just become too complex. If you haven’t paid attention to the game’s mechanics then you’re going to have a hard time finishing it.
The learning curve is good; you’ll start off with the absolute basics and then just work your way through the levels, gaining more and more functions as you go. There are 11 functions in total and these functions will apparently simulate most of a computer’s algorithm, which I was actually unaware of. You learn something new every day!
You can start and stop a puzzle, fast-forward as well take steps backward and forward. The sound can be muted in the level itself and there are also buttons to delete, copy and undo functions and use three sheets. You also have a clear button that removes all of your used functions so that you can quickly start over again. This is sometimes more useful than just rearranging everything and also gives a better overview if things are not going your way.
If you’re looking for more advanced programming puzzles then I’m sorry to have to disappoint you. Even casual gamers can eventually finish this game with a little patience. And to be honest, I don’t think the game would’ve been as fun if the puzzles would’ve been even more difficult. If you want advanced programming lessons then I suggest you go read a book or follow a training course.
In fact, I think that there will be plenty of players who might want to give programming a try after having played this, either as a hobby or a study/job.
Where I normally don’t get a sense of accomplishment whenever I manage to solve a tough puzzle, in HRM this is a completely different story. Solving the puzzles felt rewarding and great. I felt… smart. That’s not normally a feeling I get when I play games. It’s maybe because these are logical (to-the-point) puzzles whereas other puzzles usually require a bit trial-and-error gameplay because things aren’t always clear(ly explained) and are shown in an entirely different context, relative to the game’s story and atmosphere. And no, this doesn’t apply to *all* puzzle games, of course.
After finishing a puzzle you will be shown a results screen (called Optimization Challenges) that shows you have many steps (speed) and functions (size) you should have used and how many you used to actually finish the level. Since sometimes you can do (much) better this is a good incentive to go and replay a level. Plus, you will ultimately learn to program more efficiently this way. And the levels are also usually just a few minutes long (and previous attempts are saved you when exit the level), which is another kind of bonus I guess.
With such a relaxing game you will need relaxing audio as well, right? You are absolutely correct and thankfully the music that has been implemented suits the game well. It remains in the background and doesn’t become the focus of attention. Other than that there are some relatively basic sound effects: similar to the sound effects used in their previous games.
The visuals of HRM are instantly recognizable as Tomorrow Corporation’s work. There’s no doubt about it: the weird looking big lipped and/or big eyed characters and the brownish color palette. It’s all part of the developer’s famous art style. Everything looks stylish and sharp, the animations are done well, although the animations in general are quite limited. But then again, this isn’t a game about the visuals, but about the gameplay. The graphics are there so you know you’re dealing with a game here, but underneath it all is actually a basic programming tool. One that has just been dressed up.
Fortunately there are more than enough puzzles to be solved. There are 44 levels in total and while they start off by showing you the absolute basics the difficulty will increase not long after you have started. Add to this the optional, more advanced puzzles and you should be able to finish it in 10-30 hours. All of this naturally depends on your current programming knowledge and intelligence, though (hence the big gap).
They have done it again: the people of Tomorrow Corporation have managed to surprise me once more. HRM has become a beautiful, little educative game that shows everyone can have fun programming… as long as it’s a little dressed up.
I’ve had tons of fun playing it, even if it’s at times frustratingly hard/difficult/complex. But try to keep going, though, it’s worth it for the feeling of accomplishment alone.
In any case, I suggest you add this to your cart right now and press that big ‘Buy’ button immediately. Trust me!*
(*Just don’t hold me responsible if you end up not liking the game ;))
Pros:
+ Famous Tomorrow Corporation art style
+ You’ll learn the basics of programming in a fun, but still challenging way
+ Plenty of puzzles
+ Optional, advanced puzzles
+ Optimization Challenges make you want to do better and be more efficient
Mixed:
+/- If you want to learn/know more about advanced programming functions you will have to look further
Cons:
- Even though it has a good difficulty curve it may still prove too difficult for people with little or no interest in PC's (e.g. casual users).
(Ratings aren’t calculated based on a formula, but on my personal feelings)

Human Resource Machine is a challenging puzzle-based programing game from the devs who brought us Little Inferno and World of Goo. In HR Machine you’re presented with tasks to complete and in order to complete said tasks you need to program your little office worker to complete whatever steps need to be taken in order to complete it. As you’d expect the puzzles get harder as you progress through the game but they’re not exactly easy to begin with, making this one of the most challenging games I’ve come across.
I’ve never done any kind of programing before and while the game is very good at explaining how to do it within the game it is still pretty tough to wrap your head around. If you do have programing experience you may find it slightly easier but there are bonus levels along the way to test the best!
HR Machine brings back the style that Little Inferno and World of Goo had and as expected it looks great and fits perfectly with the game. There’s not much else to say about this other than the fact that it’s a great looking game. All the models are good, the UI is clean, simple and easy to use as is the menu.
Starting the game with two different commands you’ll gradually work your way up to eleven different commands, making up a simple language. Using this language you’ll program your little office worker to complete tasks set by the management. Each task has its own floor, completing the task will earn you a promotion to the next floor and a harder task to complete. While the main objective is of course to complete each task, the management are also looking to see how many commands you use and how many steps it takes for you to complete the task. While these aren’t tied to progression they add an extra challenge if you wish to push yourself though it’s not always possible to complete them both in one program.
The tasks set are of a wide variety but they always involve taking items (numbers at the beginning but letters are introduced later on) from the inbox and then manipulating them somehow before moving them to the outbox. Some tasks involve taking items from the inbox before subtracting them from the next item in the inbox, some involve multiplying a number by itself x number of times etc.
All of the levels with tasks have spaces on the floor where you can copy inbox items to/from. These are used in pretty much all of the tasks in order to manipulate the items or swap their order etc.
As I mentioned earlier there are bonus tasks which provide a challenge for even the best programmers! The different tasks are displayed as what looks like an elevator floor control. Every so often you’ll come across a branch that breaks away from the rest of the levels, generally about four or five levels. The tasks given to you on these levels are incredibly challenging, I found the regular tasks mind numbing but these take it to a whole new level of mind numbingness! So whether you’re a programming wizard or a complete newcomer there’s something here to get your grey matter going.
Audio is great across the board for HR Machine. The music fits nicely with the game and it’s reasonably subtle so it doesn’t steal the show from the game itself. Sound effects are also fitting and sound pretty good.
Human Resource Machine is a truly fantastic puzzle-based programing game with a charming aesthetic and challenging puzzles. If you’re a fan of puzzle games or just like a good challenge, do yourself a favour and buy this game.

Ever wanted a glimpse into the world of logic and assembly programming? That's what Human Resource Machine does: translates the world of some assembly based programming into a corporate like infrastructure in a puzzle like format. And they've done it rather well, allowing for teaching the concepts and ideas behind logical programming in a way that people can understand, at least coming from a software engineers perspective. It still captures the Tomorrow Corporation's aesthetic and goofy nature rather well, and while it's a game that will frustrate others with no hint system, it's countered by the use of the “debugger” to see what's going on. : Square-Enix
: Square-Enix
==========
What was old has been made anew! Final Fantasy IV, perhaps the most cherished game of my childhood, now feels as fresh as anything else in modern gaming. For newcomers to the series, this is an excellent point of entry that showcases traditional Japanese RPG gameplay with one of the best stories ever told in the genre.
Final Fantasy IV is about a hero saving the world from pure evil. Beyond that reductive outline, the game's plot is actually unusual, even by today's standards. Cecil, the protagonist, begins the game as an intimidating Dark Knight who is sent to murder innocent people and steal their valuable crystal. After the deed is done, he begins to question his loyalty to the king, due to the wickedness of these orders. Your first task as a player is to deliver a package that, unknown to Cecil, is a weapon designed to murder an entire village of summoners. At a pivotal moment in the story, Cecil undergoes a dramatic transformation and plays like a completely different character from that point forward. Throughout the game, characters will enter and leave your party at the story's whim. Some of them will turn against you; others will sacrifice themselves for your cause and never return. Clearly, this is serious material, and it's told through a new translation with a more consistent tone and some additional details that were lost in the SNES version. There is also a small amount of voice acting of admirable quality, though some of the actors don't quite match the gravity of the plot.
==========
A complex plot demands linearity of game progression, and there is no doubt that Final Fantasy IV is a linear game. It's like a roller coaster...a very slow roller coaster, and you're strapped in for the ride. Your party can include up to five characters at a time, but you have no choice as to the lineup, and every playable character has unique abilities. Although restrictive, this format keeps the gameplay fresh throughout a very long adventure. Your party changes every few hours of game time, so you have to develop new battle strategies on a regular basis. A feature in the Steam and DS versions allow you to collect Augments when some characters leave your party; these items let you teach the departed character's unique abilities to other characters. This feature is made more interesting by the fact that these versions also includes a lot more unique abilities for each character.
Some abilities, like Edward's songs, are much more useful now and continue to grow and flourish via Augments long after the original practitioner has retired from the party. There is even a customizable Auto-Battle feature in which you can assign specific skills or magic spells to be used automatically in battle, for when you are facing easier monsters that don't require your full attention. These and other gameplay tweaks will not only delight long-time fans of the game but also make it more accessible and streamlined for new players.
==========
The presentation has been overhauled far more dramatically than the gameplay. An impressive engine by Matrix Software provides some great 3D graphics. The visuals are not only easy on the eyes but also allow some of the more dramatic scenes in the game to be played out with full cinematography. Being so familiar with the original graphics, I enjoyed seeing the new 3D models for all the characters and locations, and most of them look great while staying faithful to the original designs.
==========
The classic soundtrack has been re-recorded with higher quality instruments, but the compositions themselves are untouched, so every song will be immediately recognizable to veteran players. Composed by Nobuo Uematsu, Final Fantasy IV has a ton of great tracks that match up well with what you encounter in game, and definitely get you pumped for boss battles! Just check these out:
==========
PC specs are on my profile. This game ran beautifully. I didn't run into any issues, bugs, glitches, or weird crashes. I played with a controller that worked just fine the entire playthrough. No tweaking had to be made for it to work.
==========
Final Fantasy IV is one of those classic games that nearly everyone should play at some point. It was an unparalleled experience in the early 90s and holds up remarkably well today. If you have never played Final Fantasy IV or haven't touched it since it was called Final Fantasy II for Super Nintendo, this is absolutely worth experiencing all over again. My only problem with this Steam version is that it is not the Final Fantasy IV Complete Collection that was released on PSP, that included FF4, Interlude, and The After Years.

is a point-and-click horror game about a man battling his inner demons on his way to becoming a psychotic killer. It's a completely story-driven experience. You take on the role of Hamilton and wander through the game's painting-like world and talk with the people and creatures you encounter (and yourself). The six chapters take approximately two hours to complete.
On the plus side, the artwork is excellent and disturbing as is the musical score.
Did I feel creeped out? Yeah, the story is harsh, and the warnings about this game are serious.
Particularly if you are squeamish. It's based on a true story. I found a Wikipedia article that recounted the actual events and people involved, and no names had been changed. The game is remarkably faithful to the source material, but the real-life story is even worse. If you plan on playing this game I'd avoid looking it up until after as it will give away various plot elements.
But is it a good game?
That's debatable. I would be more inclined to call this a visual novel, well ... novella, due to length. It reminded me mostly of
, another creepy Steam title with several design similarities. However that game has puzzles in it, so it takes some brain work to finish. In this game there is only one puzzle, and it's not terribly hard to figure out if you are paying attention to the clue being dropped.
Of course horror novels exist purely to creep out their audience. That's a part of their allure. Horror games do this too, but in this case I'm inclined to think it's not enough to make this rise above being a mediocre experience because it only challenges you on how tolerant you are to the scenes being depicted. Maybe that's because it stays too close to the source material? Real life events might be notorious but that doesn't mean they make a good game. By the end the only thought I was left with was, "there are some sick people in the world who are f---'d up beyond all hope." The end.
In short, if you want to walk through a deeply disturbing and horrific short story and you have two hours to kill (heh), then play it. Otherwise there isn't much else here.

From developer/publisher Oldblood comes the short, psychological horror game Masochisia; a title that in story may be familiar to a very niche group of people. To others who don't have the same macabre interests, it's simply a mysterious tale based off a true story, wherein you battle and succumb to inner demons. If you're seeking complex riddles to solve, you need look elsewhere as this game is one that relies primarily on thought provoking dialogue and exploration.
I'll start by saying right off the bat that Masochisia will not be for everyone. Those with a weak mental state, who are easily pressured into feeling like they don't have control of their thoughts, and victims of physical abuse, especially during their childhood, will not enjoy this title. It's an experience that challenges even the most mentally healthy, as it breaks the fourth wall a lot and places you deep inside the mindset of a real serial killer. Though many have been skeptic if this game is actually based on a true story, I can confirm that it is indeed heavily based on prolific killer Albert Fish. As so not to spoil the plot, I will stop here and say that if you question whether or not you can handle the mentality and subject matter of the game, look him up.
You play as a young man named Hamilton, and it becomes obvious very early on that his father physically abuses him on a regular basis. His mother is little to no help, and his brother is a deranged masochist. Through a series of hallucinations, which are sometimes calmed by medication and self harm, Hamilton encounters an angel by the name of Michael who has promised to help him understand his fate and destiny. The dialogue in this title, though small and given in one or two sentence waves, is superb, and it's the main focus of the game. As you venture on into Hamilton's psychopathic hell, the game forces you to think like him; pretty soon you will catch yourself thinking very, very morbid and deranged thoughts.
The gameplay is nothing outstanding, and that's the way it should be; simple and mindless, so your thought can be absorbed by the dialogue and story, as you think deeper about your fate. You can move your cursor to the left or right to scroll the screen, and there are arrows to click that will take you to other areas; all very similar to Year Walk. You will find some items along your way, but most will be given to you by your "friends". The game does a good job of pointing you in the direction that will lead you to your next destination. An extra additive to send you into a further delusional psychosis is that the game likes to drop text files onto your desktop every now and then, similar to IMSCARED.
On the other hand, the artwork is beautifully detailed and its style is extremely unique; though I apologize, as the genre in question is eluding me. It's not every day that you see this particular art style in any game, so it's a very fresh and welcomed change of pace from the abundance pixel art games and drab, uninspired graphics of others. There's also a hefty CRT TV filter that creates progressive scan lines, and the graphics are warped in a fish-eye or tube-like manner that makes you feel as though you're watching from a video feed.
As much of a horror game veteran that I am, Masochisia made me stop and put it away for a little while. The game sets out to expose the deepest, darkest recesses of your mind, and it does so with great malevolence. That being said, this is a true psychological horror game, that will have you taken aback by the capability of your own devious thoughts that unexpectedly rise to the surface. As well, if you're in any way a serial killer enthusiast, this game is a must play; being one myself, I personally think that we need more games based off of true crime. Even though Masochisia only lasts a couple of hours at best, its unique journey and visual style is worth every bit of the asking price.

Tharsis is a real ♥♥♥♥♥ of a game. Similar to cooperative board games such as Arkham Horror, you'll face overwhelming odds that require smart allocation of your limited resources. Four crew members, each with their own unique ability, are chosen from a pool of astronauts and each one represents your actions within the ship. It is up to you to decide how to best utilize them and, thanks to the very random nature of the game, the tactics and strategy behind a successful run are going to change every game from one to the next.
Hard mode requires nearly optimal play with a hand-picked crew but even the normal game is no walk in the park. Tharsis is a game that successfully walks that very thin line where the balance is just on this side of favoring the player. Making mistakes more often than not means entering a downward spiral where mission success is impossible. Don't worry though, runs are relatively short so many attempts can be made within a single play session.
Even once you develop a strategy for consistently getting to Mars, Tharsis continues to provide a challenge through random crew selection, hard mode, and missions (which are one-off challenges presenting the player with unique scenarios). Then again many players break before even reaching this point as more than half the people who played have never made it to Mars. Some have even gone so far as to call the devs liars about the balance of the game and claims that it can be consistently beaten without relying on luck. One year for Christmas I got the newer top loading NES and one of the games I got with it was the original Ducktales. The show had been out for a while and I was a massive fan and I still remember that day-after-Christmas morning, sitting down on the floor in front of the TV, blanket wrapped around my shoulders, everyone still in bed and loading up Ducktales (after blowing into the cartridge of course.) Hearing the midi version of the Ducktales theme, it was amazing. This was my favorite cartoon and now I could CONTROL my favorite character. No matter how many new games I got, I always went back to Ducktales. Must have beaten it over 20-30 times til I got my SNES. I knew that game inside and out and could play it blindfolded.
So when I saw DuckTales Remastered...I was skeptical. The show, the original game, completely different era...Could you really remake that game with the standards, ideas and selling points of modern day games? The short answer is no, you couldn't. Call of McDuck just wouldn't work but this game doesn't try to do that. It is 100% faithful to the original game but with the addition of an actual story. It's like watching a DuckTales movie except you get to play the thing.
Overall, bias aside, this is as the original game was: an extremely solid topnotch platformer with great enemies, varying levels and fun to fight bosses.
Not a fan of Ducktales but like platformers? Definitely a must have.
Fan of Ducktales AND platformers? Why don't you own this already.
Also, as an ending note, one of the best things about DuckTales the game was the music, each stage had its own though of course none will ever be as popular and well loved as the Moon theme. They faithfully brought the music back, it's so amazing to hear those tunes remastered. I love this game, it was such a huge part of my childhood and instantly hit me right in the Nostalgia Feels.
In closing: I could NOT recommend this game more highly.

I'm halfway through the game as I write this. Although I've played DuckTales 2 on the NES as a kid, I've never played the original version of its sequel. So even though nostalgia wasn't a big part of it, I'm glad to report I still find this game entertaining (and even challenging at times). However, I do have a couple of complaints:
1. The 2D character sprites look great but they do not fit in well with the rest of the art (backgrounds, chests, gems, etc.), which is unfortunately 3D. IMO, they should've kept everything in the iconic cartoon style of the Donald Duck universe. This is by far my biggest gripe with the game.
2. At the time of writing, I'm aware of two major bugs:
(a) The level is not reset when you respawn. Hence, the baddies will continue doing whatever they were up to when you lost your previous life. This is unfortunate, as it means that losing your first hit point may be unavoidable. And while bosses do indeed respawn, their effects do not (e.g., if you die at the wrong time during the fight with the boss in the Amazon, the ground might still be shaking from when it slammed into it before).
(b) Lots of people report that the game crashes for them when they reach the final boss. I don't know whether it will be the case for me as well but I thought I'd give you a heads up.
3. Even though they were probably never a part of the original version, they should've added special-case animations for talking characters. It's a little silly to see them talk with their mouths closed.
That said, I'm hoping for a remastered version of DuckTales 2.
Cheers,

Deep Dungeons of Doom is a casual mobile title ported to PC by Bossa Studios, responsible for "viral" games like Surgeon Simulator and I Am Bread.
That first sentence is key - this is a mobile title with slightly higher than usual production values. It is not some deep, dark dungeon delving title, it is a phone game and comes with all of the caveats of a phone game, caveats that make it extremely hard to recommend this title to anyone.
Biggest caveat of them all is the sheer lack of content.
First things first - the gameplay is fun. It plays on the established "Punch-Out!" formula of reading enemy telegraphs, reacting with a block and then responding with an attack. There are some other elements - you're able to "charge" your attack to different effects and can bring an item into the dungeons, but those amount to little more than superficial additions.
While it does have the usual touchscreen-to-cursor conversion for the interface, the actual battles themselves are able to be played with a keyboard and are better for it, it's just a shame (and somewhat confusing) that the game doesn't have full keyboard support.
Aesthetically it's played out - low resolution pixel art, but the animation carries it to an extent. While what's there looks good, the sheer lack of content means you'll be seeing the same few backgrounds and the same few enemies time and time again.
This comes back to that caveat.  Deep Dungeons of Doom has very, very little content. About 2 hours worth, give or take. And attempting to explore the limitations or post-game of DDD means you'll be grinding that same 2 hours for 20 hours, give or take. There's no remixed dungeons, no different patterns, every enemy generally performs 2 actions and both are incredibly easy to spot.
For a dungeon delver with so little content, the balancing is atrocious. Most of the post-game content is just finding out how useless the Mercenary is and how overbearingly powerful the Witch is (complete with a 3x damage multiplayer).
The bulk of the post-game is grinding pre-existing, 2 minute long dungeons for frustratingly rare drops and an Endless Dungeon that doesn't use any of the altered patterns or even half the bosses, leading to one of the most mind-numbing experiences I've ever had in a videogame.
This was not exciting.
This was not satisfying.
This was not fun.
It might be missing the point to attempt and evaluate Deep Dungeons of Doom on any merits beyond what it is - a casual mobile game to be played and dropped within 3 hours.
Having attempted anyway, it can safely be said that there are no merits behind that casual waste of time and attempting to treat this as anything else will lead to pure disappointment. I wouldn't recommend this to anyone but people looking for a specifically casual title.

Very Swery, which is exactly what I signed up for. There's no telling what will happen next. Though you can bet there will be plenty of breaks for food. This game has an obsession with basic pleasures, like drinking, eating with friends and acting silly. Instead of worrying about your health much, your character is more concerned with drinking coffee or tequila to smooth himself out. And despite his central focus in investigating his wife's murder, he still has other interests, and will take opportunities to bring up hockey or music. He watches cartoons. Makes jokes. Sometimes when he's alone, he remembers how dark his life is. You'd mistake him for a real guy if his accent weren't so ridiculous. Many other games would make him a far bleaker character.
So this guy has the ability to travel through time and space at will, provided he has an item tied to a specific event. It's his special advantage over others, allowing him to solve mysteries that would be impossible otherwise. As a trade-off, his own memories become distorted.
The gameplay is a mix of searching the environment, talking to people and occasionally taking part in bizarre QTE sequences. A lot of collection is involved, including searching your own home each day and carefully going over each new area. The pace is very laid back, especially since you can hop back and forth in time at-will, as well as replay previous chapters with items you find later in time. Backtracking for certain sidequests can be quite clever in its use of time travel.
The main draw here is the story and overall personality of the world. It's a version of America filtered through the beer-goggles of an eccentric Japanese cinephile. Familiar, but weird. It isn't afraid to run with an idea, especially if it's over the top. Yet it still takes itself seriously. I appreciate that kind of thing.

There are many things I can say about Final Fantasy IV. The second Final Fantasy game I have played, Final Fantasy for the NES preceding it is probalby my favorite Final Fantasy game out of the whole bunch, and I've played all of them except XII. The characters all have unique abilities (though augments were added in this version to share abilities between characters) that make having them at specific parts of the game useful. The storyline is rich and engaging, and you generally start to develop an emotional attachment to some of them (depending on your playstyle and level up depth you get into games I suppose). A good time sink, and luckly this version includes both Easy Type (Final Fantasy II US Release) and the original Hard Mode from the Japanese release of Final Fantasy IV on the Super Famicom. So if you are looking for a challenge, you'll get it as the game get's very difficult, very quick if you don't grind to learn spells for specific bosses.
As a forewarning, this is not the Final Fantasy that most everyone and myself fell in love with when it release back in November of 1991. The game contains the core coding for all of the characters, leveling, and monsters along with all of the proper translations the 1991 US release lacked. As much as I don't care for the graphic upgrade they gave it (should have gone with the SNES / Super Famicom graphics) the graphics do NOT make the game. The storyline and the combat system make the game, and those remain flawless. I highly recommend to anyone new to the series, and to those wanting to get a whiff of nostolgia to join Cecil Harvey once again on his adventure of Love, Betrayal, and Atonement.

It's using older modeling graphics, but it's still cute enough to play around with. I can tell that Bus Driver was just a practice run to test ideas with, and anybody who has also played ETS2 would know what I'm talking about (but that's another story for some other day) - :)
I'm not a wheel controller person, I'm strictly a keyboarder who knows how to simulate a wheel on arrow keys. But the technique requires good clean coding in the game for it to work properly. Fortunately, Bus Driver does have good keyboard response times and works well with a USB keyboard.
The game is broken up into 6 scenarios across 6 different Tiers = 36 missions. Obviously Tier 6 has the tricky missions, more stops, more turns, more intersections and traffic lights, and rush traffic that deliberately gets in your way, but I still find them just as easy as the previous Tiers as long as you watch your speed.
My favorite missions are 3-5, 4-5, and 6-5 ... these are all prison bus missions where you must transport prisoners to a specific location. Now, usually you have to keep passengers Happy, but in these missions you have to keep the prisoners Unhappy while trying to keep up with a helicopter flying overhead. However, it's actually more fun to become a rogue bus driver and give the prisoners some joy by deliberately doing demolition style driving and ramming cop cars. It's hillarious entertainment for sure.
Bus Driver is okay with the low-end expectations of a simulator, so I'm not going to go there. But, what I will do is list some things the game is missing...
1. There is NO cockpit view, in fact what little you can see inside the buses is limited to side shots while stopping at bus stops and turning sharply in chase view mode.
2. The passengers are totally static. They do not move. They are not animated in any way. They just stand still, suddenly disappear during pickup, and different ones sort of teleport to the inside of the bus. I'm sorry, but this was a really lame d__khead move for the developers to stoop that cheap, and I KNOW they could have done better.
3. Bus engine SFX are not authentic. They are low grade and totally manufactured out of thin air.
4. Apparently the handicapped is SOL in this game, because there's not a chair lift in sight anywhere!
5. There are no bus trains. Not all that surprising considering the pedestrian population appears to be unrealistically tiny and wouldn't need the trains anyway.
6. There is no bus damage or malfunctions available. You just lose points for colliding into things.
7. Dual position traffic lights do not exist in this game. There's only one set of traffic lights way the h_ll over on the opposite side of the intersection and that's it. They are very wide intersections which make those traffic lights look like peanut shells with faint LED's on them. It's better to drive at night than day in this game.
8. A.I. vehicle physics are virtually non-existent in this game. Example... A.I. vehicles instantly take off at max speed when a traffic light turns green, including the other A.I. buses! They also brake instantly while you're struggling to come to a stop without brake spiking. Not fair, Not fair!
9. None of the buses have a properly configured transmission, so don't expect any of them to behave correctly especially while climbing hills, or when jab stopping to change direction.
... I'm stopping right there. That's enough for the wall of shame, I think.
Changed my mind. I think I will note some of the best features of Bus Driver...
1. Love the weather system, which includes rain, thunder, snow and slippery roads. In fact, you're not having fun unless you're driving a bus sideways down the highway. You can also sort of drift the turns, but wheel spin is not being calculated to support it fully. It's an "almost" feature - LOL. (hey, I can't help it, I'm a natural lead footer!)
2. Buses will do at least an automatic dual kneel, but since the passengers never actually walk up to the bus, this feature is mostly cosmetic.
3. Bus doors actually move open/close, but again... purely cosmetic since the passengers are expert teleporters.
4. When I mess up, the passenger screams and yells make me laugh every time.
5. You are penalized for not using turn signals properly. This is a challenge by itself especially when you come across other vehicles that are parked in the bus lane, and you're trying to race the clock for a better score.
6. In addition to being able to roam freely anywhere a road is... If you can maintain a steady speed, then you can also roam freely "off-road style", provided you don't drive off the flat Earth, or hit a barrier or ditch and get stuck. (speed is the trick). Some things you can drive completely through, others you can't.
7. For the fun of it... you can drive in reverse the wrong way and not get penalized, but you need at least 1 mirror to watch for traffic and you still have to use turn signals. Has absolutely nothing to do with the missions, but it's still fun to do. (how many of you will actually go try this, just to see if I'm lying?)
8. This should be # 1, but ... The game has NEVER crashed with me! (knock on wood).
Well, that wraps up my fun review today. I've got some bus passengers to terrorize. Cheerio!

I have hundreds of hours off steam as well as the 20 some hours I put on Steam recently. I just came back to it on a whim.
I still like this game. It's worth coming back to if you played back in 2012-2013, but it's not nearly as active. Combat is still fun.
Pros:
-Many classes that all play very differently.
-Combat feels smooth and prompts showing up to combo is still a great touch.
-Graphics have aged fairly well, and the game will run well on a potato pc (GT 440, E5500 processor, 2 gigs of ram on my old pc, got 45 fps on high at 1366x768)
-Audio is crisp and the music is pretty good. Flying on the Pegasus and hearing how it's wings beat against the air is a great touch.
-Content upto end game is fairly diverse, same with the enemies, they feel appropriate for the zone you are fighting in.
-Boss fights are pretty epic and there is a lot going on, which is exciting and fun.
Cons:
-Not many people online on the weekdays, so if you tend to play on the weekdays like I do, trying to do certain content can suck.
-Enemies are laughably easy until around 40, where there is a somewhat noticable difficulty spike to mildy dangerous.
-End game content is really straight forward and doesn't offer a lot of diversity.
-Race and Gender locked classes force your hand at character creation. No high elf ninja's for us.
-Lots of running around to different areas on opposite sides of the continents, so get used to the sandwich bird.
All in all, if you can get a group of friends to play with you, this game is a refreshing and fun mmo experience for all involved. Solo can be tough, but it is still fun.
All in all, I give it a solid 7.5/10.

No loading screens means 100% immersion that never breaks.
If this game had VR support it would take the cake.
The way you unlock mechanics through in game events is very fluid.
You can also customise the interior of your ship with a fairly powerful editor.
Then, while usually I read slowly I started reading the logs I was picking up and became enthralled in the story.
Instead of flying around to fly around. It was fly around to learn what happens next.
I won't spoil it for you because it was one of the best experiences I've had in a while, better than watching a good movie.
Exquisitely crafted and I will be watching this game for updates because it can only get better and better.

It is fantastically simple while being incredibly intricate at the same time. The combat system is so simple you can literally play it with 2 keys on the keyboard. The real depth of this game comes in timing your attacks and defense just right, depending on your response to the opponent's movements. Along with the customization and RPG aspects of the game, it becomes an almost flawless game of strategy. The graphics are crisp and clean pixels, the animations are done well, the gameplay is quick and responsive, and the music and sound effects are very fitting with the setting of the excellent story line.
The only thing that bothers me about this game is that fact that you can only have one item of equipment at a time. It makes it frustrating when you get new items in the treasure boxes and you feel like you are forced to throw you item away. I mean really.. why can't I wear a helmet if I'm holding a sword?  I suppose this was done to increase the difficulty of the game, and is only a minor issue. It's just kind of annoying and counter intuitive.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys RPGs.

I picked this game up for $5.  At that price, you really can't go that wrong.  That being said, this game really walks the line between whether or not to give it a positive or a negative review overall.
The design flaws of the Talisman game really manifest itself when you play with a rigid, impassionate interpreter of the game.   This doesn't seem like a bad thing, but Talisman has evolved over the years with very little consistency: there's a huge variety of nuances in the language used.  Phrases such as "...at any time..." implies a different expectation than what is actually practiced in the game.
The honest truth is, people zone out when they play Talisman.  You miss a few turns in jail, or wait for four other players to battle dragons, abuse spells, and ponder over quests; just so you can roll a 3 and scoop up a bag of gold.  There's a whole layer missing from the electronic version of the game that you get when you are playing on the tabletop with your friends that really is the only thing that makes Talisman an acceptable use of an afterrnoon.
The game would also benefit from an ability to remove specific cards from out of the deck; because there are some really grossly imbalanced combinations as well as cards you just get sick of seeing- like the one that takes all the face up city cards and put them on top of the adventure deck.  The electronic version of the game also takes longer to play, as every step of the game is iterated out individually.  The dice roller seems very suspect as well.  I've had back to back snake eyes when dicing with death as well as +3 Craft from the Reaper in three stops.
The game does give you something to do while your waiting in a que or auto-running to your next mission, but it's hard to recommend solely on the experience it offers.  To be honest, considering how horribly overpriced the Fantasy Flight version of the game is, I would still recommend this version of the game over the table top version.  I'm sticking with my 2nd Edition Games Workshop version.

Love it. Runs fine. Not great, but fine. I made the mistake of letting it run for a while, resulting in a crash. I had a similar problem with Deadly Premonition, though worse.
Very Swery, which is exactly what I signed up for. There's no telling what will happen next. Though you can bet there will be plenty of breaks for food. This game has an obsession with basic pleasures, like drinking, eating with friends and acting silly. Instead of worrying about your health much, your character is more concerned with drinking coffee or tequila to smooth himself out. And despite his central focus in investigating his wife's murder, he still has other interests, and will take opportunities to bring up hockey or music. He watches cartoons. Makes jokes. Sometimes when he's alone, he remembers how dark his life is. You'd mistake him for a real guy if his accent weren't so ridiculous. Many other games would make him a far bleaker character.
So this guy has the ability to travel through time and space at will, provided he has an item tied to a specific event. It's his special advantage over others, allowing him to solve mysteries that would be impossible otherwise. As a trade-off, his own memories become distorted.
The gameplay is a mix of searching the environment, talking to people and occasionally taking part in bizarre QTE sequences. A lot of collection is involved, including searching your own home each day and carefully going over each new area. The pace is very laid back, especially since you can hop back and forth in time at-will, as well as replay previous chapters with items you find later in time. Backtracking for certain sidequests can be quite clever in its use of time travel.
The main draw here is the story and overall personality of the world. It's a version of America filtered through the beer-goggles of an eccentric Japanese cinephile. Familiar, but weird. It isn't afraid to run with an idea, especially if it's over the top. Yet it still takes itself seriously. I appreciate that kind of thing.

I got to play this on Steam-PC this past week. I would say, it's a nice game. Interesting and quirky. Slightly offbeat. Strange. I enjoyed playing it, that much is certain.
However, my single biggest issue is that this is misleadingly being marketed as an episodic game, and what we have here is being called "Season 1". It's patently false, on both counts. I should know, cause I've pretty much played all the recent episodic games (KRZ, Telltale's stuff, Life is Strange).
First off, there is a Prologue, "EP1" and "EP2". Between each of them, you can't say there's any kind of "closure". Episodic games tend to have closures (however small) between episodes. It plays and feels like one continuous game throughout (except for the fact when each new episode begins, you're shown the tutorial icons again).
Then, the most damning part is that the game just ♥♥♥♥ing **ends**. Just like that! It's ultimately the biggest climax moment. The cliffhanger. And the game just...ends. Incredible. I felt cheated of the 7 odd hours I spent in the game (I explored, and went achievement-hunting, a clean playthrough is probably 4 hours).
The most disappointing thing is that, this was done despite the fact that a Season 2 was not a guarantee at the time the game first release on the X1 (though yes, now we know there will be a "Season 2"). So the devs were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in releasing a game that ended on a cliffhanger that could well have never been completed.
Now that that's out of the way, it's a fun adventure. Very story driven. Some bizarre♥♥♥♥♥♥ The
was just ♥♥♥♥ing scary...I felt disgusted.
It kinda looks and plays like a Telltale game, minus the choice aspect. You go to hubs, solve "puzzles" and talk to people.
As for the PC port quality, it's below-par. On a GTX 750 at 1080p, I got mostly 35-50fps. The reason for this is cause most of the time, the game renders two scenes at ones (like a comic pane, left and right). No graphics options except for On/Off Dynamic Shadows. There is a severe lack of AA, but I think that may have been intentional and you get used to it. The bummer though is the fact after an hour or so of playing, the game goes to 4700MB (!!!) of RAM. Some memory leak which happened continually, which hopefully they fix.
Another minor issue is with the side-missions are done. You have to move back and forth in time, and it gets irritating after a while. Also, you are confined to the same house, and in each of the three parts, you examine/inspect the same locations/objects to find collectibles.
So there's that! Hope you guys enjoy the game. I myself hope Season 2 is out soon.

I was worried from the beginning that the Kinect controls, which were actually extremely good on the Xbone version, wouldn't transfer over very well, and to an extent that seems to be the case. A lot of the more humorous actions, like slamming your fist down to crack a fortune cookie or swinging a baseball bat (in the Xbox version you're actually instructed to get into a batter's pose and swing alongside the character), are replaced with simple actions like clicking on your fist and dragging it to the cookie or swiping across the screen to swing the bat. It still feels okay, and the game itself is still fantastic, but even though I'll still continue to buy the following seasons on both platforms I'll probably only actually play them on the Xbone, because ultimately I feel like this is a game that's made for the Kinect (and probably the only game made for the Kinect, for that matter).
In the end, if you're a fan of the parts of Deadly Premonition that didn't involve combat, and you appreciate quality over quantity (from what I remember from the Xbox One version, the game is only about 5-10 hours long depending on how much effort you put into the side content, so if you need to get your money's worth you might want to wait for a sale) you'll love this game. If you have an Xbox One (why?), I'd recommend buying it there instead unless you just really really like having your games on Steam (which I wouldn't blame you for), but if you don't have an Xbox One this version is a perfectly fine port.

First and foremost, I want to say that I have played this game from start to finish multiple times on multiple systems.  I started with the "easy" Final Fantasy 2 North American release and played that at least ten times through.  I played this on PSP, Playstation 3, Gameboy Advance, and now on Steam.  Here are the pros and cons in my book for this game that still has me playing after 20 years of its inital release.
Good:
Beautiful music, decent voice acting, turn based goodness.  I will say first and foremost, I LOVE turn base RPG's.  The story is simple by today's standards (you can tell what is going on unlike some of the later Final Fantasy games, talking to you 13 and all of your weirdness).  The combat is turn based, strategic, and fast paced (even with the atrocious frame rate at times I still didn't mind grinding).
Bad:
Ok, I said "decent" voice acting.  It is ok I guess.  It is weird hearing names of the people that I thought were always pronounced differently.  Yang is pronounce Yong and I thought Cecil was pronounced SeeSeal not Sessal.  Oh well, after twenty years I know.  The game is pretty dang hard.  Some of the tricks that worked 20 years ago do not fly right now.  Notably the putting the wall spell on yourself to reflect Bahamuts special attack.  It does not work so Bahamut is not a pushover any more.  There are other things that used to never happen like tons of counter attacking and so forth but I am glad to see it get to be more challenging.
Overall:  I know that since Square and Enix merged they have been money hungry.  However, the $16 price is worth the experience to be sure.  Final Fantasy purist may cry fowl that the game has been modernized and new players to the genre that started on 7 or later may not appreciate the gem that is FFIV.  However, I fully support this game and would love to see FFVI get the same loving treatment.  I will gladly shell out $16 for it.

The base concept around Deliverance is promising but fails in the end.  What starts off as intially fun soon takes a turn for the worse with the constant restarting, recollecting and rethinking of your current strategy (the constant reviewing of the rubbery hands is enough to cause borderline paranoia in itself).  The map itself is vague and difficult to understand even though it says "Cell" on it (where you start off).  Batteries are one of the most important items needed in the game but at times seem to be far and few apart (one time I opened the lockers at the beginning near the cell and it rendered not even a single battery!) Bursting lightbulbs and pipes add a good touch to the psychological experience and jump scares (even after almost 9 hours of gameplay it still causes this scenario with me).  The concept of having stamina attached to sprinting was not well thought up as this is the only means to escape walter (which I did once by dumb luck!)
A few things that could've fixed this game a bit is the following:
1. Allow the players to save the game 1 time anywhere (then after this if they die make them start over completely).
2. Allow for the use of environmental aspects (objects or items which could slow walter down)
3. Dont make gamers sit through that extended scene at the end (where you're strapped in the chair waiting for him to kill you off as sometime it takes more than 10-15 seconds for him to show up). I found this to be constantly annoying and I could've already been making my way back through the game.
In the end, my verdict 3/10 at best

This is the best space game I have ever played, and it's only in early access. This is a truly amazing experience, and should be experienced by all sci-fi fans. I am obviously biased towards this game, but I shall try my best to display the pros and cons to this wonderful game.
PROS
-Seamless gameplay (no loading screens)
-Full scale solar system to explore (Sun, 4 planets (life size), and asteroid belt)
-Amazing soundtrack (Epic battle music!)
-Fun combat that requires movement (Sci-fi games usually line up the ships and have you wail at each other)
-Choice between 1st person and 3rd person (only while piloting the ship, I recommend 1st person)
-Variety of weapons and upgrades (note that the upgrades only negate negative planet enviroments)
-A decent variety of enemies
-A pretty good story
-Customizable ship
-Datastick collectables (expand upon the backstory/lore of the game)
CONS
-Enemies can drop fps due to the volume of particle effects. (doesn't really happen to me, I have a pretty beefy PC)
-Sometimes crashes (only happened to me once)
-All of the planets are just wastelands and mountains. (From what I know, this is being worked on, but isn't there yet)
If you are thinking about trying this game out, there is a FREE demo available. There are no restrictions to the game in the demo, just a 1 hour limit to play time.

Well. It definitely has potential, but some major flaws are noticed early game.  The landing is a bit awkward. Even when I use the docking speed and very fine tuning with the strafe/FWD/BCKWD to bring her down.. it's just that the ship seems weightless.  It wont stick to the ground in most situtations. It's almost bouncy even on a very very soft landing.
The other problem was the first planet I visit- it's littered with marks all over as you approach, indicating plenty of areas to explore.  But you have to enter the atmosphere at an angle, and there's no telling how long it'll take, so there's really no way to aim your way to a good spot.  So now I'm on the planet.... and I'm cruising. endlessly.  10 minutes go by- nothing but the same landscape. None of the points of interest show locally, nor am i finding any at cruise speed (the highest you can go in the atmosphere).  Another 10-15 minutes goes by and at this point I've put down the game. I'm all for exploring  and all- but not when there's so little to explore.  My suggestion would be to keep some of the local marks on screen so you can move toward them, instead of zig-zagging around aimlessly for half an hour, still finding nothing.
It has a whole bunch of potential if a whole bunch of stuff is added. For now, the demo is probably enough to mess around with, followed by NMS coming out in 2 months.

I have been playing TERA since launch, back when it was Pay 2 Play..
I have leveled every character to end game, and currently am playing the latest patch's end game content.
I also know all the servers and sub communities fairly well.
I will keep this short and sweet.
For a Free to Play game, TERA has a lot to offer, the combat is what keeps me coming back for more. There is a variety of classes to play, each of the races in game have unique asthetics and animations, plenty of variety in the world and dungeons.
The only downside I have with the game, is the developers in KR, have dwindled down their support and team for the game, You find that each new patch has some new content, but it seems to just mostly focus on the Cash Shop and not very much on the game itself. Class balancing is a bit all over the place, and the game is plagued by new classes being a bit overpowering compared to the original classes that came with the game.
PVP is fun, however it is no longer a primary focus of the game per the developer which is very disheartening, but you can still enjoy it if you have friends and or a guild to romp around in Open World PVP (Max Level Only.)
All in All, I would recommend this game, if you are looking for a new free to play MMO that really isn't that "restricted" or "Pay Wall" feeling, Tera is a safe bet.

Tharsis is a cruel spacefaring roguelike in which you need to get as far as you can before your ship gets destroyed or everyone on it dies. So immediately this game has to be compared to FTL, which is a match Tharsis simply cannot win.
Every turn, new events happen that will wreck your ship if you don't fix them. How do you fix them? Literal dice rolls. And because of the conditions attached to each event, such as rolling a five dealing one damage to whichever crew member rolled it, guarantees that the odds are stacked against you the whole time. This isn't strategic, this isn't tactical, the game just hates you.
I will admit though, one thing Tharsis does better than FTL is emotional impact. Around turn 3 or 4, when most likely everyone is running a bit low on food, the option to eat one of your dead crew members is presented.  If all of that crew member has been eaten by the next turn, you have the opportunity to kill one of your crew members for food. And when a crew member does this their dice get all bloody. It's an impactful experience, even if only once.
If you want a tactical spacefaring roguelike, then go to FTL. If you've already done that, then just keep looking until you've found something besides Tharsis. If you've played FTL and wish there was more of a human element to it, Tharsis has got you covered. If you want to know the result of Choice Provisions branching off from the Bit.Trip Saga, then all you can do is just wait for Bit.Trip Void 2 or something.

This is a great game for the price.  It plays like a board game and uses an actual physics based dice thrower instead of RNG.    Since the game is quite random, the difficulty of a particular run-through can vary greatly with luck.  Still, the game gives plenty of strategic options to the player for dealing with the randomness.  Players are expected to not only deal with the issues in front of them, but also to plan ahead for the next set of circumstances the game could throw at you in future turns.  Expect to play through quite a few games before you figure everything out.  I haven't run into in bugs yet.
If you expect your game to challenge your critical thinking skills, you can't go wrong here.  If you don't like a challenge and expect your game to be easy to beat, go somewhere else.
Difficlty is impossible high, and based on luck too much.

So I downloaded Tharsis, after reading all the reviews and watching the videos. Here's how it went.
Playthrough one: There's a story! Must be just the tutorial. I really dig the visuals in this game, and damn is it hard as hell just like I've heard. Still, it's a dice game built as a cooperative board game of sorts...these are never easy. Wow, I lasted three weeks! Let's try another round.
Playthrough two: Oh, the story is presented every time? Interesting. Haven't done the new Missions yet, will try them next. This time I think I get it more. You need to plan ahead who is going to be in what module. You have to make sure you're actively trying to use those research projects, always gathering assists because Void and Injury will mess with your day. Think about the functions of each module too, and the bonuses you could get, but keep that Food up or you get no dice.
Playthrough three: I get it now. I've got the rhythm. I am having a good time playing this game, I do wish some mechanics weren't QUITE so punishing, but this is very reminiscent of a traditional board game played cooperatively against a board game AI. It's tough, but there's a sort of slogging method to it that eventually you sort of fall into...or you never fall into. It's a game for a specific type of gamer.
Luckily, that type of gamer is me. I am looking forwards to the updates to Tharsis, and I will recommend it to anyone who really enjoys traditional game mechanics (yahtzee, poker, both present here), a difficult yet understandable design, and some pretty smooth visuals. There's promise here, a lot of it.

I'm a huge fan of one-offs. Usually when I have time to game, it's not hours and hours of time, but more like ten minute spurts where I'm able to sit down and play. Because of this, I love a lot of games that don't offer much plot, and allow for quick sessions of in-and-out gameplay.
Deep Dungeons of Doom offers exactly that. The gameplay requires just the arrow keys (or wasd), and puts you in the position of a character trying to defend a kingdom. There's a knight and a wizard so far, and I predict more characters later. Typical dungeon crawler in terms of aesthetic, but almost like a mobile game in ease of play.
Should you get it? The five buck price tag is a tiiiiiiny bit much, but there's certainly enough game for the value. I recommend grabbing it off a sale, but if you're like me in terms of loving easy-in-easy-out games, this is definitely for you.

I love big, complex board games. Until I don’t. I’ve played a lot of board games where I start out with a big group of friends and a lot of excitement to play. Four hours later, I wonder – will this game ever end? Talisman: Digital Edition is a very faithful port of the classic board game and allows you to play either online with friends or against AI opponents.
I’ve played a lot of this since I bought it, partially because it doesn’t require that much attention. It’s turn-based so I can play while watching an episode of some tv show, or I can tab out to do other things. I really like when board games are digitized. Not having to keep track of a tabletop full of life tokens and counters and spells, or put them away at the end, is a big plus for me.
If you like the Talisman boardgame, you’ll probably like this. It's well done and very faithful to the original.

With 270 hours at writing time, I think I have a fair say in this game.
Cities skylines has alot of positive things. It's kinda like what simcity 5 should have been. It's mechanics and variety is great and the modding community for this game is absolutely amazing. The map designer and asset editor is fairly simple to use and allows almost anyone to make their own map.
Now there's also alot of stuff that I find annoying about this game. The main point being the Traffic AI. All problems with this game evolve around this one thing that Paradox didn't take their time with. It seems as to they only missed the traffic bit adn thought "well, lets just take a cheap AI and tweak it a bit" and added it. The AI is absolutely horrible. Why? Merging. Merging lanes in this game is made in the stupid way that instead of keeping the speed of the cars steady and THEN merging  in to another lane to not slow down traffic, they brake until almost a full stop, sometimes TO a full stop. This causes traffic behind to stop for the car and make a huge traffic jam that completely messes up the entire thing. Even with mods like Traffic Manager this is inevitable to happen.
Another thing that is really annoying is junctions. Even a simple T-Junction is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥with the amount of traffic this games gives you. The problem here is not that there's alot of traffic, the problem is that if you want ANY chance of solving it, you need to be a master traffic technician and have the mod Traffic Manager. Without this mod, it's impossible. And even WITH this mod, it seems impossible at times.
Another thing that I can find annoying at times is there's no "auto complete public transport". Any public transport line has to be made manually which is something I miss. I really  can't be bothered sitting for 30 minutes, clicking on every place I want a stop just for the busses to block the road. Ofcourse it's good that you can make it yourself but it CAN be really annoying. It should be optional.
Overall I enjoy this game but sitting for hours and hours trying to solve traffic is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Pros:
- Great variation in content
- Good mechanics (roads, zoning and emergencies)
- Amazing modding community
- Manual Public Transport Lines
Cons:
- Terrible Traffic/Driving AI
- No automatic public transport
Overall opinion: Good game with some flaws that really can ruin your day occationally but most of the time can be solved with mods.

Full disclosure: review copy provided by developer/publisher!
A note before I begin: after I played D4 for review I had a few friends over to take it for a spin. One sat in rapt attention, absolutely needing to know how this weird story plays out. One spent most of it drinking and facepalming. These are the two most common reactions to SWERY.
Memory is a curious thing, isn't it? Curiouser still how we “store” them... sometimes memories stay fresh, instantly recallable despite having occurred in the forever rose-tinted, nebulous past. Memories can be locked away, buried just beneath the surface until you find the right “key;” a weathered photograph, the smell of an old coat, or the splash of rain on your face in the right place at the right time. Sometimes memories are forever locked away, and you'll always find yourself chasing that key.
Did you know that every time you recall a memory you're just remembering your last memory OF the memory? And like all things it fades and melds and changes until it's unrecognizable?
Do you know about string theory? Quantum gravity? Me neither. But I know many lemur species are matriarchal.
ANYHOO.
D4 was cultivated and harvested from the wacky mind-fields of SWERY, the same gentleman who brought us that wonderfully weird love letter to Twin Peaks - Deadly Premonitions.
And boy was the harvest bountiful.
You play the part of one David Young: Bostonian, tequila enthusiast, semi-successful husband and police officer in the narcotics unit. And like all good video game heroes his wife was murdered (semi-successful!), the trauma leaving him amnesic but with a peculiar gift – the ability to traverse (seemingly) time and space using mementos with incredibly strong ties to specific events. His mission in life now is to solve his wife's murder, prompted by her final words: “Look for D.”
A little forward for my tastes but fine, I'll bite.
Confused? That's okay! That's normal. I don't think anyone completely understands these surreal romps except SWERY... possibly. And if anyone says otherwise they are God damned liars. But despite that you'll find yourself riveted. The characters are rich, HILAROUS (intentionally and unintentionally), animated, and strange. The story, as weird as it is, leaves you glued to the edge of your seat. I think I can safely say that this might be one of the most engaging “point n' click” adventure games available on the market – you can touch everything for points and descriptions, read articles, slap around humans, owls, cats... it's nuts. And the QTE's are some of the most engaging I've ever encountered in a game of this type.
Aesthetically D4 is leagues better than Deadly Premonitions. The music, the voice acting, the charming, cartoony cell-shade art, the ever present creative hand of SWERY, all comes together to make something truly special, perhaps the most memorable and entertaining “TellTale” style title this year so far. There's a health system (can't take too much damage during fights/interactions) and a stamina system (every action costs stamina – grab or purchase food and drinks to avoid passing out). There's even a synchronization system that takes into account actions and dialogue that determines if you're really behaving as David Young would during scenarios. All the while you'll gather credit you can use to purchase outfits, hairstyles, and more (I made my David look like a pirate because I'm a ♥♥♥♥ing adult).
However, there are things to consider before parting with your hard-earned cashola. This is SEASON ONE, two episodes and one prologue, maybe three to five hours of gameplay for the average gamer. And SEASON TWO is dependent on how this game is received, so buyer beware (it also ends on a major cliffhanger). The QTE's I mentioned are weirdly difficult! Maybe it's because they're clever little combinations I've never seen, but you'll be hard-pressed to get a perfect score. Likewise, the synchronization conversations assume you're living inside David (and SWERY's) brain. Sometimes you'll choose a dialogue branch (lacking context, inflection) thinking David would say it and you'd be dead wrong, resulting in a lower synch score. And I think it goes without saying... but I'll say it: this game is not remotely for everyone. If you're a fan of Deadly Premonitions this is absolutely a must buy. If that wasn't your cup of tea you aren't likely to enjoy this. It's a western looking game with very Japanese sensibilities – keep that in mind.
And I would be remiss not to mention a certain character's terrible, awful, abysmal voice acting delivery. You'll meet him in Episode 1 (the cinematography of that scene is BRILLIANTLY TERRIFYING).
AND.
HE.
WILL.
E-NUN-CI-ATE.
EVE-RY.
SYL-LAB-LE.
I get it, I do. He's supposed to be like the G-Man from-Half Life in that way I guess. But unlike the G-Man his dialogue may represent a quarter of my initial playthrough. Just a minor gripe. And time theft.
Overall I think this if you're a fan of SWERY, of point n' click adventure types, and of weird narratives you should take the leap, entertain your friends with it for a “movie night.” It's going to leave a mark on you, that's for sure.

D4: Dark Dreams Don’t Die is a game with big problems that is all but impossible to dislike.
As David Young, former detective now out to find the culprit behind his wife’s death, D4 took me on an adventure seemingly designed for one purpose: making an impression. Swery and his team at Access Games developed a rather passionate reputation after their eccentric cult classic Deadly Premonition became a surprise hit, but where DP was overburdened by its mechanics and ambition, the significantly smaller D4 proves a far more suitable conduit for whatever insanity Swery manages to dream up.
D4 falls somewhere between the modern adventure game as told by Telltale, and the QTE heavy efforts of Quantic Dream. Hav ing been originally designed to be played exclusively with Microsoft’s Kinect, D4 focuses itself around single screens and simple gestures, an interface that at first feels moderately restrictive but ultimately works in the game’s favor. It’s always clear where you’re supposed to look, what you can interact with, and when you’ve missed something important, as well as being generally straight forward and intuitive where a more traditional control scheme may have been overbearing.
What’s so endearing to me however is in the ways D4 appropriates mechanics from other games that ultimately have no reason to be here. There’s a stamina bar you refill by picking up food that’s been for some reason stowed throughout every level, a health bar that takes a slice off when you fail a prompt, and a credit system that rewards you for almost every action you take and can be spent on a rather outrageous number of unlockable costumes. In most games I’d scoff at how pointless it was to include things like this, but with D4 it becomes part of its personality. There’s a feeling that Access Games do not completely understand how to make the game they’re trying to, which leads to them pilfering bits and bobs from other games to fill in the “game-y” portion of D4, but they display such an infectious enthusiasm in everything they do that I eventually stopped caring about the trivial bits of D4 and in some ways even found them charming.
D4 is so entirely detached from its peers in almost every way, that these little touches mostly amounted to winks and nods at a medium Access Games clearly loves working in, and thankfully never encroach upon anything else in the game. What is left then is a crash course through a world of extremes, from D4’s over-the-top characters, to its love of ridiculous dance-like fight scenes. D4 is obsessively spectacular, each scene enriched with a playful gravitas that would seem excessive if it wasn’t for how much more absurd the rest of the game is. D4 made me laugh more than any game I can remember in a long time, and I think it’s because it always seems in on the joke. It isn’t necessarily trying for comedy, but it’s aware of itself in a way most similarly bizarre games completely miss, playing to its strengths and remembering to have fun with itself instead of just the player.
My biggest disappointment with D4 is mostly in how it chooses to portray some of its characters. There’s the damseling of David’s wife right from the start, taken a step further by the way D4 infantilizes her at every point. Some characters spout blatantly sexist commentary, and in general the women of D4 end up feeling like they were included mostly to ridicule, injure, or give David someone to fall into a compromising position with. I also found the token person of color to be problematic, as he’s portrayed as almost alien in his mannerisms and how he shows up inexplicably throughout the game mostly to be unsettlingly weird in a way that isn’t shared among the other characters. None of this is done in a way that feels intentionally malicious, but they were enough for me to shake my head and wish D4 had done better, because in general it avoids most of the worst ways women and people of color are often displayed in games and at points almost came close to being one of the better instances of representation in games.
D4: Dark Dreams Don’t Die is an imperfect creation, one that’s janky, at times conflicted with itself, and which may never be finished (this being only the first season and ending on a huge cliffhanger). But it’s also one of the most earnest games I’ve ever played, with a passion that shows up in even the endearing ways D4 fails to reach its full potential. It’s a game that I want to love unconditionally because D4 deserves it. It deserves a shot and a chance to do better, and for whatever faults it may have I feel no hesitation in saying everyone should play it.
After the mess that was Deadly Premonitions’ PC port, a lot of people are no doubt justifiably concerned as to the technical state of D4. Thankfully, D4 is (mostly) a big improvement. I experienced no crashes or major bugs throughout my playthrough, and using a mouse proved a serviceable stand-in for the Kinect (though some immersion may have been lost in the transition). Optimization isn’t as lucky, with some shockingly high system requirements that seem to be mostly accurate (I experienced some serious frame-rate drops playing on a machine that hits the minimum requirements and which has managed to run far more intensive games in the past). It never became unplayable due to the lax pace of the game, but for whatever reason speaking to characters caused the frame-rate to drop into the teens where it had previously been smooth. It isn’t anywhere near the problems Deadly Premonition faced, but if you’re concerned about whether or not you can run it downloading the demo would definitely be a wise choice.

First off: I'll mention the main point anyone would give a negative review on this game. There is a major lack of content. While this is a valid point (and basically the only valid point), it is completely and totally offset by the many positive factors.
Now, to the billion GOOD reasons to buy this game
1) The Developer: ERMUHGURD! The developer! This is a one man team (hence the lack of content) and should be judged in accordance, but he works with the speed of ten. I got this game probably around 2 years ago and since then this game has changed in more ways than I could imagine, this is even better because the content changes didn't morph the game that I had come to love, but like a gem, it has slowly been chipped and polished so it can shine even brighter. Plus, if you are worrying about the game being caught in early access hell, A) did you even read what I wrote? and B) the dev has proven to be extremely aware of this issue, that is why he made the demo and seems to offer refunds to any unsatisfied customers (THATS how consumer-friendly he is)
2) The Soundtrack: Just... Just play the game and you will know exactly what Im talking about it. As any good Syfi anything, the music is soo epic and fits the tone perfectly. Speaking of...
3) The Tone: The best way I can describe the tone of this game is like the early days of minecraft. It is often overlooked just how lonely that game can feel. When you arent playing with anyone, you really get the feeling that while minecraft, with its haunting piano track and all the unkown factors, gives you unlimited freedom, it comes with this soul freezing feeling of lonelines. Rodina uses its epic soundtrack and scale to bring you the same affect. Oh I almost forgot about the scale!
4) Scale: This is probably one of the only games I have ever owned that made me comprehend much better something that would usually be considered incomprehensible in ways only a video game could. This game made me grasp just how vast and empty space really is while still making it an enjoyable experience throught how the game progression curve and the sheer size. I'm trying to avoid anecdotes because I truley belive that this game needs to be experienced first hand, but ill say this. It makes you feel like a flea.
5) Combat: While it does take some time to get used to the controls of flying in 0G, the intuitiveness of the game is unprecedented for games of its caliber. While Im flinging around in a death spin with other games of similar physics, I'm able to fly around relatively accurately in Rodina.
